Silver Plate A Petition of the several Innholders, Vintners, and used by Alehouse-keepers, within the Cities of London and

Innkeepers. minster, and the Weekly Bills of Mortality, whose Names

are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act made in the Seventh and Eighth Years of King William the Third, to encourage the bringing Plate into the Mint to be coined, and for the further remedying the ill State of the Coin of the Kingdom, it was enacted, that no Person, keeping any Inn, Tavern, Alehouse, or Victualling House, or felling Wine, Ale, Beer, or any other Liquors, by Retail, should publicly use, or exposeto be used, in such' his or her House,"any wrought or manufactured Plate whatsoever, or any Utensils or Vessel thereof, except Spoons, under the Penalty of forfeiting the fame, or the full Value thereof, together with full Costs of Suit; and that, by an Act made in the 29th Year of King George the Second, several Rates and Duties were granted to His Majesty, payable Yearly, by all Persons and Bodies Politic or Corporate, haying certain Quantities of Silver Plate; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the said . Restriction, contained in the said Act of King,

and the other Provisions therein, were chiefly calculated to encourage the bringing Plate into the Mint, for the Coinage of Silver, at that particular Time; and that the Petitioners are, in Gonsequence of the said Restriction, liable to many vexatious and frivolous Suits; and that, if the said Restriction was taken off. His Majesty’s Revenue would be increased, and the Petitioners would be enabled the better to accommodate Persons frequenting their Houses: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repealing so much of the said Act of King William the Third, as restrains the Petitioners from publicly using in their Houses any wrought or manufactured Plate, or any Utensils or Vessel thereof j and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Ditto. A Petition of several Workers, Traders, and Dealers,

in Silver Plate, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Weekly Bills of Mortality, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House and read; Taking Notice of the preceding Petition; and alledging, that the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Restriction was repealed, it would tend to the Increase of His Majesty’s Revenue, by the Payment of the Rates and Duties, which such Innholders, Vintners, and others, would become liable to Yearly, by having Silver Plate; and it would likewise be of great Advantage to the Petitioners, and all other Workers, Traders, and Dealers, in Silver Plate: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the; Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the several Innholders, Vintners, and Alehouse Keepers, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Weekly Bills of Mortality, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred.

The House proceeded to the Hearing of the Matter of the several Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Cumberland.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the said Petitions were read.

And the Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel, at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, was also read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner Henry Esquire, and for the several Freeholders of the County of Cumberland, who, upon the 10th Day of November last, petitioned this House, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said County, were heard.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

They were again called in.

And the Original Poll Books, taken at the last Election of Knights of the Shire for the said County, were produced.

And the Counsel for the said Henry Fletcher, Esquire, and for the said Freeholders of the County of Cumberland, examined several Witnesses, in order to prove that the Sheriff' of the said County solicited Votes for Sir James Lowther, one of the Sitting Members, and a<5led in other Respects with great Partiality in Favour of the said Sir James Lowther, duringjihe Time of the Election, and after the Close of the Poll.

Vol 32.

And the said Counsel having examined Thomas and having proposed that the said Thomas Benjon should be asked what Conversation passed between him and the Sheriff, relative to the Appointment of Counsel to assist the said Sheriff in taking the Poll;

The said Thomas Benjon desired to be excused answering that Question; alledging, that such Conversation passed, in Confidence between the said Sheriff and him the said Thomas Benjon, he being at that Time appointed by the said Sheriff’ to transact the Business of Under Sheriff in the said County.

Then the said Thomas Benjon was directed to withdraw.

And the Counsel were heard thereupon.

And then they were directed to withdraw.

Ordered, That the Counsel on both Sides, and the said Thomas Benjon, be again called in; and that the said Thomas Benjon be told, that the House expected he should give an Answer to that Question.

And they were called in accordingly; and Mr. Speaker acquainted the said Thomas Benjon therewith.

And then the said Thomas Benjon gave the House an Account of the said Conversation; and was further examined, in order to prove the Partiality of the said Sheriff in Favour of the said Sir James Lowther, in the Appointment of Counsel to alfift him in taking the Poll.

Then the Counsel for the said Petitioners1 examined the said Thomas Benjon, and another Witness, in order to prove the partial Conduct of the said Sheriff, in admitting certain Votes upon the First Day of the Poll, and afterwards resolving to refuse other Votes under the like Description. '

And the said Witnesses were further examined, in order to prove that the said Sheriff admitted several Votes upon the Poll with Queries, under a Pretence that they were not Freeholders; and with Assurances that he would, at the Close of the Poll, examine whether the Estates, for which such Votes were offered, were Freeholds or not; and afterwards, notwithstanding such Assurances, the said Sheriff refused to examine into the Legality of the said Votes though several Times applied to for that Purpose, and nevertheless rejected the Votes so queried.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Ordered, That the further Hearing of the Matter of the said several Petitions be adjourned till Tuesday next, at Twelve of the Clock.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Member present informed your Committee, That the Petitioner Sir Henry Cavendish is willing, on Condition the said Roads and Foot Path be (hut up and discontinued, to take upon himself to make a good Road for Carriages and Horses, and also a good Foot Path, and to oblige himself, his Heirs, and Assigns, to keep and maintain the same in good and sufficient Repair, which will answer.all the Purposes of the Old Road and Path, and be an Advantage to the Petitioner and the Public.

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Veltrymen, and " Principal Inhabitants of the Parish of St. otherwise White Chapel, in the County of Middlesex, the City of London, and in the Liberty of His Majesty’s Tower of London, and also of the Principal Inhabitants in the Precinct of Well.Close, in the said Liberty, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Streets, Squares, Lanes, Alleys, Passages, and other Places, within the said Parish and Precinct, are extremely ill paved, and greatly obstructed by Polls, and annoyed by Signs, Spouts, Gutters, and other Incroachments* projecting into and over the fame; and that the High Street of the said Parish is a principal Avenue to the Cities of London and Westminster; and that the Inhabitants of the said Parish and Precinct, although heavily burthened with Taxes towards watching, lighting, and cleansing the fame, and providing for their numerous Poor, are willing, for the public Accommodation, to submit to an additional Tax, towards paving the same in a better Manner, and keeping suchi new Pavement in Repair, and towards clearing the same from all Annoyances; and that there are several Houses, and other Buildings, within the said Parish, which project so far into the Streets and other Passages, as not only to cause the Foot Ways to be incommodious,' but render the Passage for Carriages, in many Places, dangerous; which, if taken down, and built further back, or removed, would render the same safe and commodious j and that there are several Streets, Squares, Lanes, and other Passages, which lie partly within the aforesaid Parish, and the aforesaid Precinct, and partly within other Parishes adjoining thereto, which, if included within the aforesaid Plan, for paving and removing Obllrudlions therein, would render the said Design more complete, and make the same of much greater public Utility; and that the Petitioners are willing and desirous to contribute, to the utmost of their Abilities, towards the Purposes aforesaid; but that, unless they are aided by a small daily Toll upon Horses, Mares, Geldings, and Mules, passing through the said Streets, and also upon Carriages loaded with Hay and Straw, which shall be brought, fold, or pitched, on Market Days, in any Part of the said Parish, the utmost- that their Circumstances will admit them to pay will not by any Means be adequate to the proposed Expence; and that, as the Petitioners propose paving the whole or the greatest Part of the Highways within the said Parish, they apprehend that the House will think it reasonable that they should be exempted from the Performance of any Statute Work: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. Plumer,

To' prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Joseph Parker, a Surveyor, being examined, laid.

That by a Survey made by himself, he thinks it is practicable to make a Canal for the Navigation of Boats, and other Vessels, from the Coventry Canal Navigation, near the City of Coventry, through or near the Several Places mentioned in the Petition, to the City of Oxford.

That there are great Quantities of Lime-stone near that Part of( the Canal, which will lead from Newboid upon Avon to Oxford, which at prtefent is useless, for

want of Coal to burn it; but that if the Canal is competed, Coal will be brought for that purpose; and that the Lime when burnt will be of great Use to the Farmers in manuring their Lands.

Thomas Walker, Esquire, being examined, said. That if the Navigation is completed, it will be a Means of extending Trade and Commerce; that the Inhabitants of Oxford, IVitney, Banb, and Places adjacent, are now under the Necessity of bringing divers Manufactures from Manchester, Coventry, and many other

Places by Land Carriage, which is now very high, and that the Price of Carriage will be considerably reduced by making this Canal; that the Farmers will be enabled to carry their Corn cheaper to Market; that it will be also of great Advantage to the County of Oxford, in the Article of Fuel, which is now bought at great Prices, and the Witness believes the Price of that Commodity will be reduced at lead One Half.

That the Roads are in general in very bad Repair, and in many Parts almost impassable; that if the Canal is completed, it will be a Means of keeping the Roads in much better Repair.

American: A Petition of the Representatives of Freemen in Af-Colvniet, fijmbly of Penjylvania\; signed :by the Speaker, being offered to be presented to the House, which Petition dated that the Alb impefing Duties on them are injurious to the Rights of the Petitioners; that their Ancestors carried with them to America the natural and conditutional Rights ’ of Evgli/hSubjells, one of which is, that no Taxes, for the Purposes of Revenue, can be imposed upon them legally, but by Representatives chosen by themselves; that they shall enjoy no more than the mere Shadow of Liberty, while others exercise a Power, whenever they please, to take such Proportions of their Property as they think proper, without their Consent; that they have there a Legislature veiled with full Powers ' not only to support the internal Government of their Province, but of giving and granting to their Sovereign theneceffaty Aids, whenever required, for the general Security of His Majesty’s Dominions; dating also, That, should the Parliament of Great Britain continue to exercise a Power of imposing Taxes on His Majesty’s -Subjects, who are not, nor can be, represented in this House, their Property and Estates mud become preca-

rious, as they can have no conditutional Check on the Liberality in granting the m.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to the further Hearing of the Matter of the several Petitions complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Cumberland.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the ’Counsel for Sir James Lowther proceeded, and produced Copies of several Resolutions of the Sheriff of the said County, which he published during the Course of the Poll, with relped to what Species of Votes should be admitted, and what should be rejected, at the said Election.

And the said Counsel examined several Witnesses, in order to shew upon what Occasion the said Sheriff came to several of such Resolutions; and that the same were made without respect to any of the Candidates.

Then the said Counsel having flated the Number of Votes that were queried upon the Poll;

They examined a Witness, in order to shew upon what Grounds the said Sheriff queried such Votes.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

The House being informed that the Sheriffs of the County of Middlesexattended at the Door, and desired

to communicate lomethingjo this House;

They were called in; and, at the Bar, acquainted the House, that a numerous, daring, and outrageous Mob appeared this Day at Brentford, at the Election of a Knight of the Shire for the said County; obstruded the Freedom of the said Election; and had, by Force and Violence, prevented the said Sheriffs from going on with the Poll; that several of the Poll Books were missing; and that the said Sheriffs had adjourned the Poll till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock: And therefore they did apply to this House, for their Directions how they should proceed, in taking the said Poll; and did desire the Protection of this House.

And then they withdrew.

Ordered, Nemine contradicente. That the Sheriffs for the County of Middlesex be again called in; and that Mr. Speaker do inform them, that this House doth highly approve of their Conduct, in making Application for the Directions of this House, how they shall proceed on account of the daring and outrageous Mob, which appears this Day to have interrupted the Freedom of the Election for the said County.

That they immediately do every Thing in their Power to recover all the Poll Books, if possible; but, if that cannot be done, that they do apply to the Cheque Clerks of each Candidate for the Books kept by them; and

VOL £Z.

inform such Clerks, that it is the Order of this House, that they do produce and deliver the same to them.

That they do compare the said Books, and report to this House on Saturday Morning next the State thereof.

That they do repair Tomorrow Morning to the Place of Polling, pursuant to their Adjournment; and do then further adjourn the said Poll to Monday Morning next. Nine of the Clock.

That they do apply to the Magistrates of the County of > Middlesex and acquaint them, that it is the Order of this House, that the said Magistrates do attend the said Election, and do appoint a proper Number of Constables, and take every other Means in their Power, to preserve the Peace and Freedom of the said Election.

And that Mr. Speaker do assure the said Sheriffs of the Support and Protection of this House, in the Execution of their Duty; and that this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against any Person who shall dare to violate the Freedom of the said Election.

And the said Sheriffs were again called in; and*Mr.' Speaker acquainted them therewith.

And then they again withdrew.

Ordered, That the said Order be forthwith printed and published.

Sir Joseph Mawhey reported from the Committee, appointed to draw up what may be proper to be offered to the Lords, at a Conference, on the Subject Matter of the last Conference, That the Committee had accordingly drawn up what may be proper to be offered to the Lords at a Conference; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the fame in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

That the Commons, who are equally delirous with their Lordships of preserving all good Intelligence and right Understanding between the Two Houses, and of maintaining the closest Adherence to the ancient and regular Course of parliamentary Proceedings, have taken into Consideration the Answer of their Lordships to the Message sent from the Commons on last,

Vox.. 32.

desiring that Two Peers might have Leave to attend, to be examined as Witnesses in the House of Commons.

The Propriety of that Practice, by which each House of Parliament, having Matters under their Consideration, Wherein the Testimony of Members of the other House might be materially wanted, has been reciprocally accustomed to desire the Attendance of such Members, the Commons understand to be so well warranted, not only by every Principle of parliamentary Proceeding, but also by ancient Usage, that they are not willing to suppose, that their Lordships could mean to object uhiver-sally to the receiving a Message for such Purpose from the Commons: And as their Lordships have not thought fit to specify any particular Grounds of Exception, either to any of the Circumstances attending the Message, or the Terms in which it is conveyed, the Commons are at some loss to conceive in what respect their Message can be supposed to deviate from the ancient and regular course of Parliament.

With respect to that Part of their Lordships Answer, whereby they desire to know what Grounds have been laid before the House of Commons, for suspecting Two Peers of being privy to the Subornation of Evidence with public Money, the Commons observe, that as no Grounds were laid before them for entertaining any such Suspicion concerning the Two Peers, so no such Suspicion was entertained by the Commons; nor do they conceive, that their Message to the Lords could reasonably be thought to convey such an Imputation.

The said Report being read a Second Time;

The Amendment following was proposed to be made thereto; viz.

To leave out some" and insert44 a" in (lead thereof.

And the Question being put. That the Word " some" stand Part of the said Report;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the Word 44 a" be inserted irsstead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the said Report, thus amended, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Commons, whp are equally delirous with their Lordships of preserving all good Intelligence and right Understanding between the Two Houses, and ot maintaining the closest Adherence to the ancient and regular Course of parliamentary Proceedings, have taken into Consideration the Answer of their Lordships to the Message sent from the Commons on Wednesday last, desiring that Two Peers might have Leave to attend, to be examined as Witnesses in the House of Commons.

The Propriety of that Practice, by which each House of Parliament, having Matters under their Consideration, wherein the Testimony of Members of the other House might be materially wanted, has been reciprocally accustomed to desire the Attendance of such Members, the Commons understand to be so well warranted, not only by every Principle of parliamentary Proceeding, but also by ancient Usage, that they are not willing to suppose, that their Lordships could mean to object universally to the receiving a Message for such Purpose from the Commons: And as their Lordships have not thought fit to specify any particular Grounds of Exception, either to any of the Circumstances attending the Message, or the Terms in which it is conveyed, the Commons are at a lots to conceive in what respect their Message can be supposed to deviate from the ancient and regular Course of Parliament.

With respect to that Part of their Lordships Answer, whereby they desire to know what Grounds have been laid before the House of Commons, for suspecting Two Peers of being privy to the Subornation of Evidence with public Money, the Commons observe, tl\at as no Grounds were laid before them for entertaining any such Suspicion concerning the Two Peers, so no such Suspicion was entertained by the Commons; nor do they

That the Petitioners observing that His Majesty, in His most Gracious Speech, has recommended to Parliament the Confederation of the great Commercial Interests which had been entered upon in the preceding Session, humbly apprehend, that the House will soon resume the important Object of the Trade between Asia and Europe-, and that the Petitioners hope, that the said immense Fund of Commercial Industry, Power, and Profit, may be put on as broad a National Foundation as it is capable of, and has been found to be capable of, to the establishing of the Wealth and Power of a Neighbouring Country; and the more (b, as the opulent Territories lately added to the British Possessions in Asia were acquired by the Bravery of the British Troops, and at a prodigious Expence to the Public; and that the Petitioners, in order to extend and participate this Trade, are ready to conform to such Terms and Regulations as to the Wisdom of Parliament shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Merchants, Manufacturers, Traders, and others, of the Counties of York and Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act made in tire Thirty-first Year of his late Majesty, certain Commissioners therein named, and their Successors, were impowered to extend the Navigation of the River Colder, from Wakefield, in the said County of

York, to or near to Sowerby Bridge, in the Parish of Halifax 1 and to make navigable the River Hebble, Halig, or Halifax Brook, from Brooks Mouth, to Salter Hebble Bridge, in the said County; and that, in Pursuance of the said Act, the said Navigation hath been completed to Brooks Mouth, and Salter Hebble Bridge, and hath been found of very great Benefit and Advantage to the Petitioners, and to Trade in general; and that, in 1767 and 1768, not long after the said Navigation bad been so opened, several very great and uncommon Floods happened in the said River, which so greatly damaged the Works, as to put a Stop to the Navigation upon the said River; and the same hath ever since been totally obstructed, to the great Detriment of the Petitioners and the Public; and that the Petitioners are informed, that the Money already lent on the Credit of the said Act is expended, and, the present Security being so very precarious, no Persons will risque any more Money upon the Credit of the present Act, so that the Peti tioners are likely to be deprived of the Advantages which would arise to them, from making and completing the said Navigation: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for securing tD the present Subscribers the Money they have already advanced, and for giving feme Encouragement to Persons to advance a competent Sum of Money, for completing the said Navigation, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall appear rood: proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners being Candidates at the late Election for Members to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of in the County of York, were duly elected by a very great Majority of the Persons qualified to vote, by the Constitu-t-ion of the (kid Borough, as declared by the last Determination of the House of Commons; but that William Crewe, Esquire, the Mayor of the said Borough, presiding at the said Election as Returning Officer, conduced the Poll with the most apparent Partiality to the Interest of Lord Gallway, and Henry Strachey, Esquire, the other Candidates, rejecting, without any good Reason assigned, or any just exception, a very great Majority of the Persons entitled to vote by the Constitution of the said Borough, the last Determination of this House, and the Statutes making such Determination final; and that, under Colour of an unfair Majority, obtained through those and divers other arbitrary and illegal Practices of the said Mayor, the said Lord Gallway and Henry Strachey have been returned by the said Mayor, as having been duly elected to represent the said Borough in Parliament, contrary to the Truth, the last Resolution of this House concerning the Right of Election for the said Borough, in Defiance of the Laws and Constitution requiring fair and free Elections, in manifest Violation of the Rights of the Electors, and to the great Injury of the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give the Petitioners such Relief as they thall appear to merit, and to do further therein as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, upon the 7th Day of

March next.

Ditto. A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are % thereunto subscribed, being Electors for Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of in

the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read Setting forth. That at the late Election, the Petitioners, and many other of the Inhabitants, House-holders resident within the said Borough, being a very great Majority of the Persons legally intitled, by the Constitution of the said Borough and the last Determination of this House, to vote on that occasion, gave their Voices for Sir Rowland Winn, Baronet, and Edward Winn, Esquire; but that Lord Gallway, and Henry Strachey, Esquire, the other Candidates, having found Means to engage in their Interest William Crewe,

Esquire, the then Mayor of the said Borough, who pre- tided as Returning Officer at the said Election, took upon himself to reject the Votes of the Petitioners, and divers others who voted for the said Sir Rowland Wim and Edward Winn, under various Pretences, all either void of Foundation in Truth, or, though true, insufficient, as the Petitioners conceive, to support any solid Objection to the Votes so rejected; and particularly, that the Mayor pretended, that the Quality of a Freehold of Burgage Tenure was among the Requisites to a Qualification to vote, and that the Petitioners and others, not having Burgage Tenements, had not any Right to give their Votes; although the last Resolution of this House, concerning the Right of Election for the said Borough, was produced and proved at the said Election; whereby, and by the Statute made in Confirmation of the Resolutions of this House, the Petitioners humbly conceive the Privilege of them, and all other the Inhabitants, Housholders resident in the said Borough, to vote for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was established and confirmed, and the said Mayor ought not to have violated or impeached the same and that the said Mayor, regardless of the just Rights of the Petitioners, permitted a'great Number of Perforts, who had no Right, to poll for the said Lord Gallway, and Henry Strachey; and by those and divers other partial and illegal Practices of the said Mayor, and of the said Lord Gallway and Henry Strachey, a colourable Majority was obtained for them, against the said- Sir Rowland Winn, and Edward Winn, and the said Mayor has unduly returned the said Lord Gallway and Henry Strachey, in Prejudice of the Petitioners, and also of the said Sir Rowland Winn, and Edward Winn, who were duly elected, and ought to have been returned; and that the Petitioners thus unjustly stripped of their Fran-chilcs, and they with the Electors in general, deprived of the Representatives of their Choice, and having others imposed upon them whom they have not cholen, can have no adequate Redress but from this House: And therefore praying. That their Rights and Privileges may be preserved to them, and that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and do therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, at the same Time that the Matter of the Petition of Sir Rowland Winn, Baronet, and Edward Winn, Esquire, is heard.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Harris and Mr.

Cuddon:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, having taken into Consideration the fe-> American veral Papers relating to the late D’fturbances in America, Colonie*. laid before their Lordships by His Majesty’s Command, have come to several Resolutions; and alfa have agreed to an Address to His Majesty, to which they desire the Concurrence of this House.

And ihen the Messengers withdrew.

And the said Resolutions and Address were readj and are as fol'oweth; viz.

Resolved, by the L irds Spiritual and Temporal,

in Parliament aflhmbied That the Votes, Refutations artd Proceedti.gs of the House of Represen tatives of Majachufet's Bay, in the Months of January and February last, respecting several late Acts of Parliament, so far as the said Votes, Resolutions, and Proceedings do import a Denial of, or do draw into Question, the Power and Authority of His Majesty, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in Parliament assembled, to make Laws and Statutes of sufficient Force and Validity to bind the Colonies and People of America, Subjects of the Crown of Great Britain, in all Cases whatsoever, are illegal, uncon-ftitutional, and derogatory of the Rights of the Cr&wn and Parliament of Great Britain.

Resolved, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

in Parliament assembled, That the Resolution of the' said House of Represen tatives of the Province, of Mafa-> chufet's Bay, in January last, to write Letters to she; several Houses of Representatives of the British Colonies on the Continent, desiring them to join with the said House of Representatives of the Province of -chufet's Bay, in Petitions, which dd deny, or draw intof Question, the Right of Parliament to impose Duties and Taxes upon His Majesty’s Subjects in America, and in* pursuance of the said Resolution, the writing such Let- ters, in which certain late Acts of Parliament, imposing Duties and Taxes, are stated to be Infringements of the*

Rights of His Majesty’s Subjects of the said Province;! are Proceedings of a most unwarrantable and dangerou*

Nature, calculated to inflame the Minds of His Majesty’s Subjects in the other Colonies, tending to create unlawful

io8 16° Decembris. A. 17 68.

American lawful Combination* repugnant to the Laws of Great Colonies, Britain, and subversive of the Constitution,

Resolved, by the Lords Spiritual.and Temporal,

in Parliament assembled, That it appears that the Town of Boston, in the province of Massachuset's Bay, has for some Time pad been in a State of great Disorder and Consulion, and that the Peace of the said Town has, at several Times, been disturbed by Riots and Tumults of a dangerous Nature, in which the Officers of His Majesty’s Revenue there have been obstructed by Acts of Violence in the Execution of the Laws, and their

Lives endangered,

Resolved, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

in Parliament assembled, That it appears that neither the Council of the said Province of Massachuset's Bay, nor the ordinary Civil Magistrates, did exert their Authority for suppressing the said Riots and Tumults.

Resolved, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

,in Parliament assembled, That in thefcCircumstances of the Province of the Massachuset's Bay, and of the Town of B oft on, the Preservation of the public Peace and the due Execution of the Laws became impracticable, without the Aid of a Military Force to support and protect the Civil Magistrate, and the Officers of His Majesty’s Revenue.

Resolved, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

,in Parliament assembled, That the Declarations, Resolutions, and Proceedings, in the Town Meetings at Boston, on the 14th of June^nd 12th of September, were illegal and unconditional, and calculated to excite Sedition and Insurrections in His Majesty’s Province of Massa-chufet's Bay.

Resolved, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

in Parliament assembled, That the Appointment at the Town Meeting, on the 12th September, of a Convention to be held in the Town of Boston, on the 2 2d of that Month, to consist of Deputies from the several Towns and Districts in the Province of the Massachuset's Bay, and the issuing a Precept by the Seledk Men of the Town of Boston, to each of the said Towns and Districts, for the Election of such Deputies, were Proceedings subversive of His Majesty’s Government, and evidently manifesting a Design, in the Inhabitants of the said Town of Boston, to set up a new and unconstitutional Authority, independant of the Crown of Great Britain.

Resolved, by the Lords Spirtual and Temporal, j in Parliament assembled. That the Elections, by several Towns and Districts in the Province of Massachusets Bay, of Deputies to fit in the said Convention, and the Meeting of such Convention in Consequence thereof, were daring Infijlts offered to His Majesty’s Authority* and audacious Usurpations of the Powers of Government.

The humble Address of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, , in Parliament assembled.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, , in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty our humble Thanks for the Communication Your Majesty has been graciously pleased to make to Your Parliament, of several Papers relative to public Transactions in Your Majesty’s Province of Massachuset's Bay.

We beg Leave to express to Your Majesty, our sincere Satisfaction in the Measures which Your Majesty has pursued, forsupporting the Constitution, and for inducing a due Obedience to the Authority of the Legislature; and to give Your Majesty the strongest Assurances that'we will effectually stand by and support Your Majesty in such further Measures as may be found necessary to maintain the Civil Magistrates in a due Execution of the Laws within Your Majesty’s Province of Majfachifet's Bay: And as we conceive that nothing can be more im-

mediately necessary, either for the Maintenance of Your Majesty’s Authority in the said Province, or for guarding Your Majesty’s Subjects therein from being farther deluded by the Arts of wicked and designing Men, than to proceed in the most speedy and effectually Manner for bringing to condign. Punishment the chief Authors and Instigators of the late Disorders, we most humbly beseech Your Majesty, that You will be graciously pleased to direct Your Majesty’s Governor of Massachuset's Bay to take the most effectual Methods for procuring the full-eft Information that can be obtained, touching all Trea-fons or Misprisions of Treason committed within his Government, since the Thirtieth Day of December last, and to transrhit the fame, together with the Names of the Persons who were most active in^ the Commission of such Offences, to One of Your Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, in order that Your Majesty may issue a special Commission for enquiring of, hearing, and determining the said Offences within this Realm, pursuant to the Provisions of the Statute of the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, in case Your Majesty shall, upon receiving the said Information, fee sufficient Ground for such a Proceeding.

Ordered, That the said Resolutions and Address be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the several Papers, which were presented to the House by the Lord North, upon the 28th Day of November last, and the 7th Day of this Instant December, by His Majesty’s Command.

Calder Lord John Cavendish reported from the Committee, Navigation. to whom the Petition of several Merchants, Manufacturers, Traders, and others, of the Counties of York and Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of several Persons who have lent and advanced Money on the Credit of an Act of Parliament, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for extending the Navigation of the River Calder, to or near to Sowerby Bridge, in the Parish of Halifax; and for making navigable the River Hebble, Halig, or Halifax Brook, from Brooks Mouth, to Salter Hobble Bridge, in the County of York; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report iivhis Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, the said Act was read; whereby it appeared, That Commissioners therein named, and their Successors, are impowered to make and complete the said Navigation in

such manner as the said Act directs, with Power to borrow such Sum of Money on the Credit of the said Act as they should think fit, and to assign over the Tolls and Duties thereby granted for securing the Repayment,.. Then,

Mr. Robert Charlsworth produced to your Committee an Account of Money borrowed, and of Tolls received by Virtue of the said Act, whereby it appeared that 56,900l. and upwards had been borrowed, and 7000l. and upwards raised by the Tolls granted by the said Act; and that the Sum of 64,000l. and upwards had been expended in carrying the said Act into Execution.

And Mr. CharlfwortH informed your Committee, That in pursuance of the Powers given by the said Act, the Navigation had been completed. from Wakefield to Brookfmouth, and Salter Hebble Bridge, and a considerable Progress had been made in the Works, from Brookfmouth towards Sowerby Bridge.

That in the Years 1767 and 1.768, Two very great Floods happened . in the said Rivers, which greatly injured and damaged the Works of the Navigation.

That soon after each Flood, the Works so injured and damaged were repaired, and some additional Works and Alterations made at a very great Expence; but that soon after the same were respectively completed, and the Navigation restored another great Flood happened in the Month of June last, which so far destroyed the Works as entirely to put a Stop to the said Navigation, between Salter Hebble Bridge and Brookfmouth, and between Brookfmouth and Wakefield.

That soon after this last Floodf^ a public General Meeting of Commissioners and Creditors was held to consider what Methods should be taken to raise a further1 Sum of Money in order to restore the Navigation, but no Person could be found who would adventure any more Money, on an Undertaking so hazardous, upop the Conditions of the present Act, so that no Money was subscribed at that Meeting, but to discharge some Arrears due to Workmen who had been employed in the Undertaking, and to defray the Expences of securing such Works as were not destroyed, until an Application could be made to Parliament, to alter the present Act in such Manner as to encourage Persons to advance a sufficient Sum of Money effectually to restore and complete the said Navigation.

Mr. Jeremiah Royds confirmed the Substance of the foregoing Evidence.

Streets. Middlesex, the City of Land in the Liberty of His Majesty’s Tower of Lo, and also of the Principal Inhabitants in the Precinct of Well in the said Liberty, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as f^lloweth; viz.

1 To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Edward Hawkins, being examined, said, that the Streets and other Places, within the said Parish and Precinct, are-very ill paved, and greatly obstructed by Ports, and annoyed by Signs, Spouts, Gutters, and other Incroachments.

That the High Street of the said Parish is a principal Avenue to the Cities of London and and

greatly frequented by Travellers, to and from the said Cities, to several Parts of this Kingdom.

That notwithstanding the Inhabitants of the said Parish and Precinct, are heavily burthened with Taxes, towards watching, lighting, and cleaning the feme, and providing for the Poor, which are extremely numerous, are willing to submit to an additional-Tax towards paving the feme in a better Manner.

That there are several Houses and other Buildings, which project so far into the Streets, as not only to cause the Footway to be very incommodious; but also to obstruct the Passage of Carriages, by which means Accidents frequently happen by the'overturning of such Carriages.

That there is a House on the East Side of Somerset Street, and Three Houses at the South End of the said Street, which project so far as greatly to obstruct the Passage of Carriages: That the Three last mentioned Houses are very ruinous, and the'Landlord told the Witness he had no Objection to their being taken down.

That the Two Corner Houses at the South End of White Lion Street, project so far as to make the turning very dangerous for Carriages, and ought to be taken down: That the Witness has not spoken t.o the Proprietors of any of the said Houses except the Three above-mentioned; but has not heard any Objections made to their being taken down.

That the present Rates, within the said Parish and Precinct, are so high that the Inhabitants will not be able to complete this Undertaking, unless they are aided by a small daily Toll upon Horses and other Cattle, and upon Hay and Straw, which shall be brought, fold, or pitched, on Market Days in any Part of the said Parish.

_ Mr, Samuel Wood and Mr. Samuel Hawkins confirmed the aforegoing Evidence: And Mr. Hawkins added, That the Whole of the Rates already imposed, together with the additional Expence of pavipg, will amount to Six Shillings in the Pound, and that the Parish are now 3000l. in Debt.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for paving fuel) Parts of the Parirti of Saint Mary otherwise White Chapel, and the Precinct of Close, as lie in the.;County of and Liberty of the

Tower of London, and Parts of certain Streets adjoining to the said Parish and Precinct; and for opening such Passages as are therein mentioned: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. Alderman Trecothick, and Sir John Hynde Cotton, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Devon A Petition of the High Sheriff, Gentlemen, Clergy, Poor’*Relief, and Freeholders, of the County of , was presented to the House, and readSetting forth. That the Laws in being, relating to the Maintenance of the Poor of this Kingdom, are ineffectual; and that it has been found, by Experience, that the Poor are better supported, and the Lands exonerated in many Parishes of the said County, by the Edablishment of Societies under certain voluntary Agreements among themselves, to pay a small Sum Monthly, and to receive, in Consideration thereof, Weekly Allowances, whenever they are rendered incapable of Labour? but, as it often happens, that they lose the Benefit and Advantage of such Provisions, by Frauds and other Misapplications of the said Funds, and the Members of such Societies do often enter into unwarrantable Confederacies, to the Prejudice of Trade and Agriculture; and therefore, that the Poor may be better provided for, and may be secured against such Frauds and Misapplications of their Stock, and that the same may not be applied to any illegal Purposes: Praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better Relief of the Poor of the said County of Devon, by the Edablishment of such Societies, under proper Restrictions and Regulations, and to give such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Mr. , &c.:

And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Pdrfons, Papers, and Records.

The House was moved, that the Resolution of the House, of the 24th Day of November 1763, with relation to the Privilege of Parliament not extending to the same of writing and publishing seditious Libels, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly; and is as follow-eth; viz.

" Resolved, That Privilege of Parliament does not

extend to the same of writing and publishing fe- ditious Libels; nor ought to be allowed to obstruct the ordinary Course of the Laws, in the speedy and effectual Prosecution of so heinous and dangerous an " Offence."

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That John IVilkes, Esquire, although he is con-' victed of publishing a seditious Libel, is intitled to Privilege of Parliament.

The Amendments followfhg were severally proposed to be made to the Question;

To insert after the Words "cortvicted of," these Words printing and ;" and after " seditious," to insert " and " scandalous. "

A Message from the Lord*-, by Mr. Montagu and Mr. Cuddon:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to indemnify such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments within the Time limited by Law, and for allowing further Time for that Purpose; and to indemnify Members arid Officers, in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid; and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The Counsel for the Petitioner admitted, that the Numbers on the Poll were for the Sitting Member' 24, and for the Petitioner 21; but infilled, that Ten occasional Burgesses had been made, Five of whom voted for the Sitting Member, and ought not to be allowed, as falling within the Meaning of an Act, made in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act to prevent occasional Freemen from voting at Elections of Members to serve in Parliament for Cities and Boroughs.

Then the said Counsel produced the original Charter of the said Borough, granted by King James the First, in the Eighth Year of his Reign.

And several Parts thereof were read.

Then the original Poll, taken at the lad Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, being produced, the Numbers appeared to be as stated by the said Counsel.

Then some of the Corporation Books of the said Borough were produced; and several Entries therein were read, in order to shew at what Time the Five Voters objected to were admitted Burgesses of the said Borough; and a Witness was examined with relation thereto.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners summed up their Evidence.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member were heard, and stated several Parts of the Charter, whereby Corporate Acts are directed to be done by the Bailiff and Burgesses of the said Borough.

Royal Grandfather, this Province \tt the last War If early raised a large Body of Troops, to aifift in Conjunction "With other Colony Troops, in reducing the Power

in America, the Expence whereof was very great, and

would have been insupportable, had not Part of it been refunded by Parliament, from a Conviction of the Inability of that Province to bear- the whole; and that the Loss of Men in the several Campaigns of that War was great, and to so young a Country very detrimental, and , could not be compensated by Grants of Parliament, and to which those Grants had no respect j and that the Acquisition of so large a Part of America by His Majesty’s Arms, though a great National Good, and greatly beneficial to the Colonies, as thereby they have been freed from the Hostilities of the , and, in a good

Measure, of the Indians that were under their influence, has, in divers respects, operated to the Detriment of the Colonies, particularly by diminishing the Value of Real Estates, and drawing their Inhabitants from them, to settle the new-acquired Territories; and that the said Acquisitions have occasioned new and increasing Demands for the Manufactures of Great Britain, and have opened to her Sources of Trade, greatly beneficial, and continually enlarging, the Benefits of which center in herself, and which, with the extensive Territories acquired, are apprehended to be an ample Equivalent for all the Charges of the War in America, and for the Expences of defending, protecting, and securing, said Territories; and that that Province in particular is (till in Debt, on Account of the Charge incurred by the late War; and that the Yearly Taxes, excepting the present Year, on which no Public Tax has been yet laid, by reason of general Valuation through the Province, which could not be completed before the Dissolution.of the late General Assembly, but which will probably be resumed when a new Assembly shall be called; and that the YearlyTaxes upon the People for lessening said Debt, though not so great as dbring the War, are nevertheless with more Difficulty paid, by reason of the greater Scarcity of Money in the Colonies owing to the Balance of their Trade with Great Britain being against them, which Balance, exclusive of the Operation of the several Acts of Parliament, taxing the Colonies, by laying certain Duties for the Purpose of railing a Revenue from them, drains them of their Money, to the great Embarrassment of their Trade, the only Source of it; and that that Embarrassment is much increased by the late Regulations of Trade, and by the Tax Acts aforesaid, which draw immediately from Trade the Money necessary to support it, on the support whereof the Payment of the Balance aforesaid depends; and that the said Tax Acts operating to the Detriment of the Trade of the Colonies, mull likewise operate to the Detriment of Great , by disabling the Colonists from paying the Debt due to her, and by laying them under a Necessity of using less of her Manufactures; and that, by the Use and Consumption of the Manufactures of Great which are

virtually charged with most of the Taxes that take Place there, the Colonies pay no inconsiderable Part of those Taxes; and that by several Acts of Parliament, the Colonies are restrained from importing most of the Commodities of Europe, unless from Great Britain, which occasions her Manufactures, and all Commodities coming from her, to be dearer charged, which is equivalent to a Tax upon them; and that the Colonies ar-e prohibited fending to Foreign Markets many valuable Articles of their Produce, which, giving to Great , an Advantage in the Price of them, is a proportionable and a further Tax upon the Colonies j and that the Exports of tire Colonies, all their Gold and Silver, and their whole Powers of Remittance, fall short of the charged Value of what they import from Great Britain j apd that, if it be ‘ considered what Difficulties the Colonies encountered on their Firfi Settlement; their having defended themselves, Nova Scotia and Georgia excepted, without any Expence to Great Britain; the Aflistances given by them in the Vol. 32.

late War* whereby the Empire of Great Britain is so American greatly extended, and its Trade proportionably increased; Cobniw. the Dimunition of the Value of their Estates, and the Emigration of their Inhabitants, occasioned by that Extension; the Loss of Men in the said War, peculiaVly. detrimental to young Countries; the Taxes on them to support their own internal Government $ the Share they pay of the Duties and Taxes in Britain, by . the Consumption of British Manufactures for which such valuable Returns are made; the Restraints upon their Trade, equivalent to a Tax j the Balance of Trade continually* against them, and their consequent Inabilty to pay the Duties laid by the Acts aforesaid: If those Fads be considered, the Petitioners conceive it must appear that His Majesty’s Subjects in the Colonies have been, and are at lead as much burthened as those in Great Britain j and that they are, whilst in America, more advantageous to Great Britain than if they were transplanted thither, and subjected to all the Duties and Taxes paid there:

And that the Petitioners beg Leave to lay their Represen,-tation before this House: humbly praying a favourable Consideration of it; and that the Charter Rights and Privileges of the People of that Province, and their invaluable Liberties as British Subjects, may be secured to them j and that the several Acts of Parliament, made for the Purpose of railing a Revenue in' , be repealed.

and that great Quantities of Coal arc brought to the said Town for Sale, as well for the Con- " fumption of the said Town, as of the adjacent Country; and it would be of great Advantage to the said Town and Country, if such Coals were delivered by Statute Measure, or by Weight only; but there not being any Powers vested ip any of the Inhabitants of the said Town, to compel the Delivery of Coals by such Measure or Weight only, the Buyers thereof are at present liable to be greatly defrauded, and there is Reason to believe, that great Frauds are daily practised therein; and that it would therefdre be a great Advantage, not only to the Inhabitants of the said Town, but of the Country adjacent, if Powers were given for the due measuring or weighing of all Coals brought to the said Town for Sale, and preventing Frauds in the Measure and Weight thereof, and for laying a Duty thereupon, to defray the Expence of such measuring and weighing, and of-collecting the said Duty, and for applying the Surplus thereof in and towards the paving, repairing, cleansing, enlightening, and watching, the said Streets, Lanes, A.Ueys, Public Passages, and Avenues, within and leading to the said Town: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and with such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Freeholders and Heritors of the County of Haddingtoun, and of several Gentlemen usual-

ly travelling the Roads within the said County; was presented to the'House, and read; Taking Notice of an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for repairing the Roads from Dun-glass Bridge, to the Town of Haddingtoun; and from thence to Ravenjhaugh Burn, in the County of Haddingtoun: And setting forth, That the Money collected and borrowed by virtue of the said Act, has been duly applied, and great Progress has been made in the Reparation of the said Roads; but that the same cannot be effectually repaired, and the Money borrowed on the Credit of the said Act repaid, unless the Term and Powers of the said Act be further enlarged, and continued j and that the several Roads leading into the Road abovementioned cannot be effectually repaired, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course provided by Law; and it would be highly advantageous to the Inhabitants of the said County, and other Persons travelling through the fame, if Provision was made for the effectual repairing, and keeping in Repair the said Roads: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir George Mr. Wedderburn, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Halsey reported from the Committee, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for Naturalizing Henry Uhthoffwas committed. That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment: And lie delivered the Bill in at the Clerk’s Table.

And the said Bill was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass.

Ordered, That Mr. Halsey do carry the Bill to the Lords, and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the fame, without any Amendment.

A Petition of Charles Dingley, of , Merchant, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends the same to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, in 1766 and 1767, at the Expence of Four Thousand Pounds and upwards, erected on his Estate at Lime house, near the River Thames, a Wind Saw Mill} and that the Operation of the said Mill so fully answered the Hopes and Expectations of the Petitioner, as to encourage him to give very large Orders for proper and suitable Timber, to be thereby manufactured; and that, whilst the Petitioner was in the full Use and Enjoyment of the said Mill, and, by Means thereof, was enabled to supply the Exigencies of public Demands in a suitable and advantageous Manner, he had the Misfortune to feel the Effects of the late riotous Proceedings; the said Mill, and the Works thereof, being, on the Tenth Day of May last, by a great Number of Persons riotously and tumul-tuoully assembled, destroyed, spoiled, and rendered entirely useless; and that the Petitioner hath used his utmost Endeavours to bring the Offenders to Justice; but is advised the Punishment for such Outrage can only be as for a Misdemeanor at Common Law; and that, notwithstanding the aforesaid discouraging Incidents, the Petitioner has completely and substantially repaired the said Mill, and hath necessarily laid out and expended therein the Sum of One Thousand Pounds, and upwards; and for as much as the Petitioner hath not only brought to Perfection an Engine, so manifestly for the Benefit of the Public, but hath sustained the Loss of the Interest of the large Sums expended about the fame; and moreover hath borne the Burthen of a very great Stock of Timber provided and left on the Petitioner’s Hands unmanufactured, by Means of the Outrage and Interruptions aforesaid: Therefore praying the House, to take his same into Consideration, and to grant him such Recompence and Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof ;and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Lord Mr. , &c.:

And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, in January 1743, the Petitioner’s Ship Britannia, Burthen 200 Tons, or thereabouts, failed

from the I lie of Wight, bound on a Voyage to Genoa, or Naples, with a Cargo of Wheat on Freight, and from thence to Gallipoli, and back to , and, in the

Course of her Outward Voyage, put into Port Mahon, where Ihe was stopt by Admiral Matheivs then Commander in Chief of his Majesty’s Fleet in the Mediterranean, by whose Order the Cargo was taken out of her for the Use of the Fleet, and her whole destined Voyage thereby totally defeated; that the Petitioner was prevented, by the Agents of Government, from ever regaining Possession of her, and ascertaining the Money due to him in respect thereof, either by the Arbitrement of Merchants of Reputation, or a Jury, when the legal Remedy subsisted; and never received any Satisfaction for the fame, or the Damages occasioned and fullained; but the Officers of Government, or One of them, changed her Name, and afterwards Ihe was actually employed as a Tender in his Majesty’s Service, Thirty-two Months, and upwards; and that Government, in the former War, had Two-different Methods of hiring Ships, viz. One, for Transports, to be used at their Pleasure so long as their Service required, which were generally paid about Fifteen or Sixteen Shillings a Ton per Month, taken into immediate Pay, and so continued about Two Months after a Convoy failed with them to their destined Ports, from the Place where they were discharged abroad, and, if taken or dellroyed by the Enemy, then to be paid for by Government; the other, under certain Restrictions, for particular Voyages, upon cheaper Terms, in which Cales the Owners of Ships bound to Foreign Parts in order to bring Cargoes to Europe, where the Homeward Freight was the chief Object, usually contracted to carry Stores to Places near their Outward Course at much lower Rates of Freight

A Petition of the Reverend Robert Carter, Clerk, Ancbolm* was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, Drainage. That by an Act of 7 George III. for the more effectual draining the Lands lying in the Level of Ancholme, a Tax of Two Shillings and Six Pence per Acre, with some Indulgence to certain Lands for a limited Time only, was indiscriminately laid on the whole Level; and that such a Tax, without Regard to their present State as to Value, and Degree of being drained, or their future Capability of being cither adequately improved, or even drained, is unequal and oppressive; and that such a Tax is apprehended to be contrary to the Tenor,

Spirit, and Principle of the general Laws of Sewers, as established by the Twenty-third of Henry the Eighth; and that the Mode of Taxation in the Bill, as it was brought into the House, was totally changed and altered, from that agreed upon by the Proprietors in general at their last Meeting; and that the said Tax is particularly hard, unjust, and oppressive, upon the Petitioner, whose Predecessors having a large Property of near 600 Acres in the said Level, had embanked the fame, and erected a large Engine thereon, the only regular Drainage Works in the whole Level, by which Means, and at a very great Expence, they had so effected a private Drainage, as not to have lost their Lands, in the Summer, above once these Fifty Years, whilftall the other Lands around them have been generally loft; and that the said Low Lands, belonging to the Petitioner, are intrinsically, and naturally, of so poor and barren a Quality, as to be incapable of any further Improvement, or, at least, any adequate to the Tax imposed on them; and that no particular Consideration is made to the Petitioner by the said Act, either on Account of the great Expence and Efficacy of his former Drainage, or the natural Poverty of his Land; but that he is involved in the same Predicament with those whose Lands are almost totally loft, and have had nothing expended on them, a great Quantity of which Lands will immediately, upon emerging out of the Water, without any Culture, from their superior Quality, be worth Four, Five, or even Six Times the Value of the Lands of the Petitioner: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to amend and explain the said Act, wherein the Petitioner may be relieved by a Clause, for him either to pay only Half the Assessment, or that he may be assessed according to the Rate of his Portion, Tenure, Right, and Interest, in the said Level, or according to the Proportion of the additional Benefit he shall receive from the

Mr. Thomas Prefion, Mason, who informed your Committee that the Works have been begun, and carried on, for making a large and commodious Harbour at Ramsgate, and great Progress has been made towards finishing and completing the fame, which when finished will be a very useful and commodious Harbour: And,

your Committee, was read, and is as followeth; viz. That Shipping failing between the Goodwin Sands and the Coatt of France, are not within the . Preamble or Letter of the Act, or within the actual Benefit of it: And,

A Petition of Sir Herbert Lloyd, Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That at the Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the several Boroughs of Cardigan, Aberystwyth, Lampeter, and Atpar in the County of Cardigan, Congreve,

Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that the Christian Name of the said Congreve, was not

so much as mentioned during the whole Poll, which be* gun on Thursday Morning the Fifth Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-nine, and continued till Friday Evening the Thirteenth of the same Month, though often demanded by the Petitioner, nor was the same known to any One of the Electors; and.that the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned, but that Thomas Lloyd', Esquire, the Mayor, although applied to immediately before, and several Times after the Poll was begun, to examine into the Legality of the Voice of each Burgess as he came to be polled, and particularly to examine whether the Admission of each Burgess was duly and legally stamped, pursuant and according to the Directions of the several ’ Acts of Parliament in that same made and provided, and that the Books and Papers wherein the Admission of Burgestes of the several Boroughs aforesaid were entered, should be produced in Court, in order to have Recourfip to the same as often as occasion required, absolutely refused to come into any of the said Measures proposed by the Petitioner and his Managers, but, instead thereof, promised to grant the Petitioner a fair Scrutiny at the Close of the Poll, and which Promise was made by the Mayor in open Court, and consented to on the Part of the said Congreve-, and that the Petitioner, upon

such Promises made by the said Mayor,' and consented to by the Friends and Agents of the said Congreve,

and relying on the Faith thereof, declined from that Time, either by himself, or his Managers, to dispute the Legality of the Voice of any Person claiming a flight of polling as a Burgess of either of the said Boroughs and that during the Poll, very many Persons were, by the Agents of the said Congreve, brought up to

poll, who had no Right or Colour of Voting, and others were brought to the Place of polling surrounded by the Friends and Agents of the said Congreve, who

being asked by the Managers of the said Congreve,

who they were to poll for, could give no Answer; upon which they told them publicly in the Face of the Court theymuft poll for Congreve-, and that towards

the Close of the Poll, the Mayor caused some-very few Persons to be queried on his Book by the Clerk of the Poll, to the Number of Seven or Eight of a Side, without the Desire of the Petitioner or his Managers;

A Petition of the Burgesses of the several Corporations of Cardigan, Aberystwith, Lampeter, and Atpar, whose Names are thereunto subsenbed, on Behalf of . themselves and several other Burgesses of the said Corporations, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That at the said Election Thomas Lloyd, Esquire, the Mayor of the said Borough, was guilty of several gross Acts and Partialities in the Exercise of his Office, in Favour of a Person who was not so much as. known, nor was his Christian Name in the Books during the whole Election, yet the said Mayor kept open the Poll for Nine Days, and admitted several Hundreds of People out of Seven or Eight different Counties to poll for Congreve, who had no Right or Pretence whatsoever, in Prejudice to the Petitioners who are real Burgesses; and that upon Complaint thereof made to the said Thomas Lloyd, he promised to grant a Scrutiny to inquire who were Burgesses; and that having procured a pretended Majority for Congreve, whom he was

pre-determined to return at all Events, the said Thomas Lloyd refused the Scrutiny notwithstanding the Faith which he had pledged in open Court; and that by those and many other unwarrantable Acts and Practices of the said Thomas Lloyd, the Petitioners have been deprived of their legal Rights and Franchises: And therefore praying, That the Houfo. will take the Premises into their Consideration, and do therein as shall seem just.

And then he was directed to be taken from the Bar.

He was again brought in to the Bar, and further heard.

And then he was again directed to be taken from the Bar.

Resolved, Nemine eontradicente. That Miles Burton Allen, Esquire, having presumed to challenge Sir William Meredith, Baronet, a Member of this House, for Words by him spoken in a Debate in this House, and thereby attempted to violate the Freedom of Debate in this House, is guilty of a high Breach of the Privileges of this House.

Resolved, Nemine eontradicente. That the said Miles Burton Allen, Esquire, be, for his said Offence, committed to His Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate; and that Mr; Speaker do issue his Warrants accordingly.

Mr. Willoughby reported from the Committee, to Nottingham whom the Petition of the several Justices of the Peace, Shire Hall, and of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and others, of the County of Nottingham, the Ninth Day of January 1769, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-reded him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Hurst, Clerk of the Peace for the said County, beings

examined, said. That the Shire Hall of the said County, where the Assizes and General Quarter Sessions of the Peace have been always held, and other public Bufinefe transaded, is in a very ruinous Condition.

Mr. John Sitnpfon, Surveyor, said. That he hath lately surveyed the said Shire Hall, and finds th^t the Floors (land upon Shores, and the Beams thereof are rotted off at the Ends; and the said Hall is, in other Respects, in very bad Repair, and quite unsafe; and is very uncomfortable for Prisoners who are confined in the Gaol, which is a Part of the said Shire Hall.

And he produced Plans for a new Shire Hall, which, by his Estimate, will cost £. 3500; and he added, That Part of the Ground to be used for re-building the Hall, is in the Town of the County of the Town of Nottingham, but is the Property of the County at large.

Mr. Hurst further said, That there is no Place so convenient for holding the said Assizes and Sessions,' and doing other public Business, as at the said Town of Nottingham; but there being no Law in being for that Purpose, he produced to your Committee the Consent of the Corporation undef their Seal, for the Use of their Guild Hall, till the said Shire Hall shall be re-built.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, passed in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for enlarging the Charitable Uses, extending the Objects, and regulating the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates given by Sir William and Dame Alice, his Wife, for the Benefit of the Poor, and other Objects of Charity of the Town of Bedford, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, Thirteen Common Council, and several other Persons, are appointed Trustees for executing the said Act: And,

Mr. Richard Wakefield, Clerk to the Trustees, produced to your Committee an Account of the Expenditure of the Money from the Commencement of the Act to Midsummer last:

And Mr. Wakefield said, That the Act has provided more to be done, than the Estate is able to bear the Expence of: And to prove which,

The Reverend Henry Hind said, That by the said Act, the Mailer’s House and School is to be first rebuilt or repaired; and that the Trustees have accordingly begun, and almost finished the Reparation of the Public School House, the Expence of which amounts to £.1500, in Part of which Sum £. 1300 has been paid; and that there is not Money in hand to pay the Remainder.

Mr. Richard Cave, Mr. John Hand Mr. -field, severally said. That the Act is in several Parts de-fective, particularly with respect to the Marriage Portions thereby directed to be given to poor Maidens, and the placing out Apprentices, of which the Witnesses gave your Committee several Instances of the Impropriety thereof.

'Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, to agree to the Sixth of the Resolutions sent from the Lords, and referred to this Committee;

" That the Declarations, Resolutions, and Proceedings, in the Town Meetings at , on the 14th of June, and 12th September, were illegal and unconfti-tutional, and calculated to excite Sedition and Insurrections in His Majesty’s Province of Massachuset's Bay." Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, to agree to the Seventh of the Resolutions sent from the Lords, and referred to this Committee; viz.

" That the Appointment at the Town Meeting, on the 12th September, of a Convention to be held in the Town of Boston, on the 22d of that Month, to consist of Deputies from the several Towns and Districts in the Province of the Massachuset'$ Bay, apd the issuing a Precept by the Select Men of the Town of to each

of the said Towns'and Districts, for the Election of such Deputies, were Proceedings subversive of His Majesty’s Government, and evidently manifesting a Design in the Inhabitants of the said Town of Boston, to set up a new and unconditional Authority, independent of the Crown of Great Britain," with the following Amendments; viz.

Between the Words the" and " by" to leave out the Words " issuing a Precept," and to insert instead thereof " writing a Letter."

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, to agree to the Eighth of the Resolutions sent from the 'Lords, and referred to this Committee;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, to agree to the Address sent from the Lords, and referred to this Committee; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

" We Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual, and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty our humble Thanks for the Communication Your Majesty has been graciously pleased to make to Your Parliament, of several Papers relative to public Transactions in Your Majesty’s Province of Massachuset's Bay.

We beg Leave to express to Your Majesty our sincere Satisfaction, in the Measures which Your Majesty has. pursued for supporting the Constitution, and for inducing a due Obedience to the Authority of the Legifla-ture; and to give Your Majesty the strongest Assurances, that we will effectually (land by and support Your Majesty, in such further Measures as may be found necessary to maintain the Civil Magistrates in a due Execution of the Lawswithin Your Majesty’s Province of Massachufel's Bay: and as we conceive that nothing can be more immediately necessary, either for the Maintenance of Your Majesty’s Authority in the said Province, or for guarding Your Majesty’s Subjects therein, from being further deluded by the Arts of wicked and designing Men, than to proceed, in the most speedy and effectual Manner, for bringing to condign Punishment the chief Authors and Instigators of the late Disorders, we most humbly beseech Your Majesty, that You will be gra-18

cioully please-d to direct Your Majesty's Governor of Massachuset's Bay to take the most effectual Methods for procuring the fullest Information that can be obtained; touching all Treasons, or Misprisions of Treason committed within his Government, since the Thirtieth Day of December last, and to transmit the fame, together with the Names of the Persons who were most active in the Commission of such Offences, to One of Your Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, in order that Yorir Majesty may issue a special Commission* for inquiring of, hearing* and determining the said Offences within this Realm, pursuant to the Provisions of the Statute, of the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, ill case Your Majesty shall, upon receiving the said Information, fee sufficient Ground for such a Proceeding with the following Amendments; viz.

Between the Words " December " and " and " to leave out the Word last," and to insert instead thereof the Words " One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-< seven.H
