A Petition of Robert Buttery, and all other the Proprietors and Inhabitants of Houses, on the South Side the public High Street, in the Parish of St. Mary Matfelon, otherwise White Chapel, in the County of Middlesex, where the Hay Market there hath immemorially been held, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observing, That a Petition has been presented to the House, for paving the High Street there, and for laying a Duty upon Carriages loaded with Hay and Straw, which shall be brought, fold, or pitched, on Market Days, in any Part of the said Parish; and that the Hay brought to, and sold at, the said Market, hath immemorially been pitched on the Fronts or Front-Reads of the Petitioners respective Dwelling Houses; and they have severally, during all their respective Times, and their Predecessors have immemorially received, and are, as the Petitioners apprehend, in Right of their respective Houses, entitled to receive, for every Load of Hay pitched upon the Frontsteads of the Petitioners Houses, Four Pence for each Load, which is a very great Advantage to the Petitioners, and to which they apprehend themselves entitled, in Right of their laid Houses: And therefore praying, That the said Market may continue to be held on the Petitioners Frontsteads, or that the House would take care of the Petitioners Right to the said Toll, and make the Petitioners such Satisfaction for the same as to the House VOL. 32.

Sir Robert Ladbroke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Church-wardens, Overseers of the Poor, Vestry-men, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Bartholomew the Great, whose

Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and Is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the 28th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the better enlightening and cleansing the Open Places, Squares, Streets, Lanes, Alleys, Passages, and Courts, within the Parish of Saint Bartholomew the Great, London, and regulating the Nightly Watch and Readies within the said Parish, was read: — Aud,

Mr. John Thorn informed your Committee, That the Pavement is very bad, and dangerous for Carriages; and even for Foot Passengers in the Night: That the Parish abounds with Nuisances, such as Water Spouts, Signs, Polls, Sheds, and other Incroachments and Projections; and that frequent Obstructions happen in the narrow Streets, from Carts and Drays being left there an unreasonable Time.

With respect to the Defects in the Act of the 28th Year of his late Majesty, the Witness said. That by the said Act they have no Power to enforce the Payment of the Rates from Persons who remove out of the said Parish; by which Means the Payment of the Rates is frequently evaded.

That there is no Power in the said Act to prevent throwing the Grounds and Walhings of Beer Barrels, into the Streets, which is a very great Nuisance: And that the Number of Constables appointed by the said. Act are too few, each Constable being obliged to fit up every Third Night.

Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Thomas Wit ham, who said. The said Act is defective in several other Particulars.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend, and render more effectual, an Act of the 28th of his late Majesty, for the better enlightening and cleansing the Open Places, Squares, Streets, Lanes, Alleys, Passages, and Courts, within the Parish of Bartholomew the Great, London', and regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said Parish; and for empowering the Trustees, in the said Act named* to pave the said Streets, and Other Places within the said Parish, and to remove Annoyances and Obstructions: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. Alderman Harley, Mi. Alderman Trecothick, Mr. Alderman Crefby, and Mr. Alderman Beckford, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Sir John HuJJey Delaval presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for dividing and inclosing a Moor or Common, called Trougheitd Common, in the Parish of Elfdon, in the County of And

the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Sir Charles Whitworth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Charles Dingley, of Merchant, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vit.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed your Committee, That he bad known Mr. Dingley Thirty-eight Years; that he has carried on Trade with him as a Merchant; and that the said Mr. Dingley has, for several Years past, dealt very considerably in the Importation of Timber from different Parts of the World: And,

Mr. "James Stansfield, being examined, said, That he

was concerned in erecting Mr. s Saw Mill;

that it is built upon the Construction of those he has seen in Holland, but is much more useful; and that it

wiiT cut all Sorts of Timber, and for all Uses; and that it is situated upon Mr. Dingley'% Ellate at near to the River of Thames: Then,

Mr. Dingley produced to your Committee an Account of the Expence of first erecting the said Mill, amounting to the Sum of £.4,454. 2. 2.; and,

Mr. Christopher Richardson said, That in the Year 1765, Mr. Dingley imported into England a Quantity of Timber, which amounted to £. 38,700; and that Orders pretty near to that Amount have been continued ever since: That before Mr. Dingley erected the Saw Mill, Deals and Wainscot manufactured from Timber, were imported ready cut, which now are imported in Logs, and cut by the Mill; and that upon the known Usefulness of the said Mill, Mr. 'Dingley has given Orders for large Quantities of Timber to a considerable Amount; and that great Quantities of Deals have been supplied for His Majesty’s Use, manufactured by the said Mill, and greatly approved of.

Mr. John Barrow said, That he knows Mr. s

Saw Mill; that he has seen many of the Dutch Mills, but that this exceeds any he ever saw. — That it cuts better and finer; and that it works Thirty-six Saws at one Time.

Mr. Yeomans and Mr. Payne confirmed the above Evidence, with respect to the Utility of the said Mill; and Mr. Yeomans being asked. Whether he thought this Mill

would be an Advantage ? He said. All things of that Kind was for the public Good; but it does not employ so many Men.

18

And in order to shew the general Approbation the erecting the said Mill had received, Mr. Dingley produced to your Committee a Gold Medal, which was presented to him by the Society of Arts, as a Testimony of their Opinion of the Utility of the lame: And,

Mr. Richardson, being again examined, said. That he

was upon the Spot when the Mill was pulled down by the Rioters; that it could not be worked for Six Months; and that the flopping thereof was a great Detriment to Mr. Dingley, and a public Loss.

Mr. Joseph OJbaldeJion and Mr. James Stansfield, being severally examined, laid. That they saw the Mill just after it was damaged, and that it was rendered en* tirely useless from May to Christmas last: Then,

Mr. Thomas Francis, being examined, said. That Prosecutions were carried on against Two of the Persons concerned in the above Riot; that the Opinion of the Judges was, they did not come within the Meaning of any Act of Parliament, but as for a Misdemeanor: And,

Mr. Stansfield informed your Committee, That he had been employed in repairing the said Mill, and that the same is now substantially rebuilt, and in actual Use; an Account of the Expence whereof being produced to your Committee by Mr. Richardson, amounts to the Sum of £. 1,231. 12. 4. exclusive of all other Damages and Loss of Time.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

THE Dq>uty Clerk of the Crown, attending ac-cAiding to; Order, amended the Return for the Borough of Bramber, in the county of .

Mr. Whichcot reported from the Committee,- to whom

the Petition of the several Merchants, Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of , in the County of Linco/n,vihok Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House;-and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards de-. livered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Hutton, being examined, said, That the Streets,

Lanes, and other public Passages in the said Town, are very ill paved and incommodious; that it would be a great Advantage to the Inhabitants and Persons resorting thereto, if the same were properly paved, cleansed, and lighted, and duly watched, and kept free from Annoyances: '

That great Quantities of Coals are brought into the said Town; that if the same were delivered by Statute Measure, or Weight only, the Witness apprehends it would be a Means of preventing Frauds which are pra&iled therein; and if a Duty was laid on such Coals, to defray the Expence of measuring, weighing, and collecting the fame, and the Surplus applied towards the paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the said Streets, Lanes, and Passages, it would be of great Advantage to the said Town. ,: ,

Which Evidence ,was confirmed by Doctor Henry Revel Reynolds, and Mr. Gideon Wells. , 5 Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more effectual paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets, Lanes, Alleys, and Public Passages, in the Town of Gainsborough, in the County of , and for

' laying a Duty on all Coals, brought to the said Town to be sold, and for applying the same to such Purposes: And that Mr. Whichcot, Sir Cecil , Lord Bertie, and Mr. Amcotts, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

of the Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues lately obtained in the East Indies, having expired on the First Day of February Instant, (he laid United Company, at several General Courts lately held, took into their Confederation the Terms and Conditions for entering into a further Agreement with the Public, respecting the aforesaid Acquisitions and Revenues; and the following Question, being proposed, was carried by a Ballot hela at the Company’s House in Leadenhall Street, on the 9th of this Instant February, viz. " That it is the Opinion of the General Court, that the Court of Directors be empowered to make an Agreement with the Public,

" on the Terms and Conditions mentioned in the Pro-f' positions now laid before the General Courtand that the said Proportions then laid before the General Court were as follows:

1. That £.400,000 a Year be continued to the' Public for Five Years, from the First of February Instant.

t. That the Company be at liberty to increase their Dividend to Twelve and an Half perCent. during the said Term, so as not to exceed One per Cent, in any One Year.

3. That if the Company shall, during the said Term, be obliged to reduce their Dividends, from any Cause whatsoever: in such Case, there shall be deducted, from the Sum agreed to be paid for the Use of the Public, a Sum equal to such Redu^ion; and in like Manner, if the Company’s Dividends shall, at any Time during the said Term, be again raised or restored, the Public shall receive equal Benefit; but, if the said Dividends shall be reduced to Six per Cent, then the Payment to the Public shall be discontinued.

4. That the Company shall be obliged to export, in every Year during the Continuance of this Agreement, Goods and Merchandizes, of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of Great Britain, Military and Naval Stores excepted, of the like Value as they shall appear to have been exported annually, on an Average of Five Years preced i ng t h is Agreement.

5. That if any Surplus of Cadi shall remain in England during the said Term, after the Discharge of the Company’s Simple Contract Debts bearing Interest, and the Reduction of the Company’s Bond Debt to the Debt which shall be due from the Public to the Company, then such Surplus shall be lent to the Public at Two -Cent, per Annum.

And that the Petitioners beg Leave to submit the said Propositions to the Consideration of the House, as the Terms and Conditions for making a further Agreement between the Public and the said Company, in respect of the Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues lately obtained in the East Indies.

A Petition of the Merchants trading to Greenland, Davis's Straits, and the Seas adjacent, the Tanners, Curriers, Shoemakers, and others, dealing jn Leather, in the Borough and Corporation of Liverpool, was presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Trade to Greenland, in the Whale Fishery, for a few Years past, has been unsuccessful, which has induced the Merchants trading to those Parts to fend their VefTds out earlier than usual in search of Seals, a Trade but lacely used by the English, to the Westward, and about John a Main's Island, which has been attended with tolerable Success, and afterwards proceed upon the Whale Fishery* to have a double Chance on the same Voyage; hut the Duty on Seal Skins, as they are now rated, is Thirty per Cent, upon the Value, and amounts to Five Pence or Six Ponce per Pound Weight on the Tanned Leather, instead of One Penny Halfpenny per Pound for other Leather, which is a great Discouragernent to the Tanning of Seal Skins, which, when tanned, are as useful as any other Leather, in making Shoes or Boots, and would be the Means of reducing the Pi ice of Tanned Leather, which is, in the Space of Ten Years, advanced nearly One Half in Value, to the great Damage of the Poor in particular, and therefore praying. That the Duty of Excise on Seal Skips may be reduced, or such other Relief granted as to the House shall seem mofl meet.

The House proceeded to the Hearing of the Matter of the several Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of New Radnor.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the said Petitions were read.

And the Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, was read.

And the last Determination of the House, made upon the 12th Day of November 1690, concerning the Right of electing a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of New Radnor, (whereby it is resolved, That the Right of Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of New Radnor, is in the Burgesses oL Radnor, Ryader, Knighton, Knuckles and

Jice only) was also read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner were heard.

Then, Mr. Robert Pardo being called in, and having, at the Bar, delivered in the original Poll, taken at the last Election of a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough; he was examined by the Counsel for the Petitioner, as to the Time when, and as to the Manner in which, the said Poll, and also other Books and Papers belonging to the said Borough, came into his Custody.

And he also delivered in at the Bar Two Corporation Court Books of the said Borough; and also several Polls, taken at former Elections of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and was further examined.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner examined several Witnesses, in order to shew that the said Polls, and other Books and Papers, were sent, by Mr. John James, Town Clerk of the said Borough, to the said Mr. Pardo.

Then the said Counsel examined a Witness, in order to prove that the Copy of the Poll taken at the last Election, which was signed by the Returning Officer as a true Copy, and delivered by the said Town Clerk to the Agents for the Petitioner, by Order of the said Returning Officer, varied from the Original.

And the said Witness was further examined by the Counsel for the Petitioner, in order to prove the Handwriting of the said John James-, and to thew in what Jn-stances the said Copy of the Poll varied from the Original; and likewise to prove that One of the said Corporation Books had in several Instances been altered, and several Additions made thereto, by the said John James.

Then the said Counsel examined a Witness, in order to shew, that several Leaves had been taken out of, and many other Alterations made to, the said Book.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Exeter, &c. A Petition of the Trustees for the Sub-division of Roads. the Turnpike Roads leading from in Devon,

to the City of Exeter, was presented. to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners find a Petition is presented for a Bill to make a new Road, leading from Crediton, to the Outskirts of the said City, from St. David's Hill, through Howell's and Part of Pound Lane and Longb Street, to the Oxford Inn, Outside the East Gate of the said City, which Petition is founded on an Order made by a very few Trustees, without any previous Notice given of the said Meeting, and is made directly contrary to an Order, made by a vast Majority, at a Meeting held for that Purpose, on the 8th Day of AjtguJl last; and that these Petitioners, in pursuance of their Power, have borrowed £.5,400; and that the Expences of that Road, for Seven Years last pall, have exceeded the Income; and that much Interest is due, and several Bills unpaid; and that a large Sum is Wanting to put the Roads in a proper Repair; and that, if the new Road should be made as praposed, no Part of it being a Public Road, the Expence will be so great, that a moderate Toll raised thereon will not be sufficient to pay the Expence of purchasing Lands necessary to make and keep such a Road in Repair; and therefore the Creditors will be much injured, and the Travelling and Resort to the said City, from and to the Eastern and Western Parts of that Country will be much lessened, to its great Detriment and Loss; and that they find a Petition is also presented against the said Petition, praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against it: And therefore praying, That these Petitioners may also be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Petition; and rnay have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem most just and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the acting Trustees, appointed by an Act of Parliament, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of his late Majesty King George the Sedond, intituled, An Act for amending several Roads leading from the City of Exeter; and also of the several Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Occupiers of Land, residing near and travelling on the Roads therein mentioned,-in the County of Devon, and County and City of Exeter; is referred; and that these Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Coventry Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending before the House, for making a Navigable Canal, from the Coventry Canal Navigation, at or near the City of,

to the City of Oxford; and that the Petitioners observe, that several Petitions have lately been presented to the House, praying. That the Course of the said Canal may be carried in a different Direction than is proposed by the Bill; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners have, at a very great Expence, proceeded to make the Navigation from Fradley Heath, to the City of Coventry, and that so much thereof as lies between Bedworth and Coventry, is now nearly completed; and that the Petitioners conceive it will be of great public Advantage if the Point of Junction of the proposed Canal with the Coventry Canal Navigation be made as near the said City as may be, without losing the Level, or occasioning any additional Lockage* which may be done at Longford, within Three Miles of the said City, and" from thence to be carried through or near the several Parishes of Anjly and Shilton, and the North East Part of the Lord ship or Liberty of Coombe, to Brinklow, and from thence to the City of Oxford, in the Course proposed by the Bill: And therefore praying. That Provision may be made in the said Bill, for making the Junction of the Two Canals at Longford aforesaid, instead of Gosford Green, and that the said proposed Canal may be tarried from such Point of Junction, through or near Anjly, Shilton, and the North East Part of Coombe aforesaid, to Brinklow.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereofj and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Richard Glyn, Sir Roger Newdigate,&c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Jockey, in the Parish of Box, in the said County; and also of the Mortgagees of the Tolls arising from the several Turnpike Gates erected by virtue of the said Act, and of the Inhabitants of the Town of,

and the adjacent Parishes, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of a Petition from the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough of We ft bury, in the county of ; of the Inhabitants of Semington, in the said County; and of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the same County; and setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, that they have not only an undoubted Right to erect a Gate ou the Road leading from Melhsham to Semington by virtue of the first-mentioned Act, but that it is neceflfaiy towards the Support of the Roads comprised therein; and though it is alledged, that the Wtfibury Trustees have laid out £. 600 on the Road between Yarnbrook and Melhsham, yet the several Parishes, through which

that Road lies have been at the chief Expence, and that little or no Assistance hath been received from the said West bury Trustees; and representing to the House, that it'would be injurious to the Town of Melhsham, and the several neighbouring Parishes if the Trustees for putting in Execution the West bury Act, should be impowered to erect any other Gate for Collection of Tolls, than what tl^ey are already impowered to set up by their present Act, between Melhsham and; and

that, though the Tolls collected at the Gate leading to Semington may have amounted Annually to £. 50 and which, with the Collections at the other Gates, may have amounted to near £. 700 Annually, yet the Revenue of such Tolls has never been more than sufficienc to support the said Road; and that of late there ba!s been such a Decrease of Tolls that almost Two Years Interest for the Money borrowed on the Credit of the said Tolls still remains in Arrear; and that, in the said Act of the Thirty-first Year of his late Majesty, there is a Clause exempting Persons travelling between West-bur y and Melhsham from Payment of more than One Toll, as soon as the Sum of £. 500 should be laid out bn such Part of the Roads thereby intended to be re-

Saired as leads from Yarnbrook, up West Ashton Bill, to ielkfkam; and that the said Sum of £. 500 has been accordingly laid out on that Road; and praying, that they may not be deprived of the Benefit of the said Exemption, to which they are so entitled by the said Clause; and further setting forth, that, by a Clause in the last mentioned Act, the Trustees are restrained from erecting any Gate, in or upon any Part of the Road in the First District that lies between the present Turnpike Road at Melhsham, and the Turnpike Road leading from Steeple Ashton to Trowbridge, by the Repeal of which Clause, the Petitioners are of Opinion, the Country would be great Sufferers: And therefore praying.

That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill now depending as materially affect the Petitioners, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

at Melksham, in the County of Wilts; and for repairing

not only the Roads mentioned in the said Act, but also the Roads leading from Latchetts Bridge, to the Turnpike Road at Connock, and from the End of Market Lavington Road, near Dewey's Water, to the Turnpike Road, at or near the Ninety-third Mile Ston^? in the Road leading to Melksham, and from the Turnpike Road, at the End of Market Lavington Field, over the Downs, to the Turnpike Road, at or near the Ten Mile Stone, in the Road leading from Redhone Hill to Fisherton , and the Road from the said Turnpike Road at the Top of Market Lavington Hill, to the Top of the Hill on Easterton Down, leading to Net her haven; and the Petitioners doubt not but to pro\e that the Roads mentioned in the said Bill to be repaired, are in all at lead:

Forty Miles in Length, and most of them unfrequented Roads; that many of the said Roads lead over the large, open, extensive, and Champion Dcommonly called Salisbury Plain, which may at all Times of the Year be travelled on with the greatest Ease; and that the Roads over the said Downs never have been repaired, to the Knowledge of the Petitioners, except by the ordinary Methods appointed by Law; nor will they ever have Occasion to be repaired by any other Method; and that the said Road from Market Lavington to Dewey's Water is in so founderousa Condition, that it is dangerous for any Person on Horseback to ride through the fame; and that the Road from Dewey s Water to the Ninety-third Mile Stone in Seend, through Warton and Bulkington, hath a good Horie Causeway, but is so founderous and miry that there is no passing in the Winter Time for Carriages of any Kind, and cannot be repaired for less than £. 1 coo Mile; and that, if the said Roads should be made through the said several Villages for Carriages of all Sorts to pass thereon, the Petitioners shall be always subject to Indictments for not repairing the fame, as they are convinced that the same cannot be repaired either by the Labour appointed by Law', the Pound Rate to be raised on them, and the Tolls which shall be appointed to be received in case the same Bill shall pass into a Law: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill, or such Parts thereof as may affeCl and prove injurious to the Petitioners, or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Henry Lord Viscount Conyngham, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Year 1749, the Trustees appointed by Act of Parliament, for building a Pier for the Protection of the Harbour of Ramsgate, in the County of Kent, pof-. sessed themselves of a certain Tract of Land, Part and Parcel of his Estate and Manor of Minftre Court, in the Me of Thanet, and County of Kent, and occupied the fame, digging Chalk thereout for building the said Pier, without having first made an Agreement with him for the said Land, or receiving his Permission so to take Possession and make use thereof; and that the Petitioner, being willing to promote the said Undertaking, did, in the Year 1754, consent and agree to fell to them the said Land, which had been so occupied and made use of by them; but, upon inquiring into his Power to sell and convey the fame, it appeared that he was only a Tenant for Life of the said Estate, the same being settled on the I flue of his Marriage, and therefore could not make a sufficient Title for the Sale and Conveyance

Vol. 32.

of the Fee and Inheritance thereof, no Provision having been made in the Act, which gave the said Trustees Power to purchase Lands for the Purpose of building and maintaining the said Pier, to enable such Tenants for Life under Marriage Settlement to sell and convey the Lands so settled, and to confirm and ratify such Sales and Conveyances so made by them of such Lands; in Consequence of which Omission in the said Act to remedy such his Inability to make the necessary Title and Conveyance of the said Lands, the Petitioner has, ever since that Time, been barred from receiving the Price and Value agreed by the said Trustees to be paid to him for the said Lands, though they have continued in the undisturbed Possession and Use thereof; And therefore praying, That the House will take the Hardships under which he labours into Consideration, and grant him such Relief in the Bill now depending in the House, to explain and amend an Act, made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for enlarging and maintaining the Harbour of Ramsgate, and for cleansing, amending, and preserving the Haven of Sandwich, as the Nature of the same requires.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Acts for the Encouragement of the Coinage of Monies.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Charles Whitworth took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Charles Whitworth reported from the Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Resolved^That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The other Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Petition of the Court of Directors for the Affairs of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies

Ordered, That the several Papers which were presented to the House, upon the 14th Day of this Instant February, by Mr. Michell, Secretary to the said Company, be re-

ferred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the East India Company’s Affairs, made up the 30th June, which was presented to the House upon the 21st Day of December, 1767, be referred to the said Committee.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee; it passed in the Negative.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Chipping A Petition of the Bailiffs and Burgesses of Chipping Norton Norton, in the County of Oxford, and of divers other ncoure. persons> whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Reign of King Richard the First, the Lord of the Manor of Chipping Norton granted to the Ville of Chipping Norton aforesaid certain Pasture Grounds, called by the several Names of The Great Common below the Town, Over Norton, Feme Hill, The Heath, and South Come; and that the Owners and Occupiers of Lands and Tenements there have Time immemorial enjoyed the said Ground called The Verne Hill, as their separate Common; and that The Great Common and South Come have been ever since executively enjoyed in Common, by the Owners or Occupiers of the Messuages and Lands in the Town, Hamlet, or Division, of Chipping Norton-, and that such Owners and Occupiers have also Right of Common in The Heath, the Open Fields, and all other the Commonable Lands, in the said Division; and that the Petitioners observe, a Bill is depending before the House, for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, and Commonable Lands, in the Parishes of Chipping Norton and Salford, in the said County of Oxford, which, the Petitioners are informed, is intended to include all the Premises granted as aforesaid; and that

Vol. 32.

some of the said Grounds furnish the Poor of the said Town, which are very numerous, with Fuel, a very scarce Commodity, which will bean extreme Hardship upon the Parties mterested therein; and that the Petitioners likewise apprehend. That some other Parts of the said Bill, as it now stands, may prejudice them and others: And therefore praying. That so much of the said'

Bill as tends to the inclosure of the said Grounds, called The Great Common, The Heath, and South , may not pals into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be beard, by their Counsel, against the fame, and such other Parts of the said Bill as may affect them; and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing, and inclosing certain Open and Common Fields, and Commonable Lands, in the Parishes of Chipping Norton, and Salford, in the County of Oxford, is committed; and that the Petitioners be "heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their said Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be hea d, -at the same Time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

M

9 Geo. III. 28° FebruariL 255

An ES TIM AT E of the Expence of Maintaining the Children received into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Children, on or before the 25th Day of March 1760, from the 31st Day of December 1768 exclusive, to the 31st Day of December 1769, inclusive.

The Number of the said Children living under the Care of the Governors and Guardians of the said Hospital on the 31st Day of December 1 768, is Two thousand Four hundred and Sixteen.

The Expence of Maintaining whom, at Seven Pounds Ten Shillings each, amounts to Eighteen thousand One hundred and Twenty Pounds.

N. B. Besides the above 2,416 Children, therehave been taken into this Hospital fmcethe 25th of March 176b, 279 Children; mod: of whom were under the most distressed Circumstances, or Orphans of Soldiers and Sailors, whole Parents died in His Majesty’s Service; whereof 25 have been apprenticed, 7 claimed, and 80 dead: So that there are 167 Children, now alive, which are wholly maintained and provided for, out of the Income arising from private Donations; and are not, nor ever have been, charged in the Estimate of the Public Account. Accounts of which have been Annually delivered in to Parliament.

Signed by Order,

Tho' Collingweod, Secretary.

The Counsel for the Petitioner then objected to 99 Persons, who voted for the Sitting Member, as Burgesses of the Contributary Borough of Knuclafs, as not appearing to have been entered in any public Books, or Court Rolls, belonging to the said Borough, now in being.

there were no such Entries existing; the said Books and Court Rolls having been destroyed by Fire.

The Counsel for the Petitioner then examined several \Vitnesses, in order to disqualify 14 Persons, who voted for the Sitting Member, as Burgesses of the Borough of New Radnor;Three, as having polled Twice; One who appeared upon the Poll to have voted as a Person redding within the said Borough, there being no such Person within the Borough; Six, as not being entered in the Corporation Books; One, as never having redded within the Borough; One, as ne^er having been sworn a Burgess; One, as being a Minor at the Time he was sworn a Burgess; and One, as not redding in the Borough when he was made a Burgess.

The said Counsel then objected to 46 Persons, who voted for the Silting Member, as Burgesses of the said Borough of New Radnoron account of the Entries of their Names in the Corporation Books not being stamped; which was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

The Counsel for the Petitioner then examined several Witnesses, in order to prove Partiality in the Returning Officer, in Favour of the Sitting Member.

And the Journal of the House, of the 17th Day of March 1725, with relation to the Election of Burgesses for the Borough of Cheping IVicomb, in the County of Bucks, was read; whereby it appeared, that Persons admitted to poll, under a Charter which had not been accepted or inrolled, were declared by the House, to have no Right of voting.

The Counsel for the Petitioner then objected generally to all the Votes of the Sitting Member, on account of their Admissions as Burgesses not having been stamped.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner having closed their Evidence;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

African A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Company. Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House.

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, that the Petitioners have laid before the House, an Account of the Sums granted for 1767, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act passed in the Year 1750, for extending and improving the Trade to; and

that they have expended the Monies granted in 1768, for the Support of the Forts on the said Coast, in Goods, Stores, and Necessaries; and that the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast, having been delivered to the Petitioners in a very bad State by the Royal African Company, and the Sums annually granted by Parliament being almost wholly expended in the Maintenance and Pay of the several Garrisons, with other necessary Charges, leaving very little for the Repairs of the said Forts, many of them are in Length fallen into Decay and Ruin; and that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa, therefore pray the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, and likewise for the extraordinary Repairs now wanted, as to them shall seem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, George Furfdon, Esquire, being examined, said, That the present Laws for Relief of the Poor have been found ineffectual though very burthensome to the Owners and Occupiers of Lands in that County: And,

Mr. Robert Pullen informed your Committee, That several Societies have been established within the said County, whereby several poor Persons have engaged themselves to Pay Six Pence per Month while they are in Health and able to work; in Consideration whereof, they receive when sick or disabled, the following Allowances, that is to say. Six Shillings a Week while confined to their Beds by Sickness or Accidents; Three Shillings a Week when able to walk abroad till they can go to Work j and when they are unable to labour on Account of Age, Half a Crown a Week during the Remainder of their Lives.

That the several Funds have been found more than sufficient to answer these Purposes, and considerable Sums have accumulated which now remain in Hand.

But that the Subscribers have frequently applied such surplus Sums in an improper Manner, to support themselves in Idleness, when they have entered into Combinations for raising Wages, and have been guilty of several other Irregularities in the Disposition thereof.

That if an Act of Parliament were obtained for putting such voluntary Subscriptions under proper Regulations, it would tend to the better Provision for the Poor, and be of public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more effectual Relief of the Poor, in the County of Devon: And that Mr. Parker and Sir John worth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Bacon, according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Morpeth, in the County of Northumberland', together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; and be read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Upon the Petition of Francis Eyre, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Mathew White Ridley, for the Borough of Morpeth, in the County of Northumberland.

The Committee have examined the Merits of tips Election.

The Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for retraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination of the House of Commons, was read.

And the last Determination of the House, upon the 9th Day of March 1695, concerning the Right of Electing a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Morpeth, whereby it is resolved. That the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Morpeth, in the County, of Northumberland, is only in the Bailiffs and free Burgesses of the said Borough, was also read.

There was no Dispute concerning the Election of Mr. Beckford.

The Poll was:

For Sir Math. White Ridley - - 29

For the Petitioner - - - 24

And it appearing upon the Face of the Poll, that Twelve other People were polled for the Petitioner with Queries, but were afterwards struck out by Order of the Bailiffs who are the Returning Officers;

The Counsel for the Petitioner then examined Mr. William Tate, One of the Bailiffs, who laid the said

*7

Persons were eroded out just after the Poll was taken. — They retired into the Grand Jury Room immediately after the Poll, and they were there struck out} Mr. Cleaver went into the Grand Jury Room with them, but don’t know that he said any thing to Fenwick, the other Bailiff.

And being asked what the Reason was for refuting those Votes ? — he said. That the Candidates agreed that the Mandamus Men were to be set dowp and queried: — That an Argument was held before the First of them was polled, and after the Twelve were set down with Queries: — Being asked if the Argument was resumed after the Twelve were set down with a Query ? he said. No, but there was aConteft about their Titles; — and then repeated, that after the Twelve polled, there was no Argument: — That the Witness and the other Bailiff thought they were not legal Votes, and advised with Counsel upon it.

And being asked if the Names were struck out in the Grand Jury Room, where they had retired immediately after the Poll, or in open Court in the Presence of all Parties? — He said, To the best of his Remembrance, in the Grand Jury Room; that the other Bailiff struck them out — and Nobody made any Objection, when he said they were not good.

Being asked if the Returning Officers, before they went into the Room, declared that those Votes were to be struck off — he said, No, — Or if Cleaver said any thing when he came into the Room — he said nothing to him, if he said any thing, it was to Fenwick; but at last admitted, that he believed Cleaver did whisper to Fenwick: — -That the Sitting Member had Counsel, and the Petitioner none.

The Counsel then proceeded to shew the Partiality of the Returning Officer, and what passed at the Poll; and for that Purpose called,

Robert Swan — who being asked by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, if he had subscribed to the Expence of that Petition, an Objection was taken, but he said, That the Aldermen had given so much out of their Boxes to fend Witnesses up to London — there was some of his Money to be sure: And the Witness and Counsel being ordered to withdraw;

The Committee were of Opinion — That Robert Swan having declared, that he had contributed to carry on the Expence of the Petition, could not be admitted an Evidence to prove the Allegations thereof.

The said Counsel then proceeded to establish the Franchises of the Twelve People so objected to on the Poll; and having produced the Corporation Books, the Counsel for the Sitting Member admitted that the Twelve Persons queried were elected Freemen of their Companies, and tendered themselves to be admitted at a Court Leet, at Michaelmas 1767.

The Counsel for the Petitioner examined Edward Newton: — And being asked whether the Twelve were admitted Burgesses in 1767 — he said, They were elected about Two Years before; that they tendered themselves at a former Court Leet, previous to their applying for their Mandamus’s. That was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member; and that the Steward of the Court, refused to admit them both Times.

And the Witness being asked if any of the Twelve are Freemen of Morpeth ? — he said, He believed so — that he knew them all: — And being asked, if John Hall (One of the Twelve) was an Alderman, he said. Yes, of One of the Companies; — and that it is needflary a Man should be a Freeman before he is an Alderman: — That the Twelve had exercised their Offices ever since last Year — They were elected by their Companies — in the Companies where some are Free Men, and some Free Brothers: — That the Majority of each Company elect the Aldermen: — There are more Free Brothers than Free Men: — And being asked if he knew the Tanners Company ? — he said. He believed there are

more

o Geo. III. 3 0 Mart o

more Free Men in that Company: — That Burgesses are Free Brothers before they can be elected of their Companies: ‘

That in the Borough are Seven Guilds, Two Bailiffs, and Seven Aldermen; but he did not know how many Burgesses. — Both Free- Men and Free Brothers are elected by the Majority of the Company they belong to — some Companies elect more than others: — Twenty-four are elected in all by the several Companies, and presented by their Aldermen to the Court Leet, to be sworn: — -These Twelve were refused at the Court, and afterwards brought Mandamus’s in the Court of King’s Bench; that he alw'ays thought the Steward is obliged to swear them; — that several were made Burgesses afterwards, and not objected to; — that Morpeth is a Borough by P refcriprion; and it has always been customary to present to the Court Leet to be sworn And being asked if any of the Inhabitants of Morpeth are intitled to their Freedom by Birth ? — he laid,'They always go to EledionsAnd being asked whether any were intitled by Servitude: — he laid, All by their Companies:

— That either Birth or Servitude gives a Right to be a Free Brother; — he knew some of the Twelve were intitled by Birth, and others by Servitude: — That at the Time the Twelve were refused by the Steward, Thirty-three offered in all, some of which had been elected Twenty Years.

Then William Jones, One of the Clerks of the Crown Office, produced Thirty-three Mandamus’s: — And the Counsel for the Petitioner laid. They were issued to swear in- Thirty-three Freemen of Mof whom the Twelve

are a Part: — That the Steward of the Court, to whom they were directed, made a Return, that they were noc duly elected; and that they could not be sworn in without the Approbation of the Lord: — Whereupon Issue was joined, and a Consent Rule, that the Trial of One should bind all the rest. — A Verdict was found, that they were duly elected, and that there was no such Custom in the Borough; in consequence whereof, in Michaelmas Term 1767 — Judgment and peremptory Mandamus’s issued, which were served: — A new Trial was moved for, which the Court refused to grant, being satisfied with the Verdict The peremptory Mandamus’s issued the 9th Novemb, returnable the 28th, and Were served the 24th.

Then Christopher Fawcett, Esquire, Stewart} to Lord

Carlisle, as Lord of the Court Leet of Morpeth, was called, and produced the Thirty-thfee peremptory Writs of Mandamus, which he said were served on him at Newcastle the 24th of November 1767: — One of them was read; and he said, The Returns were all alike; — That they were all sworn at Newcastle.

The Witness being asked if these People had applied to him at the Court Leet to be admitted in pursuance of their Election ? — he said, Upon the 4th of 1766, a Paper was delivered to him signed by the Names mentioned in the Mandamus’s, to inform him,

' that they would present themselves at the next Court: — He believed they did appear — and he refused them; — they all presented themselves again the 6th of October 1767: Being asked if they were satisfied there was a Verdict ? — he said. Yes, That he was in his Diningroom at Newcastle when he was served with the peremptory Mandamus: — It was the 24th of November very late at Night, and they were returnable the 28th.

And being asked if he was desired to go to Morpeth to admit them ? — He said. Yes; and to the best of his Recollection, he said, He would certainly go, if the Writs required him: — Being asked if he did not understand that the Writ required him to swear them in a legal Manner ? — he said, That he did not consent to go to Morpeth, nor insist that they -should go to Newcastle — nor did he say he would swear them there — they were sworn at Newcastle — he was desirous of leaving nothing undone on his Part.: — That the Witness’s Business is to hold Courts on prescriptive Days; — and said,

Vol. 32.

If they would come and tender themselves, he would do all he could and he understood he could hold no Court but on a prescriptive Day; and that he told them, if they would come and tender themselves, he-would do all he could: — He sent a Messenger t;o the Clerk of the Court for the Form of the Oath, and Admittances, which tho Clerk sent the Witness the next ’ Day, and desired that he would secure his Fees, as he Was not able to come himself: — Whereupon he told the Persons they mud pay the Fees to the Clerk; — there was nothing due to the Witness: — There was some Debate, and then they saidit was not usual to pay Fees.

And being asked if he thought an Action would hot lie for the Fees - he said, he supposed the Clerk would bring Actions the next County Court against every one of them; and that he meant they should not withhold the usual Fees due to the Clerk of the Court.

Being asked if he gave them Joy of their Admission ?

— he said. He believed in the usual Way — he thought it not a good Admission — paid them the usual Compliment — gave him a Receipt for the Fees-and the Receipt was produced, which he owned to be his Handwriting.

And being asked if he at any other Time said these People were legally admitted ? — he said he. could not recoiled — he believed he could not say so — his Opinion was otherwise.

Being asked Whether at the Time the Thirty-three were admitted, there were not others admitted also ? — he said. There were.

And being asked if he knew that any were admitted but at Court Leets ? — he said. No — nor did he believe there ever were any — he always understood it should be at a Court Leet — has known some admitted at an adjourned Court Leet — has heard there is an instance, where the Stile of the Court appears a Court Baron; — but that must have been a Mistake — he never examined it.

Being asked if he knew in any modern Times of PeN fons being admitted but at a Court Leet ? — he said. No — he remembered to have had an Order from Lord Carlisle'% Guardian for Two Persons, who had received peremptory Mandamus’s: — The Witness could not attend at that Court; but it being allowed they had an undoubted Right to be admitted, he thought there was no Occasion to let them wait for Half a Year, therefore sent a Deputy to swear them in at an adjourned Court LeetThat he was not j;equested to keep the Court open to swear in the Thirty-three: — Being asked if he at any other Time swore in any at Newcastle at an adjourned Court;

He said, Upon the 25th of November 1767, the Day the Thirty-three were sworn, he had a special Order from the Lord of the Manor to swear in Richard John Morton, a Smith, John Spencer, and Taylor; they had not Mandamus’s — 26th Novembe 1767, swore

in Robert Shotten, a Weaver, Oliver another, Edward Reaunt, a Fuller and Dyer. — 7th December, swore in Ralph Steel, a Merchant Taylor, and another Person: thinks there were Nine in all. — They had all been presented the same as Mandamus Men, but did not bring the Writs; those were all he ever swore at Newcastle, except George Fenwick, the 16th of 1768: — It

was no voluntary Act of the Witness — he had the Orders of the Lord of the Manor; — he said. The Election was after this, on the 21st of March: Being asked if he thought the Orders of the Lord of the Manor more binding than those of the King’s Bench j he said. He did not: Being asked why he did it, as being illegal; he said. As an Officer of the Court, where no Injury could be done, he thought it his Duty to obey the Lord’s Order, and did not know any thing of the Illegality of it, and did not say he Was bound to obey the Order of the Lord to do an illegal Thing.

That the Petitioners are of Opinion, that every Inland Navigation which is likely to interfere with the Coal or Coasting Trade of these Kingdoms must be very prejudicial to the Nursery and Increase of Seamen; and that, if the said Bill should be carried into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend the same will affect the Northern Navigation, and thereby reduce the Number of those useful Subjects the Seamen; And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Considerstioa, and grant them such Relief therein as the Importance of the same shall require.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of several of the Nobility, and the humble Westminster Petition of several Gentlemen,' Vestrymen, and other Paving. Gentlemen and Tradesmen, Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, in the County of sex, and Liberty of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, for raising a Fund for completing the several Purposes of the Acts passed, for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, in the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, and for other Purposes; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, jf the said Bill should pass into a Law, they would be greatly aggrieved thereby, and a heavier Burthen would be thrown upon the said Parish than upon any other within the said City and Liberty; and that the Petitioners are desirous of being excepted out of the said Bill, in order to apply to Parliament in the next Session for a separate Bill, for paving, cleansing, and lighting the said Parish, in the same Manner as Bond Street is now paved, cleansed, and lighted: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Accounts do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Mr. Thompson reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Open Arable Fields, Meadow, and Pasture Grounds, in the Township of Lelley, in the Parish of in in the East

Riding of the County of York, was committed, That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true j and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee hod gone through the Bill $ and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One: and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be

ingrafted.

An ingrafted Bill for dividing and inclosing that Part or Share of Belper Ward, Which belongeth Xo Highedge, in the County of Derby, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, an Act for dividing and inclosing that Part or Share of Belper Ward, which belongeth to Highedge, in the County of Derby.

Offered, That Lord George do carry the Bill

A Petition of Barnet Falck, his Danish Majesty’s Consul residing in Great Britain, on Behalf of many of the Danish Merchants trading to this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in order to protect and assist all Ships and other Vessels passing through or lying at Anchor in The Downs, an Act was made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for enlarging and maintaining the Harbour of Ramsgate, and for cleansing, amending, and preserving the Haven of Sandwich; by which Act certain Rates and Duties, therein particularly mentioned, are laid upon every Ship or Vessel, as well British as Foreign, above a certain Burthen, from, to, or by Ramsgate, or coming into the Habour there, to be applied for the Purposes of making and maintaining the said Harbour, and the Purposes of the said Act; and that no Ship or Vessel whatsoever, belonging to any of the

Subjects of his Danish Majesty, which are only navigated to or from any Part of his said Danish Majesty’s Dominions, to and from any Port or Place South of The South Foreland, can poflibiy receive any Benefit or Advantage from the said Harbour; and, as the said Act now stands, no such Ship or Vessel so navigated is subject or liable to pay any of the Rates or Duties directed to be paid and collected by virtue of the said Act; and that a Bill is depending in the House, which, if it should pass into a Law as it now stands, the Petitioner conceives, will subject all Danish Vessels and Ships, trading to or from any Port or Place South of The South , to the said Rates

or Duties: And therefore praying the House, That he may be heard, by Counsel, against certain Parts of the said Bill; and that the fame, as it now stands, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Con-lideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to explain and amend an Act, made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of King George the Second, for enlarging and maintaining the Harbour of Ramsgate; and for cleansing, amending, and preserving, the Haven of Sandwich: is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his said Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill against the said Petition.

Trades, residing within the Bills of Mortality, and other Places within this Kingdom, was presented to the Hiufe, and read; Setting forth. That, by a Statute made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, Provision was made for preventing the wilful and negligent galhing, slaughtering, and cutting, the raw Hide of any Ox, Bull, Steer, or Cow, or the Skin of any Calf, in the flaying thereof,; and by several other Statues now in Force, the raw Hides of Oxen, Steers, and Cows, and the Skins of Calves, are to be brought to Public Markets to be sold; and that if such or the like Provisions and Regulations as are contained in the said Acts were extended to Sheep and Lamb Skins, it would be of great Advantage to the several Trades and Manufactures, of the Petitioners, and be of considerable public Utility, by the increase of Leather, and the Reduction of the present high Price of that Commodity:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

forth, That the Petitioners having observed, by the Votes Canal, of the House, That a Petition hath been presented, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a navigable Canal, between the Towns of Leeds and Liverpool, whereby a safe, easy, and expeditious Communication will be opened between the Ports of Liverpool and Hull, and that the Petitioners conceive, that such a navigable Canal will be highly beneficial to a great Parc of the County of York, and will also much conduce to the Public Good, by affording a new Nursery for Seamen, and a new Inducement for the Growth and Preservation of Timber, besides the many other Advantages mentioned in the said former Petition: And therefore praying. That a Bill may be brought in, for making and maintaining such navigable Canal, as hath been so applied for, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations^ of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Adder ley, being examined, said, That the Vicarage of Kingston comprehends the Chapelries or Curacies of Petersham, Richmond, Kew, East Moulsey and Thames

Dillon.

And in order to prove the ancient Dependence of the said Chapelries or Curacies, upon the Mother Church of Kingston aforesaid — several Extracts from the Register of the Bishop of Winchester, bearing Date respectively in the Years 1303, 1352, and 1377, were produced and read, by which it appeared, that the Vicarial Tythes, Obventions, and Dues, of the said Chapelries or Curacies, were heretofore received by the Vicar of; and

by an Extract from the Office of Remembrancer of First Fruits, and also by an Extract from the Cotton Library, bearing Date in the Year 1266, and ilfo by an Extract from the Archives of the Corporation of Kingston in the Time of Henry the 8th, it appeared that the several Curacies were considered as being within the Parish of Kingston, and contributing to the fame: And,

Mr. — Collins, Mr . — Mr.------------ Prime, the

Reverend Doctor John Thomas, and the Reverend Mr. George Harvest, being severally examined, said. That the said several Curacies have now distinct Parish Officers and Rates.

And the said Witnesses further laid. That the Vicarial Tythes or Sums of Money, in lieu thereof, are now received by the several Curates, though it appeared by the Extract from the Cotton Library aboverhentioned, that originally the said Vicarial Tythes were allowed by the Vicar to the Curates, in lieu or in Aid of their Stipend.

And Doctor Thomas said, that the Constitution of the Vicarage in these respects is irregular.

And Mr. Adderley, being examined, said. That the Vicar of Kingston has immemorially enjoyed the Right of Nomination to the said several Chapelries or Curacies.

And Doctor Thomas said, That the Right of the Curates to continue to hold their Curacies, notwithstanding the Avoidance of the said Vicarage, and independent of the Vicar, has been litigated, and never has yet been decided.

Then the Form of the Induction of the Vicar was produced, and read; and also One of the Extracts from the Register abovementioned being again read, it appeared, that the Vicar may by Law hold all the said Chapelries or Curacies.

And Doctor Thomas and Mr. Adderley said, That the Vicar has a Right to remove from one of the said Chapelries or Curacies to another as the Vacancies happen, and that such Removal has frequently been practised.

Doctor Thomas further said, That the best Method of preventing Litigation for the future, as well as pro-Vol. 32,

viding for the more decent and regular Service of the Churches in the Vicarage, would be a Division of the same into distinct and independent Vicarages or Curacies.

Then an Extract from a Presentment made by Commissioners under the Great Seal, and now in the Custody of the Archbishop of Canterbury, bearing Date in 1657, was produced, and read; by which it appeared that a Division of the said Vicarage was then recommended by the said Commissioners.

And the said several Witnesses laid. That the Distance of the said several Curacies and Mother Church aforesaid, from each other, is such as to admit of a threefold Division of the said Vicarage: And,

Mr.---- Collins, Mr.----- Bellamy, and the Reverend

Mr. Aggate, severally laid, That the Value of the Church of Kingston, and the Three several Chapelries of Petersham,

Richmond, and Kew, was such as would Supply an ample Maintenance for Two Vicarages.

But it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Ash, the Reverend Doctor Thomas, and the Reverend Mr. HarVeft, that from the particular Situation of the i'wo several Chapelries or Curacies of East Mouljey, and Thames Ditton, as well as upon account of certain D ^nations, which have been settled upon the respective Ministers of the fame, under certain Conditions and restrictions, the said Chapelries ought to be distinct from each other, and not being of sufficient Value to form distinct Vicarages, ought to be established as distinct and independent perpetual Curacies.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for dividing the Vicarage of Kingston upon Thames, in the County of Surrey, with the several Chapelries or Curacies thereto belonging, or thereon dependent, into Two lepa-rate Vicarages, and Two separate perpetual Curacies, in such Manner as is therein to be mentioned: And that Mr. Dyson, and Mr. Bacon do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Pennant reported from the Committee, to whom the African

Petition of the Committee of the Company of Merchants Company, trading to Africa, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof, to the House; and he read the Report ill his Place;

and

and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read} and is as followeth;

A State of the Fads contained in the said Petition, is &s followeth:

Joseph Champion, Esquire, One of the said Committee,

being examined, said, That the Money granted for fqpporting the several Forts on the Coast of in

the Year 1768 has been expended} but that the Account thereof is not yet made up.

It appeared to your Committee, by a Report entered in the Journal of this House, upon the Sixth Day of June 1758, that the Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa* were delivered to the Committee of the Company in a very bad State, by the Royal African Company.

And it appeared to your Committee, by an Account of Six Months Expences of the lfiid Committee, from the First Day of January 1767, to the 30th Day of June following, taken from the Books kept upon the Coast of Africa, and which were the last that the Committee have received, that the Annual Expence of Salaries to white and black Men, Presents to the Natives, and other incidental Charges for maintaining and supporting the said Forts, amounts to 11,538. in 3 d.

That the net Sum received from Government, by the said Committee, \s per Annum 12,657. 6s. 6

And that cpnfequently the Money remaining applicable tO'Repairs is no more than 1,118. 151. 3

Your Committee then proceeded to inquire into the present State of the several Forts; which from the Accounts referred to your Committee, appears to be as follows;

Dixcove, in good Repair. Seventeen of the Carriages belonging to the Guns entirely useless, and all the others much decayed; and Two Six-Pounders dismounted.

Succondee, in exceeding bad Condition, and (the Dwelling Part excepted) a Heap of Ruins. — Two Nine-Pounder Carriages, and Twelve Four-Pounder Carriages, are good; all the other Carriages much broken, and useless.

Commonda, in good Repair.

Cape Coafi Castle, in general in bad Condition, several Parts having lately fallen down, and others so old and crazy, and composed of such bad Materials, that they must soon, if not rebuilt, fall also.

Anamaboe, in very good Repair, except that it wants plaistering, and that the Roofs, Doors, and Window Shutters, of some of the Apartments, are beginning to decay.

T antumquery, in a very ruinous Condition, except the

Hall and Chief’s Room.

Winnebah, the Hall, Tower, and every Room in the Fort, wants Roofing, as do also some of the Rooms in the Spur. — The Bastions are all trunked, and in a very feeble Condition. — The Walls of the Fort are in tolerable Condition.

Accra, is in extreme bad Repair.

Your Committee then inquired into the Utility of the several Forts: And,

William Devaynes and John , Esquires, being

examined, said. That Dixcove Fort is a Place of the utmost Consequence, and absolutely necessary to be kept up, as it supplies the best Timber for repairing the Forts and Ships, and also Coral for Lime, in great Quantities * and that both the Forts and Shipping depend upon this Fort for a Supply of Corn.

That there is more Palm Oil here than in any other Part of the Coast; and it is the best Place for Ships to water at, and the only Place where a Ship can go in to clean.

As to Commenda, Mr. Roberts informed your Committee, That it is of great Consequence, as the best Stone in Africa is got there.

As to Cape Coast Castle* Mr, Barnes informed your Committee, That it is the principal Fort the Company possess on that Coast, and that is very near falling down: And,

Colonel Bramhatn* being examined, confirmed the

Evidence of Mr. Barnes, and added. That he thought, it would be more advisable to repair than rebuild it.

Mr. Barnes said, That Anamaboe Fort is of great Consequence.

Mr. Deveyne said. That many Slaves are purchased at Tantumquery, and that it is very necessary to have it kept up.

That when he left the Coast, Five Years ago, Whydah was in a very bad Condition; and that a great Trade was carried on there during the War, but none at present.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor labouring Coalheavers, work- Coalheavcn. ing upon the River Thames* was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for a Series of Years, laboured under the greatest HardftnY>s, through the cruel Impositions of a Set of Men called Coal Undertakers, to which they have been obliged to give One Fourth Part of what they earn, or could never expert to be any more employed by them 1 and that the said Coal Undertakers are, in their Profession an unnecessary Body of Men; and that the Bu-finess of the Coal Trade can be better carried on without them, by an Office properly established by the Aur thority of Parliament: And therefore praying. That the House would take their miserable same into Consideration, and cause an Amendment to be made to the Act passed in 1758 for their Relief and Regulation, which Act, through the artful Contrivances of the said Coal Undertakers, has been found to be deficient; and therefore implore, that such an Amendment may be made as the Hobfe shall determine, that the Petitioners may enjoy the Fruits of their Labour, without being imposed on by a Set of mercenary Men, which, the Petitioners presume, has been the Occasion of all those Disturbances that have happened where the Petitioners reside.

Resolved, That the Inhabitants of the Borough of Bridgewater, paying Scotland Lot, have a Right to vote in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

It passed in the Negative*

A Representation of the Genera^ Assembly of the Amerten Colony of New York, being offered to oe presented to Colon*-the House; humbly shewing the high Sense of the distinguished Blelfings under His Majesty’s Government, ana our happy Constitution: Firm in these Sentiments, the Inhabitants of the Colony acknowledge that augult Body, the High Court of Parliament, as the Supreme Legislature over all His Majesty’s Dominions: They conceive that it is not essential to preserve the just Dependence of the Colonies, that the Parliament of Great Britain, in which they are not nor can be equally or effectually represented, should be veiled with the Power of taxing His Majesty’s Subjects in America:

That it is a fundamental Principle in the Constitution, that no Tax can be imposed, or any Property be taken from the Subject, without his Consent, given by himself, or his Represen tat ive in Parliament:

That they were early invested with the Powers of Legislation, in virtue of which, the Right of impoting Taxes has been invariably and exclusively exercised by their Representatives, in General Assembly convened:

That with great Anxiety they observe the Acts of the late Parliament, imposing Duties on the Colonies for the declared Purpose of railing a Revenue, which they lament as subversive of the natural and constitutional Rights of the People they represent, whole Property is by these Acts granted without their Consent:

That the Act of the same Parliament, suspending the Legislative Power of this Colony, until they shall have made the Provision required, for quartering His Majesty’s Troops, is still more alarming, as destrudive of the very End of Representation.

The Subjects of this Colony have always cheerfully complied with the Requisitions of the Crown; and they are therefore the more afflicted at the passing of those Laws which not only tend to the Infringement of their natural Rights as Ettglijkmen, but seem to imply a Dif-

trust of their Readinels to grant such Assistance as the Public Exigence may require.

Urged by these Realous, they presume, with the utmost Deference to the Wisdom of Parliament, to lay before them the Dillrcfles of their Constituents; and fully trolling that the Grievances of His Majesty’s Subjects in America, and the united Voice of all the Colonies, will prevail on His Majesty, and the Parliament, to grant them such Relief, as they shall think necessary, to maintain an equal Participation of Rights, among his faithful Subjects, in every Part of the -tish Empire;

Signed by Mr. Levingston, as Speaker of the General Assembly.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Representation be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

meant to extend to the Inhabitants of the said Eastern and Western Divisions.

And the Counsel were again called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were again directed to withdraw.

A Petition of the Tanners, whose Names are there-unto subscribed, residing within the Counties of Nor- 6ark folk and Suffolk, was presented to the*House, and read; PfefCTvw»®n. Complaining of the great Scarcity of Oaken Bark, which, the Petitioners alledge, is owing to the felling or lopping of Oak Wood out of the Peeling Season, or by not peeling the same when felled.or cut within the Barking Season; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if the present Waste and Spoil of Oak Bark continue, the Amount of the Duties charged on Leather, and payable on the Weight thereof as it comes out of the Vat, must considerably decrease; and that the Revenue will be thereby considerably lessened, and the Consumer injured; and that the Superiority of English Leather to other Leather manufactured abroad is lolely owing to the peculiar Qualities of Oak Bark, when used in proper Quantities, in the Tanning thereof; and that such Scarcity may in great Measure be remedied, if not totally avoided, by niitable Regulations to prevent the future Waste and Spoil thereof: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give Leave for the bringing in a Bill for prohibiting the present Waste and Spoil of Oaken Bark, and for preserving and peeling the fame, so that the Tanners may be supplied with the Quantities of Oaken Bark which the real Growth thereof will furnish, by such Ways and Means, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think fit, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Sir Edward Act ley, Mr. Bacon, See.:

And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Lord Frederick Campbell reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of the City of was referred.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition} and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table.* Where the same was read; and is followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act made in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for improving the Navigation of the River Clyde, was read: And,

Mr. John Golborn, being examined, said, That he

made*a Survey of the River Clyde, in < lash:

That it is, in many Places, from Four Feet to One Foot deep, with many Bars, by which the Navigation, in its present State, is unfit to answer the necessary Purposes of the Public.

That he has considered the said Act, and is of Opinion that the Navigation may be better improved by straitening, embanking, and dredging the River, than by the Method prescribed in the said Act; which is by Locks and Dams.

That the most proper Method, in the Opinion of the Witness, is by confining the Channel to a proper Breadth, which is now much too wide; and by dredging the Bottom, which is in many Places so hard a Gravel, that the Current cannot operate so as to scour it: But that he is of Opinion, that if these Beds of Gravel were dredged or ploughed, and the Channel contrafted, a proper Depth of Water would be obtained, as the Reflux of the Current will then be sufficient to scour the Channel, so as to procure Seven Feet Water, at moderate Spring Tides, at Broomy Law, and at least Four Feet Water at all Tides.

That he estimates the Expence at 8,640} and think it may be done without any Increase of Tolls.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, made in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for improving the Navigation of the River Clyde, to the City of Glafgcnv, and for building a Bridge cross the said River, from the said City, to the Village of Gorbells: And that the Lord Frederick Campbell, Sir Charles Whitworth, and Mr. Edmoiftone, do prepare,

and bring in, the fame.
