Sir Robert Ladbroke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr, Robert Mylne, Surveyor, being examined, said, That the Fleet Prison, situate on the East Side of th Fleet

Market, in the City of London, is in so ruinous a Condition as to be unfit for the Purpose, unless the same be totally rebuilt.

That Ely House, situate in Holborn, in the County of Middlesex, and the Ground thereunto belonging, would afford proper Room and Accommodation for Prisoners usually committed to the said Fleet Prison, and might be fitted up for that Purpose at a much less Expence than rebuilding the said Prison; and that the Scite of the said Prison would be a proper and convenient Spot for the Fleet Market, the Removal of which would open a grand Communication between the Northern and Southern Parts of the Metropolis, and be of Public Utility.

Peter Roberts, Esquire, informed your Committee, That it hath been agreed between the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, the Bishop of Ely, and the City of London, That Ely House and Premises shall be vested in His Majesty, to be converted into a Prison for the Reception of Prisoners usually committed to the Fleet Prison; and that the Scite of the said present Prison, with the Messuages and Grounds thereunto belonging, shall be vested in the Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens of London, to be converted into a Market, in lieu of the said Fleet Market; but that such Agreement cannot be carried into Execution without the Aid of Parliament,

And a Motion being made. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for vesting Ely House, in Holborn, with the Appurtenances, in the Crown, and the Scite of the Fleet Prison, with the Appurtenances, in the Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London, for the Purposes therein mentioned; and for making Compensation to the Lord Bishop of Ely and his Successors;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, informed the House, that His Majesty, having been acquainted with the Purport of the said Bill, had commanded him to acquaint the House, that His Majesty gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for vesting Ely House, in Holborn, with the Appurtenances, in the Crown, and the Scite of the Fleet Prison, with the Appurtenances, in the Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London, for the Purposes therein mentioned: and for making Compensation to the Lord Bishop of Ely and his Successors: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. Alderman Beckford, Mr. Willoughby, Mr. Alderman Trecothick, and Mr. Alderman Harley, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Sir Francis Vincent reported from the Committee, to Blackfrian whom the Petition of several Persons, being Inhabitants, Bridge Merchants, Tradesmen, and Proprietors of Estates, in Road* Blackman Street, Kent Street, Long Lane, Dirty Lane, and Gravel Lane, in the several Parishes of St. George, and St. Saviours Southwark, Newington, and Bermondsey, in the County of Surrey, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth }

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Edward Cole, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Road from Blackman Street, towards Black Fryars Bridge, is along a Lane, called Dirty Lane, which is in a very ruinous and dangerous Condition; and that the Entrance from Blackman Street is only Nine Feet Three Inches wide; that the Witness saw Men crushed to Death there, occasioned by the Narrownefsof the Passage.

'Mr Alderman Trecothick reported from the Com- Preventing mittee, to whom the Petition of the Leather Dressers, the gating Leather Sellers, Tanners of Sheep Skins, Glovers, ot8k,us* Breeches Makers, and Taylors, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others interested in the said Trades, residing within the Bills of Mortality, and other Places within this Kingdom, was referred,. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fa6t contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Fads contained in the said Petition is as follows;

It appeared to your Committee, by an Act made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne; that a Penalty of Two Shillings and Sixpence is laid upon every Butcher or other Person who shall wilfully or negligently gash, (laughter, or cut, any raw Hide of any Ox, Bull, Steer, or Cow, or offer such Hide to Sale, and of One Shilling for every Calf Skin so galhed,

Haughtered, and cut, or offered to Sale; and it also appeared to your Committee, by an Act made in the First Year of King James the First, that a Penalty of Six Shillings and Eight Pence for every Hide, was laid upon every Person who should forestall any Hides coming to any Fair or Market, or should buy any Hide but in Open Fair or Market, except of Persons killing any Beast for their own Use: And,

Mr. Richard Russell, a Fellmonger, being examined, said, That great Damage is done to Sheep, and Lamb Skins in the flaying, both through Carelefness, and often by wilful Negligence; and that the Witness had seen many of them so much damaged, that they were not.fit to be manufactured into Leather; and that the Witness has had Five Pounds flopped in Two or Three hundred Skins, on Account of the same being damaged in flaying: — That he has bought Skins by Contract before the Sheep or Lambs were killed by the Butcher; and that it has frequently been the Pradiceof the Trade so to do.

Mr. John Browning, being examined, said, That he has seen Numbers of Sheep and Lamb Skins gashed and cut to such a Degree, that they were not fit to be dressed into Leather.

Then some Skins were produced to your Committee, which appeared much gaflied and cut, and unfit for Use.

Mr. George Shipley, a Leather Dresser, being examined, laid. That last Year, out of Two hundred and Three thousand Skins, he was obliged to fell Eighty thousand for Twenty Shillings a Hundred less than theycoft, on account of their being cut, gaflied, and damaged in the flaying; and that Three thousand more

which

9 Geo III. 2i

Which cost him One hundred ajid Fifty Pounds, only fold for Forty-five Pounds j they being so extremely cut, were unfit for Manufacture.

And the Witness said. That the Method of purchasing Sheep and Lamb Skins of Butchers, was frequently by Contract by the Year or Season, so that the Purchaser was obliged to take them good and bad together; which was confirmed by Mr. John Warriner, a Leather Dresser.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for preventing the cutting and gashing of Sheep and Lamb Skins, and for enforcing the Sale of such Skins in Public Markets: And that Mr. Alderman and

Sir Edward Blackett do prepare, and bring ip, the fame.

Mr. Waljh reported from the Committee, to whom Severn the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens of BridJS the City of Worcester, under their Common Seal; and of several Gentlemen and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Gwynn, Surveyor, being examined, said. That the present Bridge over the River Severn is an ancient Structure, and so ruinous, that he is surprised that it stands; and he is of Opinion, that One bad Season will destroy it.

That the Passage over the said Bridge is not more than Twelve Feet wide, and the Avenues thereto very narrow and dangerous; and that building a new Bridge, and making convenient Avenues thereto will be a great Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said City, and to all Persons having Occasion to pass over the said River there.

That he has made an Estimate of the Expence of building a proper Bridge there, which amounts to £. 6,000, and upwards.

Mr. John Thornet oe, being examined, confirmed Mr.

Gwynn's Evidence, as to the Necessity of building the said Bridge, and opening the Avenues thereto; and said, That he thinks the Expence of purchasing Houses, for making the Avenues, will not amount to more than £. 1,000, as most of the Buildings that it will be necessary to be purchased are very old and ruinous.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge cross the River Severn, in the City of Worcester, and for opening convenient Avenues to and from the same: And that Mr. Waljh, and Mr.

Harbord do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon the Importation into this Kingdom, from Ireland, or from His Majesty’s Dominions in America, of Raw or Undressed Hides of Steers, Cows, or any other Cattle, except of Horses, Mares, or Geldings, and of Calve Skins or Goat Skins, Raw or Undressed, be discontinued for a limited Time.

Sir Charles Whitworth reported from the Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Sir Charles Whitworth also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday, the 7th Day of April next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of Daniel Earl of Wand Not ting- Fleet Prison, ham, was *prefenfed to the House, and read; Setting fcc* forth, That the Petitioner observes, by the Votes of the House, that Two Petitions of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, have been presented to the House, for a Bill for carrying into Execution an Agreement between those Petitioners and the Lords of the Treasury, and the Bishop of Ely, for removing the Fleet Prison to Ely House, in Holborn; and that a Bill has been brought in for such Purposes; and representing to the House, that the Petitioner is feiled in Fee of a very considerable Estate, consisting of Ground to a great Extent, and Houses to a considerable Number, in the Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, in the County of Middlesex, most of which are inhabited by Persons of great Wealth and Fortune* particularly of a Street called Hatton Garden, which, through the Care and Attention of the Petitioner and his Predecessors, is now, and for a long Time past hath been, the Residence of Persons of the most respectable Characters; and that the Removal of the Fleet Prison to Ely House will be necessarily followed by the assigning to the same a certain Precinct, or Liberty, called The Rules, which will at once be a Refuge to Prisoners, and a Temptation to others to become so; and that the bare Apprehension, that the Rules of the said intended Prison will be of such an Extent as to include the Street called Hatton Garden, has determined many of the Inhabitants thereof to quit their, Houses, in case the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Consequence whereof will be, that, instead of a Set of reputable and responsible Men, the Petitioner will have for his Tenants hardly any but Bankrupts, Insolvents, and Persons of the most infamous and profligate Characters: And therefore praying. That he may be heard, by himself or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Rector, and Churchwardens, and Ditto. Overseers of the Poor of the Parish of St. Andrew, -born, in the County of Middlesex; and’ also of the Pari fhioners of the said Parish, inhabiting the several Streets and Places following, that is to say, Hatton Garden, Kirby Street, Crops Street, Grevill Street, Brook Street, Holborn below the Bars, and the Parts adjacent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Persons interested therein, was also presented to the House and read; also taking Notice of the said Petitions of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, and of the said Bill; and representing to the House, That the Removal of the said Prison out of the City, into the County of Mid- -dlesex, is by no Means necessary: and that theerefting a Prison of such a Magnitude as to contain the Prisoners usually secured in the Fleet, and the consequent Exten-fion thereof, so ds to include within the Rules or Liberties of the same the Street called Hatton Garden, and the other Places before-mentioned, will be productive of many mischievous Consequences, and will tend to the great Injury of the Petitioners; and that if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Resort of indigent and ne-ceffitous Persons thereto, as being within the Rules of the Fleet Prison, will be so great, as to render the Burthen of maintaining their Poor intolerable: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

The Order of the Day being read, for the Attendance Cumberland of Sir GilfredLawfon, Baronet, late High Sheriff of the Eie<aion*

County of Cumberland;

The said Sir Gilfred Lawson, Baronet, and the Counsel on both Sides, were called in.

And the Charge made against the said Sir son, upon Thursday the 9th Day of March last, for unduly returning Sir fames Lowther, Baronet, as Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Cumberland, contrary to the Majority of Votes received by the said Sheriff upon the Poll, was read.

And the Counsel in support of the said Charge was heard; and examined several Witnesses, in order to prove the said Charge.

Then the Counsel for the said Sir Gilfred Lawson waS heard; and examined several Witnesses, in answer to the said Charge. ' ‘

And the Counsel on the other Side having been heard, by way of Reply;

The said Sir Gilfred Lawson, Baronet, and the Counsel on both Sides, were directed to withdraw.

Resolved, That it appears'to this House, that Sir G/7-fred Lawson, Baronet, late High Sheriff of the County of Cumberland, did, at the last Election of Knights of the Shire to serve in Parliament for the said County, unduly return Sir James Loivther, Baronet, contrary to the Majority of Votes received by him upon the Poll; and did, after the Poll was closed, take upon himself to reject several Votes, which had been received upon the Poll in Favour of Henry Fletcher, Esquire, in order td create a Majority in Favour of Sir James , Ba-

ronet, without hearing Counsel, or admitting Evidence, in Favour of the said Votes, at the Time of rejecting them, notwithstanding his Promise to hear such Counsel, and receive Evidence in their Support.

Resolved, That the said Sir Gilfred Lawson, Baronet, has thereby acted partially and illegally, in manifest Violation of the Rights of the Freeholders of the said County, and in Breach of the Privilege of this House.

A Motion- was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Sir Gilfred Lazvfon, Baronet, be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out " taken into the-Custody of " the Serjeant at Arms attending this House," in order to insert " committed to His Majesty’s Gaol of " gate," instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words "taken " into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this " House" stand Part of the proposed Question;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Tellers for the Yeas, "3-

Tellers for the Noes, f fo‘

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That the said Sir Gilfred Lawson, Baronet, be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for granting, for " a limited Time, a Liberty to carry Rice, from His Majesty’s Provinces of South Carolina, and Georgia, directly to any Part of Am, to the Southward of " the said Provinces, subject to the like Duty as is now " paid on the Exportation of Rice from the said Colonies to Places in Europe, situate to the Southward of Cape Finisterre," which was to continue in Force for Five Years from the Twenty-fourth Day of June, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-four, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament j and also, a Clause in an Act passed in the Fifth Year of His said Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for more effectually securing and encouraging the Trade of His Majesty’s American Dominions; for repealing the lnland Duty on Coffee, imposed by an Act made in the *k- Thirty-second Year of His late Majesty King George " the Second; and for granting an Inland Duty on all Coffee imported, except Coffee Of the Growth of the

A Petition of the Governor and Company of the

Company* Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, haying been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read j Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey, has, for a long Series of Years, been carried

on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; that, in order to tarry on the said Trade with Safety, and for protesting His Majesty’s Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary that there should be an Ambafla-dor sent from England, to reside at; and

that there should be Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, in the other Parts of the Turkish Dominions, where any Subjects reside; or where

the English carry on Trade the whole Expence whereof has hitherto been borne by the Turkey Company, and, together with other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on the said Trade, has of late Years amounted to upwards of Ten tfioufand Pounds per Annum; and that the said Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and the Petitioners are sensible, that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent upon them by their Charter, nor the -Justice they owe to the Public, if they did not declare their Inability to proceed any further, unless relieved by Parliament; and'that the Petitioners arc very thankful for the Assistance granted them by Parliament in the last' Session, which was duly applied. And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Chnfi-deration, and grant the Petitioners such further Assistance as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to

the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Seven hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds be raised, by way of Lottery, such Lottery to consist of Sixty thousand Tickets, at Thirteen Pounds each; and that the Contributors towards the same shall, on or before the 20th Day of this Instant April, make a Deposit with the Cashiers of the Bank of,

of One Pound, in respect of the Monies to be paid for every such Ticket, as a Security for making the future Payments to the said Cashiers on or before the Times herein after limited; that is to say, for and in respect of every such Ticket, Two Pounds on or before the ift Day of June next, Three Pounds on or before the 10th Day of July next, Three Pounds on or before the 25th Day of August next, and Four Pounds on or before the 3d Day of October next* and that Tickets, as soon as the same can be prepared, shall be delivered to the Contributors so completing their Payments^ that the Sum of Six hundred thousand Pounds shall be distributed into Prizes for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery, which Prizes shall be charged upon the Aids and Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament for the Service of the Year 1769, and be paid at the Bank of England, in Money, to such. Proprietors, upon Demand, on or at any Time after the 12th Day of January 1770, without any Deduction whatsoever; and that all the Monies to be received by the said Cashiers shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, to be applied, from time to time to such Services as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament; and that every Contributor, who shall pay in the Whole of his Contribution towards the said Sum of Seven hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds on or before the 22d Day of AuguJ? next, shall be allowed an Interest, by way of Discount, alter the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, on the Sums so completing his Contribution respectively, to be computed from the Day of completing the same to the 3d Day of next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty thousand Pounds, out of such Monies as shall be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, after the 4th Day of April 1769, and on or before the 5th Day of April 1770, of the Produce of all or any of the Duties and Revenues, which, by any Act or Acts of Parliament, have been directed to be reserved for the Disposition of Parliament, towards defraying the necessary Expences of defending, protecting, and securing, the British Colonies and Plantations in America, be applied towards making good such Part of the Supply as hath been granted to His Majesty for maintaining His Majesty’s Forces and Garrisons in the Plantations, and for Provisions for the Forces in North America, Nova , Ne'wfoundland, and the ceded Islands, for the Year 1769.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such of the Monies as shall be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer after the 4thjDay of April 1769, and on or before the 5th Day of April 1770, of the Produce of the Duties charged by an Act of Parliament made in the 5th Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, upon the Importation and Exportation of Gum Senega and Gum Arabic, be applied towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of the Representatives of the People of the Parbadors Wand of Barbadoes, in their General Assembly assembled, for

being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Purport of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That, before the Inhabitants of the said Island had well recovered from the deplorable Situation to which they had been reduced, by Two severe Fires, in the Years 1756 and 1758; on the 14th Day of May 1766, another lamentable Fire broke out in their principal Town, which laid in Allies about One thousand Stores and other Buildings, with large Quantities, of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize; and that on the 27th Day of December, in the same Year, a like melancholy Accident consumed the most valuable Part of the Houses and Stores which had providentially escaped the Severity of the former Fires; and that the Loss sustained by the People in general, by the Two last mentioned Conflagrations, is supposed to exeed Half a Million Sterling Money of Great Britain; and that, although large Sums, raised from the Royal Bounty, and the charitable Contributions of many worthy Persons in Great Britain, and other Parts of His Majesty’s Dominions, have been sent over, for the Relief of the most

indigent

380 13a Aprilis. A. 1769.

indigent Sufferers, yet many of them remain dill in the lowed State of Poverty, and are unable to comply with the common and necessary Taxes of their Country; and that, besides the dismal Consequences of a Loss so fe-verely felt by the Inhabitants of the said Island, they have another Misfortune, which they share in common with every Part of the Dominions that are connected with them in Commerce, their Channel being at present so choked up by the Filth which has been many _ Years gathered about their that the smalled

Craft, when loaded, can hardly find a Passage to their Wharfs and Landing-Places; and that, without a speedy Remedy to the said Evil, their Trade with , as well as with Africa and mud be inevitably ob-

structed; and that the Petitioners, seeing that the Progress of the late Fires was in a great Measure occasioned by the Irregularity of their Buildings, have already passed an Act, for re-building their Town upon a safer and better Plan; but that cannot be carried into Execution without great Expence to the Community; and that the Petitioners have likewise had in Contemplation a Means to cleanse their Channel, and give freer Access to Trade; and, with the Affidance of an able Engineer in His Majesty’s Service, they have determined upon a Method, which, they conceive, will effectually answer their Purpose; but the impoverished State of their Finances, and the Incapacity of the People to bear the Burthen of heavy Taxes, have hitherto discouraged them from entering upon the Work; inasmuch, therefore, as the Petitioners, in the Execution of the Plan for rebuilding their Town, mud necessarily exhaud their Treasury, and be rendered incapable of providing for the Expence of cleansing their Channel and repairing their Mole, a Work not merely of local Advantage to the Inhabitants of the Island, but of the most extensive Utility to the Mother Country, and all the Parts of the BritiJIiDominions, whose Manufactures they consume; and inasmuch, likewise, as the melancholy Circumstances of the People will not admit of any additional Impod, they are entirely without the Hopes of Affidance but from the British House of Commons, who have been always attentive to the Didreffes of their Fellow Subjects in the most remote Parts of their Sovereign’s Dominions: And therefore praying That the House will grant the Petitioners such Affidance and Relief, as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of One million Six hundred Sixty-four thousand Eight hundred and Twenty-two Pounds Four Shillings and Five-pence Half-penny, out of such Monies as shall or may 20

That such Part of the Duties which have been, or shall be, paid upon Iron imported in Foreign-built Ships navigated by Foreigners, as exceeds the Duties payable, upon Iron imported in British-built Ships, navigated by British Subjects, be not drawn back upon Re-exportation.

That the Drawback, which was formerly payable upon the Exportation of Foreign rough Hemp, and which was discontinued by an Act made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, be redored, upon Condition that the Pre-emption thereof be offered to the Commissioners of the Navy.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown, do attend this House immediately, with the Return to the Writ for electing a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Middlesex, in the room of John Wilkes, Esquire, whole Election and Return were resolved by this House to have been null and void.

The House was moved, that the Entries in the Votes of the House, upon the 17th Day of February last, in relation to the Proceedings of the House, upon the Return to the Writ for electing a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Middlesex, in the room of John Wilkes, Esquire, expelledthis House, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Resolved, That the Election and Return of John Wilkes, Esquire, to serve in this present Parliament for the said County, are null and void.

Ordered, That Mr. John Smith, under Sheriff* of the County of Middlesex, do immediately attend this House.

And the said Mr. John Smi, attending according to Order; was called in; and, at the Bar, gave the House an Account who were the Candidates, and for whom a Poll was demanded and taken.

And then he was directed to withdraw.

Ordered, That the Sheriffs of the County of Middlesex do attend this House immediately, with the original Poll taken at the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament, for the said County.

And the said Sheriffs attending according to Order; they were called in; and, at the Bar, produced the original Poll Books, and also a Paper from which the Sheriffs had declared the Numbers of Votes for each Candidate upon the Poll.

And then they withdrew.

And the total Numbers for each Candidate, contained in the said Paper, were read.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That the Poll taken at the last Election of a Knight of the Shire for the County of Middlesex, be taken into Confederation Tomorrow Morning;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Word " Tomorrow," in order to insert the Word " Monday" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Word " To- morrow " Hand Part of the said proposed Question.; Vox,. 3a.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Mom- Supply, ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

May 1744. A Letter from the Commissioners of the Victualling to Thomas Cor Esquire, Secretary to the Admiralty, mentioning that they had discoursed Mr. Dolby on the several Points contained in his Petition or Memorial, and apprehended there was not then sufficient Light whereon to ground an Opinion with respect to the Damage which he set forth he should sustain j but, as they thought it very reasonable the Freight of the Ship should be paid as far as Genoa, they therefore proposed to him, that if the Owner of the

Wheat, and he, could adjust the Amount thereof, according to the Charter Party, they had no Objection to its being paid here, on Security being given to indemnify the Crown in case it had been already paid to the Matter, or otherwise, by their Agent at Mahon; but Mr. Dalby tinting, that this Method might occasion Delay, and be greatly injurious to him, as he wanted the Money at Genoa, or Credit to purchase a Freight Home, they proposed to fend a Copy of the Charter Party to Mr. Birtles, His Majesty’s Consul at Genoa, and to desire him to make up the Freight agreeable thereto, as if the Ship had arrived at Genoa, and to draw Bills on the Commissioners for the fame, and to, follow the Directions of Mr. Dalby in the Disposal of the Money } which Method Mr. Dalby having consented to, they intended, if their Lordships had no Objection, to write to Mr. Birtles accordingly.

9 Nov. Dalby's Letter to Birtles, mentioning he Was greatly surprised on the 29th of last Month, to fee by a public Lift, That the Britannia was again stopt at Mahon; and more especially as he had no Letter from Birtles, the Captain, or any other Person; that, upon Inquiry, he found that (he was detained for a 200 Bill of Green and Hall, which Birtles had informed him he had or would discharge; and Dalby orders Birtles in that Letter immediately to pay Messieurs Green and Hall, and every other Person whatsoever, any Demand they had against the Ship or Cargo in the Britannia, to order the Ship to be supplied with Provisions, and what else he himself thought necessary; and to take Satisfaction therefor out of the Money in his Hands.

28 April 1755. A Protell made by William Mo* ran, the Mailer of the Ship, before. James Gill, a Public Notary, and sworn to by the said William

Moran,

9 Geo. III. i8° Aprilis^405

Moran, and by Robert Elwood, Chief Mate, Laurence Farrell, Second Mate, Robert Mullegan, Carpenter, Michael Everiy, Christian Cock, and ‘Thomas

Silvia, Seamen, of and belonging to the said Ship; Hercules Rice, and Thomas Williams, Passengers on beard her, the same Day; wherein he declares as follows:

That the ('aid Snow being of the Burthen of 180 Tons or thereabouts, properly equipt, and loaded with Sugar, Rum, Wine, and sundry ether Merchandize, Tailed from St. Kitts, bound for London, on the 14th then lad

jdaft.

That on the 2 2d Day of April aforesaid, about Eight in the Morning, the Wind being at South by Wed, and in the fair Way proceeding on his Voyage up Channel, and being near a-bread of the Start, Didance or 5 Leagues -, One of His Majesty’s Tenders brought the Vessel to, and impressed Three of their bed Seamen, and, in lieu of them, the Commander of the Tender put on board the Snow Three very indifferent Men; viz — One a Taylor, who had never been on board a Ship above Three Weeks — another a Bricklayer who had never acted as a Sailor for more thart Three Months — and the Third a Husbandman, who had never been on board a Ship as a Sailor more than a Fortnight before that Time: and, as they severally declared to the said Mailer and others above named, wholly unacquainted with the Navigation ofa Ship or Vessel.

That he attempted afterwards to proceed on his Voyage, and next Day, being 23d, about Seven in the Evening, being between Pepperell Point, and the at lead Four Leagues from the Land, with the Wind at South South East; another Tender belonging to His Majesty’s Ship Royal George, and whereof Richard Sixth Lieutenant of the said Ship was the Commander, fired a Shot over the said Snow, which dropped within Thirty or Forty Yards on the Starboard Side, in order to bring the said Vessel to.

That the said Moran being apprehensive of the Indraft of the Island, and the Distress the Snow was then in, consulted with his Officers and Crew what was bed to be done under their unhappy Circumstances, having a just Dread of losing their Ship and Cargo; and it was thereupon determined to make Sail, to avoid being brought to; but that Attempt soon appearing fruitless, he, with the Approbation of his Mate and Crew, brought to.

That the said Lieutenant Williams, notwithstanding the distressed Condition of the said Snow as aforesaid, carried away another, the best Seaman left on board, and in his (lead left one Nicholas; alluring the said

Master that the said Mahon was a Seaman and a Helmf-man; which said Nicholas had the Helm at the Time of the Accident herein after mentioned.

That after the Snow was detained in Manner aforesaid, till near 12 o’Clock, in which Time (he unavoidably made a great Leeway, the said Lieutenant left her.

That the said Master being greatly fatigued under the Whole of this Transaction, having first given Directions to his Second Mate, Laurence Farrell, to (leer a direct East South East Course, laid himself down to get a little Rest; and, in Two Hours Time, the said Vessel was on Shore, the said Mahon being at the Helm, and {truck near Atherfield Rocks, and notwithstanding he, the Master, got out an Anchor, and used all other possible Means to get her off, she parted her Cable, and soon went on Shore; and, a prodigious large and folding Ground Sea going at that Instant, soon broke to Pieces, and was totally loft, together with the greatest Part of the Cargo.

That by Means of the Confusion he was put into, the Distress the Ship was left in, and other the Premises particularly described; the said Ship, and Part of her Cargo, was totally loft, and not by Means of any Neglect or Default of him or any of his Ship’s Company.

28 April 1755. A Deposition and Examination of Vol. 32.

William Moran, and the several other Persons mentioned Dalbyrs in the foregoing Protest, (worn before Barnabas Eveleigh Petition for Leigh, El'quire, One of His Majesty’s Justices of the Compen£iUlwa' Peace for the County of Southampton, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for enforcing the Laws against Persons who shall‘deal or detain ship-wrecked Goods, &c. Whereby it appears, that the said Snow was of the Burthen of 180 Tons or thereabouts, and was the sole Property of Mr. Dalby, and failed from St. Kitts at the Time, and with such Loading on board, as is mentioned in tire said Protest, and was loft in Brixton Bay at the Back of the Isle of Wight-, which was absolutely occasioned by the Detention of the Snow, and the Impressing several of her Hands; and that only a small Part of her Cargo was saved.

Alexander Clunie, of London, Merchant, formerly Commander of a Ship, produced by Mr. Dalby, — having pe-rufed the said Protest, and being asked,

1 ft. What Flood the Ship had at that Time, being Four Miles in the Offing ?

Answered, ’Till near Eleven o’Clock in the Offing.

2. Was the Wind at 9.S.E. a dead Wind to bring the Ship ashore ?

Anf. Undoubtedly it was.

3. By the Course the Master directed the Mate to (leer, do-yoti think the Wind was at South, or to

the Westward of South ?

Anf. It must have been to the Westward of South.

' 4. Would you not, in that Cafe, have hauled up to a more Southerly Course ?

Anf.Yes. ' .

5. If you had been in the Situation described by

the Captain, would you have flood to the East-ward ?

Anf.I think I should have flood to the Westward, after haying lain to, as he did,- Five Hours, if the Wind had been South; if to the Westward of South,

I should have flood more to the Southward.

6. Do you think, if there had been double the Number of Hands on board, it would have been a Means of saving the Ship ?

Anf. The Ship went to Pieces immediately; I apprehend, if any Thing was the Loss of the Ship, it was the Detention — (he was Two Hours Sail from the Place where (he -went on Shore when brought to — With the Wind at South, if it blew hard, I don’t know whether (he would have cleared the Land. I suppose the Master apprehended himself far enough from Shore when he went to deep. \

Said he knew the Master, Moran; that he was esteem-ed a very good Seaman, and a Man of a fair Character.

And as to the subsequent Proceedings of the Ship, as stated in the Petition, the Time of her Discharge from the Public Service at Mahon, her proceeding from thence to Madeira, and taking on board a Cargo of Wine, viz. 40 Pipes on Dalby*s Account, and her being taken by the Enemy on her Voyage to Carolina in 1745:

Dalby read Part of an Answer, put in by the Commissioners of Victualling, to a Bill filed by Captain Diddear, in the Court of Exchequer, in 1745, against Dalby, and to which the Commissioners were made Parties; and read also several Parts of the Deposition of Richard Burnley, examined as a, Witness in the said Cause.

28 Jan. 1744-5. A Letter from Dalby to the Commissioners, inclosing the Certificate of the Ship’s Discharge at Mahon, 21 November 1745; and mentioning his Demand on account of the Breach of the Charter Party, and Deviation from the stipulated Voyage, and Mif-em-ployment of his Ship; and denring Satisfaction.

4 March 1744-5. A Letter wrote by Dalby to the Commissioners, proposing to have the Matter settled in an amicable and reasonable Way.

10 July 1745. Dolby’s Letter to the Commissioners, requesting £. 300 on Account of this Ship j which was refused.

The Commissioners of Victualling having produced several Pieces of Evidence, to shew on what Terms they had settled with several Owners of other Ships employed in carrying Provisions for the Fleet in the Mediterranean, under similar Charter Parties with that for the Francis, in order to establish that Settlement as a Rule in this Cafe;

Dalby, in order to shew a material Difference between his Cafe, and that of the Frederick, and others, which were mentioned, produced the following Evidence:

11 May 1745. Certificate from the Custom House in London, of the Entry of the Ship Frederick; whereby it appeared, (he had on board a full Loading of Tobacco from Virginia, viz. 553 Hogsheads, besides other Goods.

Several Bills of Lading, signed by William Loney, the Master of the Ship Frederick, for Tobaccos, the Freight, of which was £.\<b person, of Hogsheads, which for 553 Hogsheads amounts to J. 2,200, and upwards.

To prove the Value of the Ship Francis at the Time (he failed from London;

Alexander Clunie, a Merchant, formerly a Commander of a Ship, acquainted, with the Outfit of Ships between London and Carolina, and with Shipping, above 30 Years; having inspected an original Account of the first Cost at Boston of the Ship Francis, formerly proved by Mr. Alderman Trecothick, a Member of the Committee, upon a Calculation made, declared the Ship, fitted as (lie was, rauft, at the Time of her failing, be worth about 11 or £.12 pa Ton.

And, being further examined, declared, That to be let by the Month to the Government, and to be insured by them, (lie was worth about £ 140 per Month.

To shew by Analogy from a Determination in a similar Cafe, That the Charter Party for the Francis was broke, by Law; Dalby produced the Record of the Court of King's in the

" Cause between Black and the Commissioners of Victualling, and the Postea indorsed thereon;

' and several Rules of the Court of King's Bench, in that Cause; whereby it appeared,

That the Jury on the Trial of that Cause found Two Facts, to wit. That Government were to find the Convoy; and, that there was no Necessity for the Ship’s going into Lisbon: And they assessed the Damages for taking the Ship in there, at One Penny.

That the Verdict found was subject to the Opinion of the Court, whether a new Trial should be granted or not; and, in Easter Term 1747, the Court, on solemn Argument, established the Verdict of the Jury, and refused a new Trial.

Dalby produced a Report of the Commissioners of Victualling to the Lords of the Admiralty, bearing Date 27 April 1764, upon a Reference to them of a Petition presented by Dalby and Downes to His Majesty, praying to be relieved, in respect to some Hardships, whereby they alledged Dalby and his Family had been injured; Upon which, the Commissioners were directed to re-consider what had before passed between their Lordships and the Commissioners on that Subject; and to lay before them a full State of the Cafe, with their Opinion thereon.

Whereby it appears. That the Commissioners in that Report omitted to date the Penny Breach above mentioned, in the Trial of Black and the Commissioners, and the Two several Facts found by the Jury, as above mentioned — And,

That in their said Report, in dating the Charter Party for the Ship Hope, they omitted to (late that the Ship was to proceed on the Voyage, Wind and Weather permitting — that the Owner was bound in a large Penalty, for the true Performance of the Charter Party — And for what was to be paid, done, and performed on his Majesty's Part, the Commissioners had set the Seal of Office.

The Commissioners of Victualling, as a Justification o( their Conduct, in refusing to pay Dalby any more Money on account of the said Ship Francis, than the Freight stipulated by the Charter Party, and Demurrage at the same Rate as had been allowed by them to other Ships, which had been hired for the same Service; having produced the Record in the Court of Exchequer, in a Cause between Harley and the Commissioners of Victualling, touching the Ship Hope; whereby it appeared, That the Jury in that Trial had found a Verdict for the Plaintiff, and assessed the Damages at £. 1,307.13*. r\d. And having, for the same Purpose, proved by the Evidence of Robal Baxter, the Commissioners Solicitor, That they had, on the 17th January 1756, tendered to Dalby the Sum of £. 939. 17 4 as a full

Satisfaction with what they had before paid him, for all his Damages on account of the Ship Francis; and had shewn to him at the same Time, by a Computation thereof in Writing, that the same was made up agreeable to the Verdict in the Court of King’s Bench, in the Cause of Black and Blifs, and the Verdict in the Court of Exchequer above mentioned;

Dalby referred to the Evidence herein before stated, touching the said Trial in the King’s Bench, and as to the Verdict in the Exchequer, in the Cause of the Hope.

He produced Two of the Jurors on that Trial, to wit, John Irish, and Charles Cojler, who being severally examined, declared to the following Effect; That, upon the Cause being opened, and a Witness called for the Plaintiff, the Counsel for the Crown would not admit

him

o Geo. III. i 8* Jprilk. 405

him to be examined, facing. It was a Matter of Law — That One of the Jury observed thereupon to the Court,

That such Cases were frequently tried at Guildhall, and Witnesses allowed to be called — That they do not remember particularly for what the Action was brought, nor what the Witness so refused was called to prove, excepting, that the Action was about the Hire of a Ship; and they believe the Evidence was called to prove the Voyage and Damage — That no Witness was examined upon the Trial, the Court having joined in Opinion with the Counsel for the Crown: That thereupon, the Attorney General prepared an Account in writing, of the Damages which he admitted to be due: The Jury, by Direction of the Court, gave a Verdict to be recorded, according to the Admission of the Attorney General.

Being asked, On the Part of the Commissioners, whether any Objection' was made by Dalby's Counsel. at the Trial to the Sum, answered, They believe there was an Objection.

An Application was made to the Court for a new Trial; which was refused, because no more could be recovered under the Charter Party.

Mr. Dalby, at the Time the Record of the Trial, relative to the Ship Hope, was first offered to be produced in Evidence before the Committee, objected, That it was not admissible; as being no way relative to the Matter of his Petition: But the Victualling Commissioners infilled on it.

And your Committee finding it necessary to order the Commissioners for Victualling His Majesty’s Navy, to attend with such Papers, relating to the Matter of the said Petition, as weref in their Custody: It appears from the Papers by them produced.

As to the Ship Britannia,

First, with regard to the original Destination of the Ship, and the Correspondence between Dolby, and his Agent, relative to the Plan afterwards purposed by Dolby for loading the Ship back, partly with Oil to be bought for him by Births, and partly on Freight to be procured by Births-, That,

19th OC?. 1743. By a Charter Party between Francis Dalby, Owner of the , of the Burthen

of Two Hundred Tons, then in the River of Thames, whereof William Henry was Master, of the One Part; and Jonathan Collier, of London, Merchant, of the other Part; Dalby let the Ship to Freight to Collier, and covenanted that (he should depart out of the River, and fail directly to Cowes, and there receive such Wheat as Collier should put on board; that (he should mount 14 Guns, and carry 20 Men, and proceed with the first Convoy j or, at the Choice of the Merchant, be manned - with 23 Men, and proceed without Convoy to Genoa directly, and there lay 3d Days to unload, and so to end her Voyage; (the Perils and Dangers of the Seas, Enemies, and the Restraint of Princes and Rulers excepted:) and Collier covenanted fully to load the Ship with Wheat at Cowes, and discharge her at Genoa within the 30 Days, or Days of Demurrage after mentioned; and pay to Dalby for the Freight, if (he proceeded with Convoy and 20 Men, at 45 s. per Ton; it without Convoy, and with 25 Men, at 47 s. 6 d. per Ton, for every Ton of Wheat loaden at Cowes, and delivered at Genoa; the same to be paid upon the said Ship’s Delivery at Genoa, with Two Thirds of Port Charges, and Pilotage, and Primage and Average accustomed, with a Provish that Collier might keep the Ship on Demurrage, at either of the Places aforesaid, for 10 Days over and above the Days above limited, paying to Dalby £. 3 Sterling per Day; and for the Performance, the Owner bound the Ship, and the Merchant the Goods: Upon which Charter Party a Memorandum was indorsed, subscribed by Collier and Dalby, whereby it was agreed that Collier should be at Liberty to keep the Ship at the Height of Genoa 48 Hours, for Orders from Collier's Factor, whether to unload there, or proceed to Naples to unload; for which

Collier was to pay Freight, if Unloaded at Genoa, 47 per Ton, If at Naples, 52 s.6 d.per Ton; , .

By a written Agreement between Dalby, and Henry, the Master of the Ship; wherein the Britannia is described to be then bound on a Voyage from Cowes, to Genoa or Naples; and from thence either to load at Gallipoly, or any other Port in the Mediterranean, for London or Boston in New England, as Dalby should appoint — Dalby covenants to pay him per Month Wages, without the Allowance of Primage or any thing elle whatsoever.

You are hereby directed, jointly with the said Mailer, to choose a Bag of the said Wheat, which is to be sealed by him and you, and sent to John Birtles, Esquire, His Majesty’s Consul at Gen, to whom the said Cargo is tonsigned j that the said sealed Bag may serve as a Sample, in order to determine the Price the said Wheat bore at Genoa at the Time the said Ship might reasonably be supposed to have arrived there, had (he not been detained here on the Government’s Account. So soon as you have received all the Cargo of Wheat, and compared and agreed your Account thereof with the said Mailer, specifying whatever Quantity shall be found damaged, you are to correspond with the said Consul Birtles, thereby advising him of my Orders, and the Steps you take in this Affair: And that the Crown may not be put to an additional Expence by any Demand the Proprietors of the said Wheat might make, in case it was not immediately paid for; as also to prevent the Rilk that attends the remitting the Amount thereof in Specie; you are, by the first Opportunity that offers after you have received said Cargo, to remit the Amount thereof, as near as you can calculate, to the said Consul Birtles, for the Use of the Proprietors, in your Bills of Exchange on the Commissioners for Victualling his Majesty’s Navy; advising them of my Orders to you for this and your other Transitions herein.

You are at the same Time to desire the said Consul Birtles, to fend you, as soon as possible, authentic Certificates of the Prices that Wheat of the same Quality of the Sample sent him sealed up, would have fold for at

1 Genoa for ready Money, at the Time the said Ship could

reasonably be judged to have arrived there as aforesaid; and upon receipt of such Certificates, and his Account of the Cargo, you are to determine the Cost thereof in your Public Accounts for the Victualling Service: For all which this shall be to you a sufficient Warrant. 8th March 1743-4, O.S. Mr. Revelladvised the Commissioners, by Letter, of the Order he had received from Admiral Matthews, saying, That the Admiral had ordered him to receive a Cargo of Wheat shipped at Corves -on the Britannia, and consigned to Mr. Birtles, which

the Admiral stopt there for his Majesty’s Service, and directed him to pay for it at the Price it would have fold for at Genoa, at the Time the Ship might be reasonably supposed to have arrived there.

13 th Sept. 1744. , Mr. Revell writes to the Board as follows; viz. First to acquaint your Honours that had not the Britannia's pargoof Wheat been taken for the use of the Government here, it must have been landed at this Port, the Ship having sprung a Leak, which could not be Hopped but by careening; and the Mailer had got his Ship dole ashore in a Cove to that end before he was ordered to deliver his Cargo to me; therefore the Wheat's being taken here proved a great Advantage to the Concerned both in Ship and Cargo, by laving a considerable Expence in landing and re-shipping the Cargo, Warehouse Room, Guards, (Ac. The Warrant given by Admiral Matthews to the Matter of the Britannia, to deliver his Cargo to me, was dated 9th 1743-4, his Order to me the 14th of the same Month, and my Receipt to the Mailer for the Wheat the 4th April following. If he had been obliged to unload his Ship with his own People only, he could not have done it in that Time; therefore there cannot be any Claim for Demurrage occasioned by this Office. I repeatedly told the Matter of the Britannia, if he wanted any Money here for the Ship’s Use, I would supply him, in order to his going to the Port he was destined to, and that he need not apply himself to any body else; but he did not think proper to accept the Offer I made him, and thereby loft a great deil of Time unnecessarily, lying long idle here after he could have proceeded under Convoy of one of his Majesty’s Ships, for which this Office can never be deemed accountable. — The Surprise Mr. Birtles expressed in his Letter of nth June last at Mr. Dolby's Demands, and his Reasoning on them, is very just; for I do not fee that any one Part of his Pretensions in his Memorial to the Lords of the Admiralty is grounded on Reaion, but am sure that all his Claims are directly contrary to what has been frequently practised in parallel Cafes: — Had the Ship and Cargo, after the Ship had been made fit here for Sea, proceeded to Genoa, and the Cargo fold there, the Freight and Primage was undoubtedly payable by the Seller out of the Produce of the Cargo, and not by the Purchasers. — Now this Office is the Purchaser, having paid for the whole Cargo at the Market Price; and therefore is no ways bound to pay Freight or Primage. — There have been many Instances here of the like Nature, when Men of War have in Time of Scarcity stopt Ships loaden with Wheat at Sea, and brought them into this Port, and the Merchants concerned have been well pleated and satisfied, by being paid in the same Manner the Britannia's Cargo was paid for — as indeed they well might, since they thereby iaved very heavy Expences that would have attended the Sales of the Cargoes in Italy, especially if put into Warehouses, as is generally the Cafe.

27th August 1744. Birtles wrote to the Board, that he

5th Obi. 1744. By a Minute to the Victualling Board, it appears that Dalby applied to them, and desired, as he had no Occasion for the Money at Genoa, that they would advance him such Part of the Freight, as they might think proper, till such Time as they might hear from their Agent at Mahon, to enable them to make a Report to their Lord ships touching his other Demands; the Board told him they could not be certain of his not having ordered Birtles so pay the Freight, according to the Directions given him from the Board some Time before; but he said he was ready to give Security to indemnify the Crown against such an Accident <; whereupon the Board ordered an Imprest Bill of £. 450 to be made out to him on account of the Freight of the said Ship, upon giving Security to indemnify the Crown against his having received it from Mr Birtles, on account of the Crown or the Owners, and against his receiving it; or giving any Orders for receiving it for the future, and upon his giving an-Authority to Mr. Birtles to dispose of the Money that he had received, or might recover of the Proprietors of the Corn for Freight and Port Charges, according to such Directions as he should receive from the Board.

22d Obi. 1744. The Board having received Mr. Reveil's Letter of the 13th of September, 1744 above dated, made a Minute of this Date, dating the Purport of this Letter; and as Mr. Dalby had not given the Security required by the Board’s Minute, and the Board being of Opinion, from the Accounts given of the Affair by Mr. Revell, that Dalby had not any Claim upon that Office, either for Freight or Damages, the intended Imprest for £. 450 was therefore not made out.

5th Nov. 1744. The Board reported to the Admiralty, That it did not seem to them that Mr. Dalby had any Claim upon that Office for the Freight, the same having been paid by the Crown in the Price for the Corn, and was retained for Mr. Dalby's Use in the Hands of Mr. Birtles; and, as to the consequential Damages, that as the Ship was not detained any longer at Mahon, by means of her Cargo having been purchased there for the Use of the Fleet, than (fie mull otherwise have been in repairing the Damage (he had got before (he put in there, and their Agent repeatedly offered the Matter what Money might be wanted for fitting the Ship to proceed to Genoa, to which Place he ought to have gone by virtue of the Orders he had received from Mr. Dalby before he left England, and where the Freight, by

the Measures that had been taken, Would have been ready to have been applied to such Purposes as Mr. Dalby might be supposed to have* lodged Orders about, against the Ship’s Arrival there';- and therefore they conceived that although Mr. Dalby might have suffered from his Mailer’s Imprudence in losing his Time at and not proceeding according to his Orders to Genoa; yet the Crown ought not to be accountable for the Time the Ship lay unnecessarily at Mahon through the Matter’s Negligence, or for any Damage that might have accrued to Mr. Dalby in Consequence thereof.

30th Jan. x 744-5. The Admiralty directed the Victualling Board to take the Attorney General’s Opinion upon the Cafe.

nth Feb. 1744-5. Sir Dudley Ryder., then Attorney General, gave his Opinion, That the Damages which were naturally consequential to the taking out the Corn at Port Mahon, ought to be made good to the Owner, and

thought an Action would lie against the Admiral for. them; but thought the unnecessary Demurrage of the Captain at Port Mahon, or his going afterwards to Cagliari, and purchasing Salt, were not such Damages as either the Admiral or the Agent Victualler were liable to make good.

i$t\\ March 1744-5. By the Order of the Admiralty it appears. That their Lordships order the Board to act in the Matter according to the Opinion, and to pay the Damage therein proposed, and no other, provided Dalby gave a general Release, and would receive the same in full Satisfaction of all Demands; and it appears by the Board’s Minute, that in consequence thereof the Board desired Mr. Dalby to give them an Account of what he insisted upon as consequential Damages.

25th March 1745. The Account being laid before the Attorney General, he gave his Opinion, That under the Circumstances of the Cafe, neither the Homeward-bound Freight, nor any other of the subsequent Demands, were such consequential Damages as ought to be allowed, though this was a Matter wholly in the Bread of a

Jury.

13th April 1745. The Account and Opinion having been communicated to the Admiralty, their Lordfiiips ordered the Board to act with Mr. Dalby exactly conformable to the Opinion.

31st July 1745. It appears by a Minute of the Board,

15th OEl, 1745. Mr. Birtles, by a Letter wrote by him from Leghorn, acquainted the Board in Answer, That Mr. Dalby's Allegations were far from being grounded

on that Justice and Equity that it is needful for a Man tender of his Charadier, and desirous to establish a Mercantile Credit. — For that when he let out the said Ship Britannia, he soon after wrote to him, the said Mr.

Birtles, and acquainted him with her Burthen, &c. and desired him, if he could, to procure the Ship a Freight back to England, and, in defect of succeeding, to fend her to load a Cargo of Salt; to which he answered him.

That if he would order the Matter to put Sixteen Guns into her, and Chip Fifty or Sixty Men, (he might go, and take a Foundation of Gallipoly Oil oa his Account, and he would procure the Remainder of the Cargo of Paper and fine Goods for London: To this Propolai Mr. Dalby answered, That he could not consent to put any more Guns into the said Ship, or suffer the Matter to increase the Complement of her Crew; but that if he thought proper he might invest about £ 1000 Sterling in Oils on his Account, and fend the Bills of Lading to his, the said Mr. Birtles' Friend in London, till he had paid his, Mr. Birtles' Bills; but this Order was confined, and not to be executed unless he could fill the Ship up at Genoa; upon which he immediately answered, That as he would not consent that the Ship should carry Sixteen Guns, and Fifty or Sixty Men at least, it would be impossible to procure her an Ounce of Goods for,

and therefore, upon her Arrival at Genoa, he would get her dispatched as soon as possible, and fend her to load a Cargo of Salt; in which Manner the Correspondency ceased about the Ship’s going back to London; so that there were no Funds lodged for the Oils, nor any Hopes of the Ship’s returning to London, if Ihe had carried the Corn to Genoa; and that consequently Mr. Dalby was no Sufferer by the Ship’s Freight to Gallipoly, nor on the

Easter Term 1746. Dalby brought an Action against Admiral Matthews and Mr. Revell.

26th Nov. 1746. Dalby petitioned the Board of Admiralty, that some Persons might attend the Trial with Mr. Reveirs Letter of the 8th March 1743, before Hated, the Order of the Board of Admiralty of the 15th March 1744-5, before Hated, and Admiral Matthew's Letter to them of the 24th January 1744, desiring to be indemnified on account of the said Ship; and their Lordships having desired the Board’s Opinion thereon, they thought it advisable to consult Counsel thereupon; which Letter of Admiral Matthews was as follows — To Thomas Corbett, Esquire. Sir, — Soho,

24th January 1744. — The Bearer is the Attorney of Mr. Francis Dalby, who has been sent to me concerning the Britannia, a Merchant Ship, which I Hopped at Mahon, with her Lading of Wheat, for the Service of the Fleet under my Command. I wrote to you upon this Subject the 8th December last, and sent you the Papers relating to this Matter; but as no Anifwef has been given, 1 am now to desire, that their Lordships will be pleased to give such Directions as shall be necessary to indemnify me for the Steps I took for the Good of the Service.

31st Dec. 1746. The Board transmitted to their Lordships a Copy of Counsellor Legge's Opinion, with regard to the producing the said Letters, as follows; viz. 1 apprehend that neither the Lords of the Admiralty, nor the Commissioners of the Victualling, ought to produce, or deliver, to Mr. Dalby these Letters; and that it would be very wrong in them so to do. It is a most unprecedented and unreasonable Request. And it is to be supposed, that Mr. Dalby knew his own same before he brought his Action, and could not expect that the Defendants should make it out for him.

Easter Term 1752. Dalby filed a Bill in the Court of Exchequer against the Commissioners of the Victualling Office, praying Satisfaction for the Freight, Primage, Petty Average, and Port Charges, of the Outward-bound Cargo of Wheat, and for the Freight for a Homeward-bound Voyage to London, for the Damage by not importing the Oil, for the Loss of the Ship, and for Interest on those Demands; and that an Ilfue at Law might be directed to try how much he had been damnified by the Seizure and Detention of the Ship, and taking away her Cargo, and the consequential Lolfcs occasioned to him thereby.

22d May 1752. The Attorney General gave another Opinion upon the Two former Cafes, and also’ upon subsequent Cafe; that he thought there was no Grounds for Mr. Dalby to recover, either in Law or Equity, any Part of the Demands he had made; and he observed there was One material FaCl Hated then, which was not in the former Cafes, which was taken from Grace's Account of the TransaClion to Mr. the Board’s Solicitor: That the Captain himself agreed to the unloading the Corn in the Manner Hated, and declared it would be a great Help, and save him great Trouble and Expence.

May 1754. The Commissioners of the Victualling Board put in Three Answers to the Bill, and the Amendments; and the last Answer was put in, in May 1754.

Michaelmas 1754. Grace was examined as a Witness de bene eft'e, and no further Proceedings have been had in the Cause.

February 1757* Dalby presented another Memorial to the Admiralty, relating to his Claims, which they referred to the Victualling Board for their Opinion.

20th May 1757. The Board reported their Opinion, That they apprehended that the Question upon taking the Corn, and what Parts of the Damages claimed' by Dalby were the natural or unavoidable Consequence thereof, were Matters which would come more properly before a Court of Judicature, or the Decision of Counsel on both Sides, upon a same to be agreed upon; and till it appeared by proper Judges, whether the Crown was liable to any of the Points of Damage claimed, it would be premature to enter into any Consideration of the Quantum.

24th May 1757. The Admiralty confirmed the Opinion, and approved of the Proposal of referring the Question of Law to the Attorney General and Mr.

Dalby's Counsel.

15th June 1757. Mr. Dalby was informed of this by the Board, and they ordered their Solicitor to take the necessary Steps with Dally or his Solicitor for adjusting a joint Cafe.

30th July 1757. The several Cafes which had been laid before Sir Dudley Ryder, and the Opinions, were sent to Mr. Skinner, Mr. Dalby's Solicitor, who was desired to let the Board’s Solicitor know, whether he had any Objections or Additions to make to those Cafes; to which he sent no Answer.

26th August 1757. Dalby laid before the Board, a Paper, intituled, A same between the Crown and himself, relating to the Ship Britannia.

14th Sept. 1757. Dalby attended the Board, and laid, He was prepared to prove his same before them: He was answered by the Board, That they did not look upon that as a Thing which they could take upon themselves to determine; but if he would settle a same with the Board’s Solicitor, such same should be laid before Counsel accordingly; but if neither himself or his Solicitor would meet the Board’s Solicitor, to endeavour to settle such a joint Cafe, the Blame would lie wholly with himself.

March 1764. Mr. Dalby presented a Petition to His Majesty, which was referred to the Admiralty, who referred it to the Victualling Board.

29th April 1764. The Victualling Board made their Report, and concluded it with saying, That as Mr. Dalby had not thought proper to proceed in the Cause which he commenced in the Court of Exchequer, for the Recovery of his Demands, on account of the said Ship 1 and as His Majesty’s Attorney General, by his before-mentioned Opinion of the 22d of 1752, adviled. That there was no Ground, either in Law or Equity, for his recovering any Part of his said Demands; and as Mr. Dalby had not produced any tiling since that Time, which they apprehended could any way tend to establish the lame, it did not therefore occur to them, that any other Measures could be taken under the said Opinion, than what was proposed by the Board, in the Year 1757, viz. Hilary ‘Term 1745, Mr. Black, Owner of the Frederick, commenced an Action in the Court of King’s Bench against the Commissioners, wherein he declared (Bating the Charter Party, and that 274 Tons of Provisions were laden on board) that on the 18th December the Captain received Orders to fail for the Downs, in order there to receive'Convoy for ;which he did,

and arrived at Spithead on the 18th January — That the Ship was detained at Spithead for want of Convoy, from the aSth of January to the 18th of April, being 2 Months and 20 Days; and on the 28th of January the Captain made his Protest; and the Declaration claims a Satisfaction for the Demurrage at Spithead above the Ten Days.

Second. — He further declared, That on the 18th of April he failed under Convoy from Spithead to Torbay, and thence to Lisbon, pursuant to his Sailing Orders; and on the 3d of May arrived at Lisbon. — That the

Sailing from Torbay to Lisbon was failing far out of the direct Courie from Torbay to Gibraltar or Mahon, and he might, if Wind and Weather had permitted, have failed to Gibraltar or Mahon without touching at Lisbon; and as he did this in Obedience to his Sailing Orders, he demands a Satisfaction for Months Delay of the Voyage.

Third. — He further declares. That at Lisbon, the Commissioners ought to have found proper Convoy, but they did not find Convoy from the Time of the Arrival at Lisbon, until the 24th Day of July; whereby the Voyage was delayed contrary to the Meaning of the Charter Party.

Fourth. — He further declared, That on 24th of July, lie was ordered by Captain Osborne to fail lrotn Lisbon under his Convoy; that he did so; and at Sea, Captain Osborne ordered him to return to Lisbon \ which he did, and staid till the 50th of August, for want of Convoy, which was a further Delay to the Voyage.

Fijth. — He further declared, that on the 30th he failed from Lijloon under Convoy, and on the 14th of September arrived at Gibraltar, and was there ordered to unload. — That the Convoy did not fail with the Expedition it might, which delayed the Voyage Ten Days.

Sixth. — He also declared for the Freight.

Upon the First Count for the Detention at Spithead, the Defendants paid the Demurrage into Court, and also the Freight upon the last Count: — Upon the Second Count, for going to Lisbon from Torbay out of the Course to Gibraltar, the Jury gave One Penny Damages: — Upon the Third Count, for not finding Convoy at Lisbon from the 3d May to 24th July, the Jury gave Damages £. 641.4 s.jd. — Upon the Fourth Count, for Delay through Want of Convoy from the 24th July to the 30th August, the Jury gave Damages /. 30. And upon the Fifth Count, for Delay in failing from Lisbon to Gibraltar, the Jury gave Damages ^.35. 15s. $d. The whole Amount of the Damages added together, do come to the Rate of ft. 12. per Ton per Month, which is the Rate of Demurrage agreed upon in the Charter Party; but all the Sums separately taken do not correspond with that Rule, with respect to the Number of Days of each Detainer.

And the Attorney General, by his Answer, said, he was a Stranger to these Matters, but hoped the Court would take Care the Commissioners, or the Crown, were not charged with the Plaintiffs Demands, other than such as should clearly appear to be reasonable and just.

December 1752. Mr. Downes having replied to the Answers, and Itfue being joined, divers Witnesses were examined on both Sides, and the Cause came oil to be heard on several Days: And, on the 21st February 1753, the Court ordered and decreed, that the Bill should be, and was retained for a Year, with Liberty, in the mean Time, for the Plaintiff to bring his. Action as he should think proper, and the surviving Commissioners to admit the Execution of the Charter Party, mentioned in the Pleadings, in the Cause, as their Act and Deed, and all further Direct ions were thereby reserved, for which Purpose, all Parties were at Liberty to resort back to the Court from time to time, as there should be Occasion.

27th Nov. 1753. The Plaintiff appealed, from the Decree of the Court of Exchequer, to the House of Lords, praying their Lordships to reverie the Decree, or grant him such Relief as they should fee meet.

1754, January 28th and 29th. On the 28th and 29th of January the Appeal was heard, when their Lordships were pleased to order, that in the Decree, after the Words be retained for," the Words "aYear"be left out, and the Words "Two Years" be inserted instead thereof; and that after the Words " for the Plaintiff to " bring," the Words " his Action" be left out, and the Words " an Action in the Name of the said Henry Harley" inserted instead thereof; and that after the Words " as their Act and Deed," these Words be added,

" And in case the Deposition of the said Henry Harley " shall be offered to be read at the Trial of the said " Action, the Respondents shall not make any Objection thereto by reason of his being named Plaintiff, in

such Action, and saving to the said Respondents all " other Objections, either to the Competency or Credit " of the said Henry Harley; and upon the Consent of " the Respondent’s Counsel at the Bar, it is further " ordered, that notwithstanding the Death of the said " Henry Harley, the Appellant be at Liberty to proceed " in his Name, as if living, and "no Advantage to be " taken on the said Trial, or by Writ of Error, on " account of his, Death: And it is further ordered " and adjudged, that with these Variations and Additions, the said Decree be, and the same is hereby " affirmed."

Thirdly. — For the Demurrage of the Ship at Spithead, from the 8th of March to the 18th of April, at 12 per Ton, according to the Charter Party.

Fourthly. — For that after the Detainer at Spithead, the Plaintiff, on 18th April 1744, in pursuance of Sailing Orders from Commodore Murray, failed -front Spithead to Lisbon; but the Convoy would not permit him to fail with such Expedition as she might have done, but kept him Three Days at ’Torbay, without just Cause.

Fifthly. — That after the Detention at Torbay, viz. 23d April, she failed under said Convoy to Lisbon, and arrived there the 3d May; and was left there by 12 Men of War: That failing from Spithead to Torbay and Lisbon, was failing out of the Course of the Voyage from Spithead to Gibraltar or Mahon, and was unnecessary, and without Cause, and the Ship could and ought to have failed from Spithead to Gibraltar or Mahon, without touching at Torbay or Lisbon; and the Wind and Weather would have permitted it: That the Plaintiff on the 20th May made his Protest of these Detainers; and his being left at Lisbon: — That when she was left there, the Ship was ready to have failed from Lisbon to Gibraltar or Mahon, and the Wind would have permitted j and the Commissioners ought, according to the Charter Party, to have provided a proper Convoy, which they neglected to do till the 30th of August; and that before and at the making the Charter Party, the Plaintiff was bound on a Voyage with the Ship from London to Nevis, to take in a Cargo of Sugars there of the Growth of 1744, to be brought to London, for which Purpose (after the Charter Party, viz. 2d December) the Ship was fitted out with 12 Months Provisions for the said Voyage to Gibraltar and Mahon, and after being dischargea at Gibraltar or Mahon, the Ship was to have failed to Nevis, and there to have received Sugars of the Growth of 1744, to be brought to London; and so to finish her Voyage Out and Home; but by failing to Torbay and Lisbon, and being detained there, said intended Voyage to Gibraltar or Mahon and Nevis, and so to London, Was totally defeated: — That Defendants were requested to satisfy Plaintiff for the Damages occasioned by the Deviation, and Detention at Torbay and Lisbon, but that they had not made him any Satisfaction for the Damages occasioned by the Deviation and Detention, which they ought to have done according to the Charter Party.

Sixthly. — That after the Detentions at Torbay and Lisbon, the Ship failed the 30th August from Lisbon for

Gibraltar, but was detained Twelve Days on the Sea; and arrived at Gibraltar the 14th of September; and on the 15th made his Protest, and claims a Satisfaction for that Detainer.

Seventhly. — That the Ship was detained at from the 14th of September, till the 23d of October, without being unloaded, though Plaintiff was required to and did go into the Harbour and moor his Ship

22

there; and was ready so havfe unloaded her Cargo, or to have proceeded, without mooring the Ship at Gibraltar, directly from thence to Mahon: — That being detained at Gibraltar was a great Expence in Wages and Provisions, and refitting the Ship beyond Sea; and totally prevented his fitting her at Home j and receiving and carrying an Outward bound Freight from thence in 1745 That after the Arrival at Gibraltar, the Wind was fair fof failing to Mahon; and the Commissioners ought to have found a proper Convoy for that Purpose; but they did not, till the 30th of October, provide a proper Convoy, but neglected so to do, and thereby obstructed him from proceeding; for which they ought to have made Satisfaction, but refuse.

Eighthly. — That on the 23d of October, the Plaintiff, pursuant to Admiral Osborne's Orders, failed from Gibraltar, and, arrived at Mahon the 13th of;

and was ready to have delivered her Cargo, which the did on the 12th of December-, and took a Receipt from Mr. Revell, whereby there became due for Freight £. 267, which the Commissioners have not paid.

Ninthly. — That the Ship was detained at Mahon, Six Days beyond the Twenty working Days for which there became due for Demurrage £. 15. 15s. 6 which Plaintiffs have not paid.
