Mr. Brick dale reported from the Committee, to whom

the Petition of Henry Webb, Agent for Glover

and John Bill, Merchants and Co-partners, in the City of Bristol, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad contained in the said Petition} and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place} and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read} and is as followeth; viz.

The Petitioner informed your Committee, That he is Mailer of the Snow Betjey and Hannah belonging to Bristol; that Melfrs. Glover and Bill, in July lall, sent Orders to their Agent at James River, in Virginia, to get ready a Cargo of Wheat against the Arrival of the Snow: — That me lailed for her Voyage from Bristol the Third of August, but meeting with tempestuous Weather and great Damage, did not arrive in Virginia, till the Twelfth of October, which was a Voyage of Eleven Weeks: — That the usual Voyage is not more than Six or Seven WeeksThat by reason of the unavoidable Repairs necessary, (he could not be loaded and cleared from the Custom House there till the 24th of December: — That meeting with bad Weather in her Return, and shipping many oeas, (he did not arrive at Bristol, till the 4th of February last, which was after the Time limited by Act of Parliament, for importing Corn Duty freeThat the said Glover and Bill then applied to the Treasury and the Custom House in London, for Liberty to land the Wheat Duty free, or to re-export it: — That such Liberty could not be obtained; but upon depositing £.155 for the Duty they were allowed to land a Part to examine the Condition of the whole Cargo) when it appeared very much damaged, by having shipped so many Seas; and by the Ship being weakened in her Sides by the bad Weather: — That the Wheat continues to grow much worse, and is not fit for any foreign Market.

Ordered, That Mr. Brickdale have Leave to make a Motion.

And he moved the House accordingly.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to taker penmaen into Consideration. the Report which was made from the Maur Committee, to whom the Petition of the Nobility and R®»d. Gentry, Inhabitants of the several Counties of North Wales, on Behalf of themselves and others, and all the Nobility, Gentry, and others, travelling through the County of Carnarvon to Ireland, by Way of Holyhead, was referred.

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth,

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition;

Terence Pendegrace Williams, Hugh Davies, John Parry,

Hugh Lloyd, Esquires, and Hugh Griffith, Clerk, being severally examined, said. That the Road over Maur, is the shortest Communication between London and Holyhead, the Station of the Packets that pass from England to Dublin.

That the Tolls of the Turnpike Road in the County of Carnarvon, and from the Mountain of Penmaen Maur, through that Part of the Turnpike Road, which is not more than 15 Miles in Extent, are yet higher than the Tolls upon any Turnpike Road whatever.

That these very heavy Tolls will, in the Opinion of the Witnesses, be barely sufficient to make even that short Extent of a Turnpike Road, as it pafles through a Country naturally almost inaccessible.

That the Road of Penmaen Maur, which extends for more than a measured Mile upon the Edge of a most dangerous Precipice, in some Parts more than 30 ©Feet in Height, is now so much undermined by the Sea, that in many Places the Road is so much wore away, that it is not more than 6 Feet 5 Inches in Breadth, without any Protection from the Danger of the Precipice.

That the present Road will admit of only One Carriage to pass.

That the Mountain, which rises to a very great Height above the Road, is covered entirely with loose Stone and broken Rock, which frequently falls, and not only renders the Road often impassable, but extremely hazardous to all Travellers.

That His Majesty’s Lord Lieutenants in travelling to Holyhead to embark for Dublin, have been detained at the Town of Conway, till the Road has with infinite Labour been cleared of the large Quantities of broken Rock and loose Stones, that have rendered the Road for some Time impassable.

That the Mail and Exprefies going to and from Ireland, are frequently delayed by the Danger and Impossibility of passing this Road.

That the Road from Penmaen Maur, has at a very S P great

great Expence, and with infinite Labour, been supported fqr many Years by the Inhabitants of North Wales, and by very large Subscriptions from belaud; and that the Inhabitants of North Wales are unable any longer to support so great an Expence.

That a new Road at the Foot of Penmatn Maur has been planned, and estimated by an eminent Surveyor, which Estimate amounts to 3000.

That by this new intended Road, if carried into Execution, a certain and safe Communication will be formed between London and Holyhead, and will be of mutual Advantage to Great Britain and Ireland.

That all Intelligence between the Two Kingdoms, will be more certain and more expeditious.

That a great Expence will be saved to Government, by the Embarkation of Troops from Holyhead to Dublin, where they will be landed immediately for the Defence of the Capital of Ireland, and more conveniently stationed in Times of War or Invasion.

That by the intended new Road, the very dangerous Passage from Park-gate to Dublin may be avoided, which Passage is subject to great Delays and moil imminent Danger.

That the Port of Holyhead is so well situated for the Station of the Packets, that almost in all Weather the Packets pass from Holyhead to Dublin; that the Passage is frequently performed in Seven Hours, and generally in Eleven Hours.

That it has never been remembered, that the Packets ia passing from Holyhead to Dublin, have ever been loft.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as follows; viz.

Mr. Jeremiah Prendergarfi* a Coal Whipper, being examined, said, the Coal Undertakers have deduced from him and the rest of the Coal-heavers, Three Half-. pence per Score, without regard to the Price — That the Price is from One Shilling to Three Shillings per Score — and that when a Ship is unloaded, each Man pays One Pdhny to the Servant of the House — that they are obliged to take Beer, whether they work or not t and when they work, each Man takes a Pot of Beer on < board. — If they do not take Beer from the Coal Undertakers Houses, they are dismissed. — In opposition to the Office under the Act, the Coal Undertakers introduced a new Set of People, under the Name of Basket-Men, and gave them Two-pence per Scare more than, the Office Price, until the Office was (hut up, when they reduced the Price to its former State, and deducted Three Half pence per Score — no Obligation to take Beer

while the Office was open. — That the Office was again opened in July last — and that many of the Coal-heavers now work under the Direction of the Office; that the Coal Undertakers won’t employ any Labourers that pay to the Office, if they can get any that do not.

James Neal,a Coal Whipper, said, That the Coal Undertakers have deducted Three Pence out of One Shilling — a Score from One Shilling to Two Shillings and Six-pence j he has received Two Shillings per Score — that he worked a Ship of Ten Score at Twa Shillings per Score, for which he received Eighteen Shillings, and the Coal Undertaker took the other Two Shillings. — That last Christmas was Twelve Months he-worked a Ship of about Thirteen Score at One Shilling, for which a Deduction was made of Threfc Pence per Score. — That Labour is lower in Winter than Summer, Work being then scarce, of which they take Advantage. — The Undertakers give the Preference to those that allow the greatest Deductions.

Being asked, What Service the Coal Undertakers do them for the Money they flop

He said, None at all; if no Undertakers they should not be obliged to go to their Houses to spend their Money. VThe Office (tops One Shilling per Pound out of their Labour which is applied to defray the Charge of the Office, and to support their Poor, and bury their Dead.

Owen Harrington* a Coal Whipper, said. He and Eight more worked the Ship Dulje, Captain last

Chrijhnas was Twelve Months, for James Man* that the Work came to betwixt 11 and 12 and he stopt Jj. as a Drawback. — That their Gang, about Three Years ago, agreed with the Mailer of a Ship to unload her at 18 d. per Score; upon Application to the Master for their Wages, they were directed to go to Mr. Man. — Mr. Man would not pay them without an Allowance of Three Pence per Score; and they were obliged to arrest the Master for their Wages — That they are obliged to take a Pot of Beer a-piece on board, and another at Night, which Beer is not fit for Christians to drink * and if they do not comply with this, they will not employ than. Mr. Vane reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor and several of the Aldermen and Common Council of the City of Bath; and also, the' Petition of William Pulteney, Esquire, and Frances, his Wife, for and on Behalf of themselves, and of Henrietta Laura Pulteney, their Infant Daughter; were severally

referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the Houte; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First mentioned Petition, Mr. George Bee, being examined, said. That if the Bill depending in this House, intituled, An Act to impower the Trustees of the Will of the late General Pulteney to purchase, and exchange Lands and Grounds in the Manor of Bathwick, in the County of Somerset, for the Purpose of making certain Roads and Ways to and from a FreeBridgo, by them intended to be built over the River Avon, in the said County, and also to impower the Persons in Possession of the Estate for the Time being, under the said Will, to grant Leases of certain Lands and Houses in the said Manor, and like-wite to enable the said Trustees to grant certain Grounds, and Springs of Water, within the said Manor of Bathwick, to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens of Bath, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; should pass into a Law, and the intended Bridge shall be built, it may be attended with great public Inconvenience, unless a Claute is interted in the said Bill for extending the Jurisdiction of the Magistrates of the said City, over the Manor of Bathwick, or some Part thereof; for otherwise Felons, and Persons guilty of Crimes, would have an easy Method, by Means of the said Bridge, of escaping from Punishment, by going out of the Jurisdiction of the said City.

And it appeared to your Committee, That on the 24th of December 1768, Mr. Pulteney did lay before the Corporation of Bath Articles in Writing, setting forth his Intention of building a Bridge as mentioned in the said Bill, and agreeing to the Extension of the Jurisdiction of the Magistrates of the said City, over the said Manor, or Part of it; and the Corporation did, upon the ad o{ January 1769, come to the following Resolution at

a Hall duly summoned for that Purpose: " It is agreed " that Mr. Pulteney shall have Liberty to build a Bridge.

" from Bath to Bathwick, at or near the present Ferry,

" the Corporation allowing him a Way thereto from " High Street, provided he purchases at his own Expence

" from the present Possessors, such Houses and Lands as " interfere with the said Way, and are not in the Pofief- fion of the Corporation.*

To prove the Allegations of the Second mentioned Petition, John Garden, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Manor of Bathwick is the Property of Mrs. Pulteney; that in that Part of the District over which the Jurisdie-

Vol. 32,

rilis. ' 457

>; tion of the Magistrates of the City of Bath is intended to be extended, there are no other Houses but a Miller’s House, a Corn Mill, a Fulling Mill, and Spring Garden, which are occupied by William Pur die, and JoJias Robins, and also some Fields which are occupied by Betty Smith, who have contented to the Extension of the Jurisdiction of the Magistrates of the said City.

And the Witness said it would be of great Convenience to the said City, and to the Public, if the Powers and Jurisdiction of the Magistrates of the said City were extended over Part of the said Manor of Bathwick.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee; to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled;

An Act to impower the Trustees of the Will of the late General Pulteney to purchase and exchange Lands and Grounds, in the Manor of Bathwick, in the County of Somerset, for the Purpose of making certain Roads and Ways to and from a Free Bridge; by them intended to' be built over the River Avon, in the said County; and also to impower the Persons in Possession of the said Estate for the Time being, under the said Will, to-grant Leases of certain Lands and Houses in the said Manor, and likewise to enable the said Trustees to grant certain Grounds, and Springs of Water, within the said Manor of Bathwick, to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens of Bath; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; is committed; that they have power to make Provision in the find Bill, for extending the Jurisdiction and certain Powers of the: Magistrates of the City of Bath, over a Part of the Manor of Bathwick.

It might have been expected that the Contracts made for the Hire of Vessels, which carried such confid'erable Sums, would have been produced for taking up the Apollo, after the Conclusion of the War.

In regard of the Reasons given by Mr. Stephens, and hereto annexed, let the Whole of all these Papers be allowed of.

The Contracts for the Hire of Tenders were made by the Commissioner, who kept them in his Office, and did not give Copies of them to the Accountant, because, as he apprehends there were not any Clauses in them which related to the Naval Officers: And in regard to the Apollo Tender, taken into the Service after the Conclusion of the War, the Accountant apprehends, that the Commander in Chief gave satisfactory Reasons for her being employed, at the Time he wrote to him to contract for her, and that he was not authorized to demand any other Reasons, than what were contained in the Preamble to the Order for paying the Hire of her.

Moran, and by Robert , Chief Mate, Laurence Farrell, Second Mate, Robert , Car-

penter, Michael Everly, Christian Cock., and ‘Thomas Silvia, Seamen, of and belonging to the said Ship; Hercules Rice, and Thomas , Passengers on

board her, the same Day; wherein he declares as follows:

That the said Snow being of the Burthen of 180 Tons or thereabouts, properly-equipt, and loaded with Sugar, Rum, Wine, and sundry other Merchandize, failed from St. Kitts, bound for London, on the 14th March then last pad.

That on the 22d Day of April aforesaid, about Eight in the Morning, the Wind being at South by West, and in the fair Way proceeding on his Voyage up Channel, and being near a-breast of the Start, Distance or 5 Leagues; One of His Majesty’s Tenders brought the Vessel to, and imprefied Three of their best Seamen, and, in lieu of them, the Commander of the Tender put on board the Snow Three very indifferent Men; viz. — One a Taylor, who had never been on board a Ship above Three Weeks — another a Bricks layer who had never acted as a Sailor for more than Three Months — and the Third a Husbandman, who had never been on board a Ship as a Sailor more than a Fortnight before that Time: and, as they l'everally declared to the said Master and others above named, wholly unacquainted with the Navigation of a Ship or Vessel.

That he attempted afterwards to proceed on his Voyage, and next Day, being 23d, about Seven in the Evening, being between Pepperell , and the,

at lead Four Leagues from the Land, with the Wind at South South East; another Tender belonging to His Majesty’s Ship Royal George, and whereof Richard Williams, Sixth Lieutenant of the said Ship was the Commander, fired a Shot over the said Snow, which' dropped within Thirty or Forty Yards on the Starboard Side, in order to bring the said Vessel to.

That the said Moran being apprehensive of the Indraft of the Island, and the Distress the Snow was then in, consulted with his Officers and Crew what was best to be done under their unhappy Circumstances,- having a just Dread of losing their Ship and Cargo; and it was thereupon determined to make Sail, to avoid being brought to; but that Attempt soon appearing ffuitlels, he, with the Approbation of his Mate and Crew, brought to.

That the said Lieutenant , notwithstanding

the distressed Condition of the said Snow as aforesaid, carried away another, the best Seaman left on board, and in his stead left one Nicholas Mahon; assuring the said Master that the said Mahon was a Seaman and a Helmf-man; which said Nicholas had the Helm at the Time of the Accident herein after mentioned.

That after the Snow was detained in Manner aforesaid, till near 12 o’Clock, in which Time (he unavoidably made a great Leeway, the said Lieutenant left her.

That the said Master being greatly fatigued under the Whole of this Transaction, having first given Directions to his Second Mate, Laurence Farrell, to steer a direct East South East Course, laid himself down to get a little Rest j and, in Two Hours Time, the said Vessel was on Shore, the said Mahon being at the Helm, and struck near Atherfield Rocks, and notwithstandinghe, the Master,

got out an Anchor, and used all other possible Means to get her off, (be parted her Cable, and soon went on Shore; and, a prodigious large and folding Ground Sea going at that Instant, soon broke to Pieces, and was' totally loft, together with the greatest Part of the Cargo.

That by Means of the Confusion he was put into, the Distress the Ship was left in, and other the Premises particularly described; the said Ship, and Part of her' Cargo, was totally loft, and not by Means of any Neglect or Default of him or any of his Ship’s Company.

To prove the Value of the Ship Francis at the Time Ihe failed from London;

Alexander Clunie, a Merchant, formerly a Commander of a Ship, acquainted, with the Outfit of Ships between London and Carolina, and with Shipping, above 30 Years; having inspected an original Account of the nrft Cost at Boston of the Ship Francis, formerly proved by Mr. Alderman Trecothick, a Member of the Committee, upon a Calculation made, declared the Ship, fitted as (he was, must, at the Time of her (ailing, be worth about 11 or £.12 per Ton.

And, being further examined, declared, That to be let by the Month to the Government, and to be insured by them, (lie was worth about £. 140 per Month.

To shew by Analogy from a Determination in a similar Cale, That the Charter Party for the Francis was broke, by Law; Dalby produced the Record of the Court of King's Bench, in the Cause between Black and the Commissioners of Victualling, and the Postea indorsed thereon; and several Rules of the Court of King's in that Cause; whereby it appeared,

That the Jury on the Trial of that Cause found Two Fads, to wit. That Government were to find the Convoy; and, that there was no Necessity for the Ship’s going into Lisbon: And they assessed the Damages for taking the Ship in there, at One Penny.

That the Verdict found was subject to the Opinion of the Court, whether a new Trial should be granted or not; and, in Easter Term 1747, the Court, on folema Argument, established the Verdict of the Jury, and refused a new Trial.

Dalby produced a Report of the Commissioners of Victualling to the Lords of the Admiralty, bearing Date 27 April 1764, upon a Reference to them of a Petition presented by Dalby and Downes to His Majesty, praying to be relieved, in respect to some Hardships, whereby they alledged Dalby and his Family had been injured: Upon which, the Commissioners were directed to re-consider what had before passed between their Lordships and the Commissioners on that Subject; and to lay before them a full State of the Cafe, with their Opinion thereon.

Whereby it appears. That the Commissioners in that Report omitted to date the Penny Breach above mentioned, in the Trial of Black and the Commissioners, and the Two several Facts found by the Jury, as above mentioned — And,

That in their said Report, in dating the Charter Party for the Ship Hope, they omitted to (late that the Ship was to proceed on the Voyage, Wind and Weather permitting — that the Owner was bound in a large,

for the true Performance of the Charter Party — And for what was to be paid, done, and performed on his Part, the Commissioners had set the Seal of Office.

The Commissioners of Victualling, as a Justification of their Conduct, in refusing to pay Dalby any more Money on account of the said Ship Francis, than the Freight stipulated by the Charter Party, and Demurrage at the same Rate as had been allowed by them to other Ships, which had been hired for the same Service; having produced the Record in the Court of Exchequer, in a Cause between Harley and the Commissioners of Victualling, touching the Ship; whereby it appeared, That the Jury in that Trial had found a Verdict for the Plaintiff, and assessed the Damages at £.1,307.135. 2\d. And having, for the same Purpose, proved "by the Evidence of Robert Baxter, the Commissioners Solicitor, That they bad, on the 17th January 1756, tendered to Dalby the Sum of £. 939. 17 4 as a full

Satisfaction with what they had before paid him, for all his Damages on account of the Ship Francis; and had shewn to him at the same Time, by a Computation thereof in Writing, that the same was made up agreeable to the Verdict in the Court of King’s Bench, in the Cause of Black and Bliss, and the Verdict in the Court of Exchequer above mentioned;

JJalby referred to the Evidence herein before stated, touching the said Trial in the King’s Bench, and as to the Verdict in the Exchequer, in the Cause of the Hope.

‘He produced Two of the Jurors on that Trial, to wit, John Irish, and Charles Coster, who being severally examined, declared to the following Effect; That, upon the Cause being opened, and a Witness called for the Plaintiff, the Counsel for the Crown would not admit

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a mod. His gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Majesty* Parliament, as followeth; viz. Peec

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

pjAving thought it necessary to give so early a Com-, mencement to the present Session of Parliament, I ani glad to find, that, by your Zeal and Assiduity in the Dispatch of the Tublic Business, I am now enabled to’ relieve you from your Attendance, before the Season of the Year is too far advanced.

I cannot put an End to the Session, without expressing My entire Approbation of your Conduct: and thanking you for that clear Demonllration which your Pro-, ceedings, through the whole Course of the Session, have afforded to all the World, of the affectionate Attachment of My Parliament to My Person and Govetnment, as well as of their Heady Adherence to the true Intercll of their Country.

It

9 Geo. III. 9sMail — 14° Junii — .19° — 2o° 453

It was with much Satisfaction that I observed your particular Attention £0 those great National Objects, which, at the Opening of the Session, I recommended to your more immediate Consideration. The Result of your Deliberations respecting the late Acquisitions in the' East Indies has shewn, that you were not more attentive to the immediate Benefit arising therefrom, in point of Revenue, than to the securing, at all Events, the permanent commercial , Interests of this Country; and guarding against every possible Discouragement to Our own Manufactures, and to the Industry of My Subjects. What more remains to be done for securing the Possession of those valuable Acquisitions, you will, I doubt not, proceed to provide for with all convenient Dispatch at your next Meeting.

The Measures which I had taken regaiding the late unhappy DisturbaRces in North America, have been already laid before you. They have received your Approbation; and you have assured Me of your firm Support in the Prosecution of them. Nothing in My Opinion could be more likely to enable the well-disposed among My Subjects in that Part of the World, effectually to discourage and defeat the Designs of the Fadious and Seditious, than the hearty Concurrence of every Branch of the Legislature in the Resolution of maintaining the Execution of the Laws in every Part of My Dominions; and there is nothing I more ardently wish for, than to fee it produce that good Effect.

With respect to Foreign Affairs, My own Determination, as well as the Assurances given Me by the other Powers of Europe, continue the fame, as I communicated to you at the Beginning of this, Session. And however unfuccesful My Attempts have proved for preventing the unfortunate Rupture which has happened between Raffia and the Porte, I shall not fail to use My good Offices towards restoring Peace between those Powers j and, I trust that the Calamities of War will not extend to any other Part of Europe.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

My particular Thanks are due to you, as well for the Supplies which you have granted Me for the Services of the current Year, as for the Provision which you have made, for enabling Me to discharge the Debt incurred upon Account of My Civil Government. Your Rea-diness in relieving Me from the Difficulties increasing upon Me from the Continuance of that Debt, I shall ever consider as an additional Motive for Me to endeavour to confine the Expences of My Civil Government within such Bounds, as the Honour of My Crown can possibly admit.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It gives Me great Concern to be obliged to recommend to you, with more than ordinary Earnestness, that you would all, in your several Countries, exert your utmost Efforts for the Maintenance of public Peace, and of good Older, among My People. You must be fen-fible, that whatever obstructs, in any Degree, the regular Execution of the Laws, or weakens the Authority of the Magistrate, must lessen the only Security which My People gan have for the undisturbed Enjoyment of their Rights and Liberties. From your Endeavours in this Common Cause I promise Myself the most salutary Effect. On My Part, no Countenance or Support shall be wanting: For as I have ever made, and ever shall make, Our excellent Constitution the Rule of My own Conduct, so shall I always consider it as equally My Duty to exert every Power with which that Constitution has intrusted Me, for preserving it lafe from Violation of every Kind; being fully convinced, that, in so doing, I tKa.Il most effectually provide for the true Interest and Happiness of my People.

After which, the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, Laid;

Ufoal Orders. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Elediou of any Member to serve

in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement to the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

V©L. 32.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, to be heard at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of PriviT leges and Elections, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed either by the House, or the Committee of Privileges and Elections, as the Matter to be heard shall be before the House or the said Committee, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguiso-ing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting: And that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him j and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Care,/ that, from Eleven, of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall mall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the Passage leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise,' therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster j and that he do fee the same put in Execution,

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody hut by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That to prevent the intercepting, or losing, of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petitions for private Bills after the ioth Day of February next.

A Petition of Sir Rowland Winn, Baronet, and Edward Winn, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners being Candidates at the late Election for Members to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of in

the County of York, were duly elected by a very great Majority of the Persons qualified to vote by the Constitution of the said Borough, as declared by the last Determination of the House of Commons; but that William Crezve, Esquire, the Mayor of the said Borough, presidingat the said Election as Returning Officer, conducted the Poll with the most apparent Partiality to the Interest of William Lord Viscount Gallway, and Henry

Strachey, Esquire, the other Candidates, rejecting without any good Reason assigned, or any just Exception, a very great Majority of the Persons entitled to vote by the Constitution of the said Borough, the last Determination of this House, and the Statutes making such Determination final; and that under Colour of an unfair Majority obtained through these, and divers other arbitrary and illegal Practices of the said Mayor, the said Lord Viscount Gallway and Henry Strachey have been returned by the said Mayor, as having been duly elected to represent the said Borough in Parliament, contrary to the Truth, the last Resolution of this House concerning the Right of Election for the said Borough, in Defiance of the Laws and Constitution requiring fair and free Elections, in manifest Violation of the Rights of the EleClors, and to the great Injury of the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give the Petitioners such Relief as they shall appear to merit, and to do further therein, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard

at the Bar of this House, upon ethwrjday the First Day of February next.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Electors for Members to lerve in Parliament for the Borough of PontefraEl, in the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That at the late Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, the Petitioners and many other of the Inhabitants, House-holders, resident within the said Borough, being a very great Majority of the Persons legally entitled by the Constitution of the said Borough, and the last Determination of this House to vote on that Occasion, gave their Voices for Sir Rowland Winn, Baronet, and Edward Winn, Esquire; but that William Lord Viscount Gallway, and Henry Strachey, Esquire, the other Candidates, having found Means to engage in their Interest, William Crewe, Esquire, the then Mayor of the said Borough, who presided as Returning Officer at the said Election, took upon himself to reject the Votes of the Petitioners and divers others, who voted for the said Sir Rowland Winn and Edward Winn, under various Pretences, all cither void of Foundation in Truth, or though true, insufficient, as the Petitioners conceive, to support any solid Objection to the Votes so rejected; and particularly, that the Mayor pretended that the Quality of a Freehold of Burgage Tenure, wasamong the Requisitesto a Qualification to vote, and that the Petitioners and others, not having Burgage Tenements, had not any Right to give their Votes, although the last Resolution of this House concerning the Right of Election for the said Borough, was produced and proved, at the said Election; whereby, and by the Statute made in confirmation of the Resolution of this House, the Petitioners conceive, the Privilege of the Petitioners, and all other the Inhabitants, Householders, resident in the said Borough, to vote for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was established and confirmed, and the said Mayor ought not to have violated or impeached the fame; and that the said Mayor, regardless of the just Rights of the Petitioners, permitted a great Number of Persons who had no Right, to poll for the said Lord Gallway and Henry Strachey; and that, by these, and divers other partial and illegal Practices of the said Mayor, and of the said Lord Gallway and Henry Strachey, a colourable Majority was obtained for them against the said Sir Rowland Winn and Edward Winn; and the said Mayor has unduly returned the said Lord Gallway and Henry Strachey, in Prejudice of the Petitioners, and also

of the said Sir Rowland Winn and Edward Winn, who were duly elected, and ought to have been returned; and that the Petitioners, thus unjustly stript of their Franchises, and they, with the Electors in general, deprived of the Representatives of their Choice, and having others imposed on them, whom they have not chosen, can have no adequate Redress but from this House: And therefore praying. That their Rights and Privileges may be preserved to them; and that this House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration, and to do therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, at the same Time that the Matter of the Petition of Sir Rowland Winn, Baronet, and Edward Winn, Esquire, is heard.

Number of the Eledors of the said Borough, being assembled in a certain Place called The Croft, in or near the said Borough, the said Walden Hanmer made very large Promises of Presents and Rewards to the Electors, if he, the said Walden Hanmer, should be elected and returned to represent the said Borough in Parliament; and the said Walden Hanmer did afterwards, on the same Day, in the public Street of the said Borough, make other Promises of the like Nature to many of the Electors of the said Borough; and that the said Thomas Fenn, Abraham Griggs, and Peregrine Clarke, did bribe, and corruptly procure a great Number of the Eledors of the said Borough, to vote for the said Patrick Blake and Walden Hanmer at the said Election; and that by Means of these, and other corrupt, undue, and illegal Practices, the said Patrick Blake and Walden Hanmer did influence and procure a Majority of Votes, although the greatest Part of such Votes were illegal, and ought not to have been taken; and the said Patrick Blake and Walden Hanmer were returned, as having been elected to represent the said Borough in Parliament, in Wrong of the said Thomas Fonnereau, who ought to have been returned; and that the Actions and Proceedings of the said Pdtrick Blake and Walden Hanmer, and the said other Persons acting on their Behalf as aforesaid, being, as the Petitioners conceive, contrary to Justice, in Defiance of the Laws requiring fair and free Elections, and in manifest Violation of the Rights of the Petitioners, and other the free Electors of the said Borough: Therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to do therein as shall seem most meet and convenient.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, at the same Time that the Matter of the Petition of Thomas Fonnereau, Esquire, is heard.

A Petition of Hugh Owen was presented to the House, Pembroke and read; Setting forth, That at the late Election of Ekftion. a Knight of the Shire to serve in Parliament for the County of Pembroke, Sir Richard Philipps, Baronet, and the Petitioner, were Candidates, and that the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned; but that John Griffiths, the High Sheriff, although he in Person presided at the Election, illegally appointed several Attornies at Law, who were Friends to the Sitting Member, as Deputies to determine the Legality of Votes; which Deputies were not sworn to do indifferent Justice between the Candidates, and accordingly not being bound by Oaths or other Security, several of them behaved in the most partial, arbitrary, and illegal Manner; the Deputies in the different Booths acting by different Rules, and determining the same legal Questions directly opposite to each other, as belt suited the Purpose of the Sitting Member; and when Complaint was made early on the Second Day of the Poll, to the High Sheriff, of the unjust and illegal Con-dud of those Deputies, and he was himself desired to determine the Legality of Votes, he immediately withdrew from the Polling Places, and wholly absented himself from the Business of the Election until the Poll was just finished, which was late the following Day, when he came back to the Booths to make his Return, but refused to hear any Objections, and denied a Scrutiny of the Votes, though demanded by the Petitioner; and that by these and many other unwarrantable Practices of the said Sheriff, his Deputies, and also of the Agents of the said Sir Richard Philipps, many Persons were admitted to vote for the said Sir Richard Philipps, who were not duly qualified, and many were refused to poll for the Petitioner, who had an undoubted Right to vote* whereby a pretended Majority was procured for the said Sir Richard Philipps, and he has been accordingly returned to serve in Parliament in the said County, in manifest Prejudice of the Petitioner, and in open Defiance of the Law: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioner such Relief therein, as upon Examination shall appear just.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Tuesday the 13th Day of February next.

Election. Esquires, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. A Petition of Joseph Bullock, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the County Borough of Carmarthen, the Petitioner and Griffith Phillips, Esquire, were Candidates, and Vaughan Esquire, and George Phillips, Esquire, the Sheriffs of the said County Borough, were the Returning Officers; and that, during the Poll, the said Sheriffs behaved themselves with the utmost Partiality in Favour of the said Griffith Phillips, by refusing several Persons to give their Votes, who offered to vote for the Petitioner, and who had an undoubted Right so to do, and by accepting the Votes of several Persons in Favour of the said Griffith Phillips, who had, as the Petitioner humbly apprehends, and is advised, no Right to vote in the said Election; by which Means, and by other undue Proceedings, a pretended Majority hath been procured in Favour of the said Griffith Phillips, and he hath been thereupon returned by the said Sheriffs, as the Member to serve in Parliament for the said County Borough, in Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had a clear Majority of the legal Votes tendered at such Election, and ought to have been returned the Member to serve in Parliament for the said County Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as shall seem just.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Thursday the 15th Day of February next.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Burgesses and Electors of the County Borough of Carmarthen, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That for the Space of Twenty Years and upwards, the Petitioners and others, to the Number of Twenty, have been Burgesses of the County Borough of Carmarthen, and as such are intitled to vote for a Member to serve in Parliament for the fame; that during all such Time the Petitioners have continued in full Enjoyment of such Right, without any Impeachment or Pretence of Interruption whatsoever, until the last Election for a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, when Joseph Bullock and Griffith Phillips, Esquires, were Candidates, upon which Occasion the Petitioners, and such other Persons as aforesaid, severally tendered their Votes as usual to Vaughan Horton and George Phillips, Esquires, the then Sheriffs and Returning Officers, in Favour of the said Joseph Bullock; but the said Sheriffs, though well acquainted with such the subsisting Rights of the Petitioners, and such other Persons as aforesaid, illegally and arbitrarily rejected their several Votes, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners and the free Representation of the said Borough: And therefore praying. That such their Rights and Privileges may be preserved to them; and that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and do therein as shall seem most meet and expedient.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, at the same Time that the Matter of the Petition of Joseph Bullock, Esquire, is heard.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Lands, D-ltt0> and of the several Merchants, Maltsters, and Ship Owners, in the County of Norfolk, whose Names are thereto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by the Encouragement given by several Acts of Parliament for the Exportation of Malt, the Petitioners and others their Neighbours have built and employed a Number of Malt-houses, for the Purpose of manufacturing Barley into Malt for Exportation; that die annual Rents and Taxes of these Houses amount to the Sum of £.4000 a Year, or upwards; and that, in all Seasons when the Price of Barley was under, or did not exceed 24J. a Quarter, the Petitioners could export Malt, and were encouraged so to do by a Bounty; and that, by this Means, Barley of an inferior Quality made into Malt has been immemorially exported; that from the Port of Great Yarmouth only, 250 Sail of Ships have been in some Years employed in this Service; and large Sums of Money have through this Channel been brought into this Kingdom, a great Body of able and useful Seamen have heen employed in exporting Malt, and a great Number of Labourers in manufacturing Barley into Malt; and that the Prohibition, which for Three Years past hath prevented the Exportation of Malt, arising from the high Price of Grain, however useful, hath been severely felt by such Part of the Petitioners as are Occupiers of Malt Houses; and that unless an Exportation of Malt, with the usual Bounty, is granted, at a Time the Price of Barley is reasonable, this valuable.

Branch of Trade will be irretrievably loft to this Kingdom; and the Petitioners apprehend, the Pdrmission of exporting Malt, with the usual Bounty, will be a National Benefit: And therefore praying the House to grant the Petitioners such further Relief in the Preroife? as shall seem meet.

Sir George Osborn reported from the Committee appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty our humble Thanks for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We cannot but look upon it as a very serious Misfortune, that, notwithstanding every Precaution which could beufed for preventing the Communication of the infectious Disorder among the Horned Cattle from Foreign Parts, that most alarming Distemper appears to have again broke out in some Parts of the Kingdom: At the same Time, we are truly sensible of Your Majesty’s Paternal Care and Vigilance for the Security of Your People, in having given the earliest Directions for every Measure to be pursued, that might be most likely to give an immediate Check to the first Spreading of the Infetftion; and we will not fail to take this most important Matter into our immediate Consideration; and to make such Provisions as shall appear best calculated to carry into effectual and complete Execution Your Majesty’s falu-tary Intentions; and thereby, as far as by human Means can be accomplished, to guard against the Danger of so great a Calamity becoming general.

Your faithful Commons have too just a Sense of the Blessings of Peace, and feel with Your Majesty too tender a Concern for the Ease of their Fellow Subjects, not to rejoice at the Prospect which the Assurances given by the other great Powers of Europe afford to Your Majesty, that the present Disturbances will not extend to any Part where the Security, Honour, or Interest of this Nation frnay make it necessary for Your Majesty to become a Party. We have the fullest Confidence that Your Majesty will never be unmindful of those important Objects; and we observe, with great Satisfaction, Your Majesty’s wife Attention to the general Interests of Europe, in Your Determination not to acknowledge any Claims of any of the other Powers of , contrary to the Limitations of the late Treaties of Peace.

We sincerely lament, that Your Majesty’s Endeavours to bring back Your Subjects in America to a just Sense of their Duty have hitherto proved so little successful. The State of Your Majesty’s Government there does undoubtedly well deserve the serious Attention of Parliament; and no Endeavours shall be wanting on our Part, to make effectual Provisions against the unwarrantable Measures carried on in some of Your Majesty’s Colonies, which are so irreconcilable to every Principle of Commercial Subserviency to the Interest of the Mother ‘Country that ought to prevail in Colonies, and which, by attempting to subject the highest legal Authority to the Controul of Individuals, tend to subvert the Foundation of all Government.

‘ Your Majesty may be assured that we will, with the ‘utmost Chearfulness and Dispatch, grant the necessary Supplies for the Service of the current Year.

We acknowledge with the warmest Gratitude, that the Welfare of these Kingdoms has been the constant Object of Your Majesty’s Wishes, and the'unvaried 20

Rule of Your Actions. Permit us, Sir, at the same Time, to offer to Your Majesty our most dutiful Thanks, for the favourable Opinion which Your Majesty is pleated-to entertain of the Conduct of Your Parliament; and to assure Your Majesty, that we will steadily persevere in such Principles as are most agreeable to the true Spirit of this free Constitution, and invariably pursue such Measures as are most conducive to the real Happiness of the People.

Earnestly desirous of justifying to all the World Your Majesty’s gracious Declaration of Your Confidence in us, we will make it our Study to avoid all Heats and Aoimofities, and to cultivate that Harmony amongst ourselves, which, we arc truly sensible, is at this Time peculiarly necessary, to give Weight to our Deliberations, to establish the Prosperity, and to maintain in its true Lustre, the Reputation of this Country.

And while we on our.Part are faithfully executing the Trust reposed in us, by endeavouring to the utmost of our Power to promote these good Ends, we trust that all who live under this happy Constitution will be convinced how indispensably it is their Duty co pay that Obedience to the Laws, and just Reverence to lawful Authority, by which alone their own Rights can be preserved, and the distinguished Blessings which they enjoy above all other Nations be rendered secure and permanent.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s Most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know His Majesty’s Pleasure, when He will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That H is Majesty’s Most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty Yesterday, with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My Sincere Thanks, for your loyal and dutiful Address. I fee with great Pleasure, the Continuance of that Zeal and Public Spirit which I have always experienced from My faithful Commons, in the Affur-ances you give Me of paying an early Attention to the importaht Objects recommended to your Consideration. My Interests, and those of My People, mull ever be the fame, and in pursuing such Measures as are most conducive to their real Happiness, you will give to Me the ttueft and most acceptable Testimony of your Attachment to My Person and Government.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morn* ing next resolve itself into the said Committee.

House, to consider of the Motion made. Yesterday, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty;

feomniness The C,erk informed the House, That Mr. p attend the Speaker was taken ill, and so much out of order that it Services of was impossible for him to attend the Service of the the House. House: That Mr. Speaker had sent for him into his Bedchamber about an Hour ago, and deGred him to express, in the rood grateful Terms, his dutiful Acknowlege-ment to the House, of the great Kindness they had always shewn him, and the Assistance they had given him in the Execution of his Office: That he was extremely sorry that the Public BuGness should meet with any Delay upon his Account, but that he found himself so very ill, and the Nature of his Complaint such, as to make it impossible for him to ascertain when he should be again able to attend his Duty: That he therefore, with great. Concern, mud intreat the House to excuse him at present from any further Attendance on their Service: That Mr. Speaker would have written a Letter to have made his Excuses to the House, but was unable, from the State of Weakness he was in: That he therefore re-» peatedly deGred the Clerk to express his dutiful Thanks to the House for their kind Acceptance of his former Services, and his great Concern that his State of Health should be the Cause of the least Interruption to the Bu-fjness of the Public.

on the Credit thereof; and that the Sum of 3,500 has been borrowed, and duly expended in making the said River navigable, and, for securing the Repayment thereof W'ith interest, did legally veil the said Tolls in the several Subscribers or Proprietors of the said 3,500; that the Petitioner has purchased of the several Proprietors or Subscribers their several Shares and Interests in the said Tolls, lo that the sole Property thereof is now legally vested in the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, redeemable only on Payment of the said Sum of £. 3,500, together with Interest for the same; and that the said principal Sum still remains due to the Petitioner, and a further Sum of 1,217. 19J. for many Years Interest thereof, up to the Third Day of December last, amounting in the Whole to the Sum of £.4717. 19J. and that the Commissioners appointed by the said Act have declined to act any further in carrying the said Act into Execution; by Means whereof, the said Navigation is greatly obstructed, and in feme Parts the River lilted up, Dams broke down. A Petition of fames Dundas, of , Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That at the last Election of a Knight to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Linlithgow, Mr. John , Second Son of the honourable Charles Hope Weir, of C-raigiehall, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that, previous to the said Election, undue Means were used to procure a Majtyity of the Electors in Favour of the said Mr. John Hope, and that great Partiality was committed at adjusting the Roll of Freeholders upon the Day of Election, by admitting Three Persons to vote for the said Mr. John Hope, who at that Time, and do still stand excluded from the Roll by a final Judgment of the Court of Session, which Court has the supreme Cogni- zance of the Qualifications of Freeholders, by several Acts of Parliament in that Behalf made; and that in the same Manner, several Persons, who claimed to be enrolled upon most unexceptionable Titles, were arbitrarily refused to be enrolled, particularly the Claims of Three Persons, who voted under Protest for the Petitioner, were refused, although the pretended Objections to their Qualifications have been over-ruled by an unanimous Judgment of the Court of Session, and their Names arc ordained to be inrolled in the Lift of Freeholders} and that by these, and other improper Methods taken? previous to, and at the Time of the late Election, there were? in Appearance, Twenty Votes for the said Mr. John Hope, and only Fifteen Votes for the Petitioner; and under Colour of such pretended Majority, the said Mr. John Hope did procure himself to be'returned as Knight of the said Shire, although in Fact he was not duly elected, and the Petitioner bad a clear Majority of unexceptionable Votes at the said Election: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioner such Relief as the Circumstances of this same ap--pear to merit; and to do further therein, as shall appear meet.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar*of this House, upon Monday the 12 th Day of Marxh next.

A Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Execution an Act made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for dividing a certain Fen, called the Haute Huntre, Eight Hundr, or Holland Fen, and certain other Commonable Places adjoining thereto, in the Parts of Holland, in the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have divided and allotted the said Fen, according to the Directions of the said Act; and that the Polls and Rails, for many Miles in the Division Fences, which have been erected pursuant to the Directions of the said Act, have been pulled down, and the greatest Part thereof destroyed, together with great Part of the Materials for completing the said Fencing; and that, if the Petitioners were empowered to take down the Remainder of the Poll and Rail Fencing already erected on the said Fen, or such Part thereof as shall be found necessary, and to dispose of the fame, and of such Polls and Rails as have been pulled down and not destroyed, and the Materials provided for completing the said Division Fences which have not yet been made Use of, and, in Lieu thereof, to make Ditches of a sufficient Width and Depth, it would more effectually answer the Intention Of the said Act: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repealing so much of the said Act as directs and limits the particular Method of making the Division Fences, and for empowering the Petitioners to make proper Ditches to serve for Boundaries to the several Allotments, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had di« reded him to report to the House: which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, including One thousand Five hundred and Twenty-two Invalids, amounting to Seventeen thousand Six hundred and Sixty-six effective Men, Commission and Non-Commission Officers included, be employed for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred and Twenty-four thousand Nine hundred and . Ninety-two Pounds and Two Pence be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Seventeen thousand Six hundred and Sixty-six effective Men, for Guards, Garrisons, and other His Majesty’s Land Forces, in Great Britain, Jersey, and GueniJ'ey, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred Eighty-three thousand Two hundred and Forty-eight Pounds One Shilling and Eleven Pence and One Eighth Part of a Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for maintaining His Majesty’s Forces'and Garrisons in, the Plantations and Africa, including those in Garrison at Minorca and Gibraltar, and for Provisions For the Forces in North America, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Gibraltar, the Ceded

Mlanch, and Africa, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand Five hundred and Thirty-three Pounds Twelve Shillings and Eight Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Difference of Pay between the Britfb and Irish Establishment of Five Batallions and Four Compa--VoL. 32,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand Five hundred* and Thirteen Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Full Pay, for Three hundred and Sixty-five Days, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy, to Officers reduced, with the Tenth Company of several Batallions reduced from Ten to Nine Companies, and who remained on Half Pay at the Twenty-fourth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred and Sixty-four Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for the Paying of Pensions to the Widows of such reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, as died upon the Establishment of Half Pay in Great Britain, and were married to them before the Twenty-fifth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Sixteen, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Twenty-three thousand Two hundred and Thirty-three Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account of tire reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, net exceeding One thousand Two hundred and Eighty-nine Pounds One Shilling and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge for Allowances to the several Officers and Private Gentlemen of the Two Troops of Horle Guards reduced, and to the superannuated Gentlemen of the Four Troops of Horse Guards, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Sixty-six thousand Nine hundred and Eighty-four Pounds Eleven Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, Tor the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty thousand Nine hundred and Thirty-three Pounds Ten Shillings and Eight Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Expence of Services performed by the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, and not provided for by Parliament in One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-nine.

The said Resolution*, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring ip a* Bill for punishing Mutiny and Desertion, and for the better Payment of the Army and their Quarters: And that the Lord Barrington and Sir Charles Whitworth do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itfelfinto a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Oidered, That Mr. Thomas Edwards do, upon this Day Sevennight, the ill Day of February next, attend the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of an Act made in the Seventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act to

Well Parts of the Kingdom, and considerably promote the Trade. Agriculture, and Inland Navigation of the fame; And therefore praying. That Leave may be given

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, to prohibit, for a further Time, the Exportation of Corn, Grain, Meal, Malt, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch; and also the Extraction of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat and Wheat Flour* without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue for a further Time an Act made in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act to continue and amend an Act made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for Importation of Salted Beef, Pork, Bacon, and Butter, from Ireland, for a limited Time; and for allowing the Importation of Salted Beef, Pork, Bacon, and Butter, from the British Dominions in , for a limited

Time; without any Amendment.

Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Liberty and also the Petition of the Rector, Churchwarden, Overseers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; .

To prove the Allegations of the First mentioned Petition;

Mr. JoJ. Cox, and Mr. John Perry, being severally examined, said. That the Poor of the said Liberty are very numerous, and are at present maintained in a Workhouse hired by the Inhabitants of the said Liberty.

That the said Workhouse is in a decayed Condition, and that the Term of the Lease will expire at mei' next.

That a Meeting of the Inhabitants has been held, when it was agreed to apply to Parliament, to enable them to raise Money by an equal Pound Rate, for purchasing Ground or Houses, in or near the said Liberty, in order to build a Workhouse, for the better maintaining and employing their Poor.

To prove the Allegations of the Second mentioned Petition;

Mr. Richard Norris, and Mr. Geo. , severally said. That the Poor of the said Parish are very numerous, and are maintained in a Workhouse, which is held by Lease from John Payee, for a certain Term of Years, at the annual Rent of £. 131.

That by the said Lease it is agreed, that on Payment of a certain Sum of Money therein mentioned, the said Workhouse, and the said Payee's Term therein, should (subject to the Rent of £. 12 a Year) be assigned to the Churchwarden and Overseers of the Poor, for the Use of the said Parish.

That at a General Meeting of the Inhabitants, held the 15th Day of December last, it was resolved to purchase the said Workhouse, for the Remainder of the said Term; and that Application should be made to Parliament, to enable the Parishioners to raise Money sufficient for that Purpose, and to defray all other Expences incident thereto.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Workhouse, for the Liberty of Saffron Hill,

Hatton Garden, and Ely Rents, in the Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. William Burke and Sir Charles Whitworth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

that Mr. William Burke and Sir Charles Whitworth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of John Trevanion, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That at the late Election of a Baron to serve in Parliament for the Town And Port of Dover, in the County of , the Petitioner, and Sir Thomas Pym Hales, Baronet, were Candidates, and John Colman, Mayor, presided as Returning Officer; and that during the Poll, the said John Colman admitted several Persons to vote for the said Sir Thomas Mym Hales, who had no Colour of Right, and refused several Persons who offered to vote for the Petitioner, who Iiad an undoubted Right; and that the said Sir Thomas Pym Males was, by himself or Agents, guilty of divers illegal ond corrupt Practices, both before and during the Time of the Election, by which Means a pretended Majprity hath been procured in Favour of the said Sir Thomas Pym Males, in manifest Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had a clear Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been elected and returned for the said Town and Port: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as to the House shall seem reasonable.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Hojkins, and Mr. Elias Cole, being examined, said. That the said Parish is very populous; and the Houses, in a great measure, occupied by poor Manufacturers, and labouring Persons; and that the Expence of maintaining the Poor, amounts to about £. 1.500 one Year with.another; and that many of the Houses art let in separate Apartments, and do not pay any Thing to the Poors Rates.

Mr. Robert Hethcott said. That the Workhouse belonging to the said Parish is so ruinous, that it is absolutely necessary the same should be taken down and re-built.

And all the Witnesses said. That if Power was given for the better regulating, maintaining, employing, and governing the Poor within the said Parish, and for, obliging the Landlords and Leaseholders who let their Houses in separate Apartments, to pay the Poors Rates; it would greatly contribute to the Benefit of the said Parish, and to the Welfare and Preservation of the Poor therein.

A Petition of the Aldermen, Common Councilmen, ptynoutk and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough of Harbour. Plymouth, in the County of Devon, and of the Gentlemen and Merchants reading in or near, and trading to and from, the feme, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the Port of Plymouth, in the County of Devon is very considerable for its Extent and Harbours, and is of great Importance, as well for the Service and Safety of His Majesty’s Ships, as for other Ships and Vessels, whether Subjects or Aliens, trading thereto, or taking Shelter therein; and that near unto the said Town and Borough lies the Harbour of Catte Water, and adjoining thereto is a Pool called Sutton Pool, lying within the said Town, for the Safety and Security of which, a strong Wall was heretofore, with the Aid of Government, erected on a Neck of Land, called How Stert, otherwise Mount Button, dividing the said Harbour of Catte Water from, the Sound or main Sea; and the Entrance

trance of Sutton Pool was also defended by a Building of Bier; all which have been long since destroyed by the Violence of the Sea; and the said Neck of Land is now so much fretted and worn, by the Breach of the Sea, that it is likely the Sea will make a Passage through it, into the said Harbour of Catte and thereby

entirely ruin the fame, if not timely prevented} and that the said Harbour of Catte Water is so much filled up of late Years, with large Banks or Shoals of Ouze, Mud, Gravel, and Sand; and daily increasing; and that the said Pool is also so much filled up, that the same is rendered hurtful and very incommodious to Ships and Vessels lying the re; and that, by erecting a strong Wall on the South Side of the said Neck of Land, called How Stert, otherwise Mount B against the said Sound

or main Ocean, and a proper Pier at or before the Entrance of the said Pool called Sutton , and by enforcing the carrying into Execution an Act made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for clearing, preserving, and maintaining, the Harbour of Catte Water, lying near , in the County of Devon, and for deanfing and keeping clean the Pool commonly called Sutton Pool, lying in Plymouth aforesaid, and at the Expiration thereof to have the like or further Power given, to preserve and keep clear the said Harbour and Pool for the future, would render the said Harbour of Catte Water a very commodious and safe Station, and would be of the utraoft Consequence, as well to His Majesty’s Ships of War, as to all Ships and Vessels belonging to Merchants, either Subjects or Aliens, trading thereto, or bound down the Channel, and forced in by Stress of Weather or contrary Winds, and would likewise render the said Pool called Sutton Pool, safe and commodious for Ships to load and unload, at the Custom House, and other Quays, within the said Town , and that the Petitioners are convinced, from the Estimates already made, that this very useful Design may be carried into Execution by the Aid of a small Tonnage, or Duty, to be laid on all Ships and Vessels coming within or trading and belonging to, the said Port of Plymouth, and also of a small Duty on Coals and Culm imported into the said Fort; and that the Trade and Commerce in general, carried on to and from His Majesty’s Dominions would be thereby greatly promoted: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Merchants, Malfters, and Ship Owners from that Part of the Sea Coast, in the County of Norfolk, that lies between the Borough of King’s Lynn and the Borough of Great Yar, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That great Advantages have arisen from the Acts passed, granting a Bounty upon the Exportation of Malt, when the Price did not exceed 24 Shillings the Quarter; and that large Sums of Money have been remitted into Great Britain by such Export; but that the Prohibition for these Three Years past, though justly founded upon the high Price of Grain, hath been a heavy Grievance to such of the Petitioners as are Occupiers of Malthouses, and to others Owners ol small Vessels built and fit only for the Employment of transporting Malt, and that the for Want of their usual Supply from Great Britain, have established a Correspondence with Hamburgh,

and other Countries, for Barley; and that they do now make it into Malt in Holland; and that the total Lois of this very valuable Branch of Trade, it is to be feared, will ensue, unless the Exportation of Malt, with the accustomed Bounty, be permitted when the Price of Grain is reasonable; and representing to the House, that the present Price of Grain is very reasonable, the Medium of Barley for Mailing being but 14J. a Quarter, which is jor. a Quarter below the Bounty Price, and that of all other Grain in Proportion; and that, in this County, in which Barley is chiefly manufactured into Malt for Exportation, there is at present very large quantities of damaged Barley, owing to the Wetnels of the last Season, useless for any other Purpolo; and therefore request a Permission to export Malt, with the

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act made in the Thirty-first Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for repairing and widening several Roads in the Counties of Dorset and Devon, leading to and through the Borough of Lyme Regis, was read: And,

Mr. Benjamin Fullett, Treasurer to the said Trustees, being examined, said, That the Sum of £ 4,000 has been borrowed upon the Credit of the said Act, which has been applied towards repairing the said Roads, and is still owing upon the Credit of the said Act.

That the annual Produce of the Tolls is about f. 300, which is not sufficient to pay off the said Debt, and put the Roads in sufficient Repair, during the Term of the said Act.

That several Pow'ers are wanting to render the said Act effectual, particularly to prevent evading the Tolls.

That the several other Roads mentioned in the Petition, are narrow and ruinous, and cannot be effectually repaired and widened by the ordinary Course of Law; and that it would be of public Utility if the said Roads were properly repaired.

A Petition of Robert TreaRichard Wind, James

Cumings, Robert Coventry, William Nichoifon,

Elder, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Skippers and Keelmen employed by Hoaftmen or Fitters of Newjcafile upon Tyne, and also Skippers and Castors employed by Fitters of Sunderland, in the County Palatine of Durham, in working, navigating, unloading, or delivering Keels, upon the Rivers Tyne and Wear, on Behalf of themselves and others. Skippers, Keelmen, and Castors, so employed there, was presented to the House, and read: Setting forth. That several Statutes have been made for the better Maintenance of Keels and Keel Boats, in the Port of Newcastle and the Members thereof, and particularly a Statute of the Sixth and Seventh Years of King William the Third, whereby several Regulations are therein provided for the Benefit of the Coal Trade; and that several Abuses and Impositions have for some Time past been practised by a greater Measure having been put upon the Petitioners than is warranted by the said Regulation, not only tending to the Diminution of His Majesty’s Customs and other Duties, but to the great Loss of the Petitioners; and that the Keelmen employed in navigating Keels upon the said Rivers, being very numerous, and obliged to reside in some few Places near the said Rivers, and have, together with their Wives and Children, in Cafes of Distress, arising from Sickness, Age, and other Causes, been truly miserable, for want of Parochial or public Relief, and especially as to such of them as were Natives of Scotland, have lately instituted a Society, for the Purpose of relieving of poor indigent Keelmen, their Wives and Children, by a Fund to be raised, from time to time, by the several Members thereof, by Stoppages out of their respective Wages; and that it would tend greatly to the Quiet and Relief of the Petitioners, to have the Measure of Coals, Ballast, isle, restrained to Eight Chaldron to each Keel, and to have the said Society established and extended, which cannot be effectually obtained without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That a Bill may be brought in for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Sir Walter Blackett, Mr. Ridley, See.:And they are to meet this Afternoon, at

Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records: And all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.
