And the Witness said. That £.32,000 has been borrowed on the Credit of the said Act, which remains due; and that it will be necessary to raise the further Sum of £. 8,000, effectually to answer the Purposes thereby intended; that several of the Powers in the said Act have been found defective and inconvenient, particularly with regard to collecting the Taxes, and for scouring out Part of the Cans Dyke; that if Power was given to cleanse, deepen, and widen the River Glen, and to erect Locks and other Works upon the new Cut and Hammond Becks, and other Cuts, and to collect a Tonnage for Vessels passing and repassing, it would be of Advantage to the Owners of the Marsh and Fen Lands, as well as the Inhabitants of several Parts of the County of Lincoln: And,

?lvmouth The Lord Barrington reported from the Committee,

Harbour. to whom the Petition of the Aldermen, Common Coun-

cil-men, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, and of the Gentlemen and Merchants residing in or near, and trading to and from, the fame, was, referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Harris, Esquire, laid. That Plymouth is a-very con fid stable Port v that there is a Harbour called within the said Port, which is defended from the Sea, by a Neck of Land called How's Stert, or Mount ten, which Neck of Land was formerly secured by a Wall erected on the South Side thereof; that the said Harbour has of late Years filled up, and the Wall is quite destroyed by the Sea; and that the said Neck of Land is so much worn by the Sea, that the Harbour will soon be rendered useless, if proper Methods are not taken to prevent it: He also said. That the Mouth of a Pool called Sutton Pool, lying within the said Harbour, and adjacent to the Town of Plymouth, was defended by a Pier, which is washed away.

Then an Act passed in the Eighth Year of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for clearing, preserving, and maintaining the Harbour of Cutwater, lying near Plymouth, in the County of Devon, and for cleansing and keeping clean the Pool, commonly called Sutton Pool, lying in Plymouth aforesaid, was produced; whereby it appeared, that Benjamin Joules had a Grant to himself, of the exclusive Privilege of ballasting and unballafting all Vessels using the said Port of Plymouth, for the Term of Seventy-one Years, on Consideration of his deepening the said Harbour and Pool, making the said Harbour capable of receiving a Ship of the Fourth Rate, and keeping it in that State during the said Term: The Witness further said, That the Conditions of the said Grant have not been fulfilled; that it would be very beneficial to the said Town of Plymouth, and to Trade in general, if a Wall was erected at Mount Batten afore-Vol. 3a.

said, and a Pier at the Mouth of Sutton Pool, which may be done by laying a small Tonnage on Ships, Vessels, and Barges, using or belonging to the said Harbour, and a small Duty on all Coals landed within the Headlands of the fame: He also laid, That the most probable Means of deepening the said Harbour and Pool, and keeping the same clean, would be, to vest the said exclusive Privilege of ballasting and unballafting Ships using the said Harbour, after the Expiration or other Determination of the said Act, in Commissioners to be appointed by Act of Parliament for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for, laying certain Duties upon Ships, Vessels, and Barges, using the Harbour of Plymouth, in the County of , or belonging thereto, for clearing, preserving, and maintaining the Harbour of Catwater, and for cleaning and keeping clean the Pool commonly called Sutton Pool: And that the Lord Barrington and Admiral Holburne do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Council of the City Glasgow* of Glasgow, and of Sir John Stewart of Castlemilk, Arch-bald Hamilton of Rofehill, Daniel Campbell of Shawfield, Navigation. James Bucbannan of Drumpellier, John of Rins,

George Nijbett of Cairnhill, Robert Coult of Garturk,

James Dougale of Easterhouse, Robert Dreghorn of Ruchill, all Proprietors of Land and Coal on the Tract of the Canal aftermentioned, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Price of Pit Coal is daily increasing in Glasgow, to the great Detriment of its Trade and Manufactures; and that there are almost in-exhaustible Funds of Coal in the Parishes of Old and New Monklands, which can be wrought at a very moderate Expence, but, on account of the Distance, cannot easily be brought to Glasgow by Land Carriage; and that, from Surveys which have been made, it appears practicable to make a navigable Cut or Canal, passing from these Collieries to Glasgow, passing mostly through, the Lands of the Petitioners, beginning at or near %

Place called The Sheep Ford, in the Parish of Old Monk-land, and County aforesaid; and passing by or near the House of Drumpellier, and may terminate at the City of Glasgow, or Broomelaw Quay, or near it, and communicate, by a Road or Waggon Way, from the West:

End of the said Canal, to the said City or Quay; and that the Petitioners conceive, that such a Cut or Canal, by reducing the Price of Carriage, will enable them to supply the City of Glasgow with Pit Coal at a moderate Rate; for which Purpose, a public voluntary Subscription has been opened, and several thousand Pounds have been subscribed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making the aforesaid Canal, and Road or Waggon Way, and for exacting, collecting, levying, and receiving, such Tolls, Rates, and Duties thereon, as shall be judged reasonable and expedient; and for giving to the Undertakers such other Powers, Grants, and Privileges, as shall be necessary for executing and completing the fame, and for maintaining, upholding, and keeping the said Canal and Road or Waggon Way in Repair, according to Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report thcfiime, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

and read; Setting forth, That, by the said Act, Lime, Limestones, Coal for burning such Limestones into 'Lime, Dung, Mold, or Compost of any Nature or Kind whatsoever for Manuring of Lands or Gardens, were exempted from the Payment of Toll j which Exemptions were, by an Act of the 30th of King George the Second, for rendering more effectual the several Laws in being for the Amendmept and Preservation of the publio Highways and Turnpik. Roads of this Kingdom, taken away, unless the Things so exempted were carried upon Broad Wheels; and that, by an Act of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the general Laws in being for regulating the Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, the said Act of 36 Geo. II. was repealed; by Means whereof Carriages employed on the said Road in carrying Lime, Limestones, Coal for burning such Limestones into Lime, Dung, Mold, or Compost of any Nature or Kind whatsoever for Manuring of Lands or Gardens, were again exempted from the Payment of Toll, although the same should be upon narrow Wheels; and that, by reason of the said last mentioned Exemption, the Tolls of the said Road have been lessened, and are not sufficient to defray the necessary Charges and Expences of putting and keeping the same in good Repair; and that the Petitioners apprehend it would require an additional Toll to put and keep the said Road in good and sufficient Repair; and that the said Act of 24 Geo. II. is in several other respects ineffectual to answer the Purposes thereby intended; and that the Petitioners apprehend it would be very beneficial to the said Road, if persons employed in leading Manure thereon werereftrained from unloading the -fame until the same should be carried to the Place it is intended to be made use of, so as such Manure, after once unloading, should not be brought again upon the said Road: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to make such Provision therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Abingdon The Order of the Day being read, for hearing at the Xleaion. gar of t jajs fjoufCj the Matter of the several Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Abingdon, in the County of Berks j

The Counsel were called in.

And the said Petitions were read.

And the last Determination of the House, concerning the Right of eleaing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of , made the 18th Day

of January 1708, was read; whereby it was resolved, " That the Right of electing a Burgess to serve in Parliament, for the Borough of Abingdon, is in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving " Alms, or any Charity."

And the Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel, at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, was also read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners was heard, and stated the Numbers upon the Poll to be, for Mr. Morion 1 26, for Mr. Bayly 124; which was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member to be as stated by the Counsel for the Petitioners.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having proposed 16

todifqualify the Votes of Three Persons who voted for the Sitting Member, Two as receiving Charity, and One being a Certificate Man;

The same was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member$ and that the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes upon the Poll.

And then the Counsel on both Sides, were directed to withdraw.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put.

That John Morton, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Abingdon, in the County of Berks

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That Nathanael Bayly, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Abingdon, in the County of Berks.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do attend this House immediately, with the Return for the Borough of Abingdon, and amend the fame, by rafing out the Name of John Morton, Esquire, and inserting the Name of Nathanael Bayly, Esquire, instead thereof.

And the Deputy Clerk of the Crown attending, according to Order, amended the said Return accordingly*

A Petition of the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the Parish of Saint Martin, in the City of New Sarum, and also of several of the principal Inhabitants of the said City, was presented to the House, and read Setting forth, That the said City consists of the Parishes of Saint Thomas, Saint Edmund, and Saint Martin; and that the Poor of all the said Parishes have, beyond the Memory of Man, been maintained out of the Collections, by an equal Number of Rates, and a like Mode of Rating in each Parish made by the respective Officers of the said Three Parishes, which Method hath hitherto been found beneficial to the whole City; and in case it should be changed, for that of maintaining the Poor of each Parish separately, it would bring a heavy Burthen on the poorer Parishes, and prove detrimental to the City; and that Doubts have arisen, whether such Maintenance of all the Poor of the said City by such Collections is legal: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for consolidating all the Rates to be made for the Relief of the Poor of the said Three several Parishes into One Common Fund, for the Maintenance of all the said Poor, in such Manner, and with such Powers and Regulations, as to the House shall feemmeet.

A Petition of Henry Fownes Luttrell, of Dunjler in the County of Somerset, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Minehead, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act passed in the 12th and 13th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for recovering, securing, and keeping in Repair, the Harbour of Minehead, certain Duties (over and besides the ancient and customary Duties and Acknowledgments before the passing of the said Act due and accustomed to be paid, to Tregonwell Luttrell, Esquire* and his Ancestors) were laid as therein particularly mentioned, for building out a new Head* and clearing the Beach, and other Works, for the securing, preserving* amending, and maintaining the Pier and Harbour of Minehead; and that, in pursuance of the said Act, a new Head was built; but the whole Duties not being sufficient to defray the Charges of completing and finishing the said Pier, exclusive of the Yearly Expence of repairing what had been done, all the Rates and Duties by the said Act granted were, by another Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for prolonging the Term for Payment of the said Duties granted by the First mentioned Act, further continued, for an additional Term of 16 Years, to commence from the Expiration of the Term granted by the First mentioned Act } and by another Act, made in the nth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, the said Terms and Powers were continued for the further Term of 40 Years, from the 24th Day of June 1738; and that all the Monies borrowed and expended for and towards building of the said new Head, and other Works, have been advanced and paid by the Lords of the Manor of Minehead, whom the Petitioner represents, and the Petitioner; and by an Account thereof, and of all other Monies received and disbursed on Account of the said new Pier, it appears that, on the 29th Day of September 1768, there was a Balance due to the Petitioner, the present Lord of the said Manor, of £. 9560. i8r. 10 j and that the Money collected by the Duties granted and continued as aforesaid hath been duly laid out, for the several Purposes in the said Acts mentioned; but the same hath proved greatly deficient to defray the Expences thereof 1 and it being necessary to keep the Mouth of the said Harbour clear from the Beach, and great Quantities of Stones that are continually forced into it by the Violence of the Sea, whereby the same is frequently choaked up, and to carry on the Works in Order to secure the said Harbour, and keep the same in Repair, which cannot be done unless the Terms and Powers granted by the said former Acts be further continued and enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for further continuing the Terms and Powers granted and given by the said recited Acts, and for the more effectual carrying the same into Execution.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the ^me, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Charles Kemys Tynte, Mr. Barrow, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber} and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of Margaret Cavendijhe, Duchess Dowager of St. M«y It

Portland, William Henry Cavendijhe, Duke of Portland, and ®one the Nobility residing in the Parish of St. Mary le bone, Church, in the County of Middlesex, and the humble Petition of the Vestrymen and other Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House. and read; Setting forth.

That the Parish of St. Mary le bone is a large and populous Parish, and the present Parish Church is much too small for the Inhabitants to assemble in for the Public Worship of God; and the Petitioners are desirous of building a larger Parish Church, and of inclosing a Piece of Ground for a Burying Place, but cannot carry their Intentions into Execution without the Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring a Bill, in such Manner and Form as to the House shall seem meet, to enable the Vestry of the said Parish to effectuate those Purposes.

A Petition of the Trustees appointed by an Act of Ode Parliament passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign h?aviSi‘t*oa» of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled.

An Act for improving the Navigation of the River Ouse, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, in the Execution of the said Act, and of another Act, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second; for rendering the said first Act more effectual, expended large Sums of Money in erecting a Lock and Dam, and otherwise in the Improvement of the Navigation of the said River; notwithstanding which, the Petitioners have, for several Years past, caused the Tolls and Duties, allowed to be taken by the said last mentioned Act, to be reduced to nearly One Half of the Rates allowed by the same Act; and that the Navigation of the said River is dill capable of much greater Improvements, which would be very beneficial to the Public; but, by reason of several Defeats in the said former Acts, and particularly in the Mode of collecting and recovering the said Tolls and Rates, the Petitioners cannot carry the same into Execution, without the farther Aid and Assistance of Parliament:

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for giving further Powers to the Trustees appointed for putting the said Acts into Execution, and for rendering the same Acts more effectual.

Watchett, in the County of Scmer/et, for which Purpose the several Rates and Dues therein mentioned were imposed; and that Sir William Wyndham, Baronet, the Petitioner’s Grandfather, and the several other Persons therein named, were thereby appointed Trufrees, for the ordering the building and making the said Harbour, and other Works in and about the fame, and the maintaining thereof from Time to Time, and the Collection and Disposition of the said Duties, of whom the Lord of the said Manor for the Time being was always to be a Trustee; and that, by an Act made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her said late Majesty, for prolonging the Term for Payment of the aforementioned Duties, all Goods shipped or discharged at a Place called ‘Ihe Blue Anchor, or Cleave Stepps, or other Places adjoining to the said Harbour and Quay of Watchett, should be chargeable with the Duties as if the same had been shipped and discharged within the said Harbour or Quay of Watchett; and that, by an Act of the Seventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, for continuing the Duties granted by several Acts made in the Sixth and Tenth Years of her late Majesty’s Reign, for Repairing the said Harbour and Quay of Watchett, the several Rates and Duties, by the said Act of the Sixth Year of her said late Majesty’s Reign, made payable for the Term of zi Years, should, from and after the Expiration thereof, be charged upon the several Goods and Merchandizes, and also the Tonnage and Keelage of Ships and Vessels in the said Act mentioned, for the further Term of n Years, and that it hath' been lately discovered, that the Term limited by the last mentioned Act, for collecting such of the said Rates and Dut ies, the Grant whereof was temporary only, did expire on the 25th of March 1750; but, through Ignorance of such Expiration, the whole of the said Rates and Duties hath been continued to be collected and applied as before; and that the said Harbour and Quay have, ever since the said First mentioned Act, been repaired and supported by the Petitioner and his Ancestors, the Lords of the said Manor; and it hath been found by Experience, that such of the said Rates and Duties, the Grant whereof was made perpetual to the Lords of - the said Manor so long as they should repair the said Harbour, have not proved, nor are likely to be sufficient to defray the current Expences of the Repairs and other incident Charges; and that, besides the ordinary Reparations now wanting, some further new Works will likewise be requisite, for better securing the Pier from the Violence of the Sea; nor can any effectual Provision be made to guard against and remedy unforeseen Accidents, without a constant Stock and Supply for that Purpose; and as the Reasons mentioned in the said First Act still continue in their original Force, and as the Preservation of the said Harbour will be of great Utility to the Navigation and Commerce of this Kingdom, and to the Inhabitants of the said Town and Counties adjacent: Therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing such of the said Rates and Duties as were granted by the said former Acts during a limited Time, for such further Term as to the House shall seem fitting, and also for the Indemnity of the Persons employed in and about collecting the same Rates and Duties since the Expiration of the Term already granted therein.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Charles Kemys Tynte, Sir Edward Bayntuu, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of Paul Methuen, Esquire, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That His Majesty’s Predecessors, Kings and Queens of England, from the Time of King Edward the First, have been seised of the Manor of Corsham, in Wilts, with all 'manerial Rights and Privileges thereunto belonging, and have from Time to Time made Grants and Leases thereof; and that his late Majesty King George the Second, by Letters Patent, und?r the Seal of 21

the Court of Exchequer, dated the 2 ad Day of June, in the Fifth Year of his Reign, in Consideration of a Fine of £. 18, demised to George Ducket, Esquire; for Twenty-five Years and an Half, mom the 18th of June 1734, the said Manor of Corsham, with all its Rights and Appurtenances, and all Fines and Profits of the Manor, excepting all Lands demised or demifeable by his Majesty for Years or Lives, and the Rents reserved for the fame, and all'o all great Trees, and Timber Trees, and all Woods, Mines, and Quarries, under the several Rents of £.73. 6x. id. 17 t> S^d.and £.4, making together,’ £. 78. 4 s.4 id.and the said George Ducket was to keep up the Buildings and Fences within the Manor, but was allowed to take from the Premilfes sufficient House Bote, Hedge Bote, or other Botes to be used upon the Pre-milfes; and that his said late Majesty, on the 9th Day of August, in the 22d Year of his Reign, in Consideration of a Fine of £. 16, demised to Thomas Ducket, Son of George Ducket, all the Premilfes comprized in the said Letters Patent, for a further Term of Twenty-five Years, from the 29th of December 1759, under the like reserved

Rents and Covenants; and that Thomas Ducket assigned over his Right and Interest in the said Demise to Daniel Bull, Esquire, and Daniel Bull assigned his Right and Interest to the Earl of Warwick, in Trust for the Petitioner; and that the Customary and Copyhold Tenants of the Manor of Corsham enjoy many special Privileges, toger ther with the Pasturage of divers Commons and Waste Grounds within the said Manor, and the Rents and Profits of the Manor have always been collected by a Bailiff chosen by the Tenants of the Manor, by whose Account it will appear, that, for Ten Years past, the Profits of the Manor and Courts have not amounted, upon an Average, to more than about 40J. a Year, over and above the Rents, amounting to 78. payable for the same to the Crown; and that there are not now any Lands within the said Manor demised or demise-' able by the Crdwn, save what are contained in the Demises herein before set forth; and that, by the Neglect of former Lessees of the Crown, the Tenants of the Manor have cut down and destroyed the Timber and1 other Trees growing upon the Commons and Waste Ground of the Manor, and applied them to theft own. Uses, so that there is not now more than sufficient left for the Botes granted to the Lessee of the Crown, and the Commons are not maintained and kept up in proper Order and Condition; and that the Petitioner hath for some Time past been engiged in a Suit with the Tenants of the Manor, at a very considerable Expence, in Defence of the Rights of the Crown to the Soil of the said Commons and Wastes, and to the Trees dill remaining thereon, and hath obtained a Verdictt in Establishment of these Rights; and the Petitioner would now proceed to clear and improve the Commons and Waste Grounds, and to replant proper Parts thereof, and guard the same from Cattle; but the Expence of such Improvements, with the Charges the Petitioner hath already been put to, will amount to more than can be expected from any Lessee for a Term of Years, and no Lease of the Premisses can be granted, sufficient to encourage such Improvements, for Want of which the Commons must remain of little Value to the Lord and the Tenants of the Manor, and the Public will be deprived of the Benefit which may result from such an Increase of Timber as is proposed to be raised by the Petitioner: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable His Majesty to grant 'the Inheritance in Fee Simple of all the said Premisses so the Petitioner and his Heirs for ever, without the Exceptions in the said Demises, under such Rent, or for such valuable Con* fidcrations, as shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tuesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Compensation. The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends the same to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That in January 1743, the Petitioner’s Ship, Britannia, Burthen Two hundred Tons, or thereabouts, failed from the Isle of Wight, bound on a Voyage to Genoa, or Naples, with a Cargo of Wheat on Freight, and from thence to Gallipoli, and back to London, and, in the Course of her Outward Voyage, put into Port Mahon, where (he was flopped by Admiral Matthews, then Commander in Chief of his Majesty’s Fleet in the Mediterranean, by whose Order the Cargo was taken out of her for the Use of the Fleet, and her whole destined Voyage thereby totally defeated; that the Petitioner was prevented, by the Agents of Government, from ever regaining Possession of her, and ascertaining the Money due to him in respect thereof, either by the Arbitrament of Merchants of Reputation, or a Jury, when the legal Remedy subsisted; and never received any Satisfaction for the same or the Damages thereby occasioned and sustained; but the Officers of Government, or One of them, changed her Name, and afterwards flie was actually employed as a Tender in his Majesty’s Service, Thirty-two Months, and upwards; and that Government, in the former War, had Two different Methods of hiring Ships; viz. One for Transports, to be used at their Will and Pleasure, so long as the Service required, which were generally paid about Fifteen or Sixteen Shillings a Ton per Month, taken into immediate Pay, and so continued about Two Months after a Convoy failed with them to their destined Ports, from the Place where they were di (charged Abroad; and if taken, or destroyed, by the Enemy, then to be paid for by Government; the other, under certain Rest rict ions, for particular Voyages, upon cheaper Terms; in which Cafes, the Owners of Ships bound to foreign Parts, in Order to bring Cargoes to Europe, where the Homeward Freight was the chief Object, usually contracted to carry Stores to Places near their Outward Course, at much lower Rates of Freight and Demurrage than they could otherwise have done; and that the Petitioner’s Ship, Francis, Burthen Two hundred Tons, or thereabouts, being, in 1743, bound to Madeira a.n<l South Carolina, to take in, and carry from thence, in 1744, a Cargo of Rice to Lifbupon the Petitioner’s Account, was, about the First of December 1743, hired by the Commissioners for Victualling, under a Charter Party, for one particular described Voyage to be performed with Convoy, Wind and Weather permitting, from Spithead to Gibraltar, or Port Mahon, the Petitioner was bound in a large Penalty for the true Performance thereof; under which Government would have recovered the Value of the Provisions, if they had been loft by the Petitioner’s breaking the fame; and on the other Hand, the Justice of the Crown was the Petitioner’s Security, for Payment and Performance on his Majesty’s Part, in same of breaking the Charter Party; and that the said Ship, although hired for such Voyage only (the Sailing Part whereof, to Port Mahon, was performed in less than Six Weeks) was, by an Order from Sir Charles Hardy, dated at Saint Helens, the 31st of March 1744, and therein mentioned to be given by Directions from the Admiralty, carried to and there detained

Three Calendar Months and Twenty-seven Days, and from thence on a Cruize Twelve Days, off Cape Saint Vincent's,; therefore did not arrive at Gibraltar till the 30th of September 1744, where (he was detained till the 18th of October following, when (he was taken back to Sea; and, off Cadiz Bay, Part of her Cargo was delivered to his Majesty’s Fleet, and afterwards taken to Port Mahon with the Remainder j and, in every respect, used, without the Petitioner’s Consent, as a Ship hired Vol. 32,

for a Monthly Transport, and not discharged by Government till Twelve Months (wanting a few Days) from the Time of her Hiring, nor did any Convoy fail with her from Mahon, until above Fourteen Months after such Hiring, whereby the Petitioner loft the Benefit of his Voyage to Carolina, in 1744, and the Ship was taken by the Enemy, on her Voyage from Port Mahon thither, in 1745; notwithstanding all which, the Petitioner has not been able to obtain Payment, either upon the Terms and Conditions of other Ships hired by Government, to be used at their Will and Pleasure, or for the special Damages occasioned and sustained by the several Breaches of the Charter Party, but received from the Commissioners for ViClualing, £.637. ns, id. and no more, in Part of the Money due to him, on Account of, this Ship; and that about the 15th of March 1755, the Petitioner’s Ship Ann, Burthen One hundred and Eighty-six Tons, or thereabouts, departed from Saint Kitts, with a valuable Cargo, and arrived in the British Channel, on the 27th of April following, when (he was brought-to by one of his Majesty’s Tenders, and Three of the Petitioner’s bed Seamen were imprest, and Three Persons wholly unacquainted with the Navigation of a Ship placed in their Stead; and about Seven of the Clock in the Evening of the next Day, the said Ship was again brought-to, between Pepperil Point and The Needles, by another of his Majesty’s Tenders, the Commander whereof, notwithstanding the distressed Condi- ' tion (he was then in for Want of Hands to navigate her, detained her in that dangerous Situation till near Midnight, and then impressed One of the best Seamen left on Board; by Means of which said Detention, and Impressing the Hands, the said Ship was, in a few Hours afterwards, beat to Pieces, at the Back of the Isle of Wight, and only a very small Part of her Cargo and Materials were saved; for which Damage, the Petitioner has not received from Government any Redress whatsoever; and that the Petitioner applied to this House the last Session of Parliament by Petition, and some Proceedings were had thereupon; but the Petitioner has not received any Relief in the Premises; and that the Petitioner, in Consequence of the above Fasts, having been greatly injured in his private Fortune, and his Family now reduced to theut-most Distress, arising from many unwarrantable and unjustifiable Delays, implores the Interposition of the House: And prays, That they will take the Premises> into their ferions Consideration, and grant such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and Hate to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition:

num, which, until within -Two or Three Years, was raised by a Re-assessment on the real, and an Assessment on the personal Estates within the said Parish, and that, by the Diminution of the Inhabitants, Rents, and Trade of the said Parish, the remaining Inhabitants have loft the Assistance thereof, towards the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish, which are very numerous and heavy, and which by the above heavy Losses and other additional Charges, they will be rendered wholly unable to support, unless timely relieved by the House i and that the Building erected by the University and County aforesaid, being for public Use, the Inhabitants are advised they can have no Relief in the Premises without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem proper.

the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was readand is as followeth; t. viz.

To' prove the Allegations of the said Petition; an Act made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty was read; And,

Mr. Luke IJffon, Vettry Clerk of the said Parish, being examined, laid. That the said Act is defective, in re-sped to paving, cleansing, and enlightening:

That the Vestrymen who are appointed to carry the Ad into Execution, have not Power to compel the Inhabitants to contribute to the necessary Repairs, or any new Pavement to be made with any particular Kind of Stone, or in an uniform and regular Manner:

That sufficient Power is not vested in them by the said Act, to remove Pods, Signs, Sign Irons, and many other Nuisances; and those very Nuisances which the Ad im-powers the Commissioners to remove, may continue fcvc-ral Days, which often causes great Mischief.

And with regard to lighting; if the Inhabitants put up Lamps at their Doors, they are not compelled to contribute to the Rate for lighting, whereby a great Burthen falls upon the poor Inhabitants; and that in particular, where there are Dead Walls, or Houses uninhabited, there is no Power to compel the putting up Lamps. Southampton Sir John Molesworth reported from the Committee, to Streets. whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town of Southampton, in Common Council assembled, and of several Gentlemen and others Inhabitants of the said Town, and the Liberties thereof, whole Names arc thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of Houses, Buildings, and Ground, within the said Town and Liberties; and also the Petition of many of the Members of the Corporation, Common Council, &c. of Southampton, and also of a very considerable Number of Proprietors of Houses and Estates, and of several Inhabitants in the said Town, on Behalf of themselves and others, were severally referred; That the Committee had heard the Petitioners by their Counsel, and had examined the Matters of the said Petitions ;^uul had directed him to Vol. 32.

report the fame, as they appeared lothcm, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition; Captain John Woodftrd, being examined, said. That he was born in the Town of Southampton, and has lived there Twenty eight Years; that the Inhabitants have been increasing every Year, and that there has been a great many new Buildings lately erected both within and about the said Town; that the Inhabitants are double now to what they have been in the Memory of the Witness.

And being asked the Question, he said. That there is no Manufactory there; that the Trade is very trilling; and that the said Town is more resorted to for Amusement than Trade: That ever since he knew the Town he thought the Streets very badly paved, and that the High Street is so bad that Carriages can only go on one Side of the Way; that he has complained of the Badness of the Pavement, but never met with any Redress; that there are often Obstructions in the Streets by Carriages Hopping; and that the Spouts project so. much over the Foot Way that they are a great Nuisance.

Mr. Jacob Leroux, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Captain Woodford, with respect to the Badness of the Pavement, and the Obstructions by Carriages, and Nuisances by the Spouts; and added, That several of the other Streets and Passages are very badly paved, narrow, and incommodious j and that it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and Persons resorting thereto, if the Streets, Lanes, Courts, Ways, and Passages, were properly paved, cleansed, and widened, where necessary: Then,

Mr. Charles Legay, Town Clerk, produced to your Committee, the Minute Book of the Quarter Sessions, wherein are several Entries of Presentments made by the Grand Jury, of the Nuisances and Obstructions in the said Town, and of the Pitching of the Streets being bad and dangerous.

And Being asked. Why the same were not removed ? he said. He preiumed it was for want of Power in the Magistrates s Then,

Mr. — Muilman, being examined, said, Thathe knows the Town of Southampton; that the Pavement thereof in general is in a very ruinous Condition, and dangerous for Carriages, and the Foot Way very inconvenient for PalTcngers.

And being asked. Whether the Town would be benefited by the Streets being new paved ? he said, It would not only be a Benefit to the Inhabitants, but to others who resort there: That the Pavement has been the Subject of Complaint for these Four Years pall; and that the Magistrates have been reflected upon for it, by People resorting thereto.

In support of the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition; the Counsel for the Petitioners produced to your Committee, Copy of an Extract from the Rolls of Parliament of the Seventeenth Year of King Edward the Fourth, to prove that the Management of the said Town was entirely in the Corporation, and the Regulation of the Pavement particularly vested in them, as set forth in their Petition; but by the said Copy it appeared to be in the Mayor, Sheriff, and Bailiffs, for the Time being.

And to prove that the Pavements were in tolerable Repair; they called,

Air. James Knight, who said, That he ig, Forty-seven Years of Age, and has lived in the Tdwn of Southampton all his Life; that when the Pavement is bad, the Method is to apply to the Corporation by a written Notice to the Town Clerk; in Consequence of which, they have been repaired; but could not mention any particular Parts that had been so repaired.

And being asked as to some particular Places in the said Town; he said, To be sure they did run a little narrow, and would do very well if widened; but that the

The House, according to Order, proceeded to the Sudbury Hearing the Matter of the several Petitions, complain- ^le&ion. ing of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the said Petitions were read.

And the last Determination of the House, concerning the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Sudbury, made the 6th Day of December 1705, was read; whereby it was resolved, "That " the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Sudbury in the County of " Suffolk, is only in the Sons of Freemen born after " their Fathers were made free, and in such as have served Seven Years Apprenticeship, or are made " Freemen by Redemption."

And the Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence, touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament, for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, was also read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners were heard, and examined several Witnesses, to prove that One of the Sitting Members did, at a numerous Meeting of the Electors for the said Borough, and in the Presence of the other Sitting Member, publicly engage to give a large Sum of Money, to be distributed among the said Electors, provided he should be elected One of the Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

And a Witness was also examined, in order to prove that the said Sitting Member did, at another Time, and on the same Condition, promise a Sum of Money to the Witness, if he would give him his Vote at the Election.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners having proposed to call a Witness to prove that the other Sitting Member did attempt to bribe the said Witness, by offering to procure him aCommission in the Army;

The same was objected to by the Counsel for the Sitting Members, the said Witness having signed the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Freemen and Electors of the Borough of Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk, which was presented to the House upon the 18th Day of November, in the last Session of Parliament.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners were heard, in Answer to that Objection.

And One of the Counsel for the Sitting Members having been heard, by way of Reply;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That Henry Threlfal, Esquire, having, as an Elector, signed the Petition of the Electors of the Borough of Sudbury, presented to the House in the last Session of Parliament, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, be admitted to give Evidence in support of the several Petitions presented in this Session of Parliament, he not having signed the tame;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Counsel were again called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners examined a Witness, in order to prove that several Persons, .'who had been convicted of Bribery at the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, were Agents to the Sitting Members.

Then the said Counsel having proposed to produce Evidence, in order to prove that several of the Persons who voted for the Sitting Members at the last Election, were not legally qualified to give their Votes, as not being Freemen of the said Borough

The same was objected to by the Counsel for the Sitting Members, as not being warranted by any Allegation in either of the said Petitions.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners were heard, in Answer to that Objection.

And One of the Counsel for the Sitting Members was beard, by way of Reply.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

It passed in the Negative.

Then the Counsel were again called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners summed up their Evidence.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Members were heard; and examined several Witnesses, in order to contraditt the Evidence that had been given on the Part of the Petitioners, as to the Declaration of One of the Sitting Members, at the said Meeting of the Electors.

And then the Counsel for the Sitting Members summed up their Evidence.

And One of the Counsel for the Petitioners was heard, by way of Reply.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Sir John Rous reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Trustees for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for continuing, and making more effectual, Two Acts of Parliament, for repairing the Roads leading from to , in

the County of Suffolk, and other Roads in the said Act mentioned, and for repairing the Road from Cleydon aforesaid, to Coddenliam B, in the said County; and also of several Gentlemen, and others, of the County of Suffolk, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place j and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth , viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And, Mr. Lott , Treasurer,

to the Trustees, being examined, said, That f. 1,270 has been borrowed upon the Credit of the Toils thereby- granted, and which Hill remains due: That the Road is now extremely bid, and grows worse every Year; and particularly that Part of it which leads to Norwich, being about Eight Miles: That the Money borrowed cannot be repaid, and the said Roads put in proper Repair, and so kept, except the Term granted by the said Act be enlarged, and the Tolls increased; and that the said Act has been found defective in several other respects.

Mr. Thomas Latham Revett, a Farmer, and Mr. Joseph Simpson, Surveyor, being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence of the foregoing Witness, with respect to the Badness of the Roads; and added, That the great Weight carried on broad-wheel Waggons, and the want of proper Materials for repairing the Roads in that Part of the Country, is the principal Cause of the Roads being in so ruinous a Condition: And,

Mr. Simpson added, That last Year there was between £. 50 and f. 60 a Mile laid out upon about Four

Miles of the Road; that there was as much laid out every Year before; and that it is now in a very bad Condition, owing to the Materials being of so soft a Nature as not to be able to bear the Weight of the broad-wheel Carriages.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Terms, and enlarging the Powers, of several Acts of Parliament, made for repairing the Road from Ipswich to Cleydon, and several other Roads 18

therein mentioned, in the County of SuffolkAnd that Sir John Rous and Sir Charles Banbury do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Sir Francis Vincent reported from the Committee of State of the the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider Nation, further of the State of the Nation, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House, which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That this House, in the Exercise of its Judicature in Matters of Election, is bound to judge according to the Law of the Land, and the known and established Law and Custom of Parliament, which is Part thereof; and that the Judgment of this House, declared in the Resolution of the 17th Day of February last, " That John " Esquire, having been in this Session of Parliament expelled this House, was, and is, incapable of being elected a Member to serve in this present Parliament," was agreeable to the said Law of the Land, and fully authorized by the Law and Custom of Parliament.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time;

And an Objection being made, that the said Ilefolu-tion contained a complicated Question; and that it was the undoubted Right of any One Member of the House to have it separated, before any Question could be put upon it;

Mr. Speaker was called upon by the House, to state what he understood to be the Order of Proceeding of the House in this Respect.

And Mr. Speaker accordingly delivered to the House his Opinion thereupon.

And a Member of the House, having, in his Speech, made feme Observations upon what had b?en said by Mr. Speaker;

And Mr. Speaker offering his Sentiments to the The House, in Awfwer to what had been observed by the said Member; Exception was taken to some Words uhen 4*^ used by Mr. Speaker in such Answer; which Words being taken down by a Member of the House, were afterwards copied by the Clerk at the Table and are as followeth: " When 1 expected candid Treatment from that Member, I was mistaken; for I find I am

And the said Words, so taken down, being read to the House;

Mr. Speaker declared, That those were not the Words, which he had madeufe of, but that they were as folk>weth: " In Candor, I hoped he would have informed me of the Motion he intended to make; but " I now find, from what the Member has said, that I " am not to expect that candid Treatment from him: — uFor he said in his Speech, That, from this Time forward, he will have no Communication with the Chair."

And Mr. Speaker declared, He did not mean any general Reflection on the Character of the Member.

And, afterwards, Mr. Speaker said, " What I said, arose out of what I understood the Member to have " said. If he disclaimed Candor with the Chair, I had a Right to say, I was not to expect Candor on that 5* Subject. I did not, in Justice I ought not to have made a general Reflection upon the Member’s Cha- racter , but, if the Member had said what I under-flood he said, I had a Right to say what I did. I can " make no Apology for what I said; but will abide the " Sense of the House."

Then a Motion being made, and, the Question being put, That the Words spoken by Mr. Speaker, from the Chair, are disorderly, importing an improper Reflection on a Member of this House, and dangerous to the Freedom of Debate in this House,

It paired in the Negative.

Sunderland A Petition of the Keelmen, Skippers of Keels, and Keelmen, tec. Castors of the Port of Sunderland near the Sea, in the County of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Petition of Robert Treall, Richard Wind, and others, who call themselves Skippers and Castors, employed by Hoaftmen and Fitters of Newcastle upon Tyne, and also Skippers and Castors employed by Fitters of Sunderland, for establishing a Society for the Purpose of relieving poor indigent Keelmen, their Wives and Children, out of a Fund to be raised as therein is mentioned; and that these Petitioners were not apprized of such Petition till it appeared in the

Votes; and setting forth. That the Petitioners are mostly Natives of this Port and Neighbourhood, and earn in their Employments, which differ greatly from those of the Keelmen of Newcastle, a competent Maintenance for themselves and their Families, and, in case of Necessity, have Relief in common with other Poor from their respective Parishes; and that the Relief fought for by the said Petition would not contribute to their better Support, but would load them with unnecessary Charge for the Relief of others, with whom they have, nor desire to have, any Connexion: And therefore hope, that, with respect to them, the House will dismiss the said Petition.

Towns therein mentioned, to and through a certain Close of Ground, the Property of William , Gentleman, lying near Love Lane, on the North West Side of the said Town and Port of Liverpoole, and from thence to the River Mersey; and the Petitioners, being Trustees for the several Docks, Pier, and other Works, in and about the Harbour and Port of , under several Acts of the 8th Year of Queen , the 3d of

King George the First, the 1 ith of King George the Second, and the 2d Year of His present Majesty, have come to an Agreement (subject to the Controul of Parliament) with the Agents for the said Navigable Canal, that, provided the said Bill shall pass into a Law, the said Navigable Canal shall terminate at the Sea Bank, or Clay Bank, at or near The North Ladies , in Liverpoole, and there be locked down to the adjacent Sea Shore, or Strand, at the Expence of the Undertakers and intended Proprietors of the said Navigable Canal; and, in order that the said Navigable Canal may have a Communication with the Dock now making on the West Side of the Town of Liv, and also with the other Docks and Pier there, and that the Ships and Vessels in the Foreign and Coasting Trade, which pay considerable Dock Duties there, may not be obstructed in their Trade by the Boats or Vessels which may navigate on the said Canal taking up too much Space in the said Docks and Pier, the Petitioners have likewise agreed with the said Agents, that the Petitioners will make a Cut or Canal, from the North End of the said Dock now constructing along the Sea Strand or Shore there, to join the said Navigable Canal at the Place where it is to be locked down as aforesaid; and will also make a Dock, and Pier necessary to support the fame, proper and sufficient for the Reception of such Boats and Vessels as shall trade or be navigated on the said Navigable Canal, upon having a moderate Ton-nage granted to them for defraying the great Expence of making and maintaining such junftive Cut or Canal, Dock, Pier, and other Works necessary thereto, provided the Terms and Powers of the said Acts be prolonged and enlarged, so as to enable the Petitioners to make and finish the said junftive Cut or Canal, Dock, Pier, and other Works necessary thereto, the present Terms and Powers being inefficient and inadequate for that Purpose: And therefore praying, That such Bill for making the said Navigable Canal from Leeds to Liverpoole, may pass into a Law, on the Terms of the said Agreement between the said Agents and the Petitioners; and that such Powers and Provisions may be inserted therein, as may enable the Petitioners to perform and fulfil their said Agreement with the Agents and Undertakers of the said Navigable Canal; and that, for the Purposes aforesaid, the Terms and Powers granted in and by the before mentioned several Acts may be prolonged and enlarged to the Petitioners, in such Manner, and under such Restrictions and Regulations, as to the House shall leem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; several

Acts passed for paving, cleansing, and lighting, the Streets, Squares, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, were read: And,

Mr. Luke Idefon, being examined, said, That the Commissioners appointed for putting the said Acts in Execution, had caused several Streets within the said Parish to be paved and lighted; but that there are several Streets within the said Parish, which have not yet been new paved; and that it would be a great Advantage to the Inhabitants, to have all the Streets within the Parish well paved, cleansed, and lighted: And the Witness said, he apprehended the Work would be performed in a much Jcfs Time, and more to the Satisfodion of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, if the same were to be under the Direction of the Commissioners, who are Inhabitants of the Parish, than under the general Law: And the Wit-, . fiefs delivered in to your Committee an Account, containing the Names of the several Streets within the said Parish which want new paving, together with the Number of square Yards in each Street, and a Calculation of the Expences which will attend the new paving the said Streets: And he said, he apprehended the Expences which would be necessary to keep all the Pavements within the Parish in good Repair, and so keep the same properly cleansed and lighted, and to defray all the other Expences relating thereto, would amount to the Sum of £. 5,500

per Annum. ,.

And the Witness said, That an Eighteen-penny Rate, made according to the present Assessment, will raise, within the said Parish,1 7,^00 > so that there will Be a Surplus off. d,oooo per Annum, to discharge t he Money which will be necessary to be borrowed for the Purposes aforesaid; and that, when the Debt was paid off, a Rate of 14 <d.in the Popnd would defray the several Purposes

jiforesaid. ., '

And being asked. How he made the Calculations he had mentioned ? he said, He calculated the Expences of fjie Work, from the Prices which bad been given for new paving the Streets within the'Parish; and he made his Calculation for raising the Mohey to defray those Ex-.. perices from the present Assessments of the Parish: And ' . added. That he did not doubt but the whole Pavements

within the Parish might be finished in Three Years Time, if an A.d was passed for tho Purposes aforesaid; and, that such-Gentlemen only as- are Inhabitants of the Parish were appointed Commissioners* to see the necessary Works carried into Execution*; .

Application has been made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for impowering the Justices of the Peace to widen and otherwise improve the present Way, or Approach, from the High Street, in the City of Exeter, to the Castle, and to apply the Sum of f. 1000, out of the County Stock, for that Purpose; and representing to the House, that, if a new Way was opened and made, from the said High Street, through Part of Castle Lane, and certain other Lands and Grounds, cross a Lane leading to the New Buildings, and from thence to the Cajtie, and a few old Building? now Handing on some Parts thereof were taken down, and some Ground was purchased for that Purpose, such new Way would be more commodious; and that the opening, making, and maintaining thereof, will be less expensive, and of greater Utility, then the repairing and widening the present Way, as prayed for by the said Petition: And therefore praying the House to grant the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Coqsideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Devon, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, the said Acts were read; and Mr. Geo. Jones, being examined, said. That great Progress has been made in the repairing the said Roads, and that the Sum of £. 2000 has been borrowed on the Credit of the said Acts, which still remains due, and cannot be repaid, and the said Road effectually repaired, widened, and kept in Repair, unless the Term thereby granted be further continued, and the Powers thereof enlarged. And, Mr. Thomas Brunfden, being examined, said, That the Road from Speenhamland, at the East Side of the Town of Marlborough, to the Turnpike Road at the West Side of the said Town, is very much out of Repair, and cannot be amended by the Laws in being And,

Mr. Jones, being further examined, said, That if the Roads, under the Management of the present Trust, were divided into Two Districts, with distinct Funds, and separate Trustees, it would be very beneficial to that Part of the Country, and would more effectually answer the Intentions of the said Acts.

And the Witness produced to your Committee, the Minute Book of the said Trustees; whereby it appeared.

That at a general Meeting of the Trustees and others, pursuant to ari Advertisement for that Purpose, it was agreed to apply to Parliament for the above Purpose.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition; Mr. Jones said, That the Road from the Turnpike Road at Speenhamland, to a Tenement, late a Blacksmith’s Shop, being about 100 Yards, is very narrow and incommodious, and cannot be repaired and widened by the Laws in being.

Which Evidence was confirmed by a Member present.

The other Order of the Day being read; mbroke The House proceeded to the further Hearing of the Matter of the Petition of Hugh Owen, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Pembroke.

And the Counsel were called in.

And John Griffiths, Esquire, of , late High

Sheriff for the County of Pembroke, wasalfo called in.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner proceeded in their Evidence; and examined a Witness, to prove the Partiality of One of the Persons appointed by the Sheriff to act as his Deputy, in favour of the Sitting Member, in admitting several Persons to poll for the Sitting Member, and rejecting others under the same Circumstances who offered to poll for the Petitioner.

And also, that the said Deputy rejected several Persons who demanded to poll for the Petitioner, and who offered to take the Freeholders Oath.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner examined another Witness, in order to prove that, in several Conversations previous to the late Election, the said Sheriff had, with great Expresslons of Bitterness, declared himself an Enemy to the Person and Family of the Petitioner; and also that, in the Booth where the Sheriff presided, another Person appeared in general to decide the Rights of the Voters; and that the Decisions of the said Sheriff, and of the other Person, were, in many Instances, very partial in favour of the Sitting Member.

And another Witness was examined, in order to prove that, though Application was made to the Sheriff to go to another Booth, in order to decide the Right of a dif-puted Vote, which had been rejected by his Deputy, he never went.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner having proposed to examine several Cheque Clerks, to prove the Number of Leaseholders and Freeholders that voted at the several Booths;

The said Evidence was objected to by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, as not being admiffable to contradict: what appears on the Original Poll Book.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner having been heard, in Answer to that Objection;

One of the Counsel for the Sitting Member was heard, by way of Reply.

And the Entry in the Journals of the House, of the 14th Day of July 1715, relating to the Election for the County of Bedford, and also the Entry in the Journals of the House of the 20th Day of January 1710, relating to the Election for the County of Rutland, being read;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

The House was moved, That an Act, made in the 7th and 8th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, inti-tujed, An Act for the further regulating Elections of Members to serve in Parliament, and for the preventing irregular Proceedings of Sheriffs, and other Officers, in the Electing and Returning such Members, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

Then the Counsel were again called in.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner proceeded in their Evidence; and examined the Cheque Clerks in the several Booths, to prove the Number of Freeholders and Leaseholders who voted at the said Election, and to shew that the Majority of Freeholders was in favour of the Petitioner.

And a Witness was examined, to prove that the Person who took the Poll, did, in many Instances, mark upon the said Poll, as Freeholders, several Persons who declared they voted only as Leaseholders; and, upon his being asked why he did so, he always replied, that he had Orders so to do.

Vo l.32.

They also examined a Witness, in order to prove, that a Voter, who offered to vote for the Petitioner as a Leaseholder, was rejected.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner having proposed to shew, that the improved Value of the Vote so rejected was above 40 s.a Year;

The Lease under which the said Voter claimed his Right of Voting was produced, bearing Date the 10th Day of September 1747.

And Objection being mad* to the said Lease being read;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Resolved, That the said Lease be now read.

The Counsel were again called in; and the said Lease was read.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were again directed to withdraw.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the Counsel for the Petitioner be restrained from producing Evidence to prove that the Voter had a Freehold, entitling him to vote for a Member to serve in Parliament, in respect of the Tenement leased to him, for One or more Life or Lives in being, under the foie Consideration of the Rent reserved;

The House was moved, That an Act made in the 8th Year of the Reign of King Henry the Sixth, intituled. What fort of Men shall be C hoofers, and who shall be. chosen Knights of the Parliament, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly j

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the House do now adjourn;

The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; an Act, made in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for making a navigable Cut or Canal, from the River Trent, at or near Wilden , in the County of

Derby, to the River Mersey, at or near Runcorn Gap; was read. And,

Brindley, the Engineer, being examined, said, That Forty Miles Open-Work of the said Canal is completed; Thirty-three from Hock Hill towards IVilden , Four Miles and a Quarter on both Sides of Hare and

Two Miles and Three Quarters on each Side of Prefion Hill.

That the Tunnel, finished at Hare Castle, is 944 Yards, and at Preston 125 Yards; that zi Locks, 60 Road- Bridges, 13 Boats, and 50 Culverts or Arches under the Canal, for carrying Brooks, Rivers, and Rivulets, under the Navigation, are finished.

That the lowest Lock, made nearest to IVilden Ferry, is opposite Burton; that there are Three below not finished; One below Swarkfton nearly finished; and that there is a Lock in some forwardness Two or Three Miles below the River Dove: That he had calculated, that the whole of the Navigation will be finished in Three Years from Christmas last. And,

Mr. — Sparrow, Clerk to the Company of Proprietors, being examined, said, That £. 130,000 was authorized to be raised by the said Act in the first Place, and £. 20,000 more if that was inefficient j that £. 86,900 has been paid into the Hands of the Treasurer, and near the Whole of it expended; and that £. 43,100 is subscribed by the Proprietors, to be paid for as the Calls are made; making together the £. 130,000. And,

Mr. Brindley, being further examined, said, That, to complete the Navigation, it will coll £. 50,000 more than the £. 150,000; and that he apprehends this Sum

will complete it; that he forms his Judgment from the Expences that have already incurred. Then,

The Agent for the Petitioners informed your Committee, That, in order to facilitate the Execution of the said Act, and make it more convenient to the Parties concerned, it is necessary to make some Amendments to several of the Provisions of the said Act; and he instanced some of them; viz. to make Transferring Shares more easy j that the Property in the said Navigation, which is now real Estate, be made Personal; to alter the Method of making Satisfaction for Damages in getting Materials; to enable the Proprietors to take Tonnage for Distances less than One Mile; to oblige Commissioners and Juries to assess the Value of the Lands and of Damages separately; to declare what Length Vessels, passing through Locks, shall be of, and what Burthen they shall carry; to alter some of the Penalties laid by the Act, relating to Satisfaction being made to Corporations in Rent, instead of a gross Sum.

And the Agent likewise informed your Committee, That Provision should be made to confirm what has been done in carrying the Navigation through the River Trent at Whichnor; to make Roads for the Convenience of Land Owners on the Outsides of the Towing Paths; to take down a certain small Building or Outhouse, at Whatcroft, in Cheshire; and that some further Powers may be necessary.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the said Report be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

To prove the Allegations of ,the first-mentioned Petition j a Survey and Plan of the intended Navigation were produced: And,

Mr. John Longbottom, being examined, said. That he had surveyed the Grounds over which the Navigation was proposed to be carried, and made that Plan; that . he thinks the Scheme practicable*-and that it will be of great "Utility to the Country, as there are Coals in some Parts, which are much wanted in others; and as it will open a safe, easy, and expeditious Communication between several trading Towns.

He also informed your Committee, That the Price Of Carriage, by the Canal, would be about Two Pence a Ton per Mile, which he apprehends, will be much cheaper than Land Carriage; but, being cross examined, as to the Distances of certain Places from each other, and the Price of Land Carriage, he owned that he could not speak particularly to either: And being asked as to the Manufacture carried on at Leyland and Ormskirk, and what Communication there was between those Towns and Liverpool ? he said, He did not know . of any.

Mr. Henry Acroyd, being examined, said, That the Price of Land Carriage from Blackbourn to is

qj. W. a Pack, or 445. a Ton; and from Burnley to rrefton, 2 s. 6d.a Pack, and the Distance 23 Miles:

That he thinks Carriage, in general, will be reduced Five Parts in Six, that is, from One Shilling a Mile to Two Pence, for a Ton of Goods; but that, in this Calculation he makes no Allowance for the Difference in Length between Land and Water Carriage; and, in regard to the Carriage between Blackbourn and,

there will still remain Four Miles Carriage to come to the proposed Canal:

That the Water Carriage will be Two Pence per Ton, including Wharfage and all other Expences, except Porterage:

That the Distance from Leeds to Liverpoole, by Land, is about 82 measured Miles, and the Price of Carriage about One Shilling a Mile fora Ton; that, by the Canal it will be io8f Miles, and the Price of Carriage Two Pence a Mile. v

Mr. Abraham Balme, being examined, confirmed Mr. Acroyd's Evidence, in regard to the Distance between Leeds and Liverpoole, both by Land and Water, and as to the Price of Carriage both Ways:

And said. That he includes the Expence of Freight and Tonnage in the 2 dper Ton, but docs not include Wharfage, Warehouses, or Porterage:

VOL. 32.

That the Wharfage is calculated at per Ton, which will be the same if Goods go the whole Length of the Canal, or ever so little a Way:

That the Course of the Canal in , will be

through a great manufacturing Country, till you come to Skipton, after which it falls off:

That Limestone is very expensive by Land Carriage, and will be cheaper by Water than the Price he mentioned.

Mr. James Brindley, being examined, said. That he had seen the Survey, and that he had gone over the whole Lands:

He delivered in an Estimate of the Expence of making the proposed Navigation, including the Purchase of Lands, amounting to £. 269,502; but he informed your Committee, that since the making of that Estimate, he had gone over Part of the Ground again, and found some Reasons for altering this Estimate ta f. 300,000, in which, he thinks, he includes every possible Expence, and that there will be Money to (pare.

Being asked. How far it would be necessary to go in order to supply the Reservoir with Water? he said. Two Miles and an Half.

Mr. Abraham Balme, being again examined, said, That upwards of £. 160,000 is already subscribed towards carrying on this Undertaking; and that, he is certain, there will not be any Want of Money.

1770.

Inhabitants of the said City, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; several Members present informed your Committee, ThatAfo*/ Sarum, eonfifts of Three Parishes, Saint Thomas, Saint Edmund, and Saint Martin; that the Poor are maintained out of the Collections, by an equal Number of Rates, and a like Mode of Rating in each Parish, assessed by the respective Officers of the Three Parishes.

That this Method has been found beneficial to the City, as it prevents Suits relating to the Settlement of the Poor; and, if it should be changed, would be very detrimental to the City, and would bring a heavy Burthen on the poorer Parishes.

But that it is apprehended, that it is not practicable to continue the present Mode of Collection, without the Authority of an Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for consolidating the Rates to be made for the Relief of the Poor of the respective Parishes of Saint Thomas, Saint Edmund, and Saint Martin, in the City of New Sarum: And that Sir Charles Whitworth, Mr. Hujfey, of Salisbury> and Mr. Harris, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Memorandum; The Deputy Auditor of the Exchequer having repeatedly declared the Impossibility of making out an Account of the Civil List Expence9, which incurred and became due at that Office for the above 8 Yean; therefore the Lords of the Treasury directed, that the same should be made out in the bell Manner possible from the Entries in the Treasury Books. — The Treasurer of the Chamber having informed their Lordships, that from want of Materials in his Office, no Account can be made up of the Charge during the same Time; the above Charge inserted in this Account, is therefore the Amount of the several Sums craved by the then Treasurer? of the Chamber for those Years, and which were actually paid upon their Memorials to the Treasury. — The Mailer of the Horse not having any Accounts in his Office to enable him to make out the Charge there, the same hath been done in respect to the Expence of that Office as in that of the Treasurer of the Chamber. — The other Charges are taken from the Accounts transmitted to the Treasury from the several other Offices above mentioned.

Aa it is impossible to make an Annual Account from the ill of January to the 31st of January^ therefore this Account is made up for 8 complete Years, commencing from the ift of January in the Year 1751.

Resolved, That this House will now proceed to the further Hearing of the Matter of the Petition of Hugh Owen, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Pembroke.

The House accordingly proceeded to the further Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

And the Counsel were called in.

And John Griffiths, Esquire, of CUnderwen, late High Sheriff for the County of Pembroke, was also called in.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner proceeded in their Evidence; and examined a Witness, in order to prove the partial Behaviour of One of the SherifPs Deputies in Favour of the Sitting Member; and that, though, at the Close of the Poll, the Sheriff was informed of the different Rules that had been observed by his Deputies in their Decisions on the disputed Votes in the several Booths, and was desired to grant a Scrutiny, he refused the fame.

Then another Witness was examined, in order to prove, that One of the Deputies rejected a great Number of Persons who offered to poll for the Petitioner, under Pretence that the Persons from whom they held their Leases had no Power to grant such Leases; and that the said Deputy appeared to act as the Friend of the Sitting Member.

He was also examined as to the Refusal of a Scrutiny by the Sheriff, at the Close of the Poll.

And a Witness was examined, to prove, that the said several Persons so rqjefted did offer to take the Freeholders Oath.

Then several Witnesses were examined, in order to prove, That One of the Deputies of the said Sheriff had, before the Election, made Application to a Person to vote for the Sitting Member; and that afterwards, when the same Person offered his Vote for the Petitioner, the said Deputy, then presiding in the Booth, receded his Vote, without giving any Reason for so doing.

And the several Cheque Clerks were examined, to shew the Number of Voters that had been rejected, who offered to vote for the Petitioner and the Sitting Mem* ber.
