BritUb A Petition of the Trustees of the British Museum. being offered to be presented to the House}

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends the same to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Petitioners represented to Parliament, that the Sum allowed for the Establishment and Support of the said Museum, was reduced to a Capital of £. 30,000 Reduced Bank Annuities, the Dividend of which, amounting to £. 900, was, notwithstanding their utmost'Attention to the forming their Establishment with Frugality, greatly insufficient for that Purpose; upon which Representation, they obtained a Grant of a further Sum of £. 2,000; and upon like Applications in the Fourth and Sixth Yean of His present Majesty’s Reign, the Trustees obtained Grants of the further Sums of £. 2,000 each' of these 'Years for the fame* Purpose; which Sums, together with the Produce of the said £. 30,000, are so far spent, that what remains is not sufficient to defray the Expences of the current Year; and that, though Major Eds Legacy is fallen in, and has been paid, yet, as that Money and the Interest and Produce thereof are by Act of Parliament appropriated for particular Purpo’fes, the same cannot be applied to-

wards the current and necessary Expences of the House:

And#therefore praying the House, to grant them such further Support, towards enabling them to carry on the Execution of the Trust repoled in them by Parliament, for the general Benefit of Learning and useful Knowledge, as to the House shall lcetn meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of African Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be pre- Company, fented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read}

Setting forth. That the Petitioners have laid before the House, an Account of the Sum granted for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-eight, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the Twenty-third of George the Second, for extending and improving the Trade to Africa; and that they have inverted the Money granted in One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-nine, for the Support and Maintenance of the several Forts and Settlements on the said Coast, and likewise the Money granted for the Repairs of Cape Coast Castle; and that the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast having been delivered to the Petitioners in a very bad State by the Royal African Company, and the Sums annually granted by Parliament being nearly expended in the Maintenance and Pay of the several Garrisons, with other necessary Charges, leaving very little for the Repairs of the said Forts, many of them still remain in a very ruinous Condition; and that the Petitioners, being sensible of the Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, therefore pray the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, and likewise for the Repairs still wanted, as to them shall feera meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Coalheavers working on the River. Coalbeavers.* Thames was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, fora Number of Years, laboured under the greatest Hardships, through the cruel Impositions of a Set of Men, who call themselves Coal Undertakers, who have obliged the Petitioners to give them a very great Part of what they earn, in order to obtain Employment from them; by which Means their Wives and Children have been reduced to starving; and in case of Sickness or Death, the Undertakers have never contributed to their Relief, but left them a Burthen to the several Parishes where they reside; and that these Coal Undertakers, are, in their Profession, an unnecessary Body of Men; and that the Coal Trade can be better carried on without them, by an Office properly established by Parliament: And therefore praying the House, to take their same into Consideration, and cause an Amendment to be made to an Act of Parliament, palfed in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-eight, for their Relief and Regulation, which Act has been found to be deficient, and ineffectual to answer the Purposes of protesting the Petitioners from the Impositions they labour under; and that such an Amendment of the said Act may be made as the House shall judge necessary, to enable the Petitioners to enjoy the Fruits of their Labour, without being imposed on by a Set of mercenary Men, which, the Petitioners presume, has been the Occasion of all the Disturbances that have happened where the Petitioners reside.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Francis Vincent, Mr. Kynaf ton, See.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber > and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records: And all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

That the Petitioners observe by the Votes, that a Bill is ordered to be brought in, for laying a Duty or Tonnage on. all Ships, Vessels, and Barges, coming within, or trading and belonging to, the Port of Plymouth, in the said County of Devon, and on Coals and Culm imported into the said Port; and representing to the House, that,

on all Ships and Vessels coming within, or trading and belonging to, the Port of the said Town of and also a small Duty on Coals and Culm imported into the said Port; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the above Duties are intended to be laid on all Vessels laden with Culm, and other Merchandize, which trade up and down the River Tamur; and if a Duty should belaid on Culm for burning Lime, or on the Limestone, it would be very prejudicial and discouraging to the Farmers; and that, as the Revenues arising on the said Duties are to be appropriated towards rendering Harbour at

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member proceeded, in their Evidence, and examined a Witness as to the general Conduct of the Sheriff, during the Time, and at the Close of the Poll; and also to prove that, when the Poll was dosed, the Sheriff directed Proclamation to be made in his Presence in the several Booths, That " if any Persons thought themselves aggrieved, they " might apply to him, and have Redress."

The said Witness was also examined, to prove that when, at the Close of the Poll, a Scrutiny Was demanded, it was declared by the Sheriff, or by his Deputy in his Presence, " That the whole Poll had been a Scrutiny j that every Freeholder had been sworn j that his Power " did not extend to oblige the Voters to produce their " Title Deeds s and that therefore a Scrutiny was not " necessary."

The said Witness was further examined, to prove that, at the Close"of the Poll, the Conduct of but On# only of the Deputies was impeached.

Another Witness was examined as to the Behaviour of the Sheriff in the County Hall, previous to the holding the Poll, and to prove, that the Cheque 1 Clerks were all sworn, the Deputies appointed, ajid their Instructions delivered to them, in the Presence of the Sheriff, and in the Presence of the Petitioner’s Friends and Agents, before the Adjournment to the Place of Polling.

Another Witness was examined, as to the Time and Manner of making out the Deputations to the several Deputies.

And several of the said Deputations being produced*

A Petition of William Bollan was presented to the Ameriean

House, Colonies.

74<*

5* Martii.

A. 1770.

House, and read; Setting forth. That, in His present Majesty’s Reign, Measures have been devised, and Laws made, for raising a Revenue, for several Purposes, out of American Commerce; the natural Augmentation whereof, thus prevented, would have caused a continual growing Consumption of British Manufactures, with a constant Increase of British Navigation, the Source of their Naval Power; would in Circuit have enriched the King and Kingdom far more by Consent, than they could be by any Compulsion; would have preserved in its former full Strength that cordial Union of the British Subjects, residing in Britain and the Colonies, which is apparently necessary to their mutual and lasting Welfare j and would moreover have augmented the Abilities of the British Americans, and given fresh Spirit to their laudable Inclination to venture their Lives and Fortunes against the Public Enemies when they shall renew their Hostilities, which, in Point of Difficulty and Danger, may equal or exceed those that were in the late War so happily l'urmounted, and which, without Question, though with uncertain Pace, are daily approaching; and that, amongst other Measures, even British Manufactures have, contrary to the plainest Principle of Commerce, been made the Subjects of Taxation, when imported into the Colonies; and that Regulations of American Commerce have been subjected to Military Execution, fitter to extirpate, than to regulate, preserve, and increase, Trade j and that Offences, Accusations, and Litigations, relative to Laws enacted touching the American Trade and Revenue have been subjected to Civil Adjudication, incompatible with the English Constitution, and pregnant with Hardships exceeding all Example; and that the King’s causing such Monies to be applied, out of certain American Revenues, as he shall think proper or necessary, for defraying the Charges of administering Justice, and supporting Civil Government, within all or any of the Colonies, would be such a Seizure of their immediate Civil Government into the King’s Hands, as would be attended with unspeakable Difficulties and Hardships; would subvert pro tanto the proper Constitution of the Colonies, which are, in their Nature, and by their Institution, distinct Members of the Commonwealth, established by the Wisdom of former Ages, and would be inconsistent with the Charter granted to the Province of Massachu-

Jet>s Bay, by their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary; and that the JunClion of the Colonies, for the Purposes of Civil Government, is manifestly repugnant to that standing Policy of their Severance, whereby they have have been so well governed from the Time of their1 Existence; and that the Application of Monies raised in a Colony, which defrays all the proper and necessary Charges of administering Justice, and supporting Civil' Government there, to pay the Charges of such Administration and Support in any other Colony neglecting its Duty in this Behalf, would be a plain Departure from the permanent Principle of natural Justice; and , that the; Hew System of defending, protecting, and fc-curing, the Colonies, devised and practised by His Majesty’s Ministers, is likewise improvident, oppressive, and ‘ dangerous, to the Kingdom and the Colonies; and that, in Consequence of the preceding and other Ministerial Measures, the British Manufactures, Trade, and Navigation, have been discouraged, and British America reduced from a State of Quiet, with chearful and profitable Obedience, to a State of great Distress and dangerous Insatisfac-tion; and that the Errors and Improvidence of Ministers, with the hostile Designs and Proceedings of France td undermine the British American Dominions, Trade, and Fishery, brought on the late expensive and dangerous War; and British America is now, in Consequence of the Errors and Improvidence of His Majesty’s Ministers, brought into a State of Invitation of Foreign War;

And therefore praying, That he may be heard before the House, in order that he may defend the Rights and Interest of the Province aforesaid, and give such necessary Information as this or the late Parliament have not received; whereby, he hopes, the House will be in some Degree assisted in taking those salutary Measures, which the Prosperity and Safety of the Kingdom, and the Colonies, at this interesting Conjuncture require.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Upon the Petition of John Williams and Thomas Arthington, Esquires, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Philip Rajhleigh and James Modyford Heywood, Esquires, for the Borough of Fowey, in the County of Cornwall,

The Committee examined the Merits of this Election. The Standing Order of the Hoyfe, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for reltraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament, for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination of the House of Commons, was read.

And the last Determination of the House, upon the 5th Day of May 1701, concerning the Ri^ht of electing a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Fowey, was also read; whereby it is resolved, That the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliamen^for the Borough of Fowey, in the County of is

in the Prince’s Tenants, who are capable of being Portreeves of the said Borough; and in such Inhabitants of the said Borough only as pay Scotland Lot.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners alledging. That they understood that the Words of the said Resolution,

Prince’s"

Account; Exchequer Bill*.

750 5° MarA. 1770.

" Prince’s Tetiahts, who are capable of being Portreeves," were not meant to restraia any Prince’s Tenants from voting; and, therefore, if they added Fifty-two Persons to the Poll of the Petitioners, who were Prince’s Tenants, and that had tendered themselves to -be admitted on the Roll of the Court Baron of the Manor of Fowey, and bad been refused, and who, at the said Election, had tendered their Votes for the Petitioners, and were rejected, the Petitioners would have a clear Majority over the Sitting Members.

The Counsel for the Sitting Members infilled. That Prince’s Tenants, who have a Right to vote at Elections, are not Prince’s Tenants at large, hut such only as are capable of being Portreeves.

And to prove what Prince’s Tenants are, by the Usage of the Borough, capable of being Portreeves, they called

Mr. Thomas Jones, who said he had known Fowey above Forty Years; and, he being examined, said, That Prince’s Tenants, capable of being Portreeves, may be intitled by Conveyance, or by Descent, but they mull first be admitted at the Court Baron of the Manor; that he never knew of but One Instance to the contrary, which was in the same of Mr. Coryton, the Returning Officer, at the Election preceding the last Election, who was presented to the Office of Portreeve at an occasional Court, held in January 1765; that, regularly. Courts ought to be held a Month after . as he be-

lieved, at leall;. all the Witness ever attended were so, except that above mentioned.

That the Meaning of holding that Occasional Court was to make a Portreeve, because Mr. Rajhleigh, the then Portreeve, was the Candidate at the Election, and it would not be proper for him to act as Portreeve; yet there was no Necessity to take Coryton, there being many Persons present who had been admitted on the Court Roll:

That he has been present at Courts, in many other Manors, and never knew any other Custom of chusing Portreeves.

And being asked. How Coryton came to be a Portreeve de fa£lo, but not dt jure ? he said, Because he was not admitted on the Roll: That he remembered Coryton adfing as Returning Officer in 1765, when, he believed, an Objection was made to his Return: that he remembered Four Portreeves of Fo, and only Coryton presented by the Homage before he was admitted; that he was made Portreeve again in 1767; that he was admitted after his first acting as Portreeve, and before the Second; and that he continued in Office Two Years and a Half after his First Election.

He then mentioned Lewis Tremain, Esquire, John

Jones, John Pomeroy, and Stephen who, he

helieved, all voted in 1765 as Prince’s Tenants; that they were on the Lift of Tenants, but did not know they were admitted; and he mentioned William Lambe who, he said, voted in 1765, and was on the Court Roll before he voted, he having done his Fealty in 1754: That there is a Difference between the Court Roll and Lift of Tenants j the Tenants are sworn and do Fealty, and then are admitted on the Roll in consequence thereof; they are put on the Lift by the Steward, which Lift is brought to the Court, when they attend to take the Oaths, and to be admitted: that a Person can serve on the Homage before he is admitted on the Roll, if he is on the Lift; that the Witness saw the Court Roll before 1757, with many Names thereto, but that none of the Persons he had mentioned were, as he believed, on it, when he saw it, except Mr. Lambe;

that, he apprehended, if a Person comes to the Court, and claims to be admitted on the Roll, and makes out a Title, the Steward, or Jury, are to admit him; that, if the Steward is not satisfied, and refuses to admit the Person, lie may apply to the Homage, and claim to be presented; and believes, that if a Person is presented by the Homage, the Steward cannot refuse to admit 21

him; and that he would do very ill if he did; that it is the Duty of the Homage to present.-.

And being asked, Whether the Steward has a Right to receive who he pleases, without Claim being made out ? he said, No: That he was of Opinion, the Steward may admit, upon his foie Judgment, when the Claim is made 01st to his Satisfaction; and that he has known a Steward admit People not presented by the Homage.

Then Mr. John Kimber, Deputy Steward of the said Manor, was called, and produced the Court Rolls of the Manor of Fowey, dated 24 1740, 19 October

1742, 7 October 1745, 10 May 1754, 14 1765,

23 October 1767, and 10 Ofl 1769; and there was allb produced a Copy of the Roll of Proceedings of the said Court, dated 9 March 1724, in order to shew the Method of presenting the Portreeves of the said Borough, the Deaths of the Tenants thereof, admitting of Tenants on the Rolls, and their doing Fealty.

Then the Counsel were directed to withdraw.

And the Committee came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Prince’s Tenants, capable of being Portreeves of the Borough of Fozvey, are such Tenants only as have been duly admitted upon the Court Rolls of the Manor, and have done their Fealty.

And the Counsel being again called in, and acquainted with the said Resolution, the Counsel for the Petitioners were again heard.

And then the Counsel were ordered to withdraw.

Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Philip Rajhleigh f Esquire, is duly elected a Bor-

gefs to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough o(Fowey, in the County of Cornwall.

Resolved, That it it the Opinion of this Committee, That James Modyford Hey wood, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Fowey, in the County of Cornwall.

;Resolved, That it appears to this House, that the Poll, taken at the late Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Pembroke, was in many Instances so irregularly taken, as to render if impo0ible for ibis: House to ascertain which of the Candidates had the Majority of legal Votes.

A:Motion was made, and the Question being put, That ;Sir Richard Phillips, Baronet, is duly elected a Knighbof the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Pembroke-,

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That Hugh Owen, Esquire, is duly elected a Knight of

the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Pembroke

Jt passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Pembroke; was a void Election.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the ciefting of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the CountyJ of Pembroke, in the room of Sir Richard Phillips, Baronet, whose Election for the said County has been declared void.

A Motion was made, That John Griffiths, Esquire, late. High Sheriff of the County of Pembroke, having opened the Election for chuling a Knight of the Shire to serve in Parliament for the said County, prelided thereat, and taken the Oath appointed to be taken by Returning Officers, to return such a Person as should appear to him, to the belt of his Judgment, to have the Majority of legal Votes; and having appointed Deputies in teveral Booths, who, during the said Poll, decided in his Abicoce on the Legality of a very great Number of Votes; and having, in some Instances, refused to take into Consideration their Decisions, although he was requested so to do, and Complaint was made to him of the Partiality of the said Deputies; and having absented himselffrom the Place, of Polling during a great Part of the Time the Poll was taking, by Means whereof it became impossible for him to form a certain Judgment who had the Majority of legal Votes, acted illegally and partially, with a View to serve Sir Richard PhBaronet, and is guilty of a great Breach of his Duty as Returning Officer.

And the Sheriff being called in, and the said Charge being read to him by Mr. Speaker;

The said Sheriff wholly denied the said Charge; and desired that he might be allowed a Month’s Time to lend for his Witnesses, and to make his Defence; and that he may be heard, by his Counsel, thereupon.

And then he withdrew.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Charge be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Monday the 2d Day of April next.

Ordered, That the said Sheriff be then heard, by his' Counsel, against the said Charge, if he thinks fit.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That, when the said Charge is heard, Witnesses be allowed to be examined in Support of the said Charge, ’ notwithstanding the Sheriff has been present during the Hearing of the Matter of the Election, and was frequently told by Mr. Speaker, that, if he thought any Matteraffeftedhim, he was at Liberty tocross-examineahy oftlie Witnesses, who were all examined in his Presence;

Speaker acquainted him with the said Orders.

And then he was again directed to withdraw.

The Order of the Day being read, for hearing at the Carmarthen Bar of this House, the Matter of the several Petitions, Election. complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County Borough of Carmarthen;

The Counsel were called in.

And the said Petitions were read.

And the last Determination of the House, concerning the Right of electing a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said County Borough, made the 19th Day of March 1727, was read; whereby it was resolved, " That " the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Carmarthen, is in the Burgesses of the said Borough."

And the Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, forreftraining the Counsel, at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence, touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, was also read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners were heard.

And the original Poll, taken at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said County Borough, was produced and read.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners having proposed, in order to establish a Majority in Favour of the Petitioner, to produce Evidence to prove, that Twenty Persons, having a Right to vote, had offered their Votes for the Petitioner at the last Election, and had been rejected; it was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, that the said Twenty Persons did offer their Votes for the Petitioner, and were rejected.

Then the Counsel were again called in.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member produced in Evidence the said Copy of a Bye Law,

Then having proposed to prove, that, since the 36th of Queen Elizabeth, the Election of Mayor has been, in Pursuance of the said Bye Law, by the Mayor and Common Council only;

The same was admitted by the Counsel for the Petitioners.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member having proposed to produce a Copy of the Record of a Judgment, obtained in the Year 1758, in a Cause between the King and Roger Phillips, to shew that the Point of the

Illegality of the Election of such Mayors was then determined; and that the Burgesses now in Question had Notice of that Judgment, and acquiesced in that Deci-fion, and submitted to it;

The said Evidence was objected to by the Counsel for the Petitioners, as not admilfable, none of the Petitioners being Parties to that Trial.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were again directed to withdraw.

Mr. Sandys reported from the Committee,' to whom the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Parish of St. , within the Liberty of Westminster, whose Name are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as fotloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; several Acts passed for paving, cleaning, and lighting, the City and Liberty of Westminster, and for removing Annoyances and Obstructions therein, were read: And,

Mr. David Salter informed your Committee, That the Commissioners appointed to execute the said Acts, have made a considerable Progress in paving the Streets, and other Places, within the said Parish; but that there are yet several Streets remaining unpaved: And he said. He apprehended, that if a seperate Commission was appointed for the Parish of St. Anne, the Pavements might be completed sooner, and at a less Expence, than they can be under the general Laws.

Then he produced to your Committee a Paper, containing the Names of the several Streets within the said Parish, distinguishing those which have been already paved by Commissioners for putting the said recited Acts in Execution, from the Streets which still remain to be paved; and he also produced an Account of the Num-2Z

Martii. A. 1776.

t 1

ber of square Yards of Pavement, in the said Parish,

together with an Estimate of the Expence which will attend the paving the several Streets, and other Places within the same, and the annual Expence of keeping the said Pavements properly repaired and cleansed, and of lighting the said Streets and other Places: And being asked, How it was proposed to defray the Expences thereof? he said. It was intended to lay a Rate of is. 6 d.in the Pound upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish, according to the present Proportion of rating the said Inhabitants towards the Relief of the Poop, which, by an Estimate he had made, will produce a . Sum more than sufficient for the Purposes aforesaid.

And being asked the Question, he said. That he was of Opinion, that the several Works aforesaid would be sooner executed, and equally as well, and cheaper, and more to the Satisfaction of the Inhabitants, under a separate Commission of themselves, than under the present . Laws, as the Works would be more immediately under their own Inspection, than they can. be under the Inspection of the present Commission, who, from the Ex-tenfiveness of the Commission, must, of Necessity, trust much more to the Care and Fidelity of their Servants, than Commissioners residing upon the Spot would be obliged to do.

William Wright, Esquire, confirmed Mr. Salter's Evidence.

RuncornGap atcr> was presented to the House, and read; Setting Navigation. forth, That an Act passed in the Thirty-second Year of King George the Second, to enable the Petitioner to make a Navigable Cut or Canal from Salford to Worjley Mill, and Middle Wood, and Hollin in the County Palatine of Lancaster; and that another Act passed in the Thirty-third Year of his said Majesty, to enable the

Petitioner to make a Navigable Cut or Canal from Worfley Mill, over the River Jrwell to , and to

Longford Bridge, in the said County Palatine; and that another Act passed in the Second Year of His present’ Majesty, to enable the Petitioner to extend the said Canal from Longford Bridge, to or near the in the County of Chester, there to communicate with the River Mersey; and that another Act passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for making a navigable Cut or Canal from the River Trent, at or near, Wilden Ferry, in the County of Derby, to the River Mersey, at, or near, Runcorn Gap; and it appearing, that if the said Navigation to be made by the Petitioner by virtue of the said Act of the Second Year of His present Majesty, and the said Navigation from the Trent to the Mersey, were to communicate with each other, at Preston Brook, near Preston on the Hill, in the said County of Chester, and be from thence carried on, by the same Canal, to the River Mersey, at, or near, Runcorn Gap, it would render both the said Navigations, more convenient and complete, and be of greater Advantage to the Public than if the same had terminated at the -fiones; the Petitioner thereupon expressed his Willing-ness to make such Communication at Preston; and, at his own Coils and Charges, to carry on, and maintain, the said Navigation, from thence, to, or near, Runcorn Gap, upon being allowed to take a small Tonnage upon the fame; and Powers were accordingly given the Petitioner, by the said last mentioned Act, to complete the said Navigation, from such Junction,. to, or near, Runcorn Gap; and that the Petitioner has made considerable Progress in the Execution of the said Work; and is now proceeding, with great Expedition, to iinish and complete the same, upon the Plan agreed and directed by the said last mentioned Act; which will be of great Service to the Public, and to all those Inland Navigations which will communicate, through it, with the Port of Liverpool; and that, by a Clause in the last mentioned Act, the Petitioner is restrained from making the said Cut or Canal within the Distance of 360 Yards from the Mansion House of Sir Richard Brook, called Norton Hall, or otherwise than above the Woods on the Southerly Side of the said Mansion House, and on the Westerly Side of the Farm House opposite the Field called The Great Grime; or to take, or divert, any Water out of the Mill Pool belonging to the said Sir Richard Brook, near the said Mansion House, or out of the Streams which flow into the said Pool; and that the Petitioner, not being sufficiently informed of the particular Restrictions intended, and how far the same might afled the Execution of the said Plan, had not an Opportunity of laying before Parliament the necessary Evidence relative thereto, at the Time of passing the said Act; and that the Petitioner finds, from the most accurate Surveys, Levels, and Observations, which he has caused to be taken and made, since the passing the said Act, that, from the Nature and Situation of the Ground, and Springs of Water, before mentioned, and from the Depth which the said Canal mull necessarily be made, to keep it in the Course described by the said Act, it will be absolutely im-pradicable to execute it, under the Restrictions therein directed and prescribed; and that the Petitioner observes, that a Bill is depending in the House, to amend the said Act made in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty, and for granting further Powers: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to make Provision in the said Bili for permitting him to vary the Course described in the said Act, under such Restrictions as to the House shall seem proper.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; John Colvill, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Price of Pit Coal is greatly increased in the City of Glasgow \ that there are great Quanties of Coal in the Parishes of Old and New Monklands, which may be wrought at a very moderate Expence; but cannot easily be brought to Glasgow by Land Carriage, on account of the Distance:

That by Surveys lately made, it appears to be practicable to make a Navigable Cut or Canal from the Collieries of Old and New Monklands to Glasgow, and to communicate by a Waggon Way from the West End of the said Canal to the City of Glasgow; and that by Means of such Canal, the Owners of those Collieries will be able to supply Glasgow with Coals at moderate Prices,

He also said. That a voluntary Subscription has been entered into, and several thousand Pounds have been subscribed, for effecting such Canal; but that the same cannot be done without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or Canal, and Waggon Way, from the Collieries, in the Parishes of Old and New Monklands, to the City of Glasgow: And that Lord Frederick Campbell and Captain Lockhart Ross do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

How the Matter was lettled ? — he said, the Keelmen complained to the Magistrates, who said, They should not have more than the legal Measure, and bid them go to Work again; which they did, not upon the Magistrates Account, but upon Mr. Hars Persuasions Being

asked, Why the Men would not go to work again when the Magistrates desired them ? — he said, The Men knowing most of the Magistrates to be Coal Owners and Fitters, they would not believe them, having been so often deceived by them: — Being asked, If he had ever been deceived by them ? — he said, He never had in any otherre-lpect than by being obliged to carry Over MeasurBeing asked, If the Magistrates did, at the above Stop, summon any Fitter, or inquire in a judicial Manner, or make any Order upon any Fitter respecting such Over Measure, or whether any Money was ordered to be paid by any Fitter for such Over Measure ? — he said. The Magistrates had never ordered any Money to be paid for that Reason; but the Men were paid for S Chaldrons only Being asked., Why they went to Work upon Mr. s Per-

suasion, and not at the pefire of the Magistrates ? — he said. It was because Mr. Harvey said he would fee them righted as far as lay in his Power. — Being asked, Whether there was any Instrument used by Persons who put off the Keels from the several Staiths, to measure the Loading of the Keels over and above the King’s Measure ? — he said. There was a Stick, which the Officer or Person that surveys the loading of the Keels commonly walked with: That there was a Nick in the Stick about Four or Five Inches from the End, to measure how deep the Keels were loaded above the King's MarkThat it was usual to load to that Notch above the King’s Mark. — He added. That he had loaded at all the Dykes in the River Being ask ed, If he knew of any Over Measure having been carried since the Stop ? — he said, Yes; and that he had carried more than the Measure for Mr.

Jon, Agent for Mr. Pereth, a Coal Owner, and for Mr. Ridley: — That they must have lost their Bread if they had refused; and that he was never paid more than the usual Dues of the River: — Being aflted, What was the Reason that when such Over Measure was imposed, the Keelmen did not usually apply to the Magistrates for Relief? — he said, It was because they were afraid of loling their Bread; as some had done, who had applied for Re-dress, and therefore they submitted to it. — Being asked, How many Keelmen reside in the Parish of All Saints Parish in Newcastle ? — be said, He believes there are about 1200; half of whom he thinks are , if not

more: — Being asked, If the Scotchmen are usually relieved as Parishioners, when they or their Families are lick or infirm ? — he said. He had never known that any Man had been relieved, although they had been employed a great Number of Years as Keelmen: — Being asked. Whether, if the loading of Keels for the future was to be restrained to the King’s Measure, it would quiet the Minds of the Keelmen, and prevent future Stops in the Coal Trade ? — lie said, It would: — That they are well contented to take the King’s Measure, and do not desire to have a Coal lei's. — Being asked, If he ever made Complaint to any Magistrate except his Master ? — he said, He had not, for fear of losing his Bread: — he said, He once complained to his Master Robin/on, who told him that he might go where he would, if he did not choose to take the Coals; for other Men would: — That he was bound to Mr. Robin/on, on certain Conditions, to take the King’s Measur, and no more. — Being asked. If, when a greater Measure had been imposed upon him at any other Time, he had complained to a Justice of Peace? — he said, iic had not, but complained to his Master; for that Men

had complained before. One of whom loft his Bread by it: — He said, He never was present when Complaint was made; That Keelmen can get £. 13 or £. 24 a Year, carrying the Quantity that has been usual for the last Two or Three Years. — Being asked, If the Men are allowed Subsistence Money ? — he said. They sometimes are, but oftener are not, as it is not a Part of the Contract. — Being asked, What Means Mr. Harvey made use of to induce the Keelmen to go to Work after the last Stop ? — he said. It was because Mr. Harvey promised to fee them righted, if he could: — The Witness said. He did not know whether Mr. Harvey had the Power to get the Men righted by Law; but they took his Advice, they did not think he would go to a Magistrate at castle to get them righted, because they had deceived them before; but they thought he would get it by applying to Parliament, which he hoped he should be able to do. — Being asked, How he had been deceived by the Magistrates at Newcastle ? — he said, That in order to prevail on the Men to go to work upon former Stops, the Magistrates had told them they should take no more than the King’s Measure; and after that the Fitters brought it on, they still intended, and got is as high as 10 or 12 Chaldrons, but not since the last Stop: — He said, He never had had Relief from the Magistrates when it came to be above Measure, nor ever applied to them: — That he was a bound Man to Mr. Pereth at the Time of the last Stop, and sometimes carried Over Measure after the Stop, during the Time he continued in Mr.

Pereth’s Service, but not always. — Being asked, If he had applied to Mr. Pereth for Redress ? — he said, He had not, but to Mr. Robin/on, jvho sent Orders to the Staith, that

no Over Measure should be offered, but yet they had it: Has had more than Measure at Sir Thomas Clavering'% Staith since the Stop:- — That he has worked at all the Staiths, and found no difference in any of them: — That it is not quite Two Years since the last Stop happened: — Being asked, If he spoke with respect to the present Practice ? — he said, He did not: — He came to London about Two Months after the last Stop. — Being asked, if he left his Work because he had no Redress when he complained to Mr . Robin/on? — he said. He did not leave it on that Account. — Being asked, If he had entered into any Agreement with Mr. Harvey? — he said, He never paid any Thing to him, nor knew him further than by Sight: — Being asked. How Mr. Harvey could prevail upon him to go to Work again, if he only knew him by Sight ? — he said, Mr. Harvey declared publicly at the Garth Heads, He was in hopes we should get a Settle-

ment; he desired us all to go to Work, and said, H® would fee us redressed: — This, he said. He only heard from others, the Number there being so great he could not hear it himself. — Being asked. Whether any written Paper was circulated among the Keelmen by Mr. Harvey / — he said. He saw none. — Being asked. How long he had worked at Newcastle, and how many Stops there had been in his Time ? — he said, He had worked there Five Years, during which Time there had been many Complaints which never were redressed, but only One general Stop, which the Keelmen made of their own Accord, and not upon the Advice of any one: — He added. That he had worked at Mr. s Works

about Three Years and a Half ago; — he has seen him several Times since, but never spoke Two Words to him.

a Surplus of above Two Chaldron and an Half: — He has loaded 40 or 50 Ships that were bound Over Sea, with the same Measure within One Year and Half before the Stop: — Since the Stop, he has only loaded Ships going Coastwise with the Over Measure; that the Keelmen have made Applications to both Matters and Magistrates for Redress with regard to the Over Measure, particularly at the Time of the last Stop, when a Skipper from every Work went to them in the Town Hall: — That the Skippers were appointed by the Fitters, who also accompanied them; — that they only required to have the just Measure, and the Magistrates told them, They should have One Quarter of an Inch above the Eight Chaldron Nail: — Being asked. If the Magistrates made the Fitters pay the Keelmen for the Over Measure they had carried? — he said. They had not; for the Keelmen never made any Application for that Pufpofethey only applied for Relief, with regard to being obliged to carry Over Measure, but never received any Satisfacticm, except the above Promise, which was made by the Mayor; which the Men not thinking enough, they refused to go to Work till Mr. Harvey persuaded them so to do; and said. He would fee us righted: — Being asked, If any Over Measure had been imposed after he had been with the Mayor ? — he said. His Keel was loaded One Inch over the Plate the Second Tide, which made her Loading amount to about Nine Chaldronthat he heard Complaints from the other Keelmen that they, were all overloaded; that a Keel of Silver top's, which he belonged to, being overloaded, he left her at the Staith at Darwent Gut upon that Account . — John Henderson,

the Staithman, told him. If he would not take her, another should, so his Men and he left the Keel there, and came to London; — this was about 18 Months ago Being asked, Why the Keelmen, when such Over Measure was imposed, did not apply to a Magistrate, instead of making a Stop ? — he said, That most of the Magistrates being Coal Owners or Fitters, they were afraid of making Complaints to them, left they should lose their Bread, and be turned away as Vagabonds; — they complained to their Masters, who promised them Relief, but gave none'That there are 8 or 900 Keelmen live in All Saints Parish, none of whom ever received any Relief from the Parish; and that it would tend greatly to quiet the Minds of the Keelmen, and to prevent future Stops, if a Law was made to restrain the Measure to Eight Chaldrons only: — Being asked. If the King’s Officers permitted Over Measure to be call on board Ships bound Over Sea ? — he said. They do not allow it when they are there; but he has done it in their Absence; — that they were forced to carry the Over Measure, but never were paid for itHe said. He has known a Vessel as full laden with 19 Keels at One Time, as Ihe has been at another Time with 24: — That Coals arc heavier in wet Weather than in dry; but that just Measure will never fink the Keel above the Top of the Plate: — That he has known Hundreds of bound Keelmen run away and leave their Masters, but never knew that any of them were taken up by Warrants from Justices of the Peace. — Being asked, Why he did not go to Work upon the Mayor’s Promises of Relief? — he said. The Keelmen doubted the Mayor’s keeping his Promise, and would not return to Work till Mr. Harvey allured them they should be relieved: — That at the Time he left his Keel at Darwent he neither applied to Mr. Harvey or a Magistrate, but acquainted his Fitter, and came away. — Being asked. If Keels loaded above the King’s Mark are not liable to Accidents? — he said, They are; and sometimes have been funk, which injures the Navigation: — That each Keel is built to carry Eight Chaldrons only, will carry about 14 Chaldrons in calm Weather before it finks; — some will not carry so much as Eight Chaldrons.

George Purvis, who, being examined; said, He had been a Keelman at Nezvcajile Two Years: And,

Thomas Oughton<, who was a Keelman there 14 Months ago, and are now Coalheavers at London: — They confirmed the Evidence of the other Witnesses as to the Over Measure imposed on Keelmen at Newcastle, and the Consequences attending it — the Impossibility of getting any Redress; — the Custom of not allowing Scotch Keelmen to gain Settlements; — the giving Over Measure to Outward-bound Ships during the Absence of the King’s Officers; and the universal Desire of the Keelmen, to have the Measure settled by Law; and the Danger they were in of being turned out of their Employments, if they made any Complaints: And,

Thomas Oughton added. That he knew a Man who

John Douglas, formerly a Keelman at Newcastle, now a Coalheaver at London, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence as to the Over Measure, and the Consequences of it; and added, That old Keels will fink two Inches lower, when empty, than new ones; so that a Keel may fink under the Mark, though (he has not more than Eight Chaldrons in her. — That he has known-a Man put in Prison for leaving his Work: — That he never applied to a Magistrate.

Then Mr. Harvey, in order to prove that the Revenue suffers by the Practice of giving Over Measure to Ships, said, That the King’s Meamre is Eight Chaldrons of Coals to a Keel; the Duty on Exportation of which is £. 5. ns. and according to that Measure the Keel is paid. — He then stated. That 8 Chaldrons, New* castle Measure, is equal to 14! Measure; in

the Manner he mentioned, according to the truest Equation between a Chaldron Newcastle Measure, and the same Quantity London Measure; and produced a List of the Loading and Delivery of Ships, from the Ports of Newcastle and Sunderland to the Port of London, brought down to February 1770; by which it appeared, that the Ships therein named had delivered much larger Quantities of Coals than they ought to have done, according to the Rate of 14! Chaldrons to the Keel: — That he had inspected the Account of Loadings and Delivery; and found, the like Over Measure had been delivered in London for Three Years past constantly That upon the Surplus Coals, above Eight Chaldrons, carried in Keels and put on board all outward-bound Ships, no Duty whatever is paid; because the Custom-house Officers reckon only Eight Chaldrons to the Keel: — That Ships clearing Coastwise, having taken in Coals from Keels carrying Over Measure, which Ships happening by Stress of Weather to be drove Over Sea, upon their Return, pay Duty only for the Number of Keels they received, by which the Revenue is injured.

With respect to establishing a Fund for Relief of indigent or sick Keelmen, and their Families, Mr. Harvey informed your Committee, That the Keelmen of Newcastle desired him to apply to Parliament for an Act for the Extension and Establishment of their Society, and to shew their Reasons for it; which are: — That great N umbers of the Keelmen employed at Newcastle are Natives of Scotland, and from the Mode of binding, hiring, and Service, arc not, as he apprehends, allowed to gain Settlements in the Parish of All Saints, where most of them reside. — Then the said,

Edward Mojely, Esquire, being examined, said, He allowed, that it will appear the Keelmen have, in some Instance9, had Over Measure imposed upon them; but not considerably so: — From his own Business as a Fitter, ,he said, he knew they sometimes had less than the Measure; for Proof of which he referred your Committee to a List of the Makings out of all Ships he loaded for London, for Three Years preceding the last Stop, since which he has not heard of any just Complaints: — That

there was no Complaint made to the Magistrates before the Stop was made on the 28th of March 1768; at which Time he sent for the Keelmen, and inquired the Cause of the Stop j — they laid, They were oppressed by being obliged to carry Over Measure; upon which, the next Day, One Keelman, chosen by themselves, out of each Work, on Behalf of the whole Body, together with the Fitters, were desired to come to the Mayor’s Chamber; where the Matter being inquired into, and, from the general Complaints of the Keelmen, believed in some Instances to be true, they’were told. That no more than' the King’s Measure should be required of them* with which they were, or seemed to be, well satisfied, and returned to their Work the 31st of March: — That on the 25 th of April following, the Keelmen put an entire Stop to the Coal Trade; not upon account of the Over Measure, but in Consequence of the Keelmen belonging to One Work refuling to join with the rest of the Keelmen in making certain Payments to Mr. for Bufi-

ness to be done by him for them, amounting to Three Shillings for every Keel’s Crew, when the Man.who had paid One Shilling and Sixpence in Part of the Sum agreed on, declared, That no Keel should go to work till every Keelman had paid his Part: — He then laid, He had exported vast Quantities of Coals; for which, when they are entered at the Customhouse, to be put on board outward-bound Ships, the Duty is paid before they are suffered to be shipped: — That the King’s Officer grantsa Sufferance, and goes with it, and permits no Keels to call On board the Ship, without his carefully examining them, to see that they have only Eight Chaldrons each: — That the Officer remains on board till the Ship is wholly loaded, and then makes his Report to the Custom-house: — That he had always found them, in the Course of his Business, careful and diligent: — That the Officer has a Power to Hop Keels that are overloaded; and so it is his Fault if over Measure is carried beyond Sea; and that he certifies that the Ship’s Loading was in proper Measure, by an Indorsement on the Sufferance. — He added. That it may sometimes happen that a Ship is forced Over Sea by Distress of Weather, where her Cargo is delivered: — That at her Return Application is made for the Acceptance of the Duty, which is always paid according to the Quantity cleared for at the Custom-house: — That after a Ship has been once entered and loaded Coastwise, under the Inspection of a Coast Officer, the future Voyages Coastwise are regulated by that Entry at the Custom-house at Newcastle’, or according to the Quantity the Ship makes out upon the Coast, the same as the London Ships are governed by; so that there can be no Loss to the Government on that Account. — He then informed your Committee, That a few Days before he came to London, he inquired of the Officers of the Parishes at Newcastle, Whether poor Keelmen, or their Families, are relieved in the Parishes ? who told him, They always have Relief, as occasional Poor, till their Settlements are found out. — And being asked, What are the Sentiments of the Fitters at , with regard to

establishing the Hospital for Keelmen ? — he said, That the Gentlemen who are concerned as Fitters at Newcastle have no Objection to such a Proposal; but are desirous to Tee it done upon a proper Plan, and are ready to do their Part, by Hopping the Contributions out of the Keelmens Wages, and paying them for that Purpose, provided the Government of the Charity be lodged in the Hands of Gentlemen of Rank and Fortune, of the Counties of Durham, Northumberland, and Newcastle upon Tyne; but they do not think it should be left in the Keelmen themselves, according as proposed by the Deed of Settlement, to which Deed they have also other Objections; and if it should be infilled on to have that Deed of Settlement established by Act of Parliament, they mud beg Leave to offer their Reasons against it. — Being asked, If Fitters receive any Advantage by the Keels carrying Over Measure ? — he said It is a Disadvantage 18

to them, because the Fitter lofeshis Fittage on the Over Measure, and is not paid for the Surplus; and that, on the contrary, it is a Prejudice to his Keels to overload them, and makes the Navigation of them dangerous. — He then informed your Committee, That there is great Difference in the sinking of Keels in the Water, for the following Reasons: — An old Keel finks much sooner than a stout new one; — that the Water near the Sea is more buoyantthan up the River; — that a Keel’s being wet finks her lower than (he would go if (he was dry, and the same with regard to the Coals being wet. — Being asked. If Ships do not often vary in the Quantity of Coals they take in ? — he said, They do, because they take in other Goods; and that a Ship being in good or bad Repair makes a Difference. — Being asked the Question, — he said. The Keels at Newcastle are marked to carry only Eight Chaldrons; which is called the King's Measure: — And being asked. Whether the Fitters can have their Keels new weighed and marked, when necessary ? — he said. That the King’s Weights for measuring Keels are brought out of the King’s Warehouses, after the 25th of March in every Year. — Being asked. If he ever knew any Keels funk before their Admeasurement ? — he said, He never had. — Being asked the Question, — he said. The Keelmen of Newcastle never applied to the Magistrates, or made any Complaint, till they were sent for upon the last Stop: That Keelmen have Hopped Keels, on Pretence of their having Over Measure; which have afterwards proved not to be over-loaded. — . That he ordered a Keel, complained of, to be call into a light Keel that swam fair to her Marks; and that, upon the Keel being so re-cast, it appeared, (he was not over-loaded; and the Man who had Hopped her, being then convinced that (he was not over-loaded, suffered her to pass. — Being asked the Question, he said. He had known Keels funk at the Dykes by bad Weather: — That, about Three Weeks ago there were several Keels funk, at and about Benton; none of which had more than Eight Chaldron of Coals on Board. — And being asked the Question, — he said, He never heard of aiqrKeelmen losing their Lives by Keels being over-loaded. — Being asked the Question, — he laid. He believed the Keelmen’s Complaints, in 1768, wero well founded; but cannot certainly tell. — Being asked. If the Fitters have any Ships, or Parts of Ships, of their own ? — he said. They have: And that, if they obtain any Over Measure from the Coal Owners, they gain more by that than they lose by the Fittage, as they do not pay the Coal Owners for such Over Measure; but in general, it is not the Fitters Interest to carry Over Measure. — Being asked. How many Magistrates there are in Newcastle f — he said, A Mayor, Recorder, and Ten Aldermen; Nine of which Magistrates are concerned in the Coal Trade, as Owners, or Fitters. — Being asked the Question, — he said, Keelmen are bound for a Year: And it has been the Custom to pass Scotch Keelmen, and their Families, to their own Country, upon their becoming indigent; that the Fitters have been applied to, by the Keelmen, to make Stoppages out of their Wages, to raise a Fund for their future Maintenance, and proposed giving the Fitters Authority so to do; that they declined doing it, because they did not think themselves warranted to do it: — That many of the Keelmen live in the Counties of Durham and Northumberland. — Being asked. If the Justices of the Peace, in those Counties, are generally Coal Owners or Fitters ? — he said, They are not. — Being asked. Which of the Magistrates are not concerned in the Coal Trade? — he said, The present Mayor, the Recorder, and One Alderman: And, he said. That the Justices of Durham and Northumberland cannot aft in;

and that only One Staith is within the Jurisdiction of that Town. Then,

Mr. Bacon, according to Order, reported from the Doter, Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter as Election., it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Town and Port of Dover, in the County of Kent, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; and be read the report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Upop the Petition of John Trevanion, Esquire, and also the Petition of several Freemen of the Town and Port of Dover, in the County of complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Thomas Pym Hales, Baronet, for the said Town and Port.

The Committee examined the Merits of this Election.

The Standing Order of the House, made upon the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel, at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination of the House of Commons, was read:

9, N And

780

And the last Determination of the House, upon the 14th Day of March 1623, concerning the Right of electing a Baron to serve in Parliament for the Town and Port of Dove*, in the County of Kent, was also read} whereby it was resolved, " That the Freemen and Free " Burgesses, Inhabitants of Dover, ought to have Voice

in the Election of their Barons to serve in Parliament."

One of the Counsel for the Petitioners opened their Cafe, by saying. They should shew that Non-resident Freemen have no Right to vote.

Wheteupon One of the Counsel for the Sitting Member declared, That if the Non»residents had no Right to vote, the Petitioner would have a Majority upon the PoH.

And, thereupon, the said Counsel for the Petitioners declared, That if Residents and Non-residents had all a Right to vote, the Sitting Member would have a Ma-jdtfty upon the Poll; but, in that Cafe, he laid in his Claim, to hive Liberty to proceed to shew that the Sitting Merribfer, by corrupt Practices of himself and Aigedts, had procured a pretended Majority.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member, in order to shew that the Usage of the said Town and Port was for Non-inhabitant Freamen to vote at Elections, offered to produce several Polls, taken at Elections of Members for the said Town and Port.

Which being objected to by the Counsel for the Petitioners;

The Committee were of Opinion, That the Counsel for the Sitting Member should be at Liberty to give Evidence of the Usage, in the Town and Port of Dover, for the Non-inhabitant Freemen to vote in the Election of Barons to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port.

Then Mr. Robert Westfield, Town Clerk of Dover, was called in, and produced the Polls taken at Elections of Barons to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port, the 8th of /htgiift 1713, the 15th of August 1727, and the 4th of May 1741, and at the lad Election.

And being asked. Whether he remembered any contested Election before the last? he said, He was never present but at One, the General Election in 1768, when the Non-resident Freemen were rejected; that the Objection was made by the Mayor: That he had been Town Clerk Four Years, and never was present at any Election where Non-resident Freemen were admitted.

Then Mr. James Hammond was examined, who said, He was born at Dover, and is a Magistrate there; that he remembered contested Elections in 1727, 1734, 1741, and the last General Election; that at those Elections, all Non-resident Freemen voted who made their Appearance, without any Objection; and that he always understood that Non-residents had a Right of voting: That, by a Freeman, he meant. One Free Born, by marrying a Freeman’s Daughter, by Purchase or Redemption, by Gift of the Corporation, or by having a Freehold of £. 5 per Annum in the Town; that the last is no longer a Freeman than he has the Estate, and is an Inhabitant; that a Man, Free Born, may take up his Freedom at any Time; but he that has his Freedom by marrying a Freeman’s Daughter, loses it when his Wife dies.

The Committee then came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Non-inhabitant Freemen, as well as the Inhabitant Freemen, and Free Burgesses, of the Town and Port of Dover, have Voice in the Election of their Barons to serve in Parliament.

And the Counsel being called in, and acquainted therewith;

The Counsel for* the Petitioners declared. They had nothing further to offer on the Part of the Petitioners.

Sir Charles Kemys Tynte reported from the Committee,

to whom the Petition of George Earl of an

Infant under the Age of Twenty-one Years, by Alicia Maria Countess of Egremont, and Percy O’Bryan, Earl of Tkomond, in the Kingdom of Ireland, his Guardians, appointed by the Will of Charles late Earl of Egremont, his Father, deceased; and also the Petition of the undersigned Merchants, Gentlemen, Traders, and others, residing in or near the Town of JVatchett , and elsewhere in the County of Somer[ei, were severally referred: That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions} and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to the'm, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same Was read: and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition; several Acts Of the Sixth and Tenth Years of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and in the Seventh Year of his late Majesty Xing George the First, for repairing the Harbour and Quay of in the County of Somerset, were read: And,

Michael Ewen, Esquire, being examined, said, That it hath lately been difeov^red that the Term limited by the last mentioned Act, for collecting certain Ratds and Duties, for repairing the said Harbour, expired in the Year 175° J but, through Ignorance of such Expiration, the' said Rates and Duties have been collected and applied as before.

That the said Harbour and Quay hath been.constantly repaired by the Lord of the Manor, at great Annual Expences, for Security of Ships and Vessels riding the rein, and the Preservation of the said Town, and the Inhabitants, from the Inroads of the Sea; that the Pier is liable to unforeseen Accidents, and 'requires a constant Fund for the Reparation thereof; and that the present Duties which Persons pay, though not compellable so to do, have, upon the Whole been found much short of the Expences incurred on Account of the said Harbour, and that betides the ordinary Reparations now wanting, some further new Works will be requisite: And that the Preservation of the said Harbour will be of great Consequence to that Part of the Country, and of public Utility.

To. prove the Allegations of the Second Petition;

The same Witness said. That all the Persons interested are defirousj that Provision may be made for continuing Certain Rates and Duties for the Preservation of the said Harbour, and that Nine Tenths of the Duties are paid by Two Persons who have signed the Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for further continuing the Duties granted and continued by several Acts made in the Sixth and Tenth Years of the Reign of Queen Anne, and in the Seventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, for repairing the Harbour and Quay of Watchett, in the County of Somerset; And that Sir Charles Kemys Tynte and Sir William Maynard do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrafted.

A Petition of the Owners and Matters of Ships and Coalheaven; Vessels belonging to the Port of upon Tyne,

employed in the Coal Trade, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes,

' that a Petition has been presented, to amend an Act passed in the Year 1 758, for Relief and Regulation of the Coalheavers working upon the River Thames; and that thele Petitioners apprehend, that the establishing £n Office, as prayed for by the said Petition, will subject the Petitioners to great Impositions and Delays in carrying oniheir Business, and will be, in every respect, very injurious to the Petitioners in particular, and to the Coal Trade in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that no Alteration may bc-made in the present Method of carrying on the Coal Trade on the River Thames, as prayed by the said Petition, but will make such Order therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the . Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Coalheavers working on the River Thames is referred.

Common Fields, Lands, and Downs, within theManorand Parish of Westwell, in the County of Oxford, was committed; That the Committeehad examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrafted.

A Petition of Woffington Earl Ferrers and Henry Lord Paget, and the humble Petition of those- whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, being Lords of Manors, and Owners of Lands, Mines, and Minerals, adjacent to, or near, the Canal now making from the River Trent to the River Mersey, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill to amend an Act made in the Sixth Ywof the Reign of His present Majesty, for making a navigable Cut or Canal, from the River Trent, at or near Wilden Ferry, in the County of Derby, to the River Mersey, at or near Runcorn Gap, and for granting further Powers for that Purpose; and letting forth. Tint the Petitioners conceive, it wifi be of great public Utility, and also of Advantage to the Company of Proprietors of the said CanaJ, ifaClause is inserted in the said Bill, to enable such Lords of Manors and Owners of Lands, whole Estates lie adjacent to or near the said Canal, to make navigable Cuts or Branches through their respective Lands into the said Canal, provided such Cuts or Branches shall be so made and done, without taking any Water out of the said Canal, or doing any Damage thereto, or to the Banks thereof, but what shall be effectually repaired, and made good by the Persons making such Cuts and Branches into the same: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given for inserting a Clause in the said Bill, to enable Lords of Manors, and Owners of Lands, lying adjacent to or near the said Canal, to make navigable Cuts or Branches into the fame, through their own respective Lands, upon the Terms and for the Purposes aforesaid, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Commute, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

A Petition of George Walker \Esquire, Agent for the Barbados Island of Barbadoes, for and in the Behalf of the Inhabit- Harbour,

ants of the said Island, being offered- to be presented to the House 1

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recom-. mends it tq the Confederation, of the House.

Then the said Petition was, brought up, and read}

Setting forth. That; before the Inhabitants of the said lflarid had well recovered from the deplorable Situation to which they had been reduced by Two Fires in the Years 17.56 and 1758,- on the 14th Day of 1766, another lamentable Fire broke out in their principal Town, which laid in Ashes about 1000 Houses, Stores, and other Buildings, with large Quantities of Goods,

Wares, and Merchandizes"; and that, on the 27th Day of December in the same Year, a like melancholy Accident confirmed the most valuable Part of the Houses and Stores which had providentially escaped the Severity of the former Fires; that the Lpfs sustained by the People in general, by’ the Two last mentioned Conflagrations, is supposed to exceed Half a Million Sterling Money of Great Britain-, and that, although large Sums,

raised from the.Royal Bounty, and the charitable Contributions of.many worthy, Persons in Britain, and other'Parts of His Majesty’s Dominions; have been sent over, for the:Relief of the most indigent Sufferers, yet nlany of them remain still in the lowest State of Poverty, and are unable to comply with the common and neceflkry Taxes of their Country; and that, besides the dismal Consequences of a t,ofs so severely felt by the Inhabitants of the said Island, they have another Misfortune, which they share In common with every Part of the Briti/k> Dominions that are connected wish them in Commerce;, the Channel to their Wharfs and Landing Places being at prefer so choked up by the Filth that has,

been many Years gathering about their Mole Head, that the smallest Crafty w^en loaded, cap hardly find a Passage; that, without a speedy Remedy to this Evil, their Trade with Fur ope, as well as Africa and America, must be inevitably obftpjfted; and that the Inhabitant* of the said Island, having ffen that the Progress of the late Fires was in a great Measure occasioned by the Irregularity of their. Buildings, have, already passed an Act, for Rebuilding their Town upon a safer and better Plan, which has been carried into Execution, so far as relates to the Purchase of private Property for wider Streets and other Openings, but not without a very great Expence to the Community j and have likewise had in Contemplation a, Means ~tQj deanfe their Channel, and give freer Acceis to Trade, and, with the Assistance of an abk Engineer, have determined upon a Method, which, they conceive, will effectually-answer their Purpose; but thb' impoverished State of thfir Finances, and the Incapacity of the People to Bear the Burthen of heavy Taxes,

SESS Copy of Address; Remonstrance, and Petition, of London, the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Livery, of the City Ac. of London,- presented to the King Aforri 14th 1770: And also,

' Copy of His Majesty’s Answer.

' And the Titles of the said Copies were read.

The said Copies are as followeth; viz.

To the KING’S Most Excellent Majesty.

The humble Address, Remonstrance, and Petition, of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Livery, of the City of London, in Common Hall assembled.

May itpleafe Your Majesty,

We have already in our Petition dutifully represented to Your Majesty, the chief Injuries we have sustained. We are unwilling to believe that Your Majesty can flight the Defines of Your People, or be regard less of their Affection, and deaf to their Complaints: Yet their Complaints remaih unanswered; their Injuries are confirmed; and the only Judge removable at the Pleasure of the Crown, has been dismissed from his high Office, for defending In Parliament" the Law and the Constitution. ",

We therefore Venture once more to address ourselves to Your Majesty, as to the Father of Your People; as to Him who must be both ablt; and willing to redress our Grievance^: And we repeat our Application with , the greater Propriety, because we fee the Instruments of

our Wrongs, who have carried into Execution the Measures of which We complain, more particularly distinguished by Your Majesty’s. Royal Bounty and Favour. ’ ‘" ’ , "

Under the same secret and malign Influence, which through each successlve Administration has defeated every' good,' and suggested every bad Intention, tlfe Majority of the' House of Commons have. deprived V our People of their dearest Rights.

K8 i:

They have done a Deed more ruinous in its Consequences, than the levying of Ship-money by Charles the First, or the Dispensing Power assumed by James the Second: A Deed which must vitiate all the future Proceedings of this Parliament; for the Acts of the Legislature itself can no more be valid without a legal House of Commons, than without a legal Prince upon the Throne.

Represen cat ives of the People are essential to the making of Laws; and there is a Time when it is morally demonstrable that Men cease to be Representatives: That Time is now arrived: The present House of Commons do not represent the People.

We owe to Your Majesty an Obedience, under the Restrictions of the Laws, for the Calling and Duration of Parliaments: And Your Majesty owes to us that our Representation, free from the Force of Arms or Corruption, should be preserved to us in Parliament. It was for this we successfully struggled under James the Second j for this we seated and have faithfully supported Your Majesty’s Family on the Throne. The People have been invariably uniform in their Object, though the different Mode of Attack has called for a different Defence.

Under James the Second they complained, that the Sitting of Parliament was interrupted, because it was not corruptly subservient to His Designst We complain now, that the Sitting of this Parliament is not interrupted* because it is corruptly subservient to the Designs of Your Majesty’s Ministers. Had the Parliament under James the Seo>nd been as submissive to his Commands, as the Parliament is at this Day to the Dictates of a Minister, instead of Clamours for its Meeting, the Nation would have rung, as now, with Outcries for its Dissolution. /

The Forms of the'Constitution, like those of Religion, were not establishedfor the Form’s Sake; but for the Substance: And we call God and Men to witness, that, as we do not owe our Liberty to those pice and subtle Distioftions, which Places and Pensions, and lucrative Employments have invented; so neither will we be deprived of it by them: But as it was gained by the stem Virtue of our Ancestors, by the Virtue of their Descendants it shall be preserved. , *

Since therefore, the Misdeeds of Your Majesty’s Ministers, in violating the Freedom of Election, and depraving the noble Constitution of Parliaments, are notorious, as well as subversive of the fundamental Laws and Liberties of this Realm; and (ince Your Majesty, both in Honour and Justice, is obliged inviolably to preserve them, accofdfug to the Oath made to God and Your Subjects at Your Coronation, We, Your Majesty’s Remonstrants, afiure ourselves, that Your Majesty will restore the constitutional Government and Quiet of Your People, by dissolving this Parliament, and removing those evil Ministers for ever from Your Councils.

Signed by Order, James Hodges.

Copy of His MAJESTY’S Answer.

I shall always be ready to receive the Requests, and to fiften to the Complaints of my Subjects: but it gives Me great Concern to fiqd, that any of them should have been so far mifled, as to offer Me an Address and Remonstrance, the Contents of which I cannot but consider as disrespectful to Me, injurious to My Parliament, and irreconcileable to the Principles of the Constitution.

I have ever made the Law of the Land the Rule of My Chnduft, esteeming it My chief Glory to reign over a free People: With this View I have always been careful, as well to execute faithfully the Trust reposed in Me, as to avoid even the Appearance of invading any of those Powers which the Constitution has placed in other Hands. It is only by perfevefing in such a Conduct, that I can cither discharge My own Doty, or secure to My Subjects the free Enjoyrfient of those Rights which My Family were called to defend; and while I ’ aft

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed. That, to deny the Legality of the present Parliament, and to assert that the Proceedings thereof are not valid, is highly unwarrantable, and has a manifest Tendency to disturb the Peace of the Kingdom, by withdrawing His Majesty’s Subjects from their Obedience to the Laws of the Realm;

And a Motion being made. That the previous Question be put, That that Question be now put;
