Then the mair*Question being put;

Resolved, That, to deny the Legality of the present Parliament, and to afiert that the Proceedings thereof are not valid, is highly unwarrantable, and has a manifest Tendency to disturb the Peace of the Kingdom, by withdrawing His Majesty’s Subjects from their Obedience to the Laws of the Realm.

A. 1770.

Resolved, That, to convey to the Crown, under Colour and Pretence of Petitioning, such an unwarrantable and dangerous Postion, is a grois Abuse of the Right of the Subjects to petition the King.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to express the extreme Concern and Indignation which we feel, at finding that an Application has been made to His Majesty in Terms lb little corresponding with that grateful and aflfeftionate Respect which His Majesty is so justly entitled to from all His Subjects; at the same Time aspersing and calumniating die Parliament, and denying its Legality, and the Validity of the Acts of the Legislature.

To allure His Majesty, that, as we are duly sensible of the Value and Importance of the-Right of the Sub. jests to petition the King, it is with the deepest Concern that we now fee the Exercise of it so grossly perverted, by being applied to the Purpose, not of preserving, but overturning, the Constitution, and of propagating Doctrines, which, if generally adopted, must be fatal to the Peace of the Kingdom, and which tend to the Subversion of all lawful Authority.

To acknowledge with Gratitude, that His Majesty has ever shewn the most tender Regard to the Rights of His People, not only in the Exercise of His own Power, but in His Care to preserve, from every Degree of Infringement or Violation, the Powers intruded to others; and to return His Majesty our unfeigned Thanks, for the fresh Proof He has now given us of His Determination to persevere in His Adherence to the Principles of the Constitution.

To express the Satisfaction it gives us, to fee His Majesty placing so just a Confidence in His People.

To represent to His Majesty, that, in whatever unjustifiable Excesses some misguided Persons may have been seduced to join, His Majesty’s Subjects in general are too sensible of what they owe, both to His Majesty and to His illustrious Family, ever to be capable of approaching His Majesty with any other Sentiments than those of the most entire Respect and Affection; and understand too well their own true Interest, to wifti to loosen the Bands of Obedience to the Laws, and of due Subordination to lawful Authority; and that we are fully persuaded, that His Majesty’s People, as well as His Parliament, will reject with Disdain every insidious Suggestion of those ill-designing Men, who are in Reality undermining the Public Liberty under the specious Pretence of Zeal for its Preservation; and that His Majesty’s Attention to maintain the Liberties of His Subjects unviolated, which His. Majesty esteems His chief Glory, will, upon every Occasion, prove the sure Means of Strength to His Majesty, and secure to Him that zealous and effectual Support, which none but a free People can bellow.

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon;

And the House having continued to fit till Half an Hour after Two of the Clock on Tuesday Morning;

Ordered, That the said Debate be adjourned till this Morning, Twelve of the Clock; and that no Public Business do intervene.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morn-

ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till this Morning, Ten of the Clock,

Afidref* The Order of the Day being fead, for refunding the ^Remjnftrancif adjourned Debate upon the Motion made Yesterday, of the City of That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, London, to express the extreme Concern and Indignation which we feel, at finding that an Application has been made to His Majesty, in Terms so little corresponding with that grateful and affectionate Respect which His Majesty is so justly intitled to from all His Subjects; at the fairie Time aspersing and calumniating the Parliament, and denying its Legality, and the Validity of the Acts of the Legislature.

To assure His Majesty, that, as we are duly sensible of the Value and Importance of the Right of the Subjects to petition the King, it; is with the deepest Concern that we now fee the Exercise of it so grossly perverted, by being applied to the Purpose, not of preserv-ing, but overturning, the Constitution, and of propagating Doctrines, which, if generally adopted, must be fatal to the Peace of the Kingdom, and which tend to the SGbversion of all lawful Authority.

To acknowledge with Gratitude, that His Majesty has ever shewn the most tender Regard to the Rights of His People, not only in the Exercise of His own Power, but in His Care to preserve, from every Degree of Infringement or Violation, the Powers intruded to others j and to return His Majesty our unfejgped Thanks, for the fresh Proof He has now given us of His Determination to persevere in His Adherence to the Principles of thcCon-stitution.

To express the Satisfaction it gives us, to fee His Majesty placing so just a Confidence in His People.

To represent to His Majesty, that, in whatever unjustifiable Excesses some misguided Persons may. have been leduced to join, His Majesty’s Subjects in general are too sensible of what they owe, both to His Majesty and to His Illustrious Family, ever to be capable of approaching His Majesty with any other Sentiments than those of the most entire Respect and Affection j land underftaiid too well their owh true Interest, to wish to laofen the Bands of Obedience to the Laws, and of due Subordination to lawful Authority; and that we are fully persuaded, that His Majesty’s People, as well as His Parliament, will reject with Disdain every iri-fidious Suggestion of those ill-designing Men, who are in Reality undermining the public Liberty under the specious Pretence of Zeal for its Preservation; and that His Majesty’s Attention to maintain the Liberties of His Subjects unviolated, which His Majesty esteems His chief Glory, will, upon every Occasion, prove the lure Means of Strength to His Majesty, and secure to Him that zealous and effectual Support, which none but a free People can bestow.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms do go with the Mace into the Speaker’s Chambers, the Court of Requests and Places adjacent, and summon the Members there to attend the Service of the House.

Essex

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Town County Gaol, of Chelmsford, in the County of Essex, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Town, was presented to the House, and read 5 Setting forth. That a Bill is depending in the House, for rebuilding the Common Gaol of the County of Essex, which Gaol is at present ligate near the said Town of Chelmsford; and that the said Town is at present well supplied with excellent Water, from a Spring called Burgess Welly and that the Petitioners are informed the said Gaol is proposed to be built upon certain Lands or Grounds, out of, or through which, the said Spring of Water runs; and many of the Inhabitants have no other Supply of Water but from the said Spring; and that, if the Gaol should be built as is supposed, the Petitioners apprehend, it will obstruct the free Course of the said Spring, or otherwise injure or damage the fame, which will be very prejudicial to the Town in general; and the said Gaol will be also very offensive; and representing to the House, that the Scite of the present Gaol, including certain Lands adjoining thereto, and which the Petitioners are informed may be purchased for that Purpose, is the rood proper and convenient Place for building the new Gaol, and where it will be the lead offensive: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises inlo Consideration; and that Provision may be made in the said Bill, that the said Gaol may be built upon or near the Place where the present Gaol now (lands: such Place to be particularly described in the Bill; and that the Petitioners may he heard, by themselves or Counsel, against any Part or Parts of the said Bill as may be prejudicial to them \ and have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Com* miitee. That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the fame^ Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. Speaker reported. That both Houses did* upon Answer Friday laid, attend His Majesty, with their Address; to *9 which His Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious rcww Answer: the

Remonstrance

of the City of London.

My Lords arid Gentlemen,

I return you My Thanks for this very loyal and dutiful Address. It is with great Satisfaction that I receive from My Parliament so grateful an Acknowledgment of My tender Regard for the Rights of My Subjects. Be assured, that \ shall continue to adhere to the true Principles of Our excellent Constitution; from which I cannot deviate, without justly forfeiting the Affections of a free People.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, Commonalty, and other Inhabitants, of the ancient Town of Rye, in the County of SuJJ'ex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for continuing, amending, and rendering more effectual, so much of Three Acts of Parliament, for repairing the Road from Tunbridge Wells, and Kipping's to Lamberhurst

Pound, and Pullins Hill, in the County of Kent, and to Flimwell, in the County of Sussex, as relates to the Road leading from Sevenoakes Common to Woodjgate, Tunbridge Wells, and Kipping's Cross, in the said County in which Bill the Petitioners are informed, is contained a Clause for repealing the Clauses of certain Acts of the Eighth of Queen Anne, the Eleventh of George the First, and the Fourteenth of George the Second, so far as they relate to that Part of the said Roads leading from Sevenoakes to Woodjgate and Tunbridge Wells, and from Woodjgate to Kipping's Cross; and that the Peti-

tioners apprehend, if such Bill should pass into a Law, it would tend to the enhancing the Price of Fish. at the London Market, and be highly prejudicial to the Inhabitants of the said Town of Rye, and of the several other Fishing Towns on this Coast: And therefore: praying. That the said repealing Clause may be taken out of the said Bill before the same pafles into a Law; and that the Petitioners may have an Opportunity of being heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as may affect the Petitioner’s Interest.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Mr. Alderman Trecothick reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Coal-heavers working on the River Thames, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House, and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it- in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vita.

To prove the Allegations of the said First mentioned Petition; Alexander , being examined,

said, Ht hks been a Coalheaver on the River ‘Thames 3 2 Years, and has, during that Time, frequently been obliged to give the Coal Undertakers a great Part of his Wages, which, if any Man complained of, they would not allow him. to work any longer in his Gang: — That a Gang has sometimes been obliged to give back a Score of Coals and the odd Measure, to the Coal Undertaker, for employing the m: — That where a Publican is a Coal Undertaker, he obliges the Men, for whom he procures Employment, to (pend 6 a Day in his House, and pay him an Halfpenny per Score for the Use of a Shovel, which they are compelled to hire of him, though they have Shovels of their own; and that the Beer, which he obliges them to pay 4d. a Quart for, is not worth a Penny; the Gin and Tobacco not worth any thing: And,

James Wood, being examined, confirmed the fore-

going Evidence; and added. That in 1758, at whatever Rate the Men delivered a Ship, the Undertaker, who recommended them, had the Price of a ScoreThat they now take i6j or a Guinea for a Ship: — That the Coal Undertakers have kept him out of Work ever since the 30th of last November-He then produced a Paper, from whence it appeared, that a Publican, who was a Coal Undertaker, had received 17;. for One Ship by way of Present.

To prove the Allegations of the Second mentioned Petition;

Mr. James Mann, a Coal Undertaker, being examined, denied the whole of the foregoing Evidence as to himself: — He said, That some Coal Undertakers do keep Public Houses, but he does notThat the Men sometimes make the Coal Undertakers a Present, not always: — He believes the Coal Undertakers, who are Publicans, do not compel the Men to spend Money in their Houses, or to hire Shovels of them: — That the Ship generally pays him for his Shovels: — Being aiked the Reason of the Men giving Presents to the Coal Undertakers; — he said. It is for getting them Employment when Work is scarce: — That the Present is sometimes One Shilling, sometimes 6d. a Man for unloading a Ship; — has lately received a Present of that Sort hunself.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for Relief of the Coalheavers working upon the River Thames; and for enabling them to make Provision for such of themselves as shall be lick, lame, or past their Labour, and for their Widows and Orphans; and for their further Relief: And that Mr. Alderman Trecothick and Mr. Ridley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Hearing of the Matter of the Petition of James "biotins, of Dundas, Esquire, complaining of an undue'Election and Return for the Shire of.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the said Petition was read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner were heard.

And the original Poll, taken at the last Election of a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for' the Shire of Linlithgow, was produced, and read.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner having proposed to add to the Petitioner’s Poll Three Perron^, who' tendered their Votes, at the Election, and were rejected;

The same were admitted, by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, to have been good Votes.

Then they examined a Witness, and produced' Evidence, to establish the Vote of another Person, who tendered his Vote for the Petitioner, and was rejected, as being a Minor.

Then having proposed to disqualify the Votes of; Three Persons who voted for the Sitting Member; as being, at the Time of the Election, excluded from the Roll of Freeholders, by a Decree of the Court of Session, at that Time unappealed from;

It was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, that, at a former Court of Freeholders, the said Th ree Persons had been refused to be admitted on the Roll; and that, on an Appeal to the Court of Session that Judgment had been confirmed; but that, at the Day of Election, having again applied, on a new Claim, they were admitted on the Roll, which was afterwards confirmed by the Court of Session; and that there was an Appeal from both those Decrees of the Court of Session to the House of Lords; and the Lords were of Opinion, that the said Three Persons were well admitted on the Day of Election, and reversed both the said Decrees of the Court of Session.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner having proposed to disqualify the Votes of Two other Persons who voted for the Sitting Member, who were admitted, at the Day of Election, on the Roll of Freeholders, which, on an Appeal to the Court of Session, was confirmed, but that Decree was afterwards reversed by the House of Lords;

It was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, that these Votes were admitted on the Day of Elec* tion, and polled; and that, subsequent to that Election, there was an Appeal to the Court of Session, who were of Opinion, That they were well admitted; and that this Decree has since been reversed by the House of Lords.

Then having proposed to produce Evidence to disqualify the Vote of a Person who voted for the Sitting Member, in Right of an Ellate which he had fold some Years before, and of which he Was not then in Pofiession.

The same was objected to by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, the said Evidence not being warranted by the Terms of the Petition; and also that the Voter appearing at the Time of the Election to stand on the Roll of Freeholders, no Evidence ought to be admitted to controvert his Right: and they were heard ia Support of that Objection.

The House was moved. That an Act made in the Third Parliament of Scotland, in the Reign of King Charles the Second, in the Year 1681, intituled, An Act concerning the Election of Commissioners for Shires; might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed toby the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the Word " inrolled" to the End of the Question.

And the previous Question, being proposed, That the Question upon the said proposed Amendment, be now put;

And a Doubt arising in the House, whether, in Point of Order, a previous Question can be put upon an Amendment;

A Motion was made, and the Question was put. That a previous Question can be put upon an Amendment;

The House divided.

Discovery Mr. Stephens, according to Order, reported from the of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred Longitude, to consider of the several Acts relating to the Rewards for discovering the Longitude at Sea, and making Expe-periments of Proposals for difeoving the Longitude, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Five thousand Pounds, be applied out of any Monies unapplied to the Use of the Navy, in the Hands of the Treasurer of the Navy, towards making Experiments of Proposals for discovering the Longitude at Sea, and towards making Improvements of the Lunar Tables constructed by Tobias deceased, late Professor at Goetingen, in Germany; and also towards making Discoveries or Improvements useful to Navigation, subject to the same Directions and Regulations as are for the like Purposes contained in Two Acts made, one in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, " for providing a public Reward for such " Person or Persons as shall discover the Longitude at " Sea;" and the other, in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, " for explaining and rendering " more effectual Two Acts, one made in the Twelfth " Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act " for providing a public Reward for such Person or " Persons as shall discover the Longitude at Sea; and " the other, in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of " King George the Second, intituled, An Act to render " more effectual an Act made in the Twelfth Year " of the Reign, of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for providing a public Reward for " such Person or Persons as shall discover the Longitude

And the Titles of the said Accounts and Estimate were read.

The said Accounts are preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Estimate is as followeth; viz.

An ESTIMATE of the Expence of maintaining the Children received into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Children, on or before the 25th Day of March 1760* from the 31st Day of December 1769, exclusive, to the 31st Day of December 1770, inclusive.

The Number of the said Children living under the Care of the Governors and Guardians of the said Hospital on the 31st Day of December 1769, was Nine hundred and Sixty-five.

The Expence of Maintaining whom, at £. 7. 10 each, amounts to only - tC*7»237 10 '

Which is no more than the Expence of Cloathing them at £. 1 each, and Two Shillings and Six Pence a Week for Nursing; but as a greater Expence will accrue this Year, of bringing the Children to London, and keeping them in the Hospital in order to be apprenticed out, will encrease the Expence the present Year, to £. 2. 10. each Child, which is £.2,412 10 — *

N. B.Besides the above 965 Children, there have been taken into this Hospital since the 25th of March 1760, 315 Children; most of whom were under the most distressed Circumstances, or Orphans of Soldiers and Sailors, whereof 32 have been apprenticed, 8 claimed, and 99 dead: So that there are 176 Children now alive, which are wholly maintained and provided for, out of the Income arising from private Donations j and are not, nor ever have been, charged in the Estimate of the Public Accounts.

Signed by Order of the General Committee,

Tho. Collingwood, Secretary.

The Bill, now ingrossed, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, was, according to Order, read the Third Time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, That if the Name of a Nominee shall happen to be drawn by Lot, his Name may be let aside, and another chosen by Lot, in his (lead; and that if the Parties, or either of them, shall not nominate One, then the Want of such Nomination shall be supplied by Lot, and such Persons shall be liable to the same Objections, as the other Persons chosen by Lot.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz,

Pr. 5.1. 24. To leave out " Agent," and insert " Agents,*’ instead thereof.

1. 26* To leave out " Agent," and inlert " Agents," instead thereof.1

Pr. 10. 1. 36. To leave out " this," and insert the," instead thereof.

Pr. 12.I. 29. After "cleared," to insert " if they " shall think proper.".

P. 13.1. 38,7 To leave out " Provided always," and 39. j insert, " And be it further enacted," instead thereof.

And the said Amendments, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament.

Ordered, That Mr. Grenville do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Sir Joseph Mawbey reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Nicholas Dunbar, at First Paymaster to the Regiment of Surrey Milita, and, after the Division of the Regiment into Two Battalions, some Time Paymaster to the First Battalion thereof was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad contained in the said Petition: a State whereof, together with the Rdolution of the Committee thereupon, they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fad contained in the said Petition, together with the Opinion of the Committee thereupon, is as followeth; viz.

It appeared to your Committee, that the Petitioner had applied to Mr. Ellis then Secretary at War, for Copies of Accounts of Surrey Militia, as passed at the War Office; but it not being customary to grant such Copies, the Petitioner applied to the Duke of Grafton 21

by Letter, wherein he told his Grace there was a Secretion of Public Money; upon which his Grace directed the proper Officers to make Enquiry into the Com-pliint, and Mr. Smith, by Lord Barrington'% Direction* desired Mr. Dunbar's Attendance at the War Office* where he attended and took Extrads Three or Four Days together: That having made Objections to several Items in Mr. Fitter's Account, the same were inquired into at the War Office, and found to be regular.

Then the Petitioner, in order to make good his Charge, desired that the Non-effectice Accounts which he alledges in his Petition to have seen at the War Office* might be produced to your Committee; which being accordingly done by the proper Officer, Mr. Dunbar fixed upon the Sum of £.4,135.19/. id. charged in the said Accounts as vacant Pay of Officers and Non-effectice Pay of Non-commission Officers and Private Men, which lie said Mr. Fitter had never accounted for to the Public.

Upon which your Committee examined John Esquire, Accountant to the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Land Forces, who produced the Paymaster General’s Books; whereby it appeared; that the said Sum of £.4,135. 19*. id. had never come the Hands of Mr. Fitter, but was Hopped at the Pay Office by vir-

tue of His Majesty's Respite Warrants, which is the uniform Practice in similar Cafes; and it further appeared, that the said Sum made Part of Two grols Sums, the Savings upon the vacant Pay of Officers, and Non-effectice Money of the several Regiments of Militia during the late War, which several Sums were applied by Parliament to the Public Service, by Votes of the 7th Day of April 1764, and the 2d Day of April 1765, in Aid of German Claims.

The Petitioner then fixed upon a Sum of £» 750. iSa. 2 d.stopt by the Pay Office for Poundage, and Hospital, and Officers Pay, which he said Mr. Fitter had charged Twice, but it appeared by the Account delivered in by Mr. Filter, that he had given Credit for the full Pay of the Regiment as voted by Parliament: That the said Sum of £. 750. 1 6s.id. had been stopt by the Pay Office; and consequently Mr. Fitter must be reimbursed by charging it against the Officers Pay, which had been, done accordingly, and appeared to be the Practice of the whole Army.

Then the Petitioner said, That Mr. Fitter had charged £. 660. 6s. 6 d.as drawn from him by the Petitioner to December 1760, for the Pay of the First Battalion of the Surrey Militia, whereas the Petitioner had only drawn for £. 659. 8r. so that there was an Over-charge of iSr. 6 d.in Answer to which Mr. Fit per produced the Petitioner’s own Account to that Tjdie by which it appeared he had only charged the Petitioner with £. 651. $s.

Then the Petitioner fixeef upon Two Articles in Mr. Fitter's Account; viz. 10 s.6d. and £. 5. 5;. for the First Sum charged as paid at the War Office, for a Warrant fora Court Martial; the 2d for a Debenture Warrants which appeared by the Teffimony of several Agents present, and the Clerks of the War Office, to be the ulua! Fees received in that Office for I'imc immemorial, from the whole Army upon the like Occasions.

He then charged Mr. Fitter with the several Sums of £. 587. 17j. 1 id. and £. 1,041. i 4 but it appeared by the Pay Office Accounts, that those Two Sums were included in the before-mentioned Sum of £-4,135- 19*. 1 d.which was stopt by the Pay Office from Mr. Fitter, as vacant Pay of Officers, and Non-effe&ive Money.

Then the Petitioner being asked. If he had any further Matter to offer in Support of his Petition ? he said* He could not answer the Question, as he found the Committee did not understand the Accounts.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, representing, in the most reljicCtful and dutiful Manner, that it appears to this House, that the Expences on His Majesty’s Civil List, from his Accession, to the 5th Lay of January 1769, have exceeded the In*

come of all His Majesty’s annual Revenues, applicable to the tJfc of His Majesty’s Civil Government, and the Support and Maiutenanc» of His Houshold and Royal Family, in the Sum of 686,116/. 5 and that it

appears also to this House, thai the Expences on His Majesty’s Civil List, in the Year ending 31st ber 1768, being the last Year for which any Account has been laid before this House, amounted to the Sum of 898,077/. ijr. ${d. which greatly exceeds the Income of all His Majesty’s Revenues applicable as aforesaid to the Use of His Majesty’s Civil Government, and the Support ind Maintenance of His Houshold and Royal Fahiily; and to express, in the most humble Manner, the Opinion of this House, that the said ExpenceS Ought to be donfined within the Income of His Majesty’s said Revenues; and humbly and earnestly to intreat His Majesty, that he will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that such Retrenchments be made in the said Expences, as may reduce them within the Income of His Majesty’s laid Revenues j alluring His Majesty, that, as this House has, upon all Occasions, given the most evident Proofs of its Zeal and Affection for His Majesty, and particularly in the late Provision for the Payment of the Debt on the Civil List, so we cannot better Discharce the Duty we owe to His Majesty, and give Proof of the Continuance of our Zeal and Affection for His Person, His Royal Family and His Government, than by humbly offering this Request to His Majesty, in order that His Servants may be induced to practise that Oeconomy, which will tend most to the Honour and Dignity of His Majesty’s Crown, the Satisfaction of His own. Royal Mind, and the Content of His People j that we shall be always willing and ready to grant such Supplies as may be Wanted, on all necessary Occasions; but that we cannot but be anxious on the Part of our Constituents, to be Relieved from the Appearance of repeated Demands, growing out of Expences, for the Continuance of which* there does not appear to this House any Necessity, and for the Reduction of which, within the Bounds of His Majesty’s Income, no Assurance has been given;

The House was moved, that so much of His Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the Ninth Day of May, in the last Session of Parliament, as allures this House, " that His Majesty will endeavour to confine the Expences of His Civil Government within such Bounds as the Honour " of His Crown can possibly admit," might be read.

And the fatne was read accordingly.

Sum of 6S6,t j6/. 5 s.8 J.; and that it appears also to this House, that the Etpences on His Majesty’s Civil List, in the Year ending 31st December 1768, being the last Year for which any Account has been laid before this House, amounted to the Sum of 898,077/. is, which greatly exceeds the Income bF all His Majesty’s Revenues applicable as aforesaid to the Use of His Majesty’s Civil Government, and the Support and Maintenance of His Houshold and Rbyal Family; and to express, in the most humble Manner, the Opinion of this House, that the said Expences ought to be confined within the Income of His Majesty's said Revenues j and humbly and earnestly to intreat His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that such Retrenchments be made in the said Expences, as may reduce them within the Income of His Majesty’s said Revenues; alluring His Majesty, that as this House has, upon all Occasions, given the most evident Proofs of its Zeal and Affection for His Majesty, and particularly in the late Provision for the Payment of the Debt on the Civil List, so we cannot better discharge the Duty we owe to His Majesty, and give Proof of the Continuance of our Zeal and Affection for His Person, His Royal Family, and His Government, than by humbly offering this Request to His Majesty, in order that His Servants may be induced to practise that Oeconomy, which will tend most to the Honour and Dignity of His Majesty’s Crown, the Satisfaction of His own Royal Mind, and the Content of His People; that we shall be always willing and ready to grant such Supplies as may be wanted, on all necessary Occasions; but that we cannot but be anxious on the Part of our Constituents, to be relieved from the Appearance of repea^fd Demands, growing out of Expences, for the Continuance of which, there does not appear to this House any Necessity, and for the Reduction of which, within the Bounds of His Majesty’s Income, no Assurance has been given;

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Pembroke thereunto subscribed. Freeholders of the County of E1«dion. Pembroke, on Behalf of themselves and other Freeholders

Aprilis.

io Geo. III. 50

holders of the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by Magna Chart a, no County Court shall be held but from Month to Month; and that by an Act of 34th and 35th Henry Eighth, made for certain Ordinances in the King’s Dominion, and Principality of Wales, it is enacted, that the Sheriffs of the Shires in Wales shall keep their County Courts Monthly as is used in England ;and that by an Act 2d of Edward the Sixth, it is enacted, no County Court or Courts, to be kept within this Realm shall be longer deferred but One Month from Court to Court, and so the said Courts shall be kept every Month, and none otherwise; and that by an Act 7th and 8th William the Third, for further regulating Elections of Members to serve in Parliament, and preventing irregular Proceedings of Sheriffs, it is enacted, that upon every Election, County Courts shall be held at the most public and usual Place of Election in the said County, and where the same has most usually been for Forty Years last part, and shall there proceed to Election at the next County Court, unless the same fall out to be held within Six Days after the Receipt of the Writ, or upon the same Day, and then shall adjourn the same Court to some convenient Day, giving Ten Days Notice of the Time and Place of Election; and that on Tuesday the Sixth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy, the then last Election for the County of Pembroke being declared void, a new Writ issued for the Election of a Knight of the Shire for that County; and that the last Monthly County Court for the County of Pembroke ought in course to have been held on Tuesday the 13th of March One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy, but instead of holding it upon that Day, the Sheriff, Thomas Colby, Esquire, caused a Notice in Writing, but dated the Day before, to be fixed up at the County Hall at Haverford West, and other Market Towns, that he would hold his First County Court on the next day the 20th Day of March, at the Town of Pembroke, and caused another Notice to be in like Manner fixed up, signifying, that he would, on the same 20th Day of March, proceed to the Election at , of a

Knight of the Shire for the County of Pembroke, having received the Writ for that Purpose; and that Hugh Owen, and John Symmons, Esquires, were the Candidates,

but Mr. Symmons, the Petitioners, and the major Part of the Freeholders, became alarmed, the Sheriff’s Proceedings being highly illegal, partial, and injurious to the Freeholders, in Two essential Points, as to the Time and Place of Election: First, Because Tuesday the 13th of March, when the Notice was fixed up, was the Day on which the Monthly County Court ought to have been held, and if the Writ had been received on that Day or within Six preceding Days, the Sheriff* ought then to have adjourned the Court, and given Ten Days Notice of proceeding to Election, or if the Writ had been received Six Days before, then he ought to have proceeded to an Election on the said 13th Day of March: Secondly, Because the Town of Pembroke lies at the extreme End of the County, so situated, that a Branch of Miljord Haven divides it from the major Part of the County, and a great many of the Freeholders live above Forty Miles from it; and that in order for a Communication with the Town of Pembroke, from the greatest Part of the County, there are Three Ferries, one called Pembroke Ferry, another called Lazvrenuy Ferry, and the third called -

ping Ferry, all of which belong to and are under the Direction or Influence of Sir William Baronet,

and Mrs. Barlow, the Father and Aunt of Hugh Ozven, Esqui re, the Candidate, and the Passage over one of those Ferries is above One Mile over, another One Mile, and over the Third about Half a Mile, and neither of the Ferry Boats are capable of carrying more than Six Horses at a Time in fair Weather, and in bad Weather they cannot pal's at all; and that Vot. 32.

West, Which is in the Center of the County, is the most Pembroke convenient Place for an Election, and the Elections Election, have been usually and constantly held there for upwards of Forty Years past, save in one Instance about Thirty Years ago; and that the Sheriff himself was apprized of the Inconvenience of the Place, and some short Time before the Writ came to his Hands, acknowledged he had waited some Time at Haverford West for the Writ, and that he had been applied to by some Persons from Pembroke, to have the Election held there, but that he had refused the same on account of the Inconveniency of the Place, and was determined it should be held at Haverjord West, as the proper and usual Place, though he afterwards changed his Opinion; and that Mr.

Symmons gave Notice in Writing to the Sheriff, that the Time and Place appointed for the Election were illegal, and that he would not attend there; and some of the Freeholders on the Day appointed went to the Polling Place at Pembroke, and in the Presence of the Sheriff and of the said Hugh Owen, Esquire, and his Friends, protested against the Sheriff’s Proceedings; but the Sheriff paying no Attention to the Notice or Protest, proceeded to the Election, received Mr. Owen's Votes, and returned him Knight of the Shire for the County of Pembrokl: And therefore praying, That as their Freedom of Election of a proper Representative in Parliament hath been taken away, and manifestly violated by the above Measures used by the said Thomas Colby, the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioners I'uch Relief therein, with such Censure upon the said Sheriff, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be, heard at the Bar of this House, upon Friday the 27th Day of this Instant April.

Ordered, That Thomas Colby, Esquire, High Sheriff for the County of Pembroke, do attend this House upon Friday the 27th Day of this Instant; and that he be served with a Copy of the said Petition.

A Petition of John Harrison, of Red Lion Square, in the County of Middlesex, Watchmaker, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is informed, that a Bill is depending in the House, for explaining and rendering more effectual several Acts, for providing a public Reward for discovering the Longitude at Sea, for improving the Lunar Tables, constructed by the late Professor Meyer, and for encouraging Discoveries and Improvements useful to Navigation; and that the Petitioner hath spent great Part of his Life in Pursuit of the Discovery of the Longitude, and conceives that he hath made a complete Discovery thereof, and that he is well entitled to the Whole of the Reward appointed by Parliament for that Purpose, although he has hitherto received only One Moiety of the same; and that the Petitioner apprehends that Part of the said Bill will be prejudicial to him, with respect to the remaining Moiety of the Reward, if the same should be 'pa{Ted into a Law: And therefore praying. That he may be heard, by himself or his Counsel, against so much of the said Bill as may tend to prejudice and affect his Interest.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and.that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it bean Instruction to the said Committee that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition

Westminster Sir Charles Whitworth reported from the Committee,

Paving. whom the Petition of the Commissioners for putting

in Execution the several Acts of Parliament, passed in the Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; Mr. John Marqnand, being examined, said, That the Commissioners appointed by the said Acts have proceeded diligently in putting the same in Execution: That they have made a great Progress therein, much to the Convenience and Benefit of the Public, but are not able to proceed without further Assistance; and that the said Acts want altering and amending in several respects.

Mr. George Box, Clerk to the said Commissioners, being asked his Opinion, what Alterations he thought necessary to be made in the said Acts, he said. He thought many were wanting:

That he was of Opinion, an additional Number of Commissioners should be chosen by the Vestry in each Parish; and that a certain Number of Persons properly qualified should be a Committee, to superintend the several Works within each Parish:

That those Committees should be impowered to make Rates for paving, repairing, cleansing, and lighting, the Streets within such Parishes respectively:

That the said Committees should appoint Collectors and Inspectors:

And he added, That several other Regulations are necessary, in order effectually to carry the said Acts into Execution.

The House was moved, That the Order made upon the 15th Day of March last, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Commissioners for putting in Execution the several Acts for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and other Places, in the said Acts mentioned, effectually to per-foriti the Works directed by the said Acts to be done, might be read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Order be discharged.

"From Michaelmas 1769 to 14 March 1770, 104 Houses, Value £.4,241: — He further informed the Committee, that it is supposed the last 104 Houses were broke open by a Number of Housebreakers, not exceeding Twenty, and few of them more than 20 Years of Age,

16 or 17 of whom are in Custody, with little Probability of their being convicted: — That the Evil increases amazingly, and never was at so great a Height as since la ft.Michaelmas. — Being asked, What is the Cause

of this Increase of Housebreaking ? — he said, That Felons formerly carried their Goods to Pawnbrokers, but by the prefertt Method of quick Notice to Pawnbrokers, Silversmiths, and others, that Plan is defeated, and the Housebreakers now go to Jews, who melt the Plate immediately, and destroy other Things that might be Evidence, which in Burglary can be nothing but the Goods, though in other Cales the Person may be sworn to -That they disguise Jewels by knocking them out of the Sockets, so that they cannot be sworn to; that the present Gang of Housebreakers are Sons of unfortunate People, and of no Trade; that they begin when Boys as Pickpockets, but turned Housebreakers when they grew up, in order to procure a greater Income to supply their increased Expences: And he informed the Committee, that for Twenty Years a Footpad has not escaped; that Highwaymen cannot escape, upon account of the early Information given to the aforesaid Office, and the great Number of Prosecutors who always appear against them, which he thinks mull in Time put an End to that Fvil — He theft laid, He had detected several Persons in Duke's Place with Plate, and has offered a Reward of Five Guineas for apprehending One Person in the same Place. — Beingalked, What he thought of the present Method of watching the Town ? — he said. The Watch is insufficient; their Duty too hard, and Pay too small: — That he has known Serjeants in the Guards employed as Watchmen: — That the Watchmen are paid 8 \d.per Night in Saint Margaret's Parish, and a Gra-

tuity of 2 Guineas a Year, out of which they find their own Candle: — That as they are paid Monthly, they borrow their Money of an Usurer once a Week: — That in other Parishes the Watch are paid from 10 to is. per Night -. — That the Watch in is in every

Parish under the Direction of a separate Commission, composed of Persons who have served the Offices of Churchwarden and Overseer: — That Commissioners of the respective Parishes appoint the Beats of their Watchmen without conferring together, which leaves the Frontiers of each Parish in a confused State, for that where one Side of a Street lies in One Parish, and the other Side in another Parish, the Watchmen of One Side cannot lend any Assistance to Persons on the other Side, other than as a private Person, except in Cafes of Felony.

James Sayer, Esquire, Deputy High Steward of Westminster, confirmed the above Evidence, and added, That St. Margaret's Parish has a select Vestry, the Majority of which is composed of Tradesmen; that they will pay no more than 8 \d.a Night to their Watchmen, and have no Way of punishing them for Neglect of Duty than by dismissing them, which, in Fact, is not a Punishment, for they find it difficult to get Men to serve in that Office; and he further said, that their Number is not sufficient.

Being asked the Reason for changing the Constables from being parochial to be Constables for the whole City and Liberty, he said, That before 29 Geo. 2. Constables were parochial; — that he apprehended the Reason for the Change was, that a Constable could not execute any official Act out of his Parish, without being specially authorized so to do He mentioned an Instance of a Constable’s being killed when he was serving a Warrant out of his Parish: — That the Person who killed him was tried, and found guilty of Manslaughter only, though he VoL. 32.

would have been guilty of Murder, if it had happened in the Parish to which the Constable belonged.

Sir John Fielding being asked, what Remedies he could suggest to prevent the above Evils, he produced Two Papers relating to Constables, Watchmen, and other Officers; which were read to, and confirmed by him; and are as follow; viz.

Watchmen too old — should be from 25 to 50 — their Beats too extensive — should not exceed 20 Houses on each Side of the Way: Watchmen too few — the Sum raised for the Watch too little, being only Four Pence in the Pound — should be Sixpence.

Ward Officers to be chosen out of those Inhabitants that have served the Office of Constable, and to have a good Salary.

One Half of the Constables to be discharged within the Year, so that One-half remaining Two Years will be able to instruct the new Officers; and the whole Duty will be done well.

If the new Provisions for the Watch can be established by the Commissioners remaining where they are, it will lave Trouble, for then the Moftey may be raised by them as it now is, and every Parish may pay and clothe their own Watchmen; so that the Appointment, Distribution, Direction, Wages, Number, and Punishment of the Watch, may be in the Magistrates, by a new Commission, and the Paying and Clothing be in the present Commissioners.

The Words " A Constable of the City and Liberty of " Westminster" to be placed over the Constables Doors; the Words " Ward Officer " over the Ward Officers Doors: — Beadles by Name, to be discharged, and the ne-ccfiary Part of the Duty they now do to be performed by the Ward Officers.

That it would be right to confine the intended Improvement and Constables to only, as the

Watch in the adjoining Parishes of Middlesex remain oft the same Footing as is originally settled by the Statute of fVinchester.

2d Paper.

1. The Watch of Westminster is extremely defective

— the Number ought to be increased, their Pay augmented, and the whole Direction of them put under One Commission, and that Commission should be Ma-gillrates of the City and Liberty of the

Watch should be attended by Ward Officers, and relieved in the Night, a whole Night’s Duty being too hard.

2. The Roundhouses should be capacious, no Liquor should be fold in them; Publicans should be punished for permitting Watchmen to tipple during their Duty; and Watchmen should be particularly rewarded for Diligence, and punished for Neglect by the Civil Power.

3. High Constables should not quit their Office at the End of Three Years: — Constables should be increased. Half the Number only discharged annually: — The Constable of the Night should be considered for his Attendance on that Duty, and punished for Neglect.

4. The Power of railing Money at present for the Watch is too confined, it should be enlarged, raised by the present Commissioners — the Watchmen paid by them — but their Number, Direction, and Appointment, be by the new Commission of Magistrates.

5. Receivers of Stolen Goods, especially of those taken by Burglary or Highway Robbery, should be made Principals, with a Power of Mitigation in the Judge.

James Sayer, Esquire, being again examined, approved of Sir John Fielding's Plan, and added. That the Beadles are an unnecessary Set of Men, advanced in Years, and Servants to the Churchwardens and Over-seers — are 40 in Number over the whole City and Liberty; — they have an Allowance of £ 20 per Ann. a-piece, which they make up £. 30: — That he appre-hendsj if the Number was increased to 60, and the City

Sir John Fielding, being again examined, said, He thought the Name of Beadle should be abolished, and that they should be called Ward Officers.

Mr. S. Rainsfortk, High Constable of , being

examined,-(aid, He had been in Office 12 Months: — That he had visited the different Night Watch Houses, in the City and Liberty of Westminster, frequently from 12 to 3 in the Morning; — found many of the Peace Officers upon Duty — some were not: That there is a general Complaint of Peace Officers neglecting their Duty; from which Neglect it is owing, that the Watchmen and Beadles are not present; and this general Neglect, he apprehends, is the reason why so many Houses are robbed: — That he has frequently found 7 or 8 Watchmen together in an Alehouse: — He thinks that the High Constable should visit the Roundhouse in the Night Time, once a Month at least> or oftener, if required; and agreed with Sir John Fielding, as to the Number and Pay of the Watchmen.

James Sayer, Esquire, being again examined, said.

That Constables are appointed under Acts 29 and 31 Geo. 2d, which Acts are in many Articles defective: — That 80 Constables, which is the Number limited, are not sufficient: — That they are appointed by the Leet Jury, which has been attended with great Partialities; for the Leet Jury being composed of the Overseers of the several Parishes of the preceding Year, they protect each other from serving the Office of Constable: — That in general opulent Inhabitants are excused, and young Tradesmen returned; That if a rich Man is now-and-then returned, he is generally got off by pleading Age or Infirmities'That Deputies are generally hired Men, and though they can’t be appointed, unless approved of by the Deputy High Steward, yet as it is impossible for him to get a true Character of the Person nominated, he finds many unfit Persons are appointed, who, he is informed, make a Trade of serving the Office; for Remedy of which, he proposed, that the Number of Constables should be increased to 120: — He thinks the Burthen of serving the Office of Constables should not lay wholly on the trading Inhabitants, as it does by the late Ad: — That by common Law, every Person, able and fit, is liable to serve: — That the Fine for not serving the Office should be enlarged from £. 8 to £ 20, which Fine should be di-ftributed among those that do serve: And he added. That 12 being obliged to attend daily during the Session of Parliament, as long as either House fits, the Duty comes round to each Individual every Sixth Day, Eight being excepted, who may be lick or kept in reserve; during which Attendance the Constables must necessarily neglect their own Business: — With relped to the High Constable, he said. It is an Office of great Burthen and Trust: — That by Law, he, the Witness, is obliged to appoint a substantial Tradesman to that Office; that the Person appointed is not to continue in Office above Three Years, and is liable to a Penalty of 20 for refusing to serve, which Penalty goes to the Poor of the Parish; upon which he observed, that the High Constable should not be a Tradesman, because his Power enables him to oblige the Keepers of Public Houses to deal with him, or those with whom he is concerned in his Way of Trade: — That the Penalty on Persons refusing to serve the Office should be increased; that the High Constable should have a Reward for his Service; and that the Constables of the Night should have a Reward also.

being again examined, said, lie was of Mr. s Opinion.

Sir John Fielding, being again examined, said, That Ballad-fingers are a greater Nuisance than Beggars, because they give Opportunity to Pickpockets, by collecting People together: — That the Songs they sing are generally immoral and obfeene; the People themselves capable of Work, and of the lowest and most abandoned Order of People: — For Remedy of which, he proposed, that all Ballad-fingers should be considered as Vagrants, and be made liable to the same Punishments, no Person being a Vagrant now but who comes within some One of the Descriptions of Vagrancy in the Vagrant Act: And the High Constable, being again examined, informed the Committee, That he has often had Warrants for taking up Ballad-fingers: That lie has apprehended a great many; notwithstanding which, their Numbers increase, and they are become a very great Nuisance: — That they have often been dispersed, but still continue the Practice.

Sir John Fielding, being again examined, said. That the City of Westminster is a Franchise under the Dean and Chapter of Westminster: — That the Common Gaol

thereof is called the Gate H, to which Offenders of every Kind apprehended within the Liberty of -

Jler have been usually committed for some Years back, to the Number of 600 or 700 annually: — That in this Gaol there is little or no Allowance or Provision for the Prisoners, but what arises from the Charity of Passengers, seldom amounting to more than 5 or 6 Shillings a Week; the greatest Part of which is given to the Beggar at the Window for the Day: — That the said Gaol appears, from Experience of the Magistrates, to be too small for the Number, and too weak for the safe Custody of Prisoners; — That to this Gaol, Persons in Execution for Debts recovered in the Court of Conscience are committed; and he said. He believed this is the only Gaol in England, where there is not some Provision for poor and distressed Prisoners; — and he added, that when a Magistrate commits a Man to that Gaol for an Assault, he does not know but he commits him there to ltarve: — for these Reafpns, as well upon the principles of Humanity as of Civil Policy, this ought to be remedied; and that on account of the vast Increase of Inhabitants, Property, and Number of Offenders, there ought to be in Westminster, a strong, capacious, and useful Gaol, and there is no such Thing at present: — That the said Gaol, called the Gate House, is a very old Building, subject to

be repaired by the said Dean and Chapter, who appoint the Gaoler: — That the supposed original Ule of this Gaol, was for the Purposes of committing Clerks Convict; the Commission of Magistrates of is

not later than Charles the 1 ft’s Reign: — They began first to commit Offenders to this Gaol, rather by Sufferance than by Right; and he observed, that however proper it may have been for its original Purposes, it is unequal to the present Occasions, and, as he apprehends, cannot be altered without a Law: And he further informed the Committee, That the Magistrates of Westminster have rc-presented this Mischief to the Dean and Chapter, who acknowledge it, are willing to pull it down, and to give a Piece of Ground in their Royalty, in Tot hill Fields, to build a new Gaol upon, and to subject the fame, with every Thing the reunto belonging, to the Magistrates of Westminster, under such Regulations as the Legislature shall think proper, provided a Sum be granted by the Public for building the fame; and he added, that Elti-mates have been made, by which it appears that a very effectual Gaol may be built for the Sum of£.2,500:

In order therefore to remedy the Inconveniencies above mentioned, he proposed, that such Gaol should be built and kept in Repair out of the County Rate, which he laid may be done without Injury to the County at large, for this Reason, that there is but one Rate at present for Middlesex and Westminster, near One Third of which

is

to Geo. III. 10° Aprilis\881

is paid by the latter since the Increase of Buildings there: — That this Proportion is much greater than the Expences required by the Act for County Rates would subject Westminster to; and he added. That the Gaol called the House of Correction in is repaired

by the Magistrates of Westminster and the Expence is paid by virtue of their Orders on the County Treasurer j that the same Thing, if allowed by Parliament for the Repair of the proposed new Gaol, will answer the Purpose, without separating the Rate.

James Sayer, Esquire, being again examined, concurred with Sir John Fielding in every Particular.

Sir John Fielding, being again examined, informed the Committee, That about 6 or 7 Years ago the Magistrates of Westminster had no other Court House but a

Place at the Bottom of the Stairs, leading to the House of Commons, called Hell, to keep their Sessions in: — The Increase of Business and of Offences in Westminster made it impradicable to carry on the Business there: The Nuisance was represented by the Magistrates to the Lord Lieutenant, Lord Northumberland, who said. He had then applied for Redress; and told the Chairman,-that it could not be taken up by Government then, but would be in future considered: In the mean Time, at his own Expence, amounting to 800, he directed the Chairman to prepare a large House in King Street,' Westminster, which was formerly a Tavern, to be made proper for a Court House, that the Magistrates, for their Sessions, the Burgesses for their Courts, the Lieutenancy for the Militia, Commissioners of Sewers for the Execution of their Business, Grand Juries for the County of Middlesex, Writs of Enquiries for the Sheriff's,

and Meeting of Inhabitants for nominating their Representatives, should ule the said Building; for all which Purposes, it has been constantly, effectually, and conveniently used: That it is scarce possible for the above Business to be traniaded without it; and the Establishment of it is as essential to the Civil Power as any Thing that has been mentioned: — That the Purchase of the said Building, and fitting it up, cost the Duke of Northumberland near J. 4,000; and he added. That this Building also might be kept in Repair by the County Rate, at an Average of J. 30 or J. 40 a Year.

James Sayer, Esquire, confirmed the foregoing Evidence: And,

Sir John Fielding said. He thinks the acting Part of the Magistrates in Westminster is in as good a state as it ever was, and more free from Imputations or Neglect of Duty: — That it would be useful to have some Persons of Rank and Condition in the Commission of the Peace for Westminster, who would attend at the Quarter Sessions, where they would become acquainted with the Conduct of the Magistrates in general, give a Dignity to the Commission, support the acting Magistrates on great Occasions, and give Encouragement to such of them as discharged their Trust becoming the Honour of the Commission, and discountenance those who did not: And he added. That for the last Two or Three Years, the Magistrates of Westminster have gone through very painful Duty, and have been very diligent in it; and having been feniible of the Necessity of their Attendance, have mutually agreed to attend at any Time or Place, upon the least Notice from their Chairman.

James Sayer, Esquire, being again examined, admitted that the Magistracy at present is composed in general of Persons of Character, and that Justice is administered with Activity, Diligence, and Skill; but alledged, that it has been otherwise formerly, and may be the same hereafter; and therefore he was of Opinion, that a Regulation in the Magistracy of Westminster is necessary: — That there should be a Qualification of Justices; — that they should have a Reward for acting, as the moll Part of their Time will be devoted to the Public Service: — That the Fees to be taken by their Clerks should be appropriated to some public Service, such as a Vagrant Hol'pital; — that there should be certain Rotation Vox. 32.

Offices established by Law; — that, as he apprehends, One such Office might be sufficient, if properly regulated; — that the Rotation Office should do all the Business, except in emergent Cafes; and that the private Offices of Justice of the Peace should be abolished, because it l'ometimes happens that a Man committed for a notorious bailable Offence, is carried to another Justice, who bails him without knowing the Enormity of his Offence: And,

Sir John Fielding laid, That in criminal Offence? that nearly regard the Public, it is impradicable to use a Rotation Office, as there are many Things that are necessary to be kept secret; — and though the Whole of the Circumstances must be known to the acting Magistrate, yet they cannot be known by a fresh Magistrate who attends in Rotation.

And he added, That the great Number of Brothels and irregular Taverns, carried on without Licence from the Magistrates, are another great Cause of Robberies, Burglaries, and other Disorders; and also of Neglect of Watchmen and Constables of the Night in their respective Duties: That these Taverns are kept by Persons of the moll abandoned Characters, such as Bawds, Thieves, Receivers of stolen Goods, and Marshalsea. Court and Sheriffs Officers, who keep lock-up Houses: The principal of these Houses are situate in Covent Garden; — about 30 in St. Mary le Strand; — about 12 in Martin*% in the Vicinity of Covent; — about 12

in St. Clement's; — 5 or 6 at Charing; — and in Hedge

Lane about 20: — That there are many more dispersed in different Parts of Westminster, in Goodman's Fields and Whitechapel, many of which are remarkably infamous, and are the Cause of Disorders of every Kind, Shelters for Bullies to protect Prostitutes, and for Thieves; are a Terror to the Watchmen and Peace Officers of the Night, a Nuisance to the Inhabitants in the Neighbourhood, and difficult to be suppressed by Prosecution,*for want of Evidence; and in short, pregnant with every other Mischief to Society: — That any Person desirous of gaining a Livelihood by keeping a Place of public Entertainment, who is of good Reputation, can obtain a Licence with Ease from the Magistrates to keep such House, when a Public House in any Neighbourhood happens to be vacant that has been licenced before; the Magistrates of Middlesex and Westminster, having long held it to be a Rule essential to the public Good, rather todiminifli, than increase, the Number of Public Houses: — That Persons of abandoned Characters, by applying to the Commissioners of the Stamp Office, may obtain a Licence for felling Wine; by virtue of such Licences it is that the Taverns above described are kept open; for the aforesaid Commissioners are impowered by Law to grant such Licences to whom they shall think fit: — That Licences, for selling Spirituous Liquors by Retail are not granted by the Commissioners of Excise, unless the Parties produce to them a Licence under the Hands and Seals of Two Justices of the Peace to sell Ale: — That Magistrates cannot by Law authorize any Person to sell Ale without a Certificate of such Person’s being of good Fame, and sober Life and Conversation; so that producing this Licence to the Commissioners establishes their Character with them, and takes away the Necessity of any Enquiry: — For Remedy of which, he proposed that Wine Licences should be placed by Law under the same Restraints as the Licences for selling spirituous Liquors now are — This Remedy, he apprehended, might probably reduce the Revenue of Wine Licences; if confined to the Bills of Mortality, it would, in his Opinion, diminish it no more than £. 400 per Ann. but if extended to Portsmouth, Plymouth, Chatham, and other Dock

Yards, it may lessen it £. 200 more: — He added, that he thinks it more necessary to correct the Evil in these Parts, as it has a direct Tendency to corrupt and destroy the very Vitals of the Constitution, the Lives of the useful Seamen, who, by means of thele Houses, become the Objects of Plunder as long as they have any Money,

and are induced to become Robbers when they have none s — And he informed the Committee, That there is another great Evil which is the Cause of these Disorders, namely, the immense Number of Common Prostitutes, who mostly from Nccelfity infeft the Streets of the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, attended

by common Soldiers, and other Bullies, to protect them from the Civil Power; These Prostitutes, when they have secured the unwary Customers, lead them to some of the aforesaid Taverns, from whence they seldom escape without being robbed: — The Cause of this Evil, as he apprehends, is the great Difficulty, as the Law now stands, to punish those Offenders, they being, as common Prostitutes, scarce, if at all, within the Description of any Statute now in being: And he added, that this subjects Watchmen, Roundhouse-keepers, Constables, and even the Magistrates themselves, to Prosecutions from low Attorneys: — That the Remedy, in his Opinion, should be to declare, that Persons walking or plying in the said Streets for lewd Purposes after the Watch is set, Handing at the Doors, or appearing at the Windows of such Taverns, in an indecent Manner, for lewd Purposes, shall be considered as Vagrants, and punished as such: — That as to the Circumstance of Street Beggars, it never came to his Knowledge that they are under Contribution to the Beadles.

Mr. ’Thomas Heath, a Burgess of the Duchy of Lancaster, being examined, said, That both the Constables and Watch within the said Duchy, are very insufficient anc^ defective.

Upon the whole of which Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That since the 29th Day of September last, 104 Houses within the Cities of London, Westminster, and the Parts adjacent, have been broke open, and Plate, Jewels, and other Goods, stolen therefrom, to the Amount of £. 4,241 Pounds; that the said Evil hath increased very much of late Years, and is likely still to increase, unless some effectual Provision be made to prevent it.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That to put a Hop to the said Evil, the Number of Constables in the City and Liberty of St.

Martin's le Grand, and such Parts of the Duchy of Lan-cafer as are within the said Liberty, should be increased; and that all Persons being Householders within the same, other than the Members of both Houses of Parliament, aClting Justices of the Peace, and certain other Officers and Persons, should be made liable to serve as Constables, or pay a Penalty for refusing to serve the said Office; and that a new Mode of appointing and discharging them should be adopted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Number of Watchmen in the said Places should be increased, more able Persons appointed, their Pay augmented, another Method adopted for appointing the m; that their Beats, or Districts, should be less ex-tehfive; their Duty be made general; and that they should be put under One general Direction.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Beadles in many Parishes are not at present of sufficient Service; that they should. for the future, be employed under another Name, and under some general Direction, as Regulators of the Watchmen, and to take up Vagrants and other disorderlv Persons, in their respective Wards; and that their Number should be inGrealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty of Constables and Watchmen, and of Beadles under another Name, should be regulated, with 8

proper Encouragements for doing their Duty, and Penalties for their Neglect of it.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the receiving of Stolen Goods, particularly Gold and Silver Plate and Jewels, should be made more penal, and the Receivers of them, particularly of those taken by Burglary or Highway Robbery, be made Principals.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision should be made for ttansporting Criminals, which now are transported to America, to the Coast of Africa and to the East Indies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That common Ballad Singers, by collecting great Numbers of People about them, give Opportunities for picking Pockets, and are a great Nuisance; and that some effectual Provision should be made for suppressing . them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present unrestrained Method of granting Licences to fell Wine, in and about the City and Liberty' of Westminster, gives an Opportunity to Persons of the most abandoned Characters, to open Houses for the retailing of Wine to be drank in the said Houses as Taverns, which are frequented by every Species of disorderly Persons, and is a great Cause of Robberies and other Disorders; and that the said Method should be restrained.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House in King Street, Westminster, called Guildhall, which is now the Property of his Grace the Duke of Northumberland, and was some Years ago fitted up by him at his own Expence, hath been of great Benefit in the holding the Sessions for the said City and Liberty, and for doing other essential public Business regarding the fame, and is absolutely necessary for those Purposes.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Prison, called the in the City of

Westminster, to which a great Number of Criminals and Debtors are committed, is too small, and totally unfit for the Purposes of a Common Gaol in the present increased State of the said City, and the Liberty thereof; and that there is no certain Allowance for the Maintenance of the Prisoners committed thereto.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a strong and capacious Gaol for the City and Liberty of Westminster should be built in another Place, and some Provision be made for the Maintenance of the Prisoners which are or shall be committed to the Gate-house, and to the said New Gaol, when built.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That larger and more convenient Roundhouses should be provided in the said City and Liberty of and in Saint Martin's le Grand, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster which is within the said Liberty; and that no Liquor should be fold therein.

Supply. Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-five thousand Five hundred Sixty-five Pounds, and Twelve Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, to discharge such unsatisfied Claims and Demands, for Expences incurred during the late War in Germany, as appear to be due to the Landgrave of HeJJe Cajftly by the Reports of the Commissioners appointed by His Majesty, for examining and stating such Claims and Demands.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Five thousand Pounds be granted to His Majesty, to be advanced to the Governor and Company of the Merchants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, to be applied in assisting the said Company in carrying on their Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Nine thousand Six hundred and Fifty Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, upon account, towards enabling the Governors and Guardians of the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education, of exposed ana deserted young Children, to maintain and educate such Children as were received into the said Hospital on or before the 25th Day of March 1760. from the 31st Day of December 1769, exclusive, to the 31st Day of December 1770, inclusive; and that the said Sum be issued and paid, for the Use of the said Hospital, without Fee or Reward, or any Deduction whatsoever.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a further Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Five hundred Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account, to enable the Governors and Guardians of the said Hospital to put out Apprentice such Children as were received into the said Hospital on or before the 25th Day of March 1760, so as the said Governors and Guardians do not give with any one Child more than the Sum of Seven Pounds; and that the said Sum be issued and paid, without Fee or Reward, or any Deduction whatsoever.

The laid Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Lord Brownlozv Bertie reported from the Committee, Roads. to whom the Bill'for repairing and widening several Hoads, leading from the Town of Louth, in the County of Lincoln, was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were, with an Amendment to One or them, agreed to by the House.

Coabheavers# A Petition of several Owners and Masters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade, on behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the Bill to explain and amend an Act passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for Relief of the Coal-heavers working upon the River Thames; and for enabling them to make Provision for such of themselves as shall be sick, lame, or past their Labour, and for their Widows and Orphans; and for their further Relief; and setting forth, that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law as it now (lands, it will be highly injurious to the Petitioners, and subject the Masters of Ships to many Restraints, wherewith it is impossible, from the 'Nature of the Trade, that they . should comply; and that it will greatly tend to increase the Misunderstandings and Disputes between the Masters and the Persons employed in unloading the Ships: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the Bill as may affect! them, and receive such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Widows of the Officers of the Royal Navy Navy, being offered to be presented to the House; Officers

The Lord Nor thy by His Majesty’s Command, ac- WKtewS# quainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That for these Six Years past the Petitioners Pensions have gradually ^decreased; and are now so greatly diminished, that for these Two Years they have received considerably leis than Half what they received in Time of War, whereby many Widows have been reduced to insuperable, and feme to insupportable, Distress, Distraction, and Despair; and therefore hope, that the House will take their very unhappy same into Consideration, and make an Addition to their Fund, which is at present so low, and upon such an uncertain Establishment, that they are not able to raise any Money on the Credit of their nominal Pensions, to procure them only a Temporary Relief, being neither certain of the Sum to be received, nor the Time of Payment; for which Reason the Petitioners cannot help thinking their Situation peculiarly singular and unfortunate; the Petitioners therefore further hope, that the distinguished Services rendered to the Public by their brave but unfortunate Husbands will recommend them and their helpless Orphans to the Notice of Parliament, that their Pensions may be fixed and regularly paid, which many of their Husbands have dearly purchased with the Price of their Blood.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
