A Petition of the Trustees, appointed by Acts of Par- Data liament, for repairing several Roads in the Counties of Surrey and Suffix, was presented to the House, and read;

Taking Notice of the said Bill; and setting forth, That the Petitioners have, in the Execution of the Trust re-posed in them, endeavoured, in all respects, to accommodate the Public, as well by opening several new Roads, as by watching and lighting the several Avenues to the Cities of London and Westminster, which are under their Direction; for which Purposes, they have been obliged to borrow a very large Sum of Money, on the Credit of the Tolls, which dill remains undischarged; and if any additional Toll should be granted, for Purposes foreign to the Design of the several subsisting Acts, it will be injurious to the Creditors who have advanced Money on the Credit of the said Acts, and a very grievous and unequal Burthen upon the Inhabitants of the said Counties: And therefore praying that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as lays any additional Toll on Horses or Carriages passing through any Turnpike under their Direction.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported

from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, The Resolutions which the Committee had dire died him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person or Persons, Bodies Politic and Corporate, who, being possessed of, or entitled to, Annnuities, after the Rate of Four Pounds per which were

consolidated by an Act of the Second of His present Majesty, shall, on or before the Seventh Day of May next, in Books to be opened at the Bank of England for that Purpose, subscribe their Names or signify their Content to accept, in lieu thereof, Annuities after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum, to commence from the Fifth Day of January 1770, and to be added to, and made One joint Stock with, certain Annuities consolidated by the Act of the Twenty-fifth of George the Second, and several subsequent Acts of Parliament, shall, for every One hundred Pounds of Capital Stock so subscribed, until the several Sums subscribed shall amount together to Two millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, be intitled to receive Two Tickets in a Lottery, to con-fist of Fifty Thousand Tickets, at the Rate of Fourteen Pounds each; and that every such Subscriber, in Consideration of such Subscription, shall have a Receipt from the Cashiers of the Bank of England for Four Pounds, in part of the said Fourteen Pounds for each Ticket, to which such Subscriber shall be intitled, and shall pay, for and in respect of every such Ticket, the Sum of One Pound, on or before the Fifteenth Day of June next; the further Sum of Two Pounds, on or before the Twentieth Day of July next; the further Sum of Three Pounds on or before the Twenty-first Day of August next; and the further Sum of Four Pounds on or before the Twenty-fifth Day of September next; that, upon such Payments being completed, Tickets shall be delivered, as loon as the same can be prepared, to the Persons holding and possessed of the Receipts, hereinbefore directed to be given by the Cashiers of thq Bank of to the several Subscribers as aforesaid; that the Sum of Five hundred thousand Pounds shall be distributed into Prizes, for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery; which Prizes shall be paid at the Bank of England, in Money, to such Proprietors, upon Demand, on the First Day of March 1771, or as soon after as Certificates can be prepared, without any Deduction whatsoever; and that every Person possessed of, and holding, such Receipts, as aforesaid, who shall pay in the whole of the Money to be paid on each Ticket, on or before the Seventeenth Day of August next, shall be allowed an Interest, by way of Discount, after the Hate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, on the Sums so completing his Payments respectively, to be computed from the Day of completing the same to the Twenty-fifth Day of September next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in case the full and entire Sum of Two Millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, in the said Four Pounds per Centum Annuities, shall not have been subscribed on or before the Seventh Day of May next; and that in conilquence thereof, any Number of Tickets, in the said Lottery, shall remain unsubscribed for; any Person or Persons shall be at liberty to contribute for the Purchase of such remaining Tickets, at the Rate of Fourteen Pounds for each Ticket, in the Manner herein after mentioned; that is to say, every such Contributor or Contributors to make a Deposit of Four Pounds, for and in respect of fugh Ticket, on or before the Tenth Vo L,3 a.

Day of May next, as a Security for making good his or

their future Payments; the further Sum of One Pound on or before the Fifteenth Day of June next; the further Sum of Two Pounds on or before the Twentieth Day of July next; the further Sum of Three Pounds, on or before the Twenty-first Day of August next; and the further Sum of Four Pounds on or before the Twenty-fifth Day of September next; Tickets to be delivered as soon as the same can be prepared, to such Contributor or Contributors, upon his or their completing their Payments; and that every Contributor, who shall pay in the Whole of the Money to be paid on each Ticket on or before the Seventeenth Day of August next, shall be allowed an Interest, by way of Discount, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, on the Sums so completing his Payments respectively, to be computed from the Day of completing the same to the Twenty-fifth Day of September next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the Monies that shall be received by the Cashiers of the Bank, for or on account of the Whole of the said Fifty thousand Tickets, shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, to be applied, from time to time, to such Services as shall their have been voted by this House, and not otherwise; and that the Sum of Five hundred thousand Pounds, herein before directed to be distributed into Prizes, for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery, shall be charged upon the Aids and Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners were further heard.

And the Deputy Clerk of the Crown attending, according to Order, with the several Returris of Knights of the Shire to serve in Parliament for the County of Pembroke; the last Return, together with the Writ thereunto annexed, were read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having proposed to produce Evidence, to shew, that, from the Year 1625, to 1696, no Elections for the County of Pembroke had ever been held at the Town of Pembroke; and that, from the Year 1696 to 1727, but Two Elections had been held at the said Town; and that, from the Year 1727 to this Time, all the Elections had been held at Haver-ford Weji, except One in the Year 1741, which was held at the Town of Pembroke;

The same was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

Then a Witness was examined, to prove that the Part of the Guild Hall at Hav in which the Elections for the County of Pembroke, have been usually held, is in the County of and not in the County of Haverford West.

Then a Witness was examined, to shew the Partiality of the Sheriff in favour of the Sitting Member, in appointing the Election to be held at the Town of Pembroke } and that that Town was in all respects very inconvenient for the Attendance of the Freeholders of most of the Hundreds in the said County.

And several Witnesses were examined, to prove what has been the Practice, with respect to the Times of holding the County Courts for the County of Pembroke.

Then a Witness was examined, to prove that the Sheriff did. Two or Three Days before he appointed the Election at the Town of Pembroke, publicly declare, that it should be held at Haverford West; and that the Notice of the Election was given but Seven Days before the Day of Election; and Evidence was produced, to shew that Mr. Symons, the other Candidate, did, some days before the Day of Election, protest against the Proceedings of the Sheriff, as being ille-

gil, in not having given proper Notice of the Time of lection, nor appointed the same to be held at the moll public and usual Place of Election within the said County, and where the same had been most usually held.

And another Witness was examined, to prove, that, at the Election, a Person did, in the Name of several of the Freeholders, object to the Sheriff’s proceeding to the Election, as the Time and Place were totally illegal.

And the said Witness was further examined, to prove the several Inconveniences to the Freeholders of the greater Part of the County, in being obliged to attend the Election at the said Town of Pembroke.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member were heard j and examined a W’itnels, to shew the usual Practice which had been held in the Manner of appointing a County Court where the former County Court had been dropt; and to prove, that the Sheriff had appointed the County Court to be held at the Town of Pembroke, before he received the Writ for the said Election; and that he appointed the Election to be held at the Town of Pembroke, as being the County Town, and not liable to the same Objections which had been made against the Sheriff on a former Occasion, for holding the Eiedtion within the Town and County of Haverford West \ and Vot. 32,

also to prove, that, in the Year 1741, a contested Election, which lasted several Days, was held at the said Town of Pembroke.

And the said Witness was further examined, to prove that the Town of Pembroke is very convenient, both in its Situation and its Accommodations, for the Holding of a County Election; and that the greater Part of the Freeholders, who are Friends to the Sitting Member, live at a greater Distance from the said Town than those in the opposite Interest.

And One of the Counsel for the Petitioners having been heard, by way of Reply;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That Hugh Owen, Esquire, is duly elected and returned a Knight of the Shire, to serve in this present Parliament, for the County of Pembroke;

Mr. Owen withdrew.

The House divided.

Scotland; A Petition of the General Assembly of the Church of Exemption* Scotland, was pretented to the House, and read; Setting cl*'med by forth, That, by several Acts of the Parliament of Scot-a®‘ land, relating to the Clergy there, the Ministers of the Church of Scotland have always enjoyed an Immunity from Taxes, not only with respect to their Stipends, commonly lo called, but also their Glebes and Manses, these having been considered as Part of their Livings; and that, as the Law. of Scotland, as explained by constant Practice, has relieved the Ministers of this Church from all Taxations upon their Stipends, in which their Glebes and Manses have been understood to be comprehended, they have been induced to consider this Exemption as Part of the Rights and Privileges of the Church of Scotland, secured by the Treaty of Union; the Church of Scotland believing themselves to be lb-cure from what they understood to be the Law of Scotland, con tuned in the Claim of Right ratified by the Articles of Union, and established by long Usage, loft the Opportunity of stating the particular Circumstances of their Cafe, when the Bill proposing a Tax on Houses and Windows was first moved in Parliament; and even after it passed into a Law, they relied on the usual Construction of the Act for levying the Land Tax, which though conceived in general Words, was never extended to their Stipends, Glebes, or Manses; but, as the Ministers of the Church of Scotland find that they are subject to Prosecutions, from time ..to time, for Payment of this Tax, and cannot be. relieved without the Aid of Parliament; Therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for relieving the Ministers of the Church of Scotland, from Payment of the Tax upon Windows, in respect of their Manses or Par-fonage Houses; or that the House will give such other „Relief to the Petitioners as shall appear just.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and others, Dealers in, and Printers or Exporters of, British and Linens, :was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Printed Linen Trade is highly advantageous to these Kingdoms, and has been so far improved as not only fully to supply Home Consumption, but also to become a considerable Article of Exportation, particularly to the Colonies; and British and Irifk Linens answering just as well as Foreign, for the Printing Trade; that Branch, so long as the former had the Benefit of a Bounty, was carried on indifferently with either; but, since the Revocation of that Bounty by the Act of the 29th of the late King, the Linens of the Manufacture of these Kingdoms are almost totally excluded from being used in the'Printing Trade, that Business being ever since almost entirely carried on with foreign Linens, which, by having a Drawback of Duties when sent Abroad, come cheaper to Market than the British and Irish, since deprived of the Bounty, can; and that the Petitioners observe, from the Votes, a Bill is depending for renewing and continuing the Bounty on certain Species of British and Irish Linens exported, for a further Term

of Years; and for extending the same to British Striped and Chequered Linens exported; and therefore praying, That the same may be extended to all Printed, Painted, or Stained Linens, of the Manufacture of Great Britain and Ireland, by taking off the Exception in the Act of 29th of George the Second, which excluded; them, and restoring them again to the Benefit they enjoyed under the Two former Bounty Acts. v '

A Petition of the several Manufacturers of Cottofis for Printing, in and near the Town of Blackburn, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, thaCa Bill is depending in the House, for further continuing the Bounties payable upon the Exportation of British and Irish Linens, granted by an Act passed in the 29th of his late Majesty; and that a Bounty is' also" to Be granted upon Printed Linens of the Manufacture of Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Petitioners and others are largely concerned in a Species of Manufacture, called Brown Cottons, which, when bleached and printed, are applicable to the same Uses as Printed Linens, and merit at least equal Encouragement, being chiefly manufactured with Irish Linen Yarn, and Yarn ipun from Cotton-Wool, of the Growth of the British Plantations; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if a Bounty is granted to Printed Linens, and not to Printed Cottons, it will greatly *m-jur® their Trade, and many Thou land Poor Families employed , therein: And therefore . praying, That if a Bounty is granted on Printed Linens exported, the like Bounty may be. extended to Printed Cottons of Bntfli Manufacture, or that they may be heard, by them (elves or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as relates to the Bounty upon Printed Linens; and that the- Petitioners may have such Relief as to the House shall feera meet.

And. the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to continue an Act, made in the 29th Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for granting a Bounty upon certain Species of British and irish Linens exported, and taking pff the Duties on the Importation of foreign raw Linen Yarns made of Flax, and for granting a Bounty on the Exportation of British Chequed and Striped Linens, is committed.

Easter Term 1752. Dalby filed his Bill in the Court of Exchequer, against the Commissioners, Rujfel Revell, and the Attorney General, for an Account and Satisfaction respecting the Ship Britannia, which was amended in Hilary Term 1753; where to the Commissioners put in three different Antwers; but the Suit being abated by the Death of Revell, nothing further was done.

8 February 1757. Memorial to the Admi-

ralty, containing a State of Facts relative to the Britannia; whereupon an Assurance was given him, that the Commissioners of Victualling should answer the Facts, and Dalby should reply thereto, and Justice be immediately done.

20th May 1757. The Commissioners Report to their Lordships upon the last mentioned Memorial, wherein they argue against the Propriety of submitting the Matters between Dalby and the Commissioners to the Arbitration of Merchants; and proposed, with their Lordship’s Approbation, to have the Affair left to His Majesty’s Attorney General, and such Counsel as Mr. Dalby might chufc, upon his Part, to determine upon a same to be agreed to by both Sides, whether any, and which of his Claims on account of the said Ship, ought to be allow'ed by the Crown; for that it appeared to them premature to enter into any Consideration of the Quantum of his Damages, till it appeared by proper Judges, whether the Crown was liable to any of the Points of Damages claimed.

15 June 1757. Mr. Dalby agreed to such Reference, and on the 22 June delivered to Mr. Baxter, the Commissioners Solicitor, as a State of his Cafe, a Copy of his Memorial to the Admiralty of the 8th February; and acquainted him at the same Time, if he had any Doubts concerning the Facts, he would meet him with a Gentleman of Character any Day to prove them; and desired he would have a Gentleman of like Character present, that some End might be put to the Affair.

Read out of the Commissioners Answers to his Bill, in the Exchequer, in 1752, as follows;

That they had heard, and believe if to be true, that before Complainant was able to release his Ship from Mahon, after the Seizure thereof by Green and Hall in September 1744, and put her again into Action, William Henry the Matter died, and that the Ship or Vessel was afterwards condemned at Mahon for Money due, or pretended to be due, for Wages to the Sailors serving on board; and that the said Ship was purchased for a valuable Consideration under the said Condemnation, or otherwise, by James Francis, who was then Clerk or Agent to the said RuJJel Revell, which said Francis was the best Bidder for the fame, as Defendants have heard and believe; and Defendants have also heard, and believe, that the Money arising from such Purchase was paid to, and divided amongst the Sailors, who had served on board the Ship, or some of them, by the proper Officer appointed to fell the Ship under the Condemnation, or some dther Person.

.28 April 1755, a Protest made by William Moran, the Master of the Ship, before James Gill, a Public Notary, and sworn to by the said William Moran, and by Robert Elwood, Chief Mate, Lawrence Second

Mate, Robert Mulligan, Carpenter, Michael Chrifiiax Cock, and Thomas Silvia, Seamen of and belonging to the said Ship; Hercules Rice, and Thomas Williams, Passengers on board her the same Day; wherein he declares as follows:

That the said Snow being of the Burthen of 180 Tons or thereabouts, properly equipt, and loaded With Sugar, Rum, Wine, and sundry other Merchandize, failed from St. Kitt’s, bound for London on the 14th March, then last part.

That on the 22d Day of April aforesaid, about 8 in the Morning, the Wind being at Sou Hr by West, and in the fair Way proceeding on his Voyage up Channel, and being near a-breast of the Start, Distance or 5 Leagues; One of His Majesty’s Tenders brought the Vessel to, and impressed Three of their belt Seamen, and in lieu of them, the Commander of the Tender put on board the Snow Three very indifferent Men;

— One a Taylor, who had never been on board a Ship above Three Weeks — another a Bricklayer, who had never acted as a Sailor for more than Three Months — and the Third a Husbandman, who had never been on board a Ship as a Sailor more than a Fortnight before that Time, and, as they severally declared to the said Mailer and others above named, wholly unacquainted with the Navigation of a Ship or Vessel.

That he attempted afterwards to proceed on his Voyage, and next Day, being 23d, about 7 in the Evening, being between Pepperell Point, and the Needles, at least Leagues from the Land, with the Wind at South South Kaft; another Tender belonging to His Majesty’s Ship Royal George, and whereof Richard Williams, 6 th Lieutenant of the said Ship, was the Commander, fired a Shot over the said Snow, which dropped within 30 Vol. 32.

or 46.Yards on the Starboard Side, in order to bring the said Vessel to.

That the said Moran being apprehensive of the Indraft of the Island, and the Distress the Snow was then in, consulted with his Officers and Crew what wa§ best to be done' under their unhappy Circumstances, having a just Dread of losing their Ship and Cargoand it was thereupon determined to make fail, to avoid- being brought to; bu,t that Attempt soon appearing fruit-lcis, he, with the Approbation of his Mate and Crew, brought to.

That the said Lieutenant Williams, notwithstanding the distressed Condition of the said Snow as aforesaid. Carried away another, the best Seaman left on, board, and in his Head left one Nicolas Mahon; alluring the said Master, that the said Mahon was a Seaman and a Helmfman; which said Nicolas had the Helm at the Time of the Accident herein after mentioned.

' Yhat after the Snow was detained in Manner aforesaid till near 12 o’Clock, in which Time she unavoidably made a great Leeway, the said Lieutenant left her.

That the said Master being greatly fatigued under the whole of this Transaction, having first given Directicns to his Second Mate, Lawrence Farrell, to fleer a direct East South East Course, laid himself down to get; a little Rest; and, in Two Hours Time, the said Vessel was on Shore, the said Mahon being at the Helm, and struck near Athei-field Rocks, and notwithstanding he, the Master, got out an Anchor, and uled.all other possible Means to get her off, she parted her Cable, a,nd soon went on Shore; and, a prodigious large and folding Ground Sea going at that lnstant, soon broke to Pieces, and was totally loft, together with the greatest Part of the Cargo.

That by Means of the Confusion he: way put into, the Distress the Ship was left in, and other the Premises particularly described; the said Ship, and Part of her Cargo, was totally loft, and not by Means of any Neglect or Default of him, or any of his Ship’s Company.

9th March 1743-4, O. S. Admiral Matthews issued a Warrant, directed to Captain Henry, in the Words following; viz-

You are hereby impowered, authorized, and directed, forthwith to deliver, for the Use of His Majesty, to Mr. Rujfel Revell, Agent for Victualling his Majesty’s Ships in this Port, the Cargo of Wheat

you now have on board the Ship Britannia, under your Command; first taking the Steps you shall think necessary and customary in like Cafes: And you are to keep an Account of the Delivery of the said Cargo, as well for your own Discharge, as for the Security an d Satisfaction of your Freighters, and the Proprietors of the said Wheat; for which the Proprietors shall be paid, by the said Russel Revell, on behalf of His Majesty, at the Rate the said Wheat would have been sold at the Market it was consigned to, at tire Time it may reasonably be computed that the said Ship would have arrived there, had not the said Cargo been stopt here for his Majesty’s Service: You are likewise, jointly with the said Mr. Revell, to chuse one of the Bags of the said Wheat, which is to be sealed by him and you, in order to be lent to the Person the Cargo is consigned to, as a Sample Whereon the Price is to be determined, and authentically certified: For all which, this shall be to you a sufficient Warrant. Dated on board the in Mahon

Harbour, 9th March 1743.

14th March 1743-4, O. S. Admiral Matthevis sent another Warrant, directed to Mr. Revell, Agent for the Victualling at Mahon, in the Words following,

viz.

By Thomas Matthezvs, Esquire, Rear-Admiral He.

Whereas, by my Warrant of 9th Instant, I have ordered :Mr. William Henry, Commander of the Ship called Britannia, to deliver to you, for the Use of his Majesty,

the Cargo of English Wheat he has now on board his said Ship: You are hereby directed to receive the same 16

from Time to Time, keeping an exact Account of the Number of Bags delivered you, as well of the Number of Quarters, as of the Mahon Measure they shall produce; and you are to cause the said Wheat to be ground into Flour, and made into ltulk, with all Expedition possible, for the Use of His Majesty’s Fleet under my Command, to prevent our being distressed in case the Supply of Provisions, ordered from England, should be delayed by the Uncertainty of the Season, or otherwise.

You are hereby directed, jointly with the said Master, to chuse a Bag of the said Wheat, which is to be sealed by him and you, and sent to John Birtles, Esquire, his Majesty’s Consul at Genoa, to whom the said Cargo is consigned; that the said sealed Bag may serve as a Sample, in order to determine the Price the said Wheat bore at Genoa, at the Time the said Ship might be reasonably supposed to have arrived there, had (he not been detained here on the Government’s Account. So soon as you have received all the Cargo of Wheat, and compared and agreed your Account thereof with the said Master, specifying'whatever Quantity shall be found damaged, you are to correspond with the said Consul Births, thereby advising him of my Orders, and the Steps you take in this Affair: And that the Crown may not be put tt» an additional Expence by any Demand the Proprietors of the said Wheat might make, in case it was not immediately paid for; as also to prevent the Risk that attends remitting the Amount thereof in Specie; you are, by the First Opportunity that offers after you have received the said Cargo, to remit the Amount thereof, as near as you can calculate, to the said Consul Birtles, for the Use of the Proprietors, in your Bills of Exchange on the Commissioners for Victualling His Majesty’s Navy; advising them of my Orders to you for this and your other Transactions herein.

You are at the same Time to desire the said Consul Birtles, to fend you, as soon as possible, authentic Certificates of the Prices that Wheat of the same Quality of the Sample sent him, sealed up, would have fold for at Genoa, for ready Money, at the Time the said Ship could reasonably be judged to have arrived there as aforesaid; and upon Receipt of such Certificates, and his Account of the Cargo, you are to determine the Cod thereof, and charge the lame, in your public Accounts, for the Victualling Service: For all which, this shall be to you a sufficient Warrant. Dated on board the Nam are, in Mahon Harbour, the 14th March 1743-4.

13th Sep? 1)44, Mr. R writes to the Board as follows, viz. First, To acquaint your Honours, that had not the Britannia's Cargo of Wheat been taken for the Use of the Government here, it must have been landed at this Port, the Ship having sprung a Leak, which could not be flopped but by careening: and the Mailer had got his Ship close alhore in a CoVe to that End, before he was ordered to deliver his Cargo to me j therefore the Wheat’s being taken here proved a great Advantage to the concerned both in Ship and Cargo, by saving a considerable Expence in landing and reship-ping the Cargo, Warehouse-Room, Guard, hie. The Warrant given by Admiral Matthews to the Mailer of the Britannia, to deliver his Cargo to me, was dated 9th March 1743-4, his Order to me the 14th of the same Month, and my Receipt to the Mailer for the Wheat the 4th April following. If he had been obliged to unload his Ship wrth his own People only, he could not have done it in that Time j therefore there cannot be any Claim for Demurrage occasioned by this Office.

I repeatedly told the Mailer of the Britannia, if he wanted any Money here for the Ship’s Ule, I would supply him, in order to his going to the Port he was destined to, and that he need not apply himself to any Body else; but he did not think proper to accept the Offer I made him, and thereby loft a great deal of Time unnecessarily, lying long idle here after he could have proceeded under Convoy of One of His Majesty’s Ships, for which this Office can never be deemed accountable. — The Surprise Mr. Birtlesexpressed in his Letter of t tth

of June lad, at Mr. Dolby's Demands, an'd his Reasoning on them, is very just; for I do not fee, that any one Part of his Pretensions in his Memorial to the Lords of the Admiralty is grounded on Reason; but am sure that all his Claims are directly contrary to what has been frequently practised in parallel Cafes: — Had the Ship and Cargo, after the Ship had been made fit here for Sea, proceeded to Genoa, and the Cargo fold there, the Freight and Primage was undoubtedly payable by the Seller out of the Produce of the Cargo, and not by the Purchasers: Now this Office is the Purchaser, having paid for the whole Cargo at the Market Price; and therefore is no ways bound to pay Freight or Primage. — There have been many Instances here of the like Nature, when Men of War have, in Time of Scarcity, stopt Ships loaden with Wheat at Sea, and brought them into this Port, and the Merchants concerned have been well pleased and satisfied, by being paid in the same Manner the Britannic?s Cargo was paid for; as indeed they well might, since they thereby laved very heavy Expences that would have attended the Sales of the Cargoes in Italy, especially if put into Warehouses, as is generally the Cafe.

Thirdly, With respect to the consequential Damages alledged to have been sustained by the Snip’s not going to Gen a for Oil and Homeward-bound Freight, and to the Manner in which the Cargo of Salt, brought from Cagliari, and the Ship, were condemned and fold.

5th Off 1744. By a Minute of the Victualling Board, it appears, that Dalby applied to them, and desired, as he had no Occasion for the Money at Genoa, that they would advance him such Part of the Freight as they might think proper, till such Time as they might hear from their Agent at Mahon, to enable them to make a Report to their Lordships touching his other Demands; the Board told him, they could not be certain of his not having ordered Birtles to pay the Freight, according to the Directions given him from the Board some Time before; but he said he was ready to give Security to indemnify the Crown against such an Accident; where* upon the Board ordered an Imprell Bill of £.450 to be made, out to him on account of the Freight of the said Ship, upon giving Security to indemnify the Crown against his having received it from Mr. Birtles, on account of the Crown or the Owners, and against his receiving it, or giving any Orders for receiving it for the future, and upon his giving an Authority to Mr. Birtles to dispose of the Money that he had received, or might recover of the Proprietors of the Corn for Freight and Port Charges, according to such Directions as he Humid receive from the Board.

22 OCT 1744. The Board having received Mr.

Revell's Letter of the 1 jth of September 1744, v above Rated; arid being of Opinion, from the Accounts given of the Affair by Mr. Revell, that Dalby had not any Claim upon that Office, either for Freight or Damages; the intended Imprest for £. 450 was therefore not made out.

5th Novr 1744. The Board reported to the Admiralty, That it aid not seem to them, that Mr. Dalby had any Claim upon that Office for the Freight, the same having been paid by the Crown in the Price for the Corn, and was retained for Mr. s Use, in the Hands of Mr. Birtles j and, as to the consequential Damages, that as the Ship was not detained any longer at Mahon, by means of her Cargo having been purchased there for the Use of the Fleet, than she mult otherwise have been in repairing the Damage she had got before ihe put in there, and their Agent repeatedly offered the Matter what Money might be wanted for fitting the Ship to proceed to Genoa, to which Place he ought to have gone by virtue of the Orders he had received from Mr. Dalby before he left England, and where the Freight, by the Measures that had been taken, would have been ready to have been applied to such Purposes as Mr. Dalby might be supposed to have lodged Orders about, against the Ship’s Arrival there; and therefore conceived that although Mr. Dalby might have suffered from his Mailer’s Imprudence in losing his Time at Mahon, and not proceeding according' to his Orders to Genoa; yet the Crown ought not to be accountable for the Time the Ship lay unnecessarily at Mahon, through the Mailer’s Negligence, or for any Damage that might have accrued to Mr. Dalby in consequence thereof.

30th Jan*9 1744-5. The Admiralty directed the Victualling Board to take the Attorney General’s Opinion upon the Cafe.

1 ith Feb* 1744-5. Sir Dudley-Ryder, then Attorney General, gave his Opinion, that the Damages which were naturally consequential to the taking out the Corn at Port Mahon, ought to be made good to the Owner* and thought an Action would lie against the Admiral for them; but thought the unnecessary Demurrage of the Captain at Port Mahon, or his going afterwards to Cagliari, and purchasing Salt, were not such Damages as either the Admiral or the Agent Victualler was liable to make good.

15th March 1744-5. By the Order of the Admiralty it appears, That their Lordships did order the Board to act in the Matter according to the Opinion, and to pay the Damage therein proposed, and no other, provided Dalby gave a general Release, and would receive the same in hill Satisfaction of all Demands and it appears by the Board’s Minute, that in consequence thereof, the Board desired Mr. Dalby to give them an Account of what he infilled upon as consequential Damages.

the Attorney General, he gave his Opinion, That under the Circumstances of the Cafe, neither the Homeward bound Freight, nor any other of the subsequent Demands, were such consequential Damages as ought to be allowed, though this was a Matter wholly in the Breast of a Jury.

nth April 1745. The Account and Opinion having

been communicated to the Admiralty, their Lordships ordered the Board to act with Mr. Dalby, exactly con-, formable to the Opinion.

15th OET 1745. Mr. Birtl, by a Letter wrote by him from Leghorn, acquainted the Board in Answer, That Mr. Dalby's Allegations were far from being grounded

on that Justice and Equity, that is needful for a Man tender of his Character, and desirous to establish a Mercantile Credit — For that when he let out the said Ship Britannia, he soon after wrote to him, the said Mr. Birtles, and acquainted him with her Burthen, csfr. and desired him, if he could, to procure the Ship a Freight back to England, and, in Defect of succeeding, to fend her to load a Cargo of Salt; to which he answeied him. That if he would order the Master to put 16 Guns into her, and ship 50 or 60 Men, (he might go, and take a Foundation of Gallipoly Oil on his Account, and he yvould procure the Remainder of the Cargo of Paper and Fine Goods for London: To this Proposal, Mr. Dalby answered. That he could not consent to put any more Guns into the said Ship, or suffer the Master to increase the Complement of her Crew; but that if he thought proper he might invest about £. 1,000 Sterling in Oils on his Account, and fend the Bills of Lading to his, the said Mr. Birtles' Friend in London, till he had paid his, Mr. Birtles' Bills; but this Order was confined, and not to be executed unless he could fill the Ship up at Genoa; upon which he immediately answered, That

as he would not consent that the Ship should carry 16 Gups, and 50 or 60 Men at lead, it would be impossible to procure her an Ounce of Goods for , and therefore, upon her Arrival at Genoa, he would get her dispatched as soon as possible, and fend her to load a Cargo of Salt: In which Manner the Correspondency created about the Ship’s going back to London; so that there was no Fund lodged for the Oils, nor any Hopes of the Ship’s returning to London if (lie had carried the Corn to Genoa; and that consequently Mr. Dalby was no Sufferer by the Ship’s Freight to Gallipoly, nor on the Oils which he (ays were to be imported, as the Scheme was. intirely laid aside before the Advice came of the Ship’s being arrived at Mahon: That as to the Master’s not being able to proceed to Genoa after the Com was taken, without being liable to be arrested, he was of Opinion, that if the Admiral was comprised within the Meaning of the Clause in the Charter Party j viz. Easter Term 1746. Dalby brought an Action against Admiral Matthews and Mr. Revell.

26th November 1746. Dalby petitioned the Board of Admiralty, that some Persons might attend the Trial with Mr. Revell's Letter of the 8th March 1743, before dated, the Order of the Board of Admiralty of the 15th March 1744-5, before dated, and Admiral Matthew'% Letter to them of the 24th January 1744, desiring to be indemnified on Account of the said Ship; and their Lordships having desired the Board’s Opinion thereon, they thought it advisable to consult Counsel thereupon; which Letter of Admiral Matthews was as follows — To Thomas Corbett, Esquire. Sir, — Soho Square,

24th January 1744. — The Bearer is the Attorney of Mr. Francis Dalby, who has been sent to me concerning' the Britannia, a Merchant Ship, which I (lopped at Mahon, with her Lading of Wheat, for the Service of the Fleet under my Command. I wrote to you upon this Subject the 8th December lad, and lent you the Papers relating to this Matter; but as no Answer has been given, I am now to desire, that their Lordships will be pleased to give such Directions as shall be necessary to indemnify me for the Steps I took for the Good of the Service.

31st Deer 1746. The Board transmitted to their Lordships a Copy of Counsellor Legg’s Opinion, with regard to the producing the said Letters, as follows; viz. I apprehend that neither the Lords of the Admiralty, nor the Commissioners of the Victualling, ought to produce, or deliver, to Mr. Dalby rhefe Letters; and that it would be very wrong in them so to do It is a most unprecedented and unreasonable Request. And it is to be supposed, that Mr. Dalby knew his own same before he brought his Action, and could not expect that the Defendants should make it out for him.

January 17th 1743. The Commissioners caused Sailing Orders to be delivered to the Captain, directing him to proceed to the Downs, to apply to the Naval Officer at Deal, to know who was to convoy the Ships to Spithead, and not to proceed thence without Convoy, and, on his Arrival there, to acquaint the Commissioners Agent at Portsmouth thereof, and then to apply to the Commander in Chief of the Convoy bound for the Straits, and proceed under his Convoy to Gibraltar, and deliver the Provisions to their Agent there;

or, if the Commander in Chief of the Fleet there, or the Commissioners Agent should so order, to proceed to Mahon, and deliver the Loading as Mr. Revell, Agent Victualler there, should direct, agreeable to Charter Party.

1743-4, Jan. 25th. The Francis arrived at Spit-head, where she continued till the 18th April following.

1744, April 18. The Francis, together with the several other Victualling Ships above named (except the Genoa Galley, Oxford, and Caroline Galley, which arefeid to be loft in the Downs) and also a large Fleet of other Store Ships and Merchants Ships, failed from Spithead for Gibraltar or Port Mahon, under Convoy of Sir Charles Hardy, with 13 Men of War: And Captain Murray, who was appointed their Commodore the

21 ft of April, ordered the Ships into Torbay, where they continued till the 23d, when they failed from thehce on their Voyage for Gibraltar or Mahon: But as the Public Affairs and Circumstances at that Time would not admit of the Fleet under which they failed, to convoy them so far as Gibraltar, the Francis and other Victuallers, were ordered to be convoyed to where they

arrived the 3d May, and were left there by Sir Charles Hardy's Fleet till Admiral Osborne came from the Mediterranean, to convoy them to Gibraltar, and Mahon: And on the 24th July they failed under Convoy of Admiral Osborne, with Six Men of War, over the Bar of Lisbon -, but Intelligence having been received of a Squadron of at least Nine French Men of War being on the Coast of Portugal, the Admiral, after having called a Council of War, wherein it was the unanimous Opinion of the Captains of all the Men of War, that it was not safe to proceed, ordered the Fleet back into Lisbon Harbour, where they continued till the 30th of August following.

1744, August 30. The Fleet of Victuallers and Stone Ships, except the Robert and Anne, which had been discharged at Lisbon, failed from Lisbon to Gibraltar, under Convoy of Captain Osborne, who was joined at Sea by Admiral llalchen, with about 20 Men of War, who kept them cruizing off Cape Saint Vincent about ia Days, so that they did not arrive at Gibraltar till the 14th September.

1744, 05V 18. The Francis, the Speedwell, the Sally, and the James Frigate, were ordered out from Gibraltar, to go to the Fleet then at Sea, and deliver Part of their Cargoes there, which they accordingly did,- and returned to Gibraltar on the 23d of same Month.

Whilst the Fleet of Victuallers and Store Ships lay at Gibraltar, Three of them, viz. the Endeavour, the Frederick, and the Constant Sally, were unloaded and discharged from the Service of the Crown.

October 23d. The Francis, and the other Victualler* and Store Ships, were ordered by Admiral Osborne, then Commander in Chief, to fail under Convoy of Admiral Rowley for Port Mahon.

Novr 13th. The Francis and other Victuallers arrived at Mahon, where the Francis delivered the Remainder of her Cargo — -21 ft November, Mr. Revell, the Agent Victualler, delivered the Captain of the , a Certificate of his having delivered the Provisions; and the Ship was thereby discharged from the Service of the Crown, which was before any other of the Ships had delivered their Cargoes, or were discharged.

1744-5 Jatly 30th. Mr. Dalby having produced the Certificate of the Delivery of the Provisions, and the Matter’s Protest, the Commissioners made him out a Bill for £.364. i8j. 7 d.being the Amount of the Freight to Mahon, which Mr. Dalby afterwards received.

March 18. The Commissioners also made out a Bill to Mr. Dalby, for £.272. 16r. for the Ships Demurrage at Spithead, from the 3d of February to the 17th April, which Mr. Dalby has also received.

The whole Amount of the Damages added together, do come to the Rate of 12 s. per Ton per Month, which is the Rate of Demurrage agreed upon in the Charter Party; but all the Sums separately taken do not corref-jtond with that Rule, with respect to the Number of Days of each Detainer.

1746, July. The above Action was tried at Guildhall, and Judgment signed 30th May 1747, and the Damage paid.

1747, July 13th. 1747, July. The Lords of the Admiralty directed the Commissioners, to pay the said Victuallers, according to the same Rate, as had been recovered by Mr. Black.

5th December 1750. Mr. Weeks died, having made his Will, and Edward Downes Executor, who, having

proved such Will, filed his Bill of Revivor against the several Defendants, and the Cause being revived, Harley put in his Answer, and declared, he was ready and willing to permit his Name to be made use of in any Action at Law, or other Proceedings to be had on the Charter Party, as the Court should direct, being indemnified.

And the Attorney General, by his Answer, said, he was a Stranger to these Matters, but hoped the Court would take Care the Commissioners, or the Crown, were not charged with the Plaintiff's Demands, other than such as should clearly appear to be reasonable and just.

December 1752. Mr. Downes having replied to the Answers, and Issue being joined, divers Witnesses were examined on both Sides, and the Cause came on to be heard on several Days: And, on the 21st February 1753, the Court ordered and decreed, that the Bill should be, and was retained for a Year, with Liberty, in the mean Time, for the Plaintiff to bring his Action as he should think proper, and the surviving Commissioners to admit the Execution of the Charter Party, mentioned in the Pleadings, in the Cause, as their Act and Deed, and all further Directions were thereby reserved; for which Purpose, all Parties were at Liberty to resort back to the Court from time to time, as there should be Occasion.

27th November 1753. The Plaintiff appealed, from the Decree of the Court of Exchequer, to the House of Lords, praying their Lordships to reverse the Decree, or grant him such Relief as they should fee meet.

1754, January 28 and 20th. On the 28 and 29th of January the Appeal was heard, when their Lordships were pleased to order, that in the Decree, after the Words " be retained for," the Words "a Year" be left out, and the Words "Two Years" be inserted instead thereof; and that after the Words "for the Plaintiff to " bring," the Words "his Action" be left out, and the Words " an Action in the Name of the said Henry " Harley," inserted instead thereof; and that after the

Words " as their Act and Deed," these Words be added, " And in case the Deposition of the said Henry Harley " Avail be offered to be read at the Trial of the said " Action, the Respondents Avail not make any Objection thereto by reason of his being named Plaintiff in " such Action, and laving to the said Respondents all " other Objections, either to the Competency or Credit " of the said Henry Harley; and upon the Consent of " the Respondents Counsel at the Bar, it is further " ordered, that notwithstanding the Death of the said " Henry Harley, the Appellant be at Liberty to proceed " in his Name, as if living, and no Advantage to be 18

" taken on the said Trial, or by Writ of Error, on " account of his Death: And it is further ordered " and adjudged, that with these Variations and Additions, the feme Decree be, and the same is hereby " affirmed."

Easter Term 1754. On the Twenty-seventh Day of 1745, at the

Request of Mr. RichdHarris, of London, Merchant, I John da Cofia Notary and Tabellion Public, dwelling in London, by Royal Authority, duly admitted and sworn, went with the original Bill of Exchange, whereof the Copy is above, to the late Dwelling House of Mr. Francis Dalby, to whom the same is directed, there to demand Payment thereof; where having exhibited the same to a Gentleman, and demanded of him, if the said Mr. Dalby was there, or had left any Orders for Payment of the said Bill ? he answered. That Mr. Dalby was just gone from thence, and had left no Orders: Upon which Answer, I the said Notary, at the Request aforesaid, did, and do solemnly protest against the Drawer of the said Bill, and all others concerned for Change, Rechange, and all Costs, Damages, and Interests suffered, and to be suffered, for want of Payment of the said Bill; thus done

The Proceedings in Regard to the Ship Britannia, whereof William Henry, of the British Nation, is Commander; in the Vice Admiralty Court of Minorca.

On the 3d Day of November 1745, Personally appeared before your Worship in the present Tribunal of the Vice Admiralty of Minorca, Mr. Michael Harris, who declared, That Captain William Henry, of the British Nation, Commander of the Ship Britannia, stands indebted unto him in the Sum of Forty-three Pounds Two Shillings and Nine Penee, Sterling, as appears by the Bill and Account he presented; which had been protested, by reason whereof he applies to your Worship* and prays that an Embargo may be laid on the said Ship, the same having been supplied for the said Ship’s Ac--count, and been p’rotefted by the Proprietor of the said Ship; the which he hopes your Worship in the Up-rightness of your Justice will grant, &c.

On the same Day appeared Mr. Joseph Miller, a Merchant, who declares to your Worship, That Captain William Henry is indebted unto him in Two hundred and Fifty Pesos, as appears by the Policy which he presented ut Inferatur, for which Credit he hypothecated his laid Ship Britannia; > and therefore prays she may be Embargoed and Sequestered for the securing his said Credit i the which he hopes your Worship in the Up-rightness of your Justice will grant, &c.

On the same Day appeared Benjamin Cransion, who declares, That Captain William Henry, of the Ship Britannia, is indebted unto him in One hundred Eighteen Pounds Ten Shillings, Sterling, which is due unto him for his Wages, as Carpenter thereof, as appears by the Account he presents ut Inferatur, and for which his Credit is admitted; and there are many others who claim a Credit against the said Ship: And therefore he prayS you will be pleased to order that the said Ship may be Embargoed and Sequestered, that he may be paid his Credit; the which he hopes your Worship in the Up-rightness of your Justice will grant, &c.

On the same Day appeared Benjamin Bryant, who set a Claim against the said Ship, of the said Captain William Henry, to the Amount of Forty-three Pounds Six Shillings, Sterling, which is due unto him for Wages, for the "Time he served on board the said Ship Britannia: And therefore he prays that his Credit may be admitted

To the Most worshipful Judge of the Vice Admiralty.

With all due Respect Benjamin Cranston, Benjamin Bryant, Edward Guffet, and John Jameson, Mariners, on board the Ship called the Britannia, whereof Captain Hrtlliam Henry is Commander, represent to your Worship, That their said Captain (lands indebted unto them in the Sum of Two hundred and Forty Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence, English Money, for their Wages; tire which Sum the said Captain declares he is not capable of paying, by reason that his Merchants do not remit him Money for that Purpose.

That their said Captain, over and besides his not paying your Petitioners their Wages, now declares, That he is not capable of supplying them with Provisions; by Teafon whereof your Petitioners, with the most profound Respect, pray your Worship to take their same into Consideration, and do them Justice, it being impossible that People can live without either Money, or any Kind of Maintenance whatsoever; and as so long a Time hath elapsed since the said Ship was employed, and there is no Appearance or Probability that the Merchants, her Proprietors, will remit Money for the paying of your Petitioners, they therefore pray your Worship would be pleased to order their said Captain immediately to pay and discharge them, or to fell the said Ship at Public Sale for that Purpose: And they pray God may preserve your Worship many Years, &c.

On the 10th Day of December 1745.

Constituted personally the most worshipful Doctor Gabriel Olivar and Pardo, Knight, Judge, Commissary of the Court of Vice Admiralty of Minorca, together with the Bartholomew Deya, Notary, and Deputy Register of the said Court, for the Ship Britannia, Cap' William Henry.

On the 11 th Day of December 1745, appeared in this present Court of Vice Admiralty, Mr. Michael Harris, and the other Persons interested; who represent to your Worship; that, supposing that the Ship Britannia Cap. William Henry, of the Nation, was fe-

questered or inventoried, and the Sale thereof delayed, the same would be a considerable Detriment, not only to the Proprietor, but also to the other Persons interested therein, by Realbn that there are Two Years that the said Ship hath laid in this Port, without being careened; and therefore it is to be supposed, without Difficulty, that file is damaged, and runs a great Rilk of sinking; especially, according to what they can learn, nukes a great deal of Water: They therefore pray your Worship would be pleased to order the Sale of the said Ship to be proceeded upon (your Worlliip previously appointing a Representative for the absent Proprietor or Proprietors, unto whom they may make and serve their Proceedings according to Custom) as w'ell for the lepa-rating the Proprietorship, aS for the other Necclfaries by Law required; it being Justice only they pray for, (Ac.

On the 13th Day of December 1743, appeared in the Kegiftry of the Vice Admiralty of Minorca, Captain William Henry, of the British Nation, Commander of the Ship Britannia; who rcprelents to your Worlliip; that the Ship Britannia is indebted unto him in One hundred and Sixty Pounds Ten Shillings, Sterling, as appears by the Account which he presents, the liuue being for Wages, as Commander thereof , and as the said Ship is in a ruinated Condition, in io much that Ihe makes Abundance of _Water; and, as lie hath not Monies sufficient for her Preservation; he therefore agrees that Ihe may be ibid, for the Benefit of the Persons

interested, and that the Produce thereof be deposited penes Curium of your Worship; which they all pray, (Ac.

His Excellency having heard the aforegoing Repre-fentation, and seen the other Requests made by the other Creditors; the whole of whom request and pray for the Sale of the said Ship Britannia, as well for the Security of their Credits, as for the Interest of the Proprietors of the said Ship themselves, on account of the Danger flic runs; doth therefore order the facie to be sold at Public Sale, and by the Voice of an Auctioneer, for the greatest Price that may offer, the Produce of which shall be de-poiited under the Authority of our Court, until such Time a Sentence of Adjucation and Liquidation shall be made thereof.

And for that Purpose, there shall be the necessary Orders and Dispatches made, according to Custom, and a Notification in Conformity, (Ac.

Olivar and Pardo, Judge of the Vice Admiralty Court of Minorca.

On the 1 ft of February 1746.

Captain Charles Conly, of Mahon, a Witness produced, of the Age of Forty Years, who, upon Oath which he took upon the Bible, tdc. by the Hands of his Worship, promised to declare the Truth, to all such Questions as should be asked him; and being interrogated on the Contents of the aforegoing Petition, which was read unto him, (dc. declared, that what he knows is. That Frederick Shepherd was One of the Mariners of Captain Henry's Ship; but he knows not what Time he served the said Captain; that he hath frequently talked with the said Captain Henry, who told him, that he would pay him with the First Money he got; and this Declarant knows that he afterwards gave the said Frederick Three Bills of Exchange, upon his Ship’s Merchant, in order to pay him; and this is the Truth, upon the Oath he had taken: This was read unto him, and he signed the same with his own Hand.

Charles Conly.

On the same Day.

Hugh Stewart, an Inhabitant of Mahon, a Witness produced, of the Age of Twenty-five Years, who, upon the Oath he took, protnifed to declare the Truth to such Questions as should be asked him; and, being interrogated upon the Contents of the aforegoing Petition, which was read unto him, he declared, That he knows that Frederick Shepherd failed Four Months with Captain Henry, but that he knows not if he was paid by the said Captain or not; nor doth he know if he gave him any Bill whatsoever, for to recover the same from the Merchant of the said Ship; which is the Truth upon the Oath he had taken: Which being read unto him, he signed the same with his own Hands.

Hugh Stewart.

Know all Men by these Presents, that I, Mary Henry, of Boston in New England, Widow of William Henry, late of said Boston, Mariner, deceased, at Port Mahon, have constituted, ordained, and made, and in my (lead and Place put, and by these Presents do constitute, ordain, and make, and in my stead and Place put, Mr. Andrew Pringle, of the City of London, in the Kingdom of Great Britain, Merchant, to be my true, sufficient, and lawful Attorney, for me, and in my Name and stead, and to my Use, to alk, demand, levy, recover, and receive, of, and from all and every or any Person or Persons, whom it doth, shall, or may concern, all Debts, Sum and Sums of Money, due, owing, payable and belonging to the Estate of my laid late Husband, whether for his Wages, Disbursements, or for the Wages of his Servant or Servants, on Board any Ship or Ships, or Vessels whatsoever, or for, or by Reason or Means of any other Matter or Cause whatsoever; and, if need be, for me to take out Letters of Administration on said Estate, and aft fully for me in that Capacity; giving, and hereby granting, unto my said Attorney, my full and whole Strength, Power, and Authority, in and about the Premises, and to take and use all due Means, Course and Process in the Law, for the obtaining and recovering the lame, and of Recoveries and Receipts thereof; in my Name to make, seal, and execute due Acquittances, and Discharges; and for the Premises to appear, and the Person of me, the Constituent, to represent before any Governor, Judges, Justices, Officers, and Ministers of the Law whatsoever, in any Court or Courts of Judicature; and there on my Behalf to answer, defend, and reply, unto all Actions, Causes, Matters, and Things whatsoever, relating to the Premises, with full Power to make and substitute One or more Attornies, under my laid Attorney, and the >4

fame again at Pleasure to revoke, and generally to say, do, aft, transeft, determine, accomplish, and finish, all Matters, and Things whatsoever, relating to the Premises, as fully, amply, and effectually, to all Intents and Purposes, as I the said Constituent myself ought, or might, or could personally, although the Matter should require more (pedal Authority than is herein comprized; I, the said Constituent, ratifying, allowing, and holding firm and valid, all and whatsoever my said Attorney, or his Substitutes, Hull lawfully do, or cause to be done, in and about the Premises, by virtue of these Presents: In Witness whereof, I have hereunto set my Hand and Seal, the Fifth Day of Annoque

Mary Henry, (L. S.)

The Most worlnipful DoCtof Gabriel Olivar and Pardo, Knight, Judge of the Vice Admiralty of norca, having seen the present Cause of the Joint Creditors of the Ship Britannia, whereof William Henry is Commander, who prayed, That the said Ship might be sold at public Sale; and that agreeable thereto Ihe hath been fold and delivered to Mr. Salvador Can/ino, for the Sum of Two thousand Eight hundred Pesos; and that the same might be paid to her respective Creditors; and as it is just and necessary to share and divide the said Money among the Creditors of the said Ship, and among those who are entitled by Law: therefore, his Worship proceeded to the said Partition and Division (previously invoking the Name of God) in Manner followings -viz.

Imprimis, He doth adjudge, in Favour of the present Tribunal, Seventy Pesos of Plate, for the Judge’s Salary, at the Rate of Two and One Half p Cent, according to Custom.

Secondly, He doth adjudge Thirty Pesos for the Register’s Charges; as well for his Instruments, as the Inventory, and Marshal’s Fees.

Thirdly, He doth adjudge to the Mariners of the said Ship their respective Wages; by Reason, that when any Ship is sold at the Request of Creditors, the Mariners of the Ship are first paid what is due unto them for their Wages, and that without their giving or taking Security for the Restitution thereof; because, in such Sum, no one is before in Time, or greater in Right, than the Mariners.

And having seen and inspected the Book of Accounts of Captain William Henry, wherein appears the Days which his respective Mariners entered in the Service of his said Ship, and also what each one earned and had received; it appears, that there is due unto Benjamin Cran-fton Five hundred and Ninety-one Pesos and Four Reals; to Benjamin Bryant, Two hundred and Thirty-one Pesos and Four Reals; to Edward Guffet, Two hundred and Eighty-nine Pesos, Five Reals, and Six Dobleros; to Samuel Wane, Fifty-six Pesos and Four Reals; to James Alexander, One hundred and Eleven Pesos and One Real; to John Hemmitt, Two hundred and Fifteen Pesos,

Five Reals, and Nine Dobleros; to John Jameson, Sc -venty-three Pesos, Seven Reals, and Twelve Dobleros; to John Wane, Two hundred and Seventy-nine Pesos

Way* Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported and Mean*, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same Were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon the Importation into this Kingdom, of Bast or Straw, Chip, Cane, and Horse-bair Hats and Bonnets, and upon certain Materials for making the lame, to ceale, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of all former Rates and Duties, all Bast or Straw, Chip, Cane, and Horle-hair Hats and Bonnets, which, from and after the 24th Day of June 1770, shall be imported into this Kingdom, shall be rated to, and pay, the old Subsidy, granted by the Act of Tonnage and Poundage, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, according to the Rates and Values of 12 s. 6 for every Dozen, each Hat or Bonnet not exceeding 2 Inches in Diameter, and 11. 5 j. for every Dozen of such Hats or. Bonnets as Khali exceed 22 Inches in Diameter each.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of all former Rates and Duties, all

Platting, or other Manufactures, of Bast or Straw,

Chip, Cane, or Horle-hair, to be used in, or proper for making of, Hats or Bonnets, which, from and after the said 24th Day of June 1770, shall be imported into this Kingdom, shall be rated to, and pay, the -laid old Subsidy, according to the Rate and Value of 6 s. and 8 d. for every Pound Weight Avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the full Amount of the several Duties, now payable for every Twenty Shillings of the Value of the said Goods, respectively, be raised and collected, according to the said respective Rates before mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Nine hundred Forty-eight Pounds Three Shillings and Steven Pence, being the final Balance of the Account of Thomas Earl of Kinnoull, formerly Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Forces, subject to the Disposition of Parliament, be applied towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, towards defraying the extraordinary Expences of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and other Services incurred, to the 26th Day of Decent* her 1769, and not provided for by Parliament.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, acknowledging with Gratitude, that Constitutional Communication which His Majesty hath always maintained with His Parliament, in every Matter which concerns the State; to return our unfeigned Thanks for that fresh Proof which His Majesty is pleased to give of that Spirit of His Government by referring to His Parliament, and by recommending to us the State of His Government in America.

To allure His Majesty, that in ready and dutiful Compliance to His Royal Recommendation, we have entered into a serious and attentive Consideration of this Matter referred to us.

With the most profound Respect and Deference, to repelent to His Majesty, that we find, that Misunder-ilandings and Disputes have arisen, in almost every one of His Colonies in America, between the Civil Governors and Military Commanders, since the Appointment of a Commander in Chief.

That we find, that in One of His Majesty’s Provinces, the Representatives of His People in the Great and General Court assembled, have complained, that according to the Arrangement of Commands in America, there is a Military Power within the said Province, without any Check by the Power of the Civil Government of the said Province, and uncontroulable by the supreme executive Power of the Province, which they conceive to be within the Limits of the fame; the just and full Representative of the supreme Exe-

Vol. 32.

cutive Power of the whole Empire, in as full and ample Manner as is the x>rd Lieutenant of Ireland, or any other His Majesty’s Lieutenants in the Dominions to the Realm of Great Britain appertaining.

That we are of Opinion, that this unhappy State of Doubts and Disputes has long called for some clear and explicit Definition and Adjustment of the respective Powers and Authorities, granted to the Governors and Commanders in Chief of His Majesty’s Provinces and Colonies, and to the Military Commanders in Chief of His Majesty’s Forces in North America, and doth require some express Directions and Instructions as to the Exercise of the said Powers.

And therefore most humbly praying His Majesty, That He will, with the Advice of His Privy Council, be graciously plealed to give His Directions for the Examination of the several Powers and Authorities contained in the respective Commissions granted, and in the respective Orders and Instructions iflfued to these several Commanders, to the End that all such Commis- lions, Instructions, and Orders, may be explained, corrected, and amended, in such Cases, wherein they clash and interfere with each other, or contain any Powers or Authorities that are not warranted by Law, and the Constitution.

A Motion tfcras made, and the Question being put, That the House do now adjourn;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the House accordingly adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of the Holders of Reconnoiflances given in Exchange for Canada Paper, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by a Declaration subjoined to the late Definitive Treaty of Peace made with the Court of France, his Most Christian' Majesty declares, that the Letters of Exchange and Bills delivered to the Canadians, for Necessaries furnirtied to the French Troops, and for other Services, shall be punctually pud, according to a Liquidation thereafter to be made; and that the Petitioners, relying on the Faith of the above Declaration, did not in the least doubt but the Canadian Paper, as soon as the same could be liquidated, would be punctually paid; but, after many Applications to different Ministers, and various Difficulties that were from Time to Time thrown in their Way by the Court of France, the Petitioners found their Property growing daily more precarious, and did therefore submit to make a considerable Reduction in their De-

so much ldfs in its Value, and so contradictory to the Sense and Meaning of the Treaty, the Petitioners applied to His Majesty’s Ministers, to be relieved from this oppressive Measure, when a Counter Edict was obtained, exempting the Petitioners from the Conversion, ^declaring, tha* *n the Year 1771 they should bring in their Reconnoiflances to be renewed; and that, on the aoth of January last, an Edict was pyblished, reducing

Petitioners must be obliged, either totally to lose their Property, or to renew their Reconnoiffances, and thereby become perpetual Creditors to the Court of France, and be deprived of the Benefit of the Convention made purposely for them, and as the Payment of their Interest for the last Year has been -refused, they take the Liberty, under these flagrant and manifest Violations of Treaty, to throw themselves upon the Wisdom of the House, not doubting Redreis from those, who, by the Constitution, are the Guardians of the Rights of Individuals, and the AffertorsofthcHonourand Dignity of the Nation; And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall teem meet.

After which. His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

THE Season of the Year, and the Dispatch you have given to the Public Business, make it proper for Me to put an End to this Session of Parliament.

The Temper with which you have conducted all Your Proceedings has given Me great Satisfaction , and I promise Myself the happiest EfTefts from the Firmness, as well as ihe Moderation, which you h&Ve manifcfled 21

in the very critical Cfrcliruflances which have attended your late Deliberations.

With rafpeft to Foreign Affairs, I have nothing ma» terial to communicate to you. 1 will continue My Endeavours to appease, if possible, the Troubles which still prevail in some Parts of Euro; or, at least, to prevent them from spreading farther. In all Events, it shall be My first and constant Care to watch over the Interests, and to preserve undiminished, the Rights of My People.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you My Thanks for the Supplies you have so chearfully granted for the Service of the current Year, as well as for your Attention to make, use of every Opportunity of reducing the National Debt. The Provision you have been able to make in this Session for discharging so considerable a Sum without laying any further Burthen on My Subjects, cannot but be highly advantageous to Public Credit.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I mufl earnestly recommend to you to exert, in your respective Counties, the same Zeal and Prudence that you have shewn in Parliament, for promoting the Peace and the Welfare of the Kingdom. Nothing can be so favourable to the Wishes of those who look with Jealously on the Strength and Prosperityof this Country, at the Prevalence of Animosities and Differ.fions actiongfl ourselves. Let it therefore be your Care, to difeounte-nance every Attempt to infuse groundless Sul'picions and Discontent into the Minds of your Fellow Subjtfts.

Make them sensible of My constant Attention to promote their Happiness; and convince them* that nothing can so effectually secure their Liberties, as the Maintenance of every Part of Our excellent Constitution in its due Force and Authority.
